Continue covertly, as the plan states it runs for 14 days
Medicines Management.w: Covert administration is lawful only while the person lacks capacity and refuses (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21). Once Ken regains capacity, the plan ends; his medicines are discussed openly and his informed decision respected (MCA 2005 s1).

n.0: The covert method ends, not the treatment; he can be offered the antibiotics openly.
n.2: Continuing covertly once he has capacity overrides his right to decide.
n.3: A plan's stated duration does not authorise covert use once capacity returns.

Medicines Management.q: Two nurses are at the bedside to start a red cell transfusion for Edith, 73, who is alert and orientated. Which method of patient identification meets the BSH standard for positive patient identification?
o: Ask 'Are you Edith Morris?' and then check her wristband details
Ask her to state her name and date of birth, then match wristband and unit
Check her wristband against the unit label and the bed-end name card
Confirm her identity with her daughter, then check the unit label
Medicines Management.w: BSH guideline on administration of blood components (2017): positive patient identification at every stage, asking the patient to state full name and date of birth where able, and checking these against the identification band and the component label, using a structured bedside checklist (SHOT recommendation).

n.0: A closed question invites a confused or hard-of-hearing person to agree to the wrong name.
n.2: Bed-end cards are unreliable, and Edith can state her own details.
n.3: Relatives may be used when a patient cannot respond; Edith is alert and should identify herself.

Medicines Management.q: A red cell transfusion for Graham, 66, started at 14:00. Baseline pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate were recorded at 13:30 and were normal. According to BSH guidance, when should the next set of observations be taken?
o: At 14:30, 30 minutes after the start
At 15:00, 1 hour after the start
At 14:15, 15 minutes after the start
At the end of the unit, within 60 minutes
Medicines Management.w: BSH (2017) observations: baseline no more than 60 minutes before starting, then pulse, blood pressure and temperature 15 minutes after the start of each unit, and again no more than 60 minutes after the end. Severe reactions often occur early in the unit.

n.0: The BSH timepoint is 15 minutes, not 30.
n.1: Waiting an hour misses the early period when serious reactions usually start.
n.3: End-of-unit observations are needed, but an observation at 15 minutes comes first.

Medicines Management.q: A unit of red cells for Hannah, 55, was removed from the blood fridge at 10:00. The transfusion was delayed while her cannula was resited and started at 10:40. By what time must the unit be completed?
o: By 14:00, 4 hours after leaving storage
By 13:00, 3 hours after leaving storage
By 14:40, 4 hours after the start
By 12:00, 2 hours after leaving storage
Medicines Management.w: BSH (2017): red cells should be transfused within 4 hours of leaving temperature-controlled storage, to limit bacterial growth. The clock starts when the unit leaves the fridge, not when the infusion starts.

n.1: 3 hours is not the BSH limit; the standard is 4 hours from leaving storage.
n.2: Timing runs from removal from storage, so 14:40 is 40 minutes too late.
n.3: 2 hours is shorter than the BSH limit for red cells.

Medicines Management.q: Ruth, 64, has chronic kidney disease and symptomatic anaemia with a haemoglobin of 68 g/L. She is not bleeding and does not have acute coronary syndrome. The doctor plans a red cell transfusion. In line with NICE NG24, what is the recommended approach?
o: Transfuse 1 unit, then reassess and check haemoglobin
Transfuse until haemoglobin reaches at least 110 g/L
Transfuse 2 units, then check haemoglobin the next day
Transfuse 3 units to avoid repeated cannulation
Medicines Management.w: NICE NG24 (updated 2026): use a restrictive threshold of 70 g/L with a target of 70-90 g/L after transfusion, and consider single-unit transfusions for adults without active bleeding, clinically reassessing and checking haemoglobin after each unit before giving more.

n.1: 110 g/L is well above the NG24 post-transfusion target of 70-90 g/L.
n.2: Two units without reassessment risks overtransfusion and circulatory overload.
n.3: Multiple units without reassessment conflicts with single-unit transfusion and raises overload risk.

Medicines Management.q: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, Martin, 70, develops rigors, lower back pain and a temperature of 38.9°C (baseline 37.0°C). His blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the transfusion, keep venous access, recheck identity and call for urgent review
Continue the transfusion and give a prescribed antihistamine for the rigors
Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, remove the cannula and dispose of the unit in clinical waste
Medicines Management.w: Features of a severe acute transfusion reaction (rigors, fever, loin pain, hypotension, possible ABO incompatibility) require the transfusion to be stopped immediately, venous access maintained for treatment, the patient's identity and unit rechecked, an ABCDE assessment and urgent medical review (NICE NG24 1.13; BSH). The unit is kept for investigation.

n.1: Continuing risks a fatal haemolytic reaction; antihistamines do not treat this.
n.2: Slowing the transfusion continues exposure to a possibly incompatible unit.
n.3: Venous access is needed for treatment, and the unit must be kept for laboratory investigation.

Medicines Management.q: Bridget, 58, is due to have her first red cell transfusion before surgery. She asks the nurse what she should know about it. According to NICE NG24, which information should the nurse include?
o: That she will be able to give blood herself once she has recovered
That she will no longer be eligible to donate blood after a transfusion
That she cannot refuse once the transfusion has been prescribed
That a transfusion has no risks if the bedside checks are completed
Medicines Management.w: NICE NG24 rec 1.14.2: give verbal and written information on the reason for transfusion, risks and benefits, the process, alternatives, that the person is no longer eligible to donate blood, and encourage questions; document the discussion (1.14.3).

n.0: NG24 states people who have had a transfusion are no longer eligible to donate blood.
n.2: A person with capacity may refuse a transfusion; consent remains her decision.
n.3: Transfusion carries risks that must be explained even with correct checks.

Medicines Management.q: Ninety minutes into his second unit of red cells, Walter, 86, who has heart failure, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases. His blood pressure has risen to 172/96 mmHg and SpO2 has fallen to 89% on air. What is the most likely complication, and the priority action?
o: Anaphylaxis; stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Circulatory overload; slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 1 hour
An allergic reaction; slow the transfusion and give an oral antihistamine
Circulatory overload; stop the transfusion, sit him up and get urgent medical review
Medicines Management.w: Breathlessness, crackles, hypertension and hypoxia in an older person with heart failure suggest transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). The transfusion is stopped, he is sat up, oxygen given and urgent medical review sought, with the reaction reported (NICE NG24 1.13; SHOT).

n.0: Hypertension without rash, angioedema or wheeze points away from anaphylaxis.
n.1: Slowing and waiting an hour lets pulmonary oedema progress.
n.2: Allergic reactions cause urticaria or itch; this picture is fluid overload, and continuing worsens it.

Medicines Management.q: At the bedside check, the nurse notices that the compatibility label on a unit of red cells for Catherine, 60, reads 'Catherine Smyth', while her wristband reads 'Catherine Smith'. Her date of birth and hospital number match. What should the nurse do?
o: Proceed, as the date of birth and hospital number both match
Do not start, and contact the transfusion laboratory to resolve it
Ask a second nurse to countersign the discrepancy and proceed
Correct the spelling on the wristband and then proceed
Medicines Management.w: BSH (2017): all identifiers on the wristband and the component label must match exactly at the bedside; any discrepancy means the component is not given until resolved with the transfusion laboratory. Wrong component transfused is a leading SHOT-reported error.

n.0: Partial matches are not acceptable; every identifier must match.
n.2: A second signature does not resolve a mismatch in identifiers.
n.3: Changing the wristband to fit the unit conceals the discrepancy and is unsafe.

Medicines Management.q: Elaine, 45, tells the practice nurse she bought a small pack of paracetamol from a supermarket, but the pharmacy said her prescribed codeine needed a prescription. She asks which legal category allows sale from premises such as supermarkets. Which category is correct?
o: Prescription only medicine (POM)
Controlled drug in Schedule 5
Pharmacy medicine (P)
General sale list medicine (GSL)
Medicines Management.w: MHRA guidance on medicine categories: GSL medicines can be sold from a wider range of premises, such as supermarkets, if the premises can be closed to exclude the public and the medicines are pre-packed. POM and P medicines are sold or supplied from a registered pharmacy, POMs against a prescription.

n.0: POMs need a prescription and are supplied through a pharmacy or other authorised route.
n.1: Schedule 5 is a controlled drug schedule, not a sale category; such products are sold through pharmacies.
n.2: Pharmacy medicines are sold under a pharmacist's supervision at registered pharmacy premises.

Medicines Management.q: Chloe, a registered nurse in a sexual health clinic, sees Zara, 22, who requests emergency hormonal contraception. No prescriber is on site. The clinic has an authorised written direction covering this medicine for defined groups of patients. Under which mechanism can Chloe supply it?
o: A verbal order from an on-call doctor
A homely remedy protocol
A patient specific direction
A patient group direction
Medicines Management.w: A patient group direction (PGD) is a written direction allowing named, authorised registered professionals such as nurses to supply or administer a specified medicine to a defined group of patients without an individual prescription (MHRA; Human Medicines Regulations 2012).

n.0: Verbal orders are for exceptional changes to existing administration details, not first supply to a new patient.
n.1: Homely remedy protocols cover non-POM medicines in settings such as care homes, not this clinic's POM supply.
n.2: A PSD is an instruction from a prescriber for a named patient after individual assessment; no prescriber has assessed Zara.

Medicines Management.q: In a GP practice, Jamal, a registered nursing associate, is asked to give influenza vaccines at a Saturday clinic. The registered nurses give the vaccine under a patient group direction (PGD). How can Jamal lawfully administer the vaccine?
o: Under a patient specific direction from a prescriber
Under the practice's homely remedy protocol for vaccines
Under the PGD, after signing it as a named practitioner
Under the PGD, while a registered nurse supervises him
Medicines Management.w: MHRA guidance lists the registered professions that may supply or administer under a PGD (including nurses, midwives, paramedics and pharmacists); nursing associates are not on the list. A nursing associate can administer against a prescription or a patient specific direction from a prescriber.

n.1: Homely remedy protocols apply to non-prescription medicines; influenza vaccine is a POM.
n.2: Signing a PGD does not authorise a profession that the legislation does not include.
n.3: Supervision does not extend PGD use to a profession that is not authorised to use PGDs.

Medicines Management.q: Doreen, 79, is fluid overloaded with worsening breathlessness. The registrar, who is scrubbed in theatre for the next 2 hours, phones the ward to add a single dose of intravenous furosemide now. Trust policy permits verbal orders in exceptional circumstances. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Accept it per policy and ask for written confirmation within 7 days
Refuse, and wait for the registrar to write it after theatre
Write the new dose on the drug chart herself and sign it as the prescriber
Accept it per policy and ensure written confirmation, ideally within 24 hours
Medicines Management.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20: in exceptional circumstances, where delay would compromise care and the medicine is not a Schedule 2 CD, verbal orders may be used under organisational policy; the prescriber then amends the chart or provides a prescription as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.

n.0: The RPS/RCN standard is ideally within 24 hours, not 7 days.
n.1: A 2-hour delay could compromise Doreen's care when policy allows a verbal order.
n.2: Transcribing cannot be used to add a new medicine; the nurse would be acting as an unauthorised prescriber.

End of Life Care.q: Frank, 68, has COPD and pneumonia. Two days ago the team thought he was dying and started an end of life care plan. Today he is more alert, has eaten some breakfast and his breathing is easier. The doctors disagree about whether he is still dying. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue the end of life care plan unchanged, as improvement is often brief
Seek advice from the specialist palliative care team about the uncertainty
Request daily full blood counts and renal function to clarify his prognosis
Stop the end of life care plan and restart all of his previous medicines
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.7: seek advice from colleagues with more experience of end of life care when there is a high level of uncertainty, for example conflicting signs, about whether a person is dying, stabilising or may recover. Rec 1.1.3: improvement could indicate stabilising or recovery.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.1.3 warns that improvement may mean the person is stabilising or recovering, so the plan cannot simply continue unchanged.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.1.4 advises avoiding investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last days of life.
n.3: Reversing all care without a shared review is premature; the guidance is to seek experienced advice when the picture is uncertain.

End of Life Care.q: Dorothy, 90, is in the last days of life on a care of older people ward. Her chart still includes daily blood tests, which were requested a week ago when she was admitted. She is comfortable and settled. What should the nurse do about the blood tests?
o: Ask the team to review whether the daily blood tests will change her care
Ask Dorothy's daughter to give consent for the tests to be stopped
Take the blood tests as charted because the request is still active
Leave the tests undone and record that Dorothy declined them
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to prevent catastrophic bleeding. The nurse should prompt a team review rather than act alone.

n.1: Relatives cannot consent for an adult; the clinical team should review whether the tests are needed.
n.2: Continuing a test that is unlikely to change care causes discomfort; NG31 rec 1.1.4 says avoid such investigations.
n.3: Recording a refusal that did not happen is falsifying the record (Code 10.3) and does not resolve the plan.

End of Life Care.q: Kwame, 64, has motor neurone disease and is now thought to be in his last days. The team are deciding who should talk with him about his prognosis. He knows the ward sister well and trusts her, and she has experience of these conversations. According to NICE NG31, what should guide the choice of professional?
o: Their seniority and grade within the treating medical team
Which professional the family would prefer to lead the conversation
Which professional first made the diagnosis of his condition
Their competence and confidence, and their rapport with the person
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.2.2: identify the most appropriate available multiprofessional team member to explain the dying person's prognosis, based on the professional's competence and confidence and their rapport with the person.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.2.2 does not base the choice on grade; a senior doctor without rapport may not be the most appropriate person.
n.1: Family views matter, but NG31 rec 1.2.2 bases the choice on the professional's competence, confidence and rapport with the person.
n.2: The diagnosing clinician is not the NG31 criterion; competence, confidence and rapport are.

End of Life Care.q: Brian, 75, has advanced prostate cancer and wishes to die in the local hospice. He is now in the last days of life, and the hospice confirms no bed will be available this week. Brian asks the nurse whether he will be moving soon. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange discharge home as the next best setting and inform him afterwards
Defer the conversation until the hospice confirms a date for admission
Reassure him that a bed will be found soon so that he does not become distressed
Explain honestly why no hospice bed is available and agree another plan
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.3.8: when a dying person's wishes cannot be met, explain the reason to them and those important to them. Rec 1.2.4: give accurate information and avoid false optimism. The plan is then revised with Brian (rec 1.3.7).

n.0: Deciding a new setting without Brian breaches shared decision-making (NG31 1.3.1) and Code 4.
n.1: Delay leaves Brian uncertain in his last days; NG31 rec 1.3.8 says explain why a wish cannot be met.
n.2: This offers false hope; NG31 rec 1.2.4 asks for accurate information that avoids false optimism.

End of Life Care.q: Peter, 74, has pancreatic cancer and is in the last days of life at home. He can no longer swallow tablets. Over the past 24 hours the community nurse has given three 'as required' subcutaneous doses of morphine for pain, each giving relief for a few hours. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue 'as required' doses and review the plan in 72 hours
Ask his wife to give oral morphine solution between visits
Discuss with the prescriber starting a continuous syringe pump
Give the next 'as required' doses by intramuscular injection
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.5.6: consider a syringe pump to deliver medicines for continuous symptom control if more than 2 or 3 doses of any 'as required' medicine have been given within 24 hours. Rec 1.5.5: avoid intramuscular injections.

n.0: Needing more than 2 or 3 doses in 24 hours is the NG31 trigger to consider a syringe pump; waiting 72 hours leaves pain poorly controlled.
n.1: Peter can no longer swallow safely, so the oral route is unsuitable (NG31 rec 1.5.4).
n.3: NICE NG31 rec 1.5.5 advises avoiding intramuscular injections in the last days of life; subcutaneous or intravenous routes are used.

End of Life Care.q: Arthur, 88, is dying on a medical ward. His breathing has become noisy with a rattling sound. He is unconscious and appears settled. His daughter is upset and asks whether he is 'drowning'. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Explain that a medicine will be given now to stop the noise completely
Start oxygen through a face mask to make his breathing feel more comfortable
Explain that the noise means fluid on his lungs that needs a diuretic injection
Explain the noise is unlikely to be causing him discomfort, and reposition him
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.29 and 1.5.30: assess the cause of noisy respiratory secretions and the impact on the person and those important to them; reassure them that although the noise can be distressing it is unlikely to cause discomfort; consider non-drug measures such as repositioning.

n.0: Medicines are considered if secretions distress the dying person (rec 1.5.31), and they may not stop the noise completely.
n.1: NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen; offer it for known or suspected symptomatic hypoxaemia.
n.2: Noisy secretions in the last days are not treated as pulmonary oedema; the guidance is reassurance and non-drug measures first.

End of Life Care.q: Hilda, 83, has end-stage pulmonary fibrosis and is in the last days of life. She says she feels breathless at rest. Her oxygen saturation is 95% on air and her chest is unchanged on examination. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
o: Use a fan and positioning, and check whether an opioid is prescribed
Arrange an arterial blood gas sample to guide oxygen therapy
Start oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula to ease her breathing
Give the 'as required' hyoscine butylbromide from her anticipatory box
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.16 and 1.5.17: consider non-pharmacological management of breathlessness (for example a fan), do not routinely start oxygen unless symptomatic hypoxaemia is known or suspected, and consider an opioid, a benzodiazepine or both.

n.1: An invasive test unlikely to change care should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.1.4).
n.2: With saturation of 95% she is not hypoxaemic; NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen for breathlessness.
n.3: Hyoscine butylbromide is used for secretions or bowel obstruction, not for breathlessness.

End of Life Care.q: Nora, 80, is dying from heart failure in a nursing home. Tonight she has become restless, keeps pulling at her sheets and is groaning. She last passed urine 10 hours ago and her lower abdomen looks swollen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the GP to prescribe an antipsychotic for terminal delirium
Ask a relative to sit with her and see whether she settles overnight
Give the prescribed 'as required' midazolam to settle her agitation
Assess her for urinary retention and pain before giving sedation
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.11 and 1.5.23: agitation in isolation is sometimes associated with unrelieved pain or a full bladder or rectum; treat reversible causes of pain such as urinary retention before considering benzodiazepines or antipsychotics.

n.0: An antipsychotic is considered for delirium only after reversible causes such as urinary retention are explored (recs 1.5.25 and 1.5.27).
n.1: Company can help, but it leaves a likely full bladder untreated; reversible causes should be assessed first.
n.2: Sedation first would mask a reversible cause; NG31 rec 1.5.23 says agitation may reflect a full bladder or unrelieved pain.

End of Life Care.q: Leonard, 77, has heart failure and advanced bowel cancer with bowel obstruction. He is in the last days of life with persistent nausea and vomiting. Subcutaneous hyoscine butylbromide was started 24 hours ago, but his symptoms have not improved. Which action should the nurse discuss with the prescriber?
o: Continuing the same hyoscine dose for 72 hours more
Changing hyoscine to the intramuscular route
Adding cyclizine as the next option
Considering octreotide as the next option
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.5.22: for nausea or vomiting with obstructive bowel disorders in the last days of life, consider hyoscine butylbromide first line, then octreotide if symptoms do not improve within 24 hours. Rec 1.5.3: take into account risks such as cyclizine exacerbating heart failure.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.22 says consider octreotide if symptoms have not improved within 24 hours.
n.1: NG31 rec 1.5.5 advises avoiding intramuscular injections in the last days of life.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.3 notes that cyclizine may exacerbate heart failure, which Leonard has; octreotide is the NG31 next step.

End of Life Care.q: Joyce, 85, is dying in hospital and can take only sips of fluid. Her husband asks the nurse, 'If she has a drip, will it keep her alive longer? And if she doesn't, will she die sooner?' Which response is most accurate?
o: Without a drip she will die sooner from dehydration, so the team will advise starting one
It is uncertain whether a drip would lengthen her life, or whether going without would shorten it
Drips are not used at the end of life because they cause fluid overload in older people
A drip would give her several more days of life, so one is usually started at this stage
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.4.5: tell the person and those important to them that clinically assisted hydration may relieve distressing symptoms of dehydration but may cause other problems, and that it is uncertain whether giving it prolongs life or whether not giving it hastens death.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.4.5 states it is uncertain whether withholding clinically assisted hydration hastens death.
n.2: Clinically assisted hydration can be a therapeutic trial (rec 1.4.8); it is not ruled out, though overload is a risk to monitor.
n.3: NG31 rec 1.4.5 states it is uncertain whether clinically assisted hydration prolongs life or the dying process.

End of Life Care.q: Samuel, 79, is in the last days of life. Yesterday a trial of subcutaneous fluids was started because he was thirsty and slightly confused. Today the nurse notes new crackles at both lung bases and increasing ankle swelling. He is more breathless. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 'as required' midazolam for breathlessness and continue the fluids
Increase the infusion rate because his thirst is still present
Continue the fluids and reassess them at tomorrow's daily review
Reduce or stop the fluids and inform the team of signs of fluid overload
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.4.9: for a person started on clinically assisted hydration, monitor at least every 12 hours for benefit or harm; continue if there is clinical benefit and reduce or stop it if there are signs of possible harm such as fluid overload, or if the person no longer wants it.

n.0: Sedating him without removing the cause of the overload is not appropriate; the fluids are causing harm.
n.1: Increasing fluid would worsen the overload; thirst is managed with mouth care and sips (rec 1.4.2).
n.2: NG31 rec 1.4.9 says reduce or stop clinically assisted hydration if there are signs of harm such as fluid overload.

End of Life Care.q: Gwen, 70, is in the last days of life with metastatic cancer and new bone pain. She has not taken opioids before. The team agree to start subcutaneous morphine for symptom control, and the nurse is planning her care. Which approach to dosing is recommended?
o: Wait until her pain is severe before giving the first dose of morphine
Start with the lowest effective dose and titrate to her symptoms
Start at the top of the prescribed range so that she is comfortable quickly
Give a loading dose by intramuscular injection, then change to subcutaneous
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.7 and 1.5.8: for people starting treatment who have not previously had medicines for symptom management, start with the lowest effective dose and titrate as clinically indicated, reassessing symptoms at least daily.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.11 asks for pain to be managed promptly and effectively once identified.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.7 recommends starting with the lowest effective dose for people not previously given symptom-control medicines.
n.3: Intramuscular injections should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.5.5).

End of Life Care.q: Julie, 58, has motor neurone disease and full capacity. She tells the specialist nurse she wants to make an advance decision refusing mechanical ventilation in the future, even if her life is at risk. In England, what is needed for this refusal to be valid and applicable to life-sustaining treatment?
o: Signed by her GP and registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Written, signed and witnessed, stating it applies even if her life is at risk
Written down and then confirmed in writing by her next of kin
Recorded verbally in her notes and countersigned by two registered nurses
End of Life Care.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 ss24-25: a person aged 18 or over with capacity may make an advance decision to refuse treatment. For life-sustaining treatment it must be in writing, signed by the person (or by another in their presence and by their direction), signed by a witness, and contain a statement that it applies even if life is at risk.

n.0: Registration with the Office of the Public Guardian applies to lasting powers of attorney, not advance decisions; no GP signature is required.
n.2: Next of kin confirmation is not a legal requirement; Julie's signature, a witness and the 'even if life is at risk' statement are.
n.3: A verbal advance decision can refuse other treatment, but a refusal of life-sustaining treatment must be in writing, signed and witnessed (MCA s25(5)-(6)).

End of Life Care.q: Raymond, 82, has a DNACPR decision recorded after a discussion with him. Overnight he develops a temperature of 39.1°C, a heart rate of 118 and new confusion, giving a NEWS2 of 7. A colleague says there is 'no point escalating because he is DNACPR'. What should the nurse do?
o: Phone his family first to ask whether he should be treated for infection
Withhold escalation because the DNACPR shows he is not for active treatment
Escalate urgently for sepsis review, as the DNACPR decision covers CPR
Start the end of life care plan, as the DNACPR shows he is now dying
End of Life Care.w: Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BMA, RCUK, RCN, 3rd edition): a decision not to attempt CPR applies only to CPR and not to any other treatment. A NEWS2 of 7 needs an emergency response (RCP 2017) and possible sepsis is managed under NICE NG253 (2025).

n.0: Raymond's deterioration needs urgent escalation now; his family do not decide his treatment and delay risks harm.
n.1: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR; all other appropriate treatment continues (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance).
n.3: A DNACPR decision does not mean a person is dying; recognising dying is a separate assessment (NICE NG31).

End of Life Care.q: Ivy, 84, now has advanced dementia and lacks capacity to decide where she lives or how she is cared for. Some years ago, with capacity, she wrote a signed letter saying she would like to be cared for at home and prefers baths to showers. How should staff treat this letter?
o: As having no weight now that she lacks capacity to confirm her wishes
As a legally binding instruction that must be followed in the same way as an ADRT
As a statement of her wishes that must be considered in best interests decisions
As binding once her GP has countersigned it and placed it in her record
End of Life Care.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(6)(a): in deciding best interests, consider so far as reasonably ascertainable the person's past and present wishes and feelings, in particular any relevant written statement made when they had capacity. An advance statement of this kind is considered but is not legally binding, unlike a valid and applicable ADRT (ss24-26).

n.0: MCA s4(6)(a) requires decision makers to consider past wishes, in particular relevant written statements made with capacity.
n.1: A statement of wishes and preferences is not legally binding; only a valid, applicable ADRT binds staff to a refusal of treatment.
n.3: A GP signature does not convert a statement of wishes into a binding document.

End of Life Care.q: Walter, 79, has a ReSPECT form recommending ward-based treatment but not admission to intensive care. He becomes acutely unwell and cannot express his views. A student nurse asks what status the ReSPECT form has. Which statement is correct?
o: Its recommendations guide the clinicians present but are not legally binding
It is a legally binding refusal of treatment that clinicians must follow
It replaces the need for clinicians to assess what treatment would benefit him
It becomes valid once Walter has also registered a lasting power of attorney
End of Life Care.w: Resuscitation Council UK (ReSPECT; RCUK 2025 Ethics guidelines): ReSPECT creates personalised recommendations for a future emergency in which the person cannot make or express choices. Preferences and recommendations are recorded on a non-legally binding form; the final decision rests with clinicians present unless a legally binding document applies.

n.1: RCUK states ReSPECT recommendations are recorded on a non-legally binding form; only documents such as a valid ADRT are binding.
n.2: Clinicians still make treatment decisions at the time, using the recommendations to inform them.
n.3: A ReSPECT form does not depend on an LPA; it records recommendations from conversations with the person and clinicians.

End of Life Care.q: Thomas, 71, has advanced lung cancer and full capacity. The registrar decides that CPR would not be in his interests and plans to complete a DNACPR form. The registrar tells the nurse they will not mention it to Thomas because 'it might upset him'. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Remind the registrar that Thomas should be consulted unless it would cause him harm
Ask Thomas's wife to decide whether he should be told about the decision
Accept the plan, as DNACPR decisions are a medical matter that need no discussion
Record the DNACPR now and plan to tell Thomas at next week's ward round
End of Life Care.w: R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals NHS FT [2014] EWCA Civ 822: Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions, and there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation causing physical or psychological harm. Lord Dyson MR (para 54) said doctors should be wary of being too ready to exclude patients from the process on the grounds that their involvement is likely to distress them; a belief that discussion would cause distress is unlikely to be enough unless the distress is likely to cause harm (para 56).

n.1: Thomas has capacity; his wife cannot decide what he is told about his own care.
n.2: R (Tracey) [2014] held there is a presumption the patient will be consulted, and warned against excluding patients because the discussion may distress them.
n.3: Delaying the conversation until after the decision is recorded still breaches the duty to consult him first.

End of Life Care.q: Maureen, 87, lacks capacity and has life-threatening pneumonia. Her daughter holds a registered health and welfare lasting power of attorney (LPA). The LPA does not contain express authority over life-sustaining treatment. Her daughter says she refuses intravenous antibiotics. How should the team proceed?
o: Delay treatment until the Court of Protection has confirmed that the LPA is valid
Ask the daughter to agree as nearest relative, which overrides the terms of the LPA
Follow the daughter's refusal, as the LPA is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Decide in her best interests, consulting her daughter, who cannot refuse this treatment
End of Life Care.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s9 (an LPA must be registered) and s11(7)-(8): a health and welfare attorney can give or refuse consent to treatment when the person lacks capacity, but this does not extend to life-sustaining treatment unless the LPA contains express provision. The team decide in Maureen's best interests (s4), consulting her daughter.

n.0: The registered LPA does not need court confirmation, and delaying antibiotics would put Maureen's life at risk.
n.1: There is no 'nearest relative' power under the MCA; decisions are made in Maureen's best interests.
n.2: Registration is required, but under MCA s11(8) an attorney cannot refuse life-sustaining treatment without express authority in the LPA.

End of Life Care.q: In 2019, Dennis made a valid written advance decision refusing artificial nutrition. In 2023, with capacity, he made a health and welfare LPA giving his son express authority to decide on that treatment, including if life-sustaining. Dennis now lacks capacity. Whose decision about artificial nutrition applies?
o: The consultant's, because the two documents conflict
His son's, as the later LPA covers the same treatment
The Court of Protection's, as both documents exist
The advance decision, because it was made first
End of Life Care.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s25(2)(b): an advance decision is not valid if the person has, under an LPA created after the advance decision was made, conferred authority on the attorney to give or refuse consent to the treatment to which the advance decision relates.

n.0: There is no conflict for the consultant to resolve; the later LPA displaces the earlier advance decision.
n.2: Court involvement is not needed when the law gives a clear answer on these facts.
n.3: MCA s25(2)(b): an advance decision is not valid if a later LPA gives the attorney authority over the same treatment.

End of Life Care.q: Stanley, 80, has end-stage heart and kidney disease and full capacity. The consultant judges that CPR would not succeed and records a DNACPR decision. Stanley tells the nurse he does not accept this and wants 'everything done'. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record that CPR will be attempted because Stanley has requested it
Ask his family to confirm the decision on his behalf at the next visit
Leave the decision unexplained to avoid causing Stanley more distress
Explain the decision sensitively and offer him a second opinion
End of Life Care.w: Decisions relating to cardiopulmonary resuscitation (BMA, RCUK, RCN): where CPR would not be successful, clinicians have no obligation to offer it, but the patient should be informed sensitively, and if they do not accept the decision a second opinion should be offered. Tracey [2014]: presumption of involving the patient.

n.0: Clinicians are not obliged to offer CPR that would not succeed; a patient request does not require it (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance).
n.1: Stanley has capacity, so his family cannot confirm or make the decision for him.
n.2: Stanley must be informed and his concerns heard (Tracey [2014]); avoiding the topic denies him the chance to seek another view.

End of Life Care.q: Phyllis, 92, dies peacefully in a nursing home. Her death was expected and a DNACPR discussion is documented. The registered nurse, who is trained and competent, begins verification of death. For how long, at minimum, should Phyllis be observed to establish irreversible cardiorespiratory arrest?
o: 10 minutes
1 minute
2 minutes
5 minutes
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK/RCN, Care after death: Registered Nurse Verification of Expected Adult Death (6th edition, 2024): observe for a minimum of five minutes to establish irreversible cardiorespiratory arrest; any spontaneous return of cardiac or respiratory activity prompts a further five minutes of observation.

n.0: Ten minutes is longer than required; a further 5 minutes is needed only if spontaneous activity returns.
n.1: One minute is the minimum time for checking the absence of a central pulse and of heart sounds, within the longer observation period.
n.2: Two minutes is shorter than the minimum observation period set in the RNVoEAD guidance.

End of Life Care.q: Albert, 85, dies at home with his wife present at 02:10. The community nurse arrives at 03:30 and completes verification of his expected death at 03:45. His wife asks what time will be recorded as the time of death. What should the nurse tell her?
o: 03:30, when the nurse arrived at the house
02:10, when she noticed that he had stopped breathing
The time the doctor completes the death certificate
03:45, when verification of death was completed
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the time of verification is recognised as the official time of death and is recorded when verification is completed, not when the death is first reported. Families should be advised there may be a difference between the time of the last breath and the official time of death.

n.0: Arrival time is not the time of death; it is recorded when verification is completed.
n.1: The guidance says families should be told that the time of the last breath may differ from the official time of death.
n.2: The MCCD is completed later by a medical practitioner; the official time of death is the time of verification.

End of Life Care.q: Ruth, 76, has died on a hospice ward and her death has been verified. During personal care after death, the nurse notices that Ruth's eyes are partly open. Her daughter would like them closed. What is the recommended way to close them?
o: Close them once rigor mortis has developed in the face
Leave them open now for the funeral director to close later
Apply light pressure to the eyelids for about 30 seconds
Tape the eyelids closed with a strip of hypoallergenic tape
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): close the eyes by applying light pressure for 30 seconds (this also protects tissue for corneal donation); do not apply tape over the eyelids; if they fail to close, explain sensitively that the funeral director will resolve this.

n.0: Care should be given soon after death, before rigor mortis sets in, which occurs 2 to 6 hours after death.
n.1: Light pressure is tried first; the funeral director is involved if the eyelids fail to close.
n.3: Hospice UK advises against taping the eyelids because tape can mark the skin.

End of Life Care.q: Mr Hussain, 69, has died on a medical ward after an expected death. The death is not being referred to the coroner. His family tell the nurse that their faith requires family members to wash his body and that they would like to do this themselves. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that hospital policy requires staff to wash all deceased patients
Leave the washing to the family and support them with the rest of his care
Ask the mortuary staff to wash him before he is released to the family
Wash him before the family arrive so that they are spared any distress
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): wash the deceased unless requested not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons, or the death is being referred to the coroner; key contacts may wish to assist and should be supported. NMC Code 1.3 and 1.5: recognise diversity and individual choice, and respect and uphold people's human rights.

n.0: Care after death guidance says wash the deceased unless asked not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons.
n.2: Washing by mortuary staff would also override the family's wish to carry out the washing themselves.
n.3: This disregards the family's stated religious wishes, which the guidance says must be respected.

End of Life Care.q: Clive, 80, had an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) that was still active when he died on a cardiology ward. The registered nurse has verified his expected death. Which action relating to the device is the nurse's responsibility?
o: Instigate deactivation and tell the mortuary or funeral director about the device
Record the device in the notes, as no further action is needed after death
Ask his family to inform the funeral director that a device is present
Remove the device before Clive is transferred to the mortuary
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the RN must instigate the process for deactivation of an implantable cardiac defibrillator where applicable, and must notify the funeral director or mortuary of any infections, radioactive implants, implantable devices and whether an ICD is still active.

n.1: An active ICD remains a hazard to people handling the body, so deactivation must be arranged.
n.2: Notifying the mortuary or funeral director is the verifying nurse's responsibility, not the family's.
n.3: Ward nurses do not remove implanted devices; the RN instigates deactivation and passes on the information.

End of Life Care.q: Gordon, 66, dies unexpectedly on a surgical ward on the day after a planned procedure. There are no suspicious circumstances, but his death will be referred to the coroner to investigate the cause. He has a peripheral cannula and a urinary catheter. How should the nurse manage these devices during care after death?
o: Leave the cannula in place and spigot the urinary catheter
Remove both and send them with him in a labelled bag
Remove the cannula and catheter before washing him
Remove the cannula but leave the catheter bag attached
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): when the death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause and there are no suspicious circumstances, leave IV cannulae and lines in situ and catheters spigotted; personal care can then be given. Deaths that may be related to a medical procedure or treatment require coroner referral.

n.1: Removing devices could affect the coroner's investigation of a death that may relate to a procedure.
n.2: Devices are left in situ when the death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause.
n.3: The cannula must stay in situ; the catheter is spigotted, and the bag contents may be discarded per policy.

End of Life Care.q: A registered nurse is reviewing four recent deaths on a care of older people ward. All were verified, and none involved suspicious circumstances. Which death should be referred to the coroner?
o: Bill, 74, who died an expected death in a hospice from motor neurone disease
Harold, 79, who died an expected death from confirmed COVID-19
Edith, 88, who died five days after a hip fracture from a fall at home
Joan, 91, who died an expected death from heart failure under her GP
End of Life Care.w: RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024), Appendix 1 (Ministry of Justice): refer to the coroner where the death may have been caused by violence, trauma or physical injury, whether intentional or otherwise, among other criteria. A notifiable disease such as COVID-19 is not a reason to refer.

n.0: An expected death from a diagnosed progressive illness is not, on these facts, reportable to the coroner.
n.1: A notifiable infectious disease such as COVID-19 is not, by itself, a reason to refer a death to the coroner.
n.3: An expected death from a known natural cause with an attending practitioner does not need coroner referral.

End of Life Care.q: A community nurse attends to verify the expected death of Lena, 83, who had advanced dementia. Lena is cold and rigor mortis is present. The nurse notices fresh, unexplained bruising on Lena's upper arms, and two relatives give conflicting accounts of the evening. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Decline to verify and request the police and the responsible doctor
Begin CPR because the death can no longer be treated as expected
Verify the death as expected and document the bruising in her record
Verify the death, then wash Lena before the funeral director arrives
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): verification by an RN applies to expected deaths not accompanied by suspicious circumstances, and the verifying nurse has the right to refuse to verify and to request the responsible doctor or the police in any unusual situation. Care after death guidance: minimal contact with the body when suspicion arises.

n.1: Rigor mortis is a sign of irreversible death, so CPR is not indicated (RNVoEAD; RCUK).
n.2: Verification by an RN is excluded where there are suspicious circumstances (RNVoEAD guidance).
n.3: Washing could destroy evidence; with suspicion, there should be minimal contact with the body.

End of Life Care.q: Daniel, 45, is on an intensive care unit in England after a catastrophic brain haemorrhage. Treatment is to be withdrawn. He has lived in England all his life and has not recorded a donation decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. What happens about organ donation?
o: His organs are retrieved without discussion because his consent is deemed
His family are approached to find out whether he held any views about donation
The consultant decides on donation at a best interests meeting
Donation cannot proceed because he did not register as an organ donor
End of Life Care.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England (opt out from 20 May 2020): adults are considered to agree to donate unless they recorded a decision not to donate or are in an excluded group, and families are still consulted when donation is a possibility, to share any knowledge of the person's decision.

n.0: Under the opt-out law the family are still consulted when donation is possible; retrieval does not proceed without that discussion.
n.2: Donation decisions follow the deemed consent law and the person's known views, not a clinical best interests meeting.
n.3: In England, adults not in an excluded group are considered to agree unless they opted out; registration is not required.

End of Life Care.q: A nurse on an intensive care unit in England is caring for four patients for whom organ donation after death may be possible. None has recorded a decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. Which patient is excluded from deemed consent?
o: Leah, 30, who had not discussed donation with her family
Amy, 17, a student who has lived in England all her life
Victor, 75, who completed treatment for bowel cancer last year
Paul, 60, who moved to England from Wales three years ago
End of Life Care.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England: the opt-out law does not apply to people under 18, people who lack capacity to understand the arrangements for a significant period before death, visitors and people not living in England voluntarily, or people who lived in England for less than 12 months before their death.

n.0: Not having discussed donation does not exclude an adult; her family are approached about any known views.
n.2: Medical history affects suitability, not whether deemed consent applies; age 75 is not an exclusion.
n.3: He has lived in England for more than 12 months and is an adult, so he is not in an excluded group.

End of Life Care.q: Mavis, 81, has died on a medical ward. Her two sons arrive an hour later and say they are unsure whether they want to see her body, as they have never seen someone who has died. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Tell them viewing is possible once she has reached the funeral director
Offer them the chance to see her and prepare them for what to expect
Advise them not to view her so they remember her as she was in life
Explain that viewing on the ward is allowed after the doctor's review
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): all key contacts should be offered the opportunity to view the deceased; there is evidence that, even in traumatic circumstances, key contacts found this helpful. Viewing can occur in acute hospitals, some hospices or later at the funeral directors. Prepare people sensitively for changes to the body.

n.0: Viewing can take place in hospitals and hospices, so there is no need to delay it until later.
n.2: Hospice UK guidance says all key contacts should be offered the chance to view; many find it helpful.
n.3: Viewing does not depend on a doctor's review once death has been verified.

End of Life Care.q: Gladys, 88, died at home this morning and her death has been verified. Her daughter, Pam, wants to help the community nurse with washing her. As they turn Gladys, there is a sighing sound from her mouth. Pam becomes frightened and asks whether her mother is still alive. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Explain gently that air can escape from the body when it is moved
Recheck Gladys's pulse and breathing and then call 999 for help
Call the GP to come and verify the death a second time
Ask Pam to leave the room while the nurse completes the washing
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): when moving the deceased, air can be released and this should not be mistaken for breathing; share this sensitively with the key contact or carer assisting. Prepare key contacts sensitively for changes to the body after death.

n.1: Death has been verified; the guidance says released air should not be mistaken for breathing.
n.2: The death was properly verified; a sound from released air is expected and is not a reason to re-verify.
n.3: Pam wishes to take part; the guidance is to prepare and support key contacts, not exclude them.

End of Life Care.q: Iris, 70, dies on a general ward. She was on the NHS Organ Donor Register as wanting to donate. Her husband asks the nurse whether her wish to donate can still be met now that she has died on the ward. Which response is accurate?
o: The ward nurse can remove the corneas before transfer to the mortuary
Donation is not possible because she did not die in intensive care
Organs can be retrieved from the ward if it is within 24 hours of death
Tissue such as corneas may still be donated, up to 24 hours after death
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): organ donation is possible only from intensive care units and emergency departments and is organised before death; whole-body and tissue donation is possible after death, and cornea donation can take place up to 24 hours after death in hospitals, hospices and funeral homes.

n.0: Ward nurses do not retrieve tissue; donation is arranged with the specialist donation service.
n.1: This is true for organs, but tissue donation, including corneas, remains possible after death.
n.2: Organ donation is organised before death from intensive care or emergency departments; it cannot be arranged after a ward death.

End of Life Care.q: Kai, 34, is on an intensive care unit, and the team have decided to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. The bedside nurse thinks organ donation may be possible and Kai's parents are at the bedside. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Raise donation with Kai's parents yourself at the bedside straight away
Contact the specialist nurse for organ donation to lead the approach
Wait to see whether Kai's parents ask about organ donation
Ask Kai's GP to discuss donation with his parents by phone
End of Life Care.w: NHS Blood and Transplant / British Transplantation Society best practice: the specialist nurse for organ donation is the main professional who makes the family approach, in collaboration with the hospital team, after checking the NHS Organ Donor Register for a recorded decision or nominated representative. Families are always approached if donation is possible.

n.0: The family approach is planned jointly and led by the specialist nurse, who checks the Organ Donor Register first.
n.2: Families are approached whenever donation is possible; waiting may lose the chance to honour Kai's decision.
n.3: The GP is not part of the donation pathway; the specialist nurse for organ donation leads it.

End of Life Care.q: Albert, a resident in a care home, died last night. This morning his close friend Ted, another resident, asks the nurse where Albert is, as he did not come to breakfast. Albert's family have been informed. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask the activities coordinator to tell residents at next week's meeting
Avoid telling Ted, to prevent him becoming upset during breakfast
Tell Ted sensitively that Albert has died and offer him time and support
Say that Albert has gone into hospital so that Ted is not distressed
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): residents in communal settings such as care homes often build significant relationships with other residents and will need to be informed; the RNVoEAD guidance asks the nurse to recognise the emotional impact on surrounding residents and prompt support. Code 2 and 20.2: act with honesty.

n.0: Delaying news for a week is not compassionate support for a close friend who is asking now.
n.1: Residents in communal settings have often built close relationships and need to be informed and supported.
n.3: Giving false information is dishonest (Code 20.2) and delays Ted's grieving.

End of Life Care.q: Mr Levi, 79, has died an expected death on a hospital ward and the death has been verified. His family explain that their faith requires burial as soon as possible, ideally within a day. It is a Friday evening. What should the nurse do?
o: Explain that his release cannot be arranged until the next working week
Advise the family to ask the coroner to speed up release of the body
Release him to the funeral director before the death certificate is issued
Tell the doctor promptly so certification is expedited, and involve chaplaincy
End of Life Care.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): spiritual, religious and cultural preferences, especially urgent release for burial or cremation, are time critical and should be acted on, with advice from the spiritual care or chaplaincy department; the RN informs the doctor of the death promptly (RNVoEAD 2024).

n.0: Care after death guidance highlights urgent release for burial as time critical; staff should act promptly.
n.1: This is not a coroner case; the doctor and medical examiner process handle certification.
n.2: Release follows the local legal process; the nurse cannot bypass certification.

End of Life Care.q: George, 86, has end-stage heart failure and lives in a nursing home. Over two days he has become harder to rouse, has stopped eating, and his knees look mottled. His breathing alternates between deep breaths and pauses. Which group of findings most suggests that George may be entering the last days of life?
o: Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and increasing peripheral oedema
New fever, a productive cough and a respiratory rate of 26 per minute
Improved alertness, taking more fluids and fewer respiratory secretions
Mottled skin, Cheyne-Stokes breathing and a falling level of consciousness
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.2 lists signs that may suggest a person is entering the last days of life: agitation, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, deteriorating level of consciousness, mottled skin, noisy respiratory secretions and progressive weight loss, alongside increasing fatigue, loss of appetite and functional decline.

n.0: These suggest fluid overload or worsening heart failure, not the recognised signs that a person may be dying.
n.1: These findings point to a possible chest infection or sepsis that needs assessment and escalation; they are not the NG31 signs of dying.
n.2: NICE NG31 1.1.3 says improvement in signs, symptoms or function may mean the person is stabilising or recovering.

End of Life Care.q: Margaret, 81, has metastatic lung cancer and is being cared for on a medical ward. The team agree she may be in the last days of life and start an individualised care plan. A newly qualified nurse asks how often Margaret should be formally reviewed for changes. Which minimum interval does NICE NG31 recommend for monitoring and updating her care plan?
o: At least every 24 hours
At least every 12 hours
At each weekly multidisciplinary meeting
At least every 72 hours
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.6: monitor for further changes in the person at least every 24 hours and update the care plan. Improvement can occur (rec 1.1.3), so regular review guards against wrongly assuming the person is dying.

n.1: Twelve hours is the NG31 minimum for monitoring a person on clinically assisted hydration (rec 1.4.9), not the general review of a dying person.
n.2: A weekly review would miss rapid changes in the last days of life; NG31 asks for monitoring at least every 24 hours.
n.3: Seventy-two hours is too long; NG31 rec 1.1.6 sets a minimum of every 24 hours because the person's condition can change quickly.

End of Life Care.q: Edna, 79, has metastatic breast cancer and has capacity. The team believe she is entering the last days of life. Her son meets the nurse in the corridor and asks that Edna is not told she is dying because 'it will crush her'. What is the nurse's most appropriate next step?
o: Tell Edna her full prognosis straight away so she is fully informed
Find out from Edna how much she would like to know about her condition
Agree with her son and avoid discussing the prognosis with Edna
Ask the consultant to decide whether Edna should be told she is dying
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.2.1 and 1.2.3: establish how much information the dying person would like about their prognosis, then discuss it with them unless they do not wish to be informed, including those important to them if the person wishes. Priorities for Care (2014): sensitive communication and involving the dying person in decisions.

n.0: This ignores her own preference about how much she wants to know; NG31 rec 1.2.1 asks staff to establish this first.
n.2: Edna has capacity and a right to information; NG31 rec 1.2.3 says discuss the prognosis with her unless she does not wish to be informed.
n.3: The decision about how much information she receives rests with Edna, not with a clinician or relative acting for her.

End of Life Care.q: Ahmed, 72, has end-stage COPD and is on a respiratory ward. He is thought to be in his last days. He tells the nurse he wants to die at home, and his wife says she wants this too and can stay with him. What should the nurse do first?
o: Explain that moving him home in the last days of life is not safe for him
Ask the GP to decide whether a home death would be appropriate
Start arranging the equipment, care and medicines needed at home without delay
Record his wish and review it at next week's multidisciplinary team meeting
End of Life Care.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.3.4 and 1.3.5: establish as early as possible the resources needed (equipment, care at night, support) and create an individualised care plan that includes the person's preferred care setting. Priority for Care 5: an individual plan of care agreed and delivered with compassion.

n.0: NG31 supports a preferred care setting where possible; transfer is not ruled out simply because he is dying.
n.1: The plan is made with Ahmed, his wife and the multidisciplinary team; deferring the decision to the GP delays action on his wish.
n.3: Waiting a week risks him dying before his wish can be met; NG31 rec 1.3.4 says establish resources as early as possible.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A public health team plans to reduce average salt intake across a region by working with manufacturers to lower the salt content of bread and processed foods. Which statement best describes this strategy?
o: Secondary prevention that detects raised blood pressure at an early stage
A high-risk approach targeting people already diagnosed with hypertension
A population approach: a small benefit to each person but a large total benefit
Tertiary prevention to reduce disability in people who have had strokes
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the population approach recognises that society influences individual behaviour and reduces risk at population level. The prevention paradox (Rose): most people who lower their risk will not benefit directly, although the total benefit across the population is large.

n.0: No one is being tested or detected; this lowers exposure to a risk factor across the population.
n.1: The change affects everyone who buys the foods, not a selected high-risk group.
n.3: This is aimed at the whole population before disease develops, not at people with established disease.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Lorraine, 59, has had type 2 diabetes for six years and has no visual symptoms. Which of the following is an example of secondary prevention for her?
o: Annual diabetic eye screening to detect early retinopathy
Rehabilitation and mobility aids after a below-knee amputation
A structured education course to prevent diabetes developing
A low-vision service after she has lost sight in one eye
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: secondary prevention detects early departures from health so treatment can begin. NHS screening: diabetic eye screening is offered from age 12 to all people with diabetes to check for early signs of diabetic retinopathy.

n.1: This reduces long-term disability from an established complication, which is tertiary prevention.
n.2: Lorraine already has diabetes; preventing its onset in people at risk would be primary prevention.
n.3: Support after sight loss limits disability from established disease, which is tertiary prevention.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A practice nurse invites people with a BMI over 40 to an intensive weight-management programme rather than offering it to the whole practice population. Which advantage is associated with this high-risk approach?
o: It tackles the social influences on behaviour in the wider community
Those invited are often more motivated, as their personal risk is high
It removes the need to assess each person's individual risk factors
It brings the largest fall in disease across the whole population
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the high-risk approach may be more cost-effective than population-wide approaches and targets people who are more motivated to change their behaviour; the population approach achieves risk reduction at population level. NICE PH49 (2014) rec 9: high-intensity interventions for people at high risk, for example a BMI over 40.

n.0: Addressing social influences on the whole community is a feature of the population approach.
n.2: A high-risk approach depends on identifying individuals by assessing their risk.
n.3: A large fall in total disease is the strength of the population approach, not a high-risk approach.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Beatrice, 67, has rheumatoid arthritis. She tells the nurse she would like to be more active but finds long walks painful. She enjoys swimming and used to garden. Which response best supports Beatrice to make an informed choice within the limits of her condition?
o: Explain that exercise is unsuitable for people with rheumatoid arthritis
Advise her to walk 10,000 steps a day, as recommended for everyone
Explore activities she enjoys and can manage, and agree a goal together
Give her a leaflet on exercise and ask her to decide at home
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.9: use appropriate communication skills and strength-based approaches to support people to make informed choices about their care within the limits of illness or disability. NICE PH49 (2014): agree goals and develop action plans with the person.

n.0: This is inaccurate and removes her choice; activity within her limits can be supported.
n.1: A fixed target ignores her pain and preferences; P2.9 asks for strength-based, person-centred support.
n.3: A leaflet alone misses the chance to build on her strengths and agree a plan with her.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A nurse on placement with the local public health team reads a report stating that 120 people in a town of 100,000 were newly diagnosed with tuberculosis between January and December 2025. Which epidemiological measure does this figure describe?
o: Prevalence
Mortality rate
Case fatality rate
Incidence
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: incidence is the number of new cases of a disease arising in a population over a given period; prevalence is the total number of existing cases at a point or over a period. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2 (epidemiology).

n.0: Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or period, not only the new cases arising in the year.
n.1: A mortality rate counts deaths in a population, not new diagnoses.
n.2: Case fatality is the proportion of people with a disease who die from it.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A GP practice annual report states that on 1 April 2026, 850 of its 12,000 registered adults were living with diagnosed type 2 diabetes. A student nurse on placement asks what this figure measures. Which term is correct?
o: Prevalence
Relative risk
Life expectancy
Incidence
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: prevalence is the total number of existing cases in a population at a point in time (point prevalence) or over a period; incidence counts new cases. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2.

n.1: Relative risk compares the risk of an outcome between an exposed and an unexposed group.
n.2: Life expectancy estimates average years of life remaining and is unrelated to this count.
n.3: Incidence counts new cases over a period; this figure counts everyone currently living with the condition.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A community nurse is learning about the NHS England Core20PLUS5 approach to reducing healthcare inequalities in adults. What does 'Core20' refer to?
o: The 20% of the population who are aged 65 and over in each region
The 20% of adults living with the highest number of long-term health conditions
The most deprived 20% of the population, by the Index of Multiple Deprivation
The 20% of local areas with the highest rates of emergency hospital admission
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS England, Core20PLUS5 (adults): Core20 is the most deprived 20% of the national population as identified by the national Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD); PLUS groups are identified locally; the 5 are clinical areas of focus.

n.0: Age is not the basis of Core20; it is the most deprived fifth of the population.
n.1: Core20 is defined by deprivation, not by the number of long-term conditions a person has.
n.3: Admission rates are not the measure; Core20 uses the national Index of Multiple Deprivation.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A practice nurse is preparing a teaching session on the adult Core20PLUS5 programme. Which of the following is one of its five clinical areas?
o: Dementia diagnosis rates and post-diagnostic support
Hypertension case-finding and optimal lipid management
Rehabilitation after hip fracture in older adults
Sexual health screening for adults under 25
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS England, Core20PLUS5 (adults): the five adult clinical areas are maternity, severe mental illness (annual health checks), chronic respiratory disease, early cancer diagnosis, and hypertension case-finding and optimal management with lipid optimisation.

n.0: Dementia is not one of the five adult clinical areas in Core20PLUS5.
n.2: Hip fracture rehabilitation is not one of the five adult clinical areas.
n.3: Sexual health screening is not one of the five adult clinical areas.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Clifford, 63, has just been prescribed a new inhaler. The nurse has explained how to use it. Clifford left school at 14 and says he 'is not one for reading'. What is the best way for the nurse to check that he has understood?
o: Ask him to explain and show, in his own words, how he will use it
Give him a detailed written leaflet to read when he gets home
Ask him 'Do you understand?' before he leaves the clinic
Repeat the explanation using the correct medical terms in full
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS England, Health literacy (personalised care): TeachBack (asking the person to explain information back), chunk and check, and plain language are recommended techniques to support people with lower health literacy. Code 7.1-7.2: use terms people understand and check understanding.

n.1: A detailed leaflet may not help someone with limited reading and does not check understanding.
n.2: A closed question invites a 'yes' and does not show whether he has understood.
n.3: Medical terms make information harder to follow; NHS England recommends plain language.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A nurse is planning patient information for an outpatient clinic and wants to account for health literacy across the local population. Which statement about health literacy in England is supported by Public Health England evidence?
o: Up to 61% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
Health literacy is measured by a person's highest school qualification
Difficulty understanding health information mainly affects people over 80
About 10% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS England, Health literacy (personalised care): a Public Health England report found that up to 61% of the English working-age population do not routinely understand the health and wellbeing information they are given. Health literacy (WHO) is the personal characteristics and social resources needed to access, understand, appraise and use information to make health decisions.

n.1: Health literacy is the ability to access, understand, appraise and use information, not a qualification level.
n.2: Low health literacy is common across working-age adults, not mainly in the oldest age groups.
n.3: The figure is far higher; PHE found up to 61% of the working-age population struggle.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: An integrated care board is using Core20PLUS5 to plan work on healthcare inequalities. Which group best illustrates the 'PLUS' element of the approach?
o: Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities identified as a local priority
People in one of the five clinical areas, such as maternity
Adults with hypertension who need case-finding and lipid checks
Adults living in the most deprived 20% of neighbourhoods
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS England, Core20PLUS5 (adults): PLUS populations are identified locally and include ethnic minority communities, people with a learning disability and autistic people, people with multiple long-term conditions, and inclusion health groups such as people experiencing homelessness and Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities.

n.1: Maternity is one of the '5' clinical areas, not a PLUS population group.
n.2: Hypertension is one of the five clinical areas rather than a PLUS population.
n.3: This describes the Core20 group, which is defined by the national Index of Multiple Deprivation.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Derek, 70, has COPD and has been admitted twice this winter with exacerbations. He tells the nurse that his flat is damp and that he cannot afford to heat it. Which action by the nurse best addresses the factors affecting his health?
o: Ask the prescriber to increase his inhaler dose for the winter months
Refer or signpost him to local housing and energy support services
Advise him to spend more time in bed to conserve his energy
Record the housing issue and note it is outside the nursing role
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.2 and P2.7: understand the wider determinants of health and explain the contribution of social influences and circumstances to health outcomes. NICE PH49 (2014): assess the context in which people live, including their physical, economic and social environment.

n.0: Medicines do not address the damp, cold housing that is affecting his health.
n.2: This does not address the housing problem and reduces his activity.
n.3: NMC P2.7 expects nurses to recognise social circumstances as influences on health and act on them.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Vincent, 48, attends the practice nurse for a wound dressing. While checking his record, the nurse sees he smokes 20 cigarettes a day. They have about a minute before the next patient. Which approach reflects very brief advice on smoking?
o: Ask about smoking and advise him to cut down gradually by himself
Ask, advise that medicines plus specialist support work best, and offer referral
Explain the diseases caused by smoking in detail over the next 20 minutes
Wait until he says he is ready to quit before raising the topic of smoking
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NCSCT Very Brief Advice on smoking; NICE NG209 (2021, updated 2025): very brief advice is Ask (record smoking status), Advise (the best way to stop is with a combination of medication and specialist support) and Act (offer referral to local stop smoking support); it takes about 30 seconds.

n.0: VBA advises that the most effective way to stop is medication combined with specialist behavioural support, not quitting unaided.
n.2: Very brief advice takes about 30 seconds; a long lecture is not the VBA model and is not feasible here.
n.3: VBA is offered to everyone who smokes at every opportunity, whatever their stated readiness.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Carol, 41, tells the nurse at a health check that she drinks most weekends: about 7 units on Friday night and 7 units on Saturday night, and nothing during the week. Which advice is most accurate?
o: Her drinking is above the weekly guideline, which is 10 units for women
Her drinking is low risk because her weekly total is within 14 units
Spread drinking over 3 or more days, as heavy sessions raise her risk
She should drink a small amount daily, as this protects her heart
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UK Chief Medical Officers' low risk drinking guidelines (2016): it is safest not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, for men and women; if drinking as much as 14 units a week, spread it evenly over 3 or more days, as one or two heavy drinking episodes a week increase the risk of death from long-term illness and from accidents and injuries.

n.0: The CMO guideline is 14 units a week for both men and women.
n.1: The CMOs advise that one or two heavy drinking episodes a week increase risks of long-term illness, accidents and injuries.
n.3: The CMOs do not advise drinking for health; risk rises with regular drinking.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Marion, 56, says she drinks four 250 mL glasses of wine a week. The wine is 12% alcohol by volume. One UK unit is 10 mL of pure alcohol. How many units does Marion drink each week?
o: 12 units
30 units
3 units
8 units
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Working: 250 mL x 12% = 30 mL pure alcohol per glass; 30 mL / 10 mL = 3 units per glass; 3 x 4 glasses = 12 units a week, within the UK Chief Medical Officers' low risk drinking guidelines (2016) limit of 14 units a week.

n.1: This treats the 30 mL of pure alcohol in one glass as units; 30 mL is 3 units.
n.2: Three units is the amount in one 250 mL glass at 12%, not the weekly total of four glasses.
n.3: This undercounts; each glass contains 3 units, so four glasses contain 12.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A ward manager is introducing Making Every Contact Count (MECC) and explains the first level of intervention to her team. Which description matches a MECC Level 1 very brief intervention?
o: Oral discussion and negotiation with follow-up and possible referral for support
High-intensity specialist sessions over several weeks for people at high risk
An individual discussion lasting more than 30 minutes over one or more sessions
Giving information or signposting, taking from 30 seconds to a couple of minutes
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS England, Making Every Contact Count consensus statement (2016): MECC uses day-to-day interactions to support positive changes to physical and mental health and wellbeing. Level 1 very brief intervention takes from 30 seconds to a couple of minutes and enables information giving or signposting; Level 2 brief intervention involves discussion, negotiation or encouragement.

n.0: This describes a MECC Level 2 brief intervention.
