n.1: High-intensity interventions are delivered by specialist services, not as MECC very brief interventions.
n.2: This describes an extended brief intervention (NICE PH49), which is more intensive than Level 1.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Ray, 58, smokes, drinks about 30 units a week and takes little exercise. He tells the nurse he wants to be healthier but feels overwhelmed by everything he 'should' change. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise him to stop smoking and drinking on the same day
Tell him to start with alcohol, as it carries the greatest risk
Give leaflets on all three topics and review him in six months
Ask which change he feels most motivated to tackle first
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) rec 8: tailor interventions by assessing the person's behaviour, capability, context and how motivated they are to change; if many behaviours need to change, assess which one or ones the person is most motivated to tackle. NMC Annexe A 2.7: assess motivation and capacity for behaviour change.

n.0: Tackling several behaviours at once when he feels overwhelmed may reduce his chance of success; PH49 asks which he is most motivated to change.
n.1: Choosing for him ignores his motivation; PH49 recommends assessing which behaviour he is most motivated to tackle.
n.2: Leaflets without a plan miss the chance to agree goals; PH49 recommends goals, action plans and planned review.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Shirley, 66, wants to eat more fruit and vegetables. She knows how to cook and is keen to change. However, her nearest shop sells no fresh food and there is no bus to the supermarket. Using the COM-B model, which component is the main barrier to her behaviour change?
o: Motivation
Health literacy
Capability
Opportunity
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014), glossary (COM-B, Michie et al. 2011): for behaviour change a person needs capability (physical and psychological), opportunity (physical and social) and motivation. PH49 gives the example that a healthy diet is harder in an area without shops selling fresh food and with poor transport.

n.0: She is keen to change, so motivation is not the main barrier.
n.1: Health literacy is not one of the three COM-B components, and she understands what to do.
n.2: Shirley has the knowledge and skills to cook, so physical and psychological capability are present.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Leon, 39, stopped smoking three months ago with support. He tells the nurse he is worried he will start again at a family wedding next month, where many guests smoke. What is the most appropriate support?
o: Help him make an 'if-then' plan for moments when he is tempted
Advise him to avoid weddings and other social events for a year
Close his episode of care, as his quit attempt is now complete
Reassure him that relapse is rare once three months have passed
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) recs 6 and 10: interventions should address relapse and recognise that it is common; help people maintain change by giving them well-rehearsed action plans such as 'if-then' plans, social support and feedback and monitoring for at least 1 year.

n.1: Avoiding all social contact is unrealistic and removes social support that helps people maintain change.
n.2: PH49 rec 10 recommends feedback and monitoring for at least a year to help maintain change.
n.3: PH49 recognises that relapse is common and asks for interventions to address it.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Ben, 30, has a learning disability and attends his annual health check with his support worker. His BMI is 35. The nurse wants to discuss diet and activity with him. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Use easy-read materials, allow extra time and involve Ben in each choice
Discuss the plan with his support worker rather than with Ben himself
Use the standard 10-minute appointment and the usual written leaflet
Postpone the conversation, as he may not understand the information
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.4: use opportunities, with reasonable adjustments, to discuss diet and exercise. Equality Act 2010 s20 (duty to make reasonable adjustments); Accessible Information Standard (2025). NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014): tailor interventions to the person's capability and needs, including any disability.

n.1: Ben should be involved in decisions about his own health; talking over him is not person-centred.
n.2: Without reasonable adjustments, Ben may be unable to take part; adjustments are a legal duty (Equality Act 2010 s20).
n.3: Assuming he cannot understand breaches MCA s1 and denies him health promotion.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Kenneth, 68, lives in England and asks the practice nurse what the NHS bowel cancer screening programme will offer him. He has no bowel symptoms. Which answer is accurate?
o: A home test kit every 2 years
A home test kit every year
A colonoscopy every 5 years
A one-off camera test at age 70
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): everyone aged 50 to 74 is offered a bowel cancer screening home test kit every 2 years; people aged 75 or over can ask for a kit every 2 years.

n.1: The bowel screening kit is sent every 2 years, not annually.
n.2: Colonoscopy is a diagnostic test offered after a positive screening result, not the routine screen.
n.3: The current programme offers a home test kit every 2 years from 50 to 74.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Ronald, 70, lives in England. He mentions to the nurse that he has never had abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) screening and asks whether it is too late. What is the most accurate response?
o: He is now too old to be included in AAA screening
Men over 65 who have not been screened can refer themselves
Screening after 65 is offered to men with symptoms of an aneurysm
He needs a GP referral for a hospital ultrasound scan
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): AAA screening is offered to men when they turn 65; men over 65 can self-refer.

n.0: Men over 65 can self-refer to the programme.
n.2: Screening is for men without symptoms; men over 65 who were not screened can self-refer, and symptoms need GP assessment.
n.3: Self-referral to the screening programme is available; a GP referral is for symptoms.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Patricia, 73, lives in England and has had regular breast screening. She asks the practice nurse why she has not received an invitation since she turned 71. Which response is accurate?
o: Invitations stop after 70, but she can refer herself for screening
Women over 70 are invited every 5 years instead of every 3 years
Breast screening ends at 70 because no benefit remains after that age
She needs a GP referral to a breast clinic to be screened
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): breast screening is offered to women aged 50 to 70; women over 70 can self-refer.

n.1: Routine invitations are for women aged 50 to 70; after 70 screening is by self-referral.
n.2: Women over 70 can still self-refer; screening is available to them on request.
n.3: A breast clinic referral is for symptoms; screening after 70 is by self-referral.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Nadia, 34, has a screen-positive result from an NHS screening programme. She is anxious and asks the nurse what this result means. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: She may have the condition and will be offered tests to confirm it
She has the condition and will now start treatment straight away
The result is likely to be a false positive, so no action is needed
She should repeat the same screening test again in 5 years' time
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): a screen-positive (higher-risk) result means you may have the condition; you will be offered diagnostic tests to confirm whether you have it, then treatment, advice and support.

n.1: A screening test is not diagnostic; diagnostic tests are needed to confirm the condition first.
n.2: Screen-positive results lead to diagnostic tests; they cannot be assumed to be false.
n.3: A screen-positive result leads to diagnostic testing, not routine re-screening.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Brenda, 58, completed a bowel screening kit six months ago and the result was normal. She now tells the nurse she has had blood in her stools and looser bowel movements for four weeks. What should the nurse advise?
o: Wait for her next routine kit, due in about 18 months' time
See her GP about these symptoms now, despite the normal screen
Her normal screening result means bowel cancer can be ruled out
Request an extra screening kit to repeat the test this month
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): screening identifies increased risk in apparently healthy people; even with a normal result you could still develop the condition, and people with symptoms should speak to a GP. Screening tests are not 100% accurate (false negatives occur).

n.0: Symptoms need GP assessment now; screening is for people without symptoms.
n.2: A normal (screen-negative) result means low risk at the time; it does not exclude disease developing later.
n.3: Screening is not a test for symptoms; she needs clinical assessment by her GP.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Agnes, 55, has received her cervical screening invitation. She tells the nurse she has heard mixed things about screening and is unsure whether to go. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that cervical screening is compulsory for women of her age group
Advise her that screening prevents every case of cervical cancer
Give balanced information on benefits and limits, and support her choice
Book her test now and explain the details at her appointment
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): deciding whether to have screening is a personal choice; benefits (early detection, preventing some deaths) are weighed against risks and limitations (false positives and negatives, anxiety, difficult decisions). Code 4.2: make sure informed consent is obtained.

n.0: Screening is a personal choice; NHS screening is offered, not mandated.
n.1: Screening tests are not 100% accurate; this overstates the benefit and is misleading.
n.3: Booking before she has decided bypasses informed choice.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A practice nurse is reviewing which patients might be contacted for lung cancer screening, available in some parts of England. Which person meets the age and smoking criteria?
o: Susan, 50, who currently smokes 15 cigarettes a day
Thomas, 78, who stopped smoking 30 years ago
Raj, 60, who smoked for 20 years and stopped 10 years ago
Ann, 65, a lifelong non-smoker who lives with a smoker
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): people aged 55 to 74 who have ever smoked may be contacted by their GP or a local NHS service to take part in lung cancer screening.

n.0: Lung cancer screening is for people aged 55 to 74; Susan is under 55.
n.1: Thomas is over 74, above the age range for lung cancer screening.
n.3: Screening is for people who have ever smoked; Ann has never smoked.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Gary, 52, tells the nurse he is thinking of paying for a private 'full body' screening scan because 'the NHS does not screen for enough things'. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: NHS programmes are offered where benefits are judged to outweigh harms
Private screening tests are more accurate than NHS screening tests
All private screening tests are approved by the UK National Screening Committee
Each GP practice chooses which screening tests to offer its patients
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): the UK National Screening Committee advises the NHS on which screening programmes to offer and recommends screening only when the benefits to the group offered outweigh the harms; some commercial tests are not recommended because it is not clear that benefits outweigh harms.

n.1: There is no basis for this; some private tests are not recommended because benefits may not outweigh harms.
n.2: Some private tests are not recommended by the UK NSC.
n.3: The UK NSC advises the NHS in all four nations on which screening programmes to offer.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A school nurse is teaching staff about adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), using the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh ACE study. Which experience is counted as an ACE in that study?
o: Living with a household member who served a prison sentence
Being born early and spending time in a neonatal unit
Moving house and changing school during the primary years
Having a parent who regularly worked night shifts
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): the nine ACEs were verbal, physical and sexual abuse, and growing up in a household with parental separation, domestic violence, mental illness, alcohol abuse, drug use or incarceration.

n.1: Prematurity is not one of the nine ACEs measured.
n.2: Moving house is not one of the nine ACEs measured in the Welsh study.
n.3: Parental shift work is not one of the nine ACEs measured.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A nurse is preparing a teaching session on how childhood adversity affects adult health. In the Welsh ACE study, how much more likely were adults with four or more ACEs to be high-risk drinkers than adults with no ACEs?
o: About 4 times
About 20 times
About 2 times
About 11 times
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): compared with people with no ACEs, those with 4+ ACEs were 4 times more likely to be a high-risk drinker, 6 times more likely to smoke, 11 times more likely to have smoked cannabis and 20 times more likely to have been incarcerated.

n.1: Twenty times relates to having been incarcerated, not high-risk drinking.
n.2: The study reported a fourfold, not twofold, increase in high-risk drinking.
n.3: Eleven times relates to having smoked cannabis, not high-risk drinking.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A health visitor explains to a student nurse why she prioritises support for pregnant women and families with babies. According to Public Health England's life course guidance, which period offers an opportunity to make a difference over a person's whole lifetime?
o: The first year after retirement from work
The teenage years from age 13 to age 18
The first year of secondary school education
The first 1,000 days of a child's life
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): there is growing evidence that intervening in the first 1,000 days of a child's life can make a difference over their whole lifetime. NMC P2.6: understand the importance of early years and childhood experiences on later health.

n.0: Retirement is a later transition; the guidance highlights the first 1,000 days.
n.1: Adolescence is an important stage, but it is not the period the guidance singles out here.
n.2: School transitions matter, but the guidance highlights the first 1,000 days as having lifelong impact.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A practice nurse is preparing a short presentation for a safeguarding update and reads the 2015 Welsh study of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) among adults. Roughly what proportion of the adults surveyed reported four or more ACEs?
o: About 47%
About 30%
About 5%
About 14%
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): 47% of Welsh adults reported at least one ACE and 14% reported four or more.

n.0: Forty-seven per cent reported at least one ACE, not four or more.
n.1: Thirty per cent is not a figure from the study for 4+ ACEs.
n.2: Five per cent was the prevalence of individual ACEs such as parental drug use or incarceration.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A nurse is helping to design a local prevention strategy and wants to apply a life course approach. Which statement best reflects that approach?
o: Accept that adult health is fixed by genes, so early action changes little
Begin prevention once a long-term condition has been diagnosed in the person
Act early and at key transitions, as health is shaped across the whole of life
Focus prevention on older adults, as most long-term disease occurs in later life
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): a life course approach considers the critical stages, transitions and settings where large differences can be made, taking action early and appropriately across the life course and reducing health inequalities throughout life.

n.0: The approach rests on evidence that early and timely action changes lifelong outcomes.
n.1: Waiting for diagnosis misses the critical earlier stages the approach targets.
n.3: A life course approach acts at every stage, including early years, not just in later life.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Jason, 26, attends the emergency department for the third time this year with injuries after drinking heavily. He tells the nurse that as a child he lived with domestic violence and that his father misused alcohol. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to use this information?
o: Refer him to children's social care about what happened in his childhood
Tell him his drinking is a choice that is unrelated to his childhood
Recognise that early adversity may underlie his current risks, and offer support
Treat his injuries and avoid discussing his past, as it is not relevant now
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): adults with 4+ ACEs were more likely to be high-risk drinkers and victims of violence. NMC P2.6: understand the importance of early years and childhood experiences on later physical, mental and behavioural health and wellbeing.

n.0: Jason is an adult; children's social care is for current concerns about children.
n.1: This is dismissive and contradicts evidence linking ACEs with high-risk drinking.
n.3: The ACE evidence links childhood adversity with health-harming behaviours, so it is relevant to his care.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A community nurse is supporting Elsie, 82, who lives alone, to plan her care. Public Health England's life course guidance identifies a main outcome to aim for across life, including in older age. What is it?
o: Reducing the number of medicines prescribed
Planning an early move into residential care
Maintaining good functional ability
Increasing the total number of years lived
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): maintaining good functional ability is the main outcome of the life course approach to health, and functional ability can be enhanced throughout life by a supportive environment.

n.0: Medicine reduction may help some people but is not the main outcome named.
n.1: Moving into care is not an outcome measure of the life course approach.
n.3: The guidance identifies functional ability as the main outcome, not length of life.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Jade, 8, lives with her mother and her mother's partner. A nurse learns that the partner is often violent towards Jade's mother, although Jade herself has not been hit. How does the Welsh ACE study classify Jade's experience?
o: An ACE, but one with no link to later health or behaviour
As an ACE, because growing up with domestic violence is counted
Not an ACE until the police have attended an incident at home
Not an ACE, because the child must be directly harmed to count
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): ACEs include direct harm (verbal, physical, sexual abuse) and the environment the child lives in, such as growing up in a house with domestic violence. Any current concern about Jade's safety would also need a safeguarding referral (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026).

n.0: The study found clear links between ACEs, including household adversity, and later health-harming behaviour.
n.2: Police attendance is not a criterion for counting domestic violence as an ACE.
n.3: Household adversities such as domestic violence count even when the child is not directly harmed.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A nurse on a postnatal ward is explaining immunity to a new mother. She says her baby is born with some protection against measles because of antibodies the mother made. Which type of immunity is this?
o: Population immunity from high vaccine coverage in the community
Active immunity produced by the baby's own immune system
Innate immunity from the baby's skin and mucous membranes
Passive immunity from antibodies that crossed the placenta
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): passive immunity is protection from antibodies transferred from immune individuals, most commonly across the placenta; it is temporary, commonly lasting a few weeks or months, and is more effective against some infections (for example tetanus and measles) than others.

n.0: Population immunity reduces exposure; it is not antibody protection inside the baby.
n.1: The baby did not make these antibodies; they were transferred from the mother, which is passive immunity.
n.2: Innate immunity is non-specific; measles-specific antibodies from the mother are passive acquired immunity.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A practice nurse is checking her understanding of vaccine types before a childhood immunisation clinic. Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
o: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV23)
Inactivated poliomyelitis vaccine (IPV)
Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine
Tetanus vaccine containing inactivated toxin
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): live attenuated vaccines include yellow fever, measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) and BCG; the weakened organism replicates in the recipient. IPV contains inactivated virus, tetanus and diphtheria vaccines contain toxoids, and pneumococcal vaccine contains capsular polysaccharide.

n.0: PPV23 contains capsular polysaccharide, not a live organism.
n.1: IPV contains inactivated virus, which cannot cause the disease.
n.3: Tetanus vaccine contains an inactivated toxin (toxoid), not a live organism.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Lucy brings her 1-year-old son for his MMRV vaccine. Her neighbour's baby is too young to be vaccinated, and Lucy asks how vaccinating her son could help that baby. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Vaccinating children means adults in the area no longer need vaccines
Her son will pass vaccine antibodies to other children he plays with
Vaccinated people are less likely to pass the infection on to others
The vaccine gives lifelong protection, so the disease disappears locally
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): vaccinated individuals are less likely to be a source of infection to others, reducing the risk of exposure for unvaccinated individuals, so people who cannot be vaccinated still benefit. This is population (or 'herd') immunity.

n.0: Population immunity does not replace the adult programme; adults are still offered vaccines.
n.1: Antibodies are not passed between children; protection of others comes from reduced transmission.
n.3: No vaccine offers 100% protection, and disease can return if coverage falls.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Priya, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant and attends her antenatal appointment in October, during the flu season. She has had no vaccines in this pregnancy. According to the UKHSA schedule, which vaccines should she be offered now?
o: Flu, pertussis and RSV vaccines, all at this appointment
Pertussis vaccine now, with the flu vaccine after the birth
RSV vaccine now, with the pertussis vaccine from 28 weeks
Inactivated flu vaccine and the pertussis (Tdap) vaccine
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: in pregnancy, inactivated flu vaccine at any stage during the flu season; pertussis (Tdap) from 16 weeks (ideally before 32 weeks but may be given later); RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) from 28 weeks.

n.0: RSV vaccine is offered from 28 weeks of pregnancy, so it is not due at 20 weeks.
n.1: Inactivated flu vaccine is offered at any stage of pregnancy during the flu season.
n.2: This reverses the timings: pertussis is from 16 weeks and RSV from 28 weeks.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Doreen, 70, gave consent for a two-dose shingles vaccine course at her first appointment. She now attends for the second dose. Nothing has changed in her health and no new information about the vaccine has emerged. What should the nurse do about consent?
o: Check that she is still happy to proceed, then give the second dose
Obtain fresh written consent from her before giving the second dose
Ask her GP to confirm the consent given at her first appointment
Give the dose without discussion, as consent covers the whole course
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): consent is a process; it may be withdrawn at any time. Where consent has been obtained for a full course it is not necessary to seek consent again for each vaccine unless new information has come to light, but it is good practice to check the person is content to proceed at each stage.

n.1: Where consent was obtained for a full course, it need not be sought again for each dose unless new information arises.
n.2: Consent is between Doreen and the person giving the vaccine; GP confirmation is not required.
n.3: The Green Book says it is good practice to check the person is content to proceed at each stage.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Ella, 14, is in school Year 9. The school nurse assesses her as Gillick competent, and Ella consents to her MenACWY vaccine. Her mother has returned a form refusing the vaccine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the vaccine, as a parent cannot override a Gillick competent child's consent
Delay the vaccine until Ella is 16 and can legally consent for herself
Ask the head teacher to decide whether the vaccine should be given
Withhold the vaccine, because a parent's refusal takes priority under age 16
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): children under 16 who understand fully what is involved (Gillick competent) can give consent, ideally with parental involvement; where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent. UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: MenACWY at 14 years (school Year 9).

n.1: Gillick competent children under 16 can consent, so waiting is unnecessary.
n.2: The head teacher has no role in consent to Ella's treatment.
n.3: The Green Book states that where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Frank, 68, has heart failure. He attends the practice in October 2026 and asks whether he is eligible for the RSV vaccine. Which answer is accurate under the UKHSA schedule from September 2026?
o: No; the RSV vaccine is offered in pregnancy and to care home residents
Yes; people aged 65 to 74 with heart failure are now offered it
No; the RSV vaccine is offered to older adults from age 75
No; RSV vaccine is offered to care home residents aged 80 or over
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) at 75 years and for all adult residents of care homes for older adults; from September 2026, also for people aged 65 to 74 with chronic respiratory or heart conditions (for example severe asthma, chronic pulmonary disease, heart failure) or immunosuppression; and in pregnancy from 28 weeks.

n.0: These groups are eligible, but the 2026 schedule also includes 65 to 74 year olds with heart failure.
n.2: The age-75 programme continues, but from September 2026 people aged 65 to 74 with chronic heart conditions are also eligible.
n.3: The care home programme covers all adult residents of care homes for older adults, and Frank is eligible anyway.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Mia, 6, is due her annual flu vaccine at school. Her parents tell the school nurse they decline the nasal spray vaccine because it contains porcine gelatine, which conflicts with their beliefs, but they want her protected. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that children under 9 must have the nasal vaccine to be protected
Give the nasal vaccine, explaining that gelatine is an inactive ingredient
Discuss the injected inactivated flu vaccine as an alternative for Mia
Advise them that Mia can have a flu vaccine once she reaches adulthood
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: the live attenuated influenza vaccine (Fluenz, nasal) contains porcine gelatine; if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used (Green Book chapter 19). UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): consent must be given freely by an appropriately informed person.

n.0: The schedule states that if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used.
n.1: Giving it against the parents' refusal would be without valid consent (Green Book chapter 2).
n.3: An inactivated alternative is available now, so she need not go unprotected.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: A practice nurse is planning activities for a GP surgery's prevention week. Which activity is an example of primary prevention?
o: Giving the MMRV vaccine to a child at her one-year appointment
Offering cervical screening to a 30-year-old woman
Sending a bowel screening kit to a 62-year-old man
Referring a man to cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: primary prevention is prevention of disease through control of exposure to risk factors. Immunisation prevents infection before it occurs (UKHSA routine schedule from 1 September 2026: MMRV at one year).

n.1: Screening detects early departures from health in people who already have changes, so it is secondary prevention.
n.2: Bowel screening aims to find cancer or polyps early, which is secondary prevention.
n.3: Rehabilitation reduces impairment from existing disease, so it is tertiary prevention.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Sunita, 52, feels well and has no symptoms. After receiving an NHS invitation letter, she attends her GP surgery for cervical screening, and the practice nurse takes a sample. Which level of prevention does this activity represent?
o: Secondary prevention
Health protection
Primary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: secondary prevention is the application of available measures to detect early departures from health and to introduce appropriate treatment; screening, such as cervical screening, is a major component.

n.1: Health protection covers measures such as infection control and immunisation, not detecting early disease in individuals.
n.2: Primary prevention controls exposure to risk factors before disease starts, for example immunisation or stopping smoking.
n.3: Tertiary prevention reduces long-term impairment and disability from established disease, such as rehabilitation.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Michael, 61, had a stroke three months ago. He now attends community physiotherapy and speech and language therapy to regain function and adjust to living with weakness in his right arm. Which level of prevention does this care represent?
o: Tertiary prevention
Primary prevention
Population prevention
Secondary prevention
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: tertiary prevention is the application of measures to reduce or eliminate long-term impairments and disabilities, minimising suffering from existing ill health and promoting the person's adjustment to their condition.

n.1: Primary prevention aims to stop the disease occurring at all; Michael has already had a stroke.
n.2: This is a population-wide strategy, not care to reduce one person's long-term impairment.
n.3: Secondary prevention detects disease early in people without symptoms, for example through screening.

Health Promotion & Prevention.q: Graham, 54, has a BMI of 34 and is at a health check. The nurse explains the health risks of his weight and the support available. Graham says he does not want to change his diet at the moment because of stress at work. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell him he must start changing his diet now to avoid a heart attack
Record that he is non-compliant and close the health promotion episode
Refer him to a weight management service even though he has declined
Respect his decision, give information and offer to revisit the topic later
Health Promotion & Prevention.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.1 and P2.9: promote health by empowering people to make informed choices, using communication skills and strength-based approaches. NICE PH49 (2014) recommends tailoring interventions to the person's motivation and planning review points; Code 4.1 respects the person's right to accept or refuse.

n.0: Pressuring or frightening him is not empowering; NMC P2.1 and P2.9 support informed choices.
n.1: Labelling him non-compliant is judgemental and closes the door on future support.
n.2: Referral needs his agreement; acting against his choice undermines informed decision-making (Code 4).

Patient Safety & Quality.q: On a surgical ward, Femi asks the ward manager about the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 because a new bariatric care pathway is being written. Which step do the regulations require the employer to take first?
o: Set a maximum weight that any member of staff may lift on the ward
Reduce the risk of injury to the lowest level by providing equipment
Avoid hazardous manual handling so far as is reasonably practicable
Assess the risk of injury from every manual handling task on the ward
Patient Safety & Quality.w: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 set out a hierarchy for employers: avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable; assess the risk of injury from any hazardous operations that cannot be avoided; and reduce that risk to as low as reasonably practicable (HSE, Manual handling at work).

n.0: The HSE states that the law does not set specific weight limits; weight is one factor in the risk assessment.
n.1: Reducing risk is the third step, after avoidance and assessment.
n.3: Assessment is the second step and applies to hazardous handling that cannot be avoided, not to every task.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Before a transfer, Rosa checks the mobile hoist on her ward. The examination label shows that its last thorough examination under LOLER was eight months ago, and no examination scheme with different intervals is displayed. What should Rosa do?
o: Use the hoist, because lifting equipment is examined every 12 months
Take the hoist out of use, report it and use another hoist that is in date
Carry out a visual pre-use check and continue if the hoist looks sound
Use the hoist for this transfer and report the overdue date at handover
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Under LOLER 1998, lifting equipment and accessories used for lifting people must be thoroughly examined at least every 6 months (other lifting equipment every 12 months) unless an examination scheme sets other intervals. A hoist overdue for examination should not be used to lift a person and should be reported (HSE, Thorough examinations and inspections of lifting equipment).

n.0: The 12-month interval applies to lifting equipment that is not used to lift people; patient hoists fall under the 6-month interval.
n.2: A pre-use check is good practice but does not replace the thorough examination by a competent person that LOLER requires.
n.3: Knowingly using equipment that is overdue for its statutory examination puts the patient at risk; the problem must be dealt with before the transfer.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: During a morning shift, Grace, a staff nurse, slips on a wet floor in the sluice and fractures her wrist. She is taken to the emergency department. The ward manager is the responsible person under RIDDOR 2013. How should this injury be reported?
o: To the HSE without delay and within 10 days, as it is a specified injury
To the HSE within 15 days, as it happened in a clinical area
Through the local incident system, as staff injuries are not reportable
To the HSE within 15 days, if Grace is off work for more than seven days
Patient Safety & Quality.w: A fracture other than to fingers, thumbs or toes is a specified injury under RIDDOR 2013. Specified injuries and work-related deaths must be reported to the HSE without delay, and within 10 days. The incident should also be recorded on the local system (HSE, RIDDOR: when do I report).

n.1: The 15-day deadline is for over-7-day incapacitation, and the location of the accident does not decide the timescale.
n.2: Work-related injuries to employees are exactly what RIDDOR covers; local reporting is needed in addition to, not instead of, the RIDDOR report.
n.3: The over-7-day rule applies to injuries that are not specified injuries; a wrist fracture is reportable whatever the length of absence.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Ben, a newly registered nurse, is asked to clean up after a patient's commode using a chlorine-releasing product he has not used before. A domestic assistant tells him the solution works better if he makes it twice as strong. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make up a stronger solution as advised, wearing gloves and an apron
Follow the COSHH assessment and data sheet for dilution and PPE
Mix the product with detergent to clean and disinfect in one step
Decant the solution into a spare spray bottle so it is easy to use
Patient Safety & Quality.w: The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 require employers to assess hazardous substances and set control measures, and employees to follow them. The product's COSHH assessment and safety data sheet state the correct dilution, ventilation and PPE (HSE, COSHH basics; Code 19).

n.0: Making the solution stronger than specified increases exposure to a hazardous substance; PPE does not make an uncontrolled concentration safe.
n.2: Mixing chlorine-releasing agents with other chemicals can release toxic gases; products are used as the COSHH assessment directs.
n.3: Decanting into an unlabelled or wrongly labelled container breaks the controls and leaves others unaware of the hazard.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Edith Morris, 81, is admitted to a medical ward with a chest infection. A colleague suggests completing a falls risk prediction score first and arranging a falls assessment if she scores as high risk. According to NICE NG249 (2025), what is the most appropriate approach?
o: Arrange a falls assessment if the prediction score places her in the high-risk band
Offer her a comprehensive falls assessment because she is a hospital inpatient aged 65 or over
Repeat the prediction score daily and refer her to the falls team if the score rises
Arrange a falls assessment if she reports a fall within the 12 months before admission
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NICE NG249 Falls: assessment and prevention (April 2025) advises not to use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling, and to offer all hospital inpatients aged 65 and over (or 50-64 at higher risk) a comprehensive falls assessment and management.

n.0: NG249 advises against using falls risk prediction tools to decide who is at risk; inpatients aged 65 or over are offered assessment whatever a score shows.
n.2: Repeating a prediction tool does not make it valid for this purpose; the assessment and interventions are what reduce falls.
n.3: A fall in the previous year is a community trigger in NG249; for inpatients aged 65 or over the assessment is offered without that history.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Joseph Adeyemi, 72, was assessed as low risk of pressure ulcers on admission. Two days later he develops sepsis, becomes drowsy and can no longer reposition himself in bed. What is the most appropriate action for his named nurse?
o: Ask the tissue viability nurse to assess his risk before any change
Wait for the weekly scheduled review before changing his care plan
Reassess his pressure ulcer risk now and update his prevention plan
Keep the admission assessment, as risk is assessed once on admission
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NICE CG179 Pressure ulcers advises assessing risk on admission and reassessing when there is a change in clinical status, using clinical judgement supported by a validated scale. Loss of the ability to reposition is a major new risk factor, so prevention must be updated now (P6.5 contemporary risk tools).

n.0: The registered nurse is competent to reassess and start prevention; specialist referral may follow but should not delay basic prevention.
n.1: Waiting for a routine review leaves a high-risk patient without updated prevention for days.
n.3: Risk assessment is not a one-off; CG179 requires reassessment when clinical status changes.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Frank Ellis, 74, uses a walking frame and fell once at home last month. He has capacity and wants to walk to the day room for lunch. His daughter asks the nurse to keep him in his chair so he cannot fall again. Which response best reflects positive risk management?
o: Let Mr Ellis walk to the day room after he signs a disclaimer accepting the risk of falling
Arrange for him to use a wheelchair to reach the day room until physiotherapy can review him
Agree with the daughter and keep him seated at lunchtimes until he is discharged home
Agree a plan with Mr Ellis for supervised walking with his frame and record the discussion
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Positive risk management weighs benefits and harms with the person and puts proportionate controls in place so they can do what matters to them, rather than removing all activity (P6.10 risk management versus risk aversion). Mr Ellis has capacity, so his decision is respected (MCA 2005 s1), and the plan and discussion are documented (Code 10).

n.0: A disclaimer does not manage the risk or remove the nurse's duty of care; it replaces planning with paperwork.
n.1: Using a wheelchair when he can walk with his frame reduces independence and mobility without a clinical reason.
n.2: Keeping him seated is risk aversion: it removes activity he values, causes deconditioning and overrides the choice of a person with capacity.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: While walking to the nurses' station, Chloe, a staff nurse, notices a large pool of spilled water on the corridor floor outside a bay where several patients walk with frames. Nobody else is nearby. What should Chloe do first?
o: Complete an incident report so the hazard is recorded for the ward manager
Ask the domestic team to mop the floor when they reach the ward this afternoon
Make the area safe straight away with a warning sign and arrange for it to be dried
Tell the patients in the bay at the next ward round to avoid that corridor
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 require nurses to act promptly on hazards, and s7 Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires reasonable care for others. Removing an immediate slip hazard comes first; reporting follows (P6.6 respond to potential hazards).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate but should follow making the area safe; the hazard remains while the form is completed.
n.1: Leaving a known slip hazard until the afternoon exposes patients with frames to falls.
n.3: Warning patients later does not remove the hazard now and relies on people remembering.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: For three weeks the call bells in one bay on Kemi's ward have failed intermittently. Each failure has been reported as an incident, but estates staff say a full replacement needs trust funding. What is the most appropriate next step for Kemi as the nurse in charge?
o: Move patients who cannot use a call bell to beds nearer the nurses' station each shift
Keep reporting each failure as an incident until the estates team replaces the system
Write to the local newspaper about the delay to replacing the call bell system
Escalate to the ward manager so the risk can be assessed and added to the risk register
Patient Safety & Quality.w: A persistent risk that cannot be fixed at ward level should be escalated so it is formally assessed, recorded on the organisation's risk register with an owner and controls, and reviewed (P6.3 local and national frameworks for managing and reporting risk; Code 16.1 and 25.1). Interim measures continue alongside escalation.

n.0: Moving patients is a sensible interim control but does not get the underlying risk managed or funded.
n.1: Incident reports record events; they do not on their own place a known, ongoing risk under managed review with an owner.
n.2: Going to the media before using internal escalation routes is not consistent with NMC raising concerns guidance.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Leah, 34, attends the emergency department after self-harm. A colleague completes a self-harm risk scale, which places her at low risk, and suggests she can be discharged on that basis. According to NICE NG225, what should happen?
o: Assess Leah's needs and agree a safety plan with her, not using the scale
Repeat the scale in four hours and discharge Leah if it is unchanged
Discharge Leah, as the scale places her in the low-risk group
Admit Leah for observation until a medium-risk score can be ruled out
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NICE NG225 (2022) advises not to use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged. Care is based on a psychosocial assessment of needs and a safety plan developed with the person.

n.1: Repeating an invalid tool does not make it a valid basis for discharge.
n.2: NG225 says scales must not be used to decide discharge; a low score gives false reassurance.
n.3: NG225 advises against global low, medium or high risk stratification; admission is decided by assessed needs, not a score band.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Marcus Bell, 66, is on a surgical ward. His observations are: respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on air, BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 84/min, alert, temperature 37.2°C. His NEWS2 total is 3. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Increase observations to at least hourly and inform the medical team
Repeat the observations in 4 hours and escalate if the total rises
Continue 4 to 6 hourly observations as the total score is below 5
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
Patient Safety & Quality.w: A respiratory rate of 26/min scores 3 in a single parameter (NEWS2, RCP 2017, Chart 1). A score of 3 in any one parameter triggers a low-medium clinical risk response: minimum 1-hourly observations and the registered nurse informs the medical team, who decide whether escalation is needed (Chart 4). Two steps: calculate the parameter score, then apply the single-parameter rule.

n.1: Four-hourly review delays recognition of deterioration when a single parameter is already scoring 3.
n.2: The aggregate of 3 is low, but a single red score of 3 overrides this and requires at least hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.3: Emergency critical care assessment is the response to an aggregate of 7 or more; this is an urgent ward-based response.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Asif, a staff nurse, is explaining risk to a group of student nurses. Which statement best describes the difference between risk management and risk aversion?
o: Risk management weighs harms and benefits with the person; risk aversion avoids any activity with risk
Risk management is the manager's task; risk aversion is the approach expected of each nurse
Risk management is completed on admission; risk aversion is used once a person has been harmed
Risk management removes every activity that could cause harm; risk aversion accepts all risk
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Risk management identifies hazards, weighs harms against benefits with the person and puts in proportionate controls so that valued activity can continue. Risk aversion avoids activity to prevent any chance of harm, often at the cost of independence and wellbeing (P6.10). Positive risk-taking is part of person-centred care.

n.1: Every registrant manages risk (Code 16, 19 and 25.1); risk management is not confined to managers.
n.2: Risk management is continuous and is reviewed when circumstances change, not a single admission task.
n.3: This describes avoiding harm at all costs, which is risk aversion, and misdescribes risk aversion as accepting all risk.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Hannah, a staff nurse, is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Derek Lowe, 58. At the bedside he tells her he is allergic to penicillin. His allergy band was missing and the chart says 'no known allergies'. No dose was given. What should Hannah do about reporting?
o: Report herself to the NMC, as she nearly gave a contraindicated drug
Record it as a near miss on the trust's patient safety reporting system
Tell the ward manager verbally, as no harm reached the patient
Correct the chart and allergy band, as no report is needed without harm
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Near misses are patient safety events and must be recorded so the system can learn, whether or not harm occurred (P6.8; Code 14 and NMC/GMC candour guidance 2024, which covers reporting near misses). Local systems feed the national Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service. The chart and band must also be corrected and the prescriber informed.

n.0: Self-referral to the regulator is not the response to a near miss caught by correct checks; this is a system issue for local reporting.
n.2: Verbal reporting alone loses the learning; near misses are formally recorded on the local system.
n.3: Correcting the records is needed, but near misses are reported because they reveal weaknesses before harm occurs.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Owen, a staff nurse, realises he gave Ruth Price, 76, 10 mg of morphine instead of the prescribed 2.5 mg. She becomes drowsy with a respiratory rate of 9/min. The doctor has reviewed her and naloxone has been given. Which action best meets Owen's professional duty of candour?
o: Tell Mrs Price's daughter what happened and leave her to explain it to her mother
Ask the doctor to decide whether Mrs Price needs to be told about the overdose
Wait until the incident review is complete before telling Mrs Price what happened
Tell Mrs Price promptly what happened, apologise, and explain what is being done
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Code 14.1-14.3 and the NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (2024): when something goes wrong, tell the person (or their advocate) promptly, apologise, explain what happened and the likely effects, put matters right where possible, and record and report the incident (P1.3).

n.0: Mrs Price is the person affected; information goes to her unless she lacks capacity or asks for it to be shared.
n.1: The professional duty of candour belongs to each registrant; Owen cannot pass the decision to another clinician.
n.2: Candour is prompt; waiting for a review delays information the person is entitled to now.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A ward manager is introducing the Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF) to her team. Which of the following is one of PSIRF's four stated aims?
o: Identifying the member of staff responsible for each incident
Reporting every patient safety incident directly to the regulator
A root cause analysis for every incident within a fixed timescale
Compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected
Patient Safety & Quality.w: PSIRF (NHS England 2022, replacing the Serious Incident Framework 2015) has four aims: compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected; system-based approaches to learning; considered and proportionate responses; and supportive oversight focused on strengthening the response system (S-PSIRF).

n.0: PSIRF focuses on how incidents happen and contributory system factors, not on attributing individual blame.
n.1: PSIRF is a framework for provider learning responses; it does not require every incident to go to a regulator.
n.2: Fixed-timescale investigation of set categories was a feature of the Serious Incident Framework; PSIRF calls for proportionate, planned responses.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A newly qualified nurse asks which national NHS service now receives the patient safety events that staff record through the trust's local reporting system in England. What is the correct answer?
o: The National Reporting and Learning System (NRLS)
The Strategic Executive Information System (StEIS)
The Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service
The MHRA Yellow Card scheme
Patient Safety & Quality.w: LFPSE is the national NHS system for recording and analysing patient safety events. It replaced the NRLS, which was decommissioned on 30 June 2024; organisations record through LFPSE-compliant local systems (NHS England, LFPSE).

n.0: The NRLS was decommissioned on 30 June 2024 and replaced by LFPSE.
n.1: StEIS remains in use for specific serious incident reporting while LFPSE develops; it is not where routine safety events are recorded.
n.3: Yellow Card is the MHRA scheme for suspected adverse drug reactions and device problems, not the general patient safety event system.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: During a patient safety study day, a nurse asks what makes an incident a Never Event rather than another serious incident. Which statement is correct?
o: It is any incident that causes harm lasting 28 days or more to a patient
It is wholly preventable because national barriers should be in place
It is any incident that a coroner later finds was caused by staff error
It is any incident in which a patient dies as a direct result of their care
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NHS England's Never Events policy and framework (2018, list updated 2021) defines Never Events as patient safety incidents that are wholly preventable because guidance or safety recommendations providing strong systemic protective barriers are available nationally and should have been implemented by all providers. They are recorded on LFPSE with a learning response under PSIRF.

n.0: Twenty-eight days is the duration used for prolonged pain or psychological harm in the statutory candour definitions, not the Never Event test.
n.2: A coroner's finding does not define the category; it is defined by the national barriers that should have prevented it.
n.3: Death is not the defining feature; a Never Event may cause no harm, and many deaths are not Never Events.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: The son of Betty Walsh, 88, approaches Daniel, the nurse in charge, upset that his mother waited over an hour for pain relief this morning. He says he wants to complain. What is the most appropriate response from Daniel?
o: Ask him to put the complaint in writing before discussing it any further
Listen, apologise for the wait, check her pain now and explain how to complain
Explain that the ward was short-staffed, so the delay was nobody's fault
Move Mrs Walsh to another bay so that the complaint does not affect her care
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Code 24.1-24.2: never let a complaint affect the care provided, and use complaints as a form of feedback to reflect and improve. Listening, apologising, dealing with the immediate need and explaining the complaints process is a compassionate, open response (Code 14; P6.9).

n.0: Complaints can be made verbally; insisting on writing first is obstructive and delays resolution.
n.2: Explaining causes can follow, but opening with a defence dismisses his concern and does not address his mother's pain now.
n.3: Moving her does not address the complaint or her pain and may itself disrupt her care.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: After Ivan Novak, 79, fell and fractured his hip on a medical ward, the trust begins a learning response under PSIRF. His wife asks whether she can contribute her account of the evening and ask questions. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Advise her to wait for the final report and then decide whether to make a complaint
Explain that incident reviews are internal and that she will receive a summary letter
Welcome her involvement and arrange for her account and questions to inform the review
Ask her to raise her concerns through the Patient Advice and Liaison Service instead
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected is one of PSIRF's four aims; families are invited to share their account and questions so the learning response reflects their perspective (NHS England PSIRF, Engaging and involving patients, families and staff). This applies P6.9, working with people and families on improvement.

n.0: Delaying her involvement until the report is final excludes her perspective from the learning.
n.1: PSIRF expects meaningful involvement of those affected, not a summary sent after the event.
n.3: PALS can support families, but it does not replace involving her directly in the learning response.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Patience Okoro, 61, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab is left in her abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital in England. Under regulation 20 (statutory duty of candour), what must the provider do?
o: Notify her in person as soon as reasonably practicable, with an apology
Send her a written notification within 28 days of the incident
Notify her if she asks the surgical team whether anything went wrong
Notify her in writing once the incident investigation is completed
Patient Safety & Quality.w: An unplanned return to surgery is moderate harm, so this is a notifiable safety incident. Regulation 20 (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014) requires notification in person as soon as reasonably practicable, including an apology, followed by a written notification, with records kept. Two steps: classify the harm, then apply the duty.

n.1: Regulation 20 requires notification as soon as reasonably practicable and in person first; 28 days is the duration test for prolonged pain or psychological harm.
n.2: Candour is proactive; the provider must notify without waiting to be asked.
n.3: The duty is not deferred until an investigation ends; further information is shared as enquiries progress.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Nurses on a surgical ward want to check whether pain scores are reassessed within 30 minutes of giving analgesia, as their trust policy requires. They plan to review 40 recent patient records against this requirement. What type of activity is this?
o: Service evaluation, because it describes current care with no standard
Research, because it collects data from patient records
A PDSA cycle, because it tests a change to practice on a small scale
Clinical audit, because it measures care against a set standard
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Clinical audit is a quality improvement cycle that measures the effectiveness of care against agreed standards and acts to bring practice in line with them (HQIP definition). Here an existing policy standard is being measured, so it is audit (P6.4, P6.7).

n.0: Service evaluation describes current care without reference to a standard; this project has a defined standard.
n.1: Research generates new knowledge, for example by testing a hypothesis; reviewing records against an existing standard is not research.
n.2: A PDSA cycle tests a change; no change is being tested here, only current practice measured.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: An audit on Ward 6 found that only 58% of patients had a fully completed fluid balance chart against a standard of 95%. The team then held teaching sessions and introduced a simpler chart. What is the next step that completes the audit cycle?
o: Lower the standard to a level the ward can meet
Re-audit practice against the same 95% standard
Start a new audit on a different topic for the ward
Publish the original results in a nursing journal
Patient Safety & Quality.w: The audit cycle is: agree the standard, measure practice, compare, implement change, then re-audit to check whether the change has improved and sustained practice (HQIP Best Practice in Clinical Audit). Re-measurement against the same standard closes the loop (P6.7).

n.0: Standards are set from evidence and policy, not lowered to match current performance.
n.2: Moving on without re-auditing leaves the cycle incomplete and the change unevaluated.
n.3: Sharing findings can be useful, but publication does not show whether the changes worked.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A ward team wants to reduce the number of missed doses of time-critical medicines. Using the Model for Improvement, which question should they answer first?
o: Who was responsible for the missed doses last month?
What change can we make that will result in improvement?
What are we trying to accomplish?
How will we know that a change is an improvement?
Patient Safety & Quality.w: The Model for Improvement (used in NHS England improvement resources) asks three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? (the aim); How will we know that a change is an improvement? (measures); What change can we make that will result in improvement? (change ideas). Changes are then tested with PDSA cycles. Setting the aim comes first (P6.4).

n.0: Improvement methods look at system causes rather than individual blame, and this is not one of the model's questions.
n.1: Change ideas are the third question, chosen once the aim and measures are agreed.
n.3: Measures are the second question; they depend on a clear aim.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Lauren is leading a test of a new structured handover sheet on one night shift. The test has finished and she is now comparing the number of omitted items with what the team predicted. Which stage of the PDSA cycle is this?
o: Plan
Act
Do
Study
Patient Safety & Quality.w: In Plan, Do, Study, Act (PDSA), Plan sets the objective and predictions, Do carries out the test and collects data, Study analyses the results and compares them with predictions, and Act decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change (NHS England PDSA guidance; P6.4).

n.0: Plan is where the objective, prediction and data collection are agreed before the test.
n.1: Act follows Study and decides what to do next with the change.
n.2: Do is the stage of carrying out the test and recording data and observations.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A ward manager has designed a new bedside safety checklist and wants every ward in the hospital to start using it next Monday. Arjun, the ward's quality improvement lead, is asked for advice. Which approach best reflects improvement methodology?
o: Pilot it on one ward for a year before deciding whether to use it more widely
Introduce it on all wards on Monday and audit compliance in six months
Test it with a few patients on one ward, measure, adapt and then scale up
Ask each ward manager to decide whether to adopt the checklist locally
Patient Safety & Quality.w: The Model for Improvement uses rapid, small-scale PDSA cycles: test a change with a few patients or one shift, measure the effect, adapt, and build up to wider implementation once it works. This limits risk and builds learning and ownership (NHS England improvement guidance; P6.4, P6.6).

n.0: A single year-long pilot is slow; PDSA relies on short, repeated cycles that allow rapid adaptation.
n.1: Hospital-wide launch without testing risks spreading an untested change, and a six-month delay in measurement slows learning.
n.3: Leaving adoption to individual choice produces inconsistent practice without any evidence that the checklist works.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A community nursing team wants to improve the written information given to people after a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Which approach best involves people who use the service in this improvement?
o: Adapt a leaflet that a neighbouring trust has used for several years
Co-design the information with people who have recently been diagnosed
Ask the diabetes consultant to approve the content before it is printed
Ask the team's nurses to agree the content at the next team meeting
Patient Safety & Quality.w: P6.9 requires nurses to work with people, their families and colleagues to develop improvement strategies. Co-design with people who have lived experience of the service makes information relevant, accessible and person-centred (Code 2.1 work in partnership).

n.0: Borrowing another organisation's leaflet may help, but it does not involve local service users in the improvement.
n.2: Clinical approval checks accuracy but does not involve people who use the service.
n.3: Staff agreement alone excludes the people the information is for.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation attempt on a medical ward, Sofia, the nurse in charge, arranges a short team debrief once the immediate tasks are complete. What is the main purpose of this debrief?
o: Identify which member of staff made an error so that it can be dealt with formally
Reflect together on what went well and what could improve, and support staff
Complete the incident report and the statutory notification to the regulator
Decide as a team what information the family should and should not be given
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Team reflection and debriefing support staff wellbeing and turn experience into learning for future practice (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; Code 8 work cooperatively; human factors and just culture principles).

n.0: A debrief is a supportive learning discussion, not a disciplinary process; a blame focus discourages openness.
n.2: Reporting is a separate governance step and is not the purpose of a team debrief.
n.3: Communication with the family is guided by candour and the person's wishes, not by a team agreement to withhold information.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A ward is running an improvement project to discharge more patients before midday. The team is already measuring the percentage of discharges before 12:00. Which additional measure would act as a balancing measure?
o: Number of patients discharged before 12:00 each day
Average time that discharge letters are completed
Number of take-home prescriptions ready the evening before
Readmission rate within 30 days of discharge
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Balancing measures check whether improving one part of a system causes problems elsewhere. Rushing discharges could increase readmissions, so 30-day readmission is a balancing measure. The other options are outcome or process measures for the same aim (Model for Improvement measures: outcome, process, balancing; P6.4, P6.7). Two steps: classify each measure, then identify the one that detects unintended harm.

n.0: This is the outcome measure itself, restated as a count.
n.1: Discharge letter timing is a process measure that supports the aim, not a check for unintended harm.
n.2: Prescriptions ready in advance is a process measure on the route to earlier discharge.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Code standard 19.2 asks nurses to take account of current evidence and knowledge about human factors. During preceptorship, Jade is asked which definition of human factors the Code refers to. Which is correct?
o: The physical and mental health conditions that may affect a registrant's fitness to practise safely
The personal values and beliefs that staff bring to their work and that can influence patient care
The study of individual mistakes so that staff responsible for errors can be identified and retrained
Environmental, organisational and job factors, and individual characteristics that affect behaviour at work
Patient Safety & Quality.w: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors refer to environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety (P5.2).

n.0: Health and fitness to practise is covered by Code 20.9 and NMC processes, not by the definition of human factors.
n.1: Personal beliefs are addressed by Code 20.7; the human factors definition is wider and centres on work systems.
n.2: Human factors looks at how systems shape performance, not at singling out individuals for blame or retraining.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A medical ward has had four medicine administration errors in a month. Review shows each occurred while the nurse was interrupted during the drug round by phone calls and queries. Which change is most likely to reduce these errors?
o: Move the main drug round to later in the evening when it is quieter
Ask each nurse involved to complete a medicines calculation test
Ask a second registered nurse to check every oral medicine given
Introduce protected drug round time with a visible do not disturb signal
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Interruptions and distraction are recognised human factors that increase error. Designing the system to reduce interruptions, for example protected time and visible signals, targets the identified cause (Code 19.2; P6.6 respond to potential hazards; P5.2).

n.0: Moving the round alters clinically timed doses and does not tackle interruptions directly.
n.1: The review identified interruptions, not calculation skills, as the contributing factor; individual testing does not change the system.
n.2: Routine double-checking of all oral medicines uses scarce staff time and still leaves both nurses exposed to the same interruptions.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Martina, a staff nurse, has just finished three consecutive 12-hour night shifts and feels exhausted. The ward manager phones asking her to work an extra day shift starting in four hours because of sickness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the shift and ask a colleague to second-check her medicines
Accept a shorter shift and leave as soon as cover can be found
Accept the shift and plan to rest during her break in the afternoon
Decline the shift, explaining that fatigue would make her practice unsafe
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Fatigue is a key human factor that impairs judgement and increases error. Code 20.9 requires registrants to maintain the level of health needed to carry out their role, and Code 19.1 requires them to take measures to reduce mistakes. Martina should explain the safety risk so the manager can seek other cover (P5.2).

n.0: A second check does not make an exhausted nurse safe across all her tasks on a full shift.
n.1: Working even part of the shift while exhausted creates the same risk, and the time cover arrives is uncertain.
n.2: A short break does not offset the fatigue from three night shifts; she would still start the shift unsafe.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: In theatre, Callum, a newly registered scrub nurse, sees the surgeon pick up the scalpel before the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist time out has been done. The team seems not to have noticed. What should Callum do?
o: Complete an incident report after the operation so the omission is recorded
Note the omission and raise it at the team debrief at the end of the list
Quietly tell the anaesthetist so that the surgeon is not challenged openly
Say clearly that the time out has not been done and ask the team to pause
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 (preserve safety) require nurses to intervene. Checklists work only if anyone can stop the process; speaking up clearly and directly at the moment of risk is the safest action, whatever the speaker's seniority (P6.6; P5.2).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate later, but the immediate risk must be addressed before the incision.
n.1: Raising it afterwards allows the operation to proceed without the safety check that prevents wrong site and wrong patient surgery.
n.2: An indirect approach delays action and may not stop the procedure in time.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Nadia, a staff nurse, reports that she gave an evening dose of a medicine to the wrong patient after two patients with similar names were moved into adjacent beds. The patient is unharmed. Which response from the ward manager best reflects a just culture?
o: Remove Nadia from medicine rounds until she has completed a formal assessment
Ask Nadia to apologise to the team for the extra work the incident has created
Record a formal warning on Nadia's file because she did not check identity
Thank Nadia for reporting, support her and review the system factors involved
Patient Safety & Quality.w: A just culture treats honest error as an opportunity to learn, supports the person involved and looks at system contributors (here, similar names placed side by side). This encourages reporting, which PSIRF and Code 14 and 16 depend on (P5.2; P6.6). Reckless conduct is handled differently.

n.0: Removing her from duties for an honest error with clear system causes discourages reporting; support and reflection are more proportionate.
n.1: Asking her to apologise to colleagues shames her and adds nothing to learning.
n.2: Formal sanctions for unintentional error undermine reporting and ignore the system factors.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Agnes, the nurse in charge of a busy surgical ward, wants the whole team to share the same understanding of which patients are at risk at the start of each shift. Which practice best supports this?
o: Each nurse reads the full medical notes of all patients before starting
Staff ask the nurse in charge about any patient they are worried about
A brief safety huddle after handover to share key risks and plans
The nurse in charge keeps a written list of risks in the ward office
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Shared situational awareness, the team's common understanding of what is happening and what may happen next, is supported by short structured safety huddles where risks (deteriorating patients, falls, staffing) are discussed and actions agreed (human factors; P5.2; P6.6).

n.0: Reading all notes is impractical on a busy ward and does not create a shared team picture or agreed actions.
n.1: Relying on individuals to ask means risks are shared reactively and unevenly.
n.3: A list kept by one person does not share awareness across the team.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Aisha, a staff nurse in an NHS trust in England, raised concerns with her ward manager about unsafe practice on night shifts. Two weeks later nothing has changed and she feels her concerns were dismissed. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Raise the concern with the trust's Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
Post an anonymised account of the problem on a nursing social media group
Contact the National Guardian's Office to request an independent review
Report the ward manager to the NMC for failing to act on the concern
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance sets stages: line manager, then a designated person in the organisation, then a higher level, then a regulator. Local Freedom to Speak Up Guardians remain in place to support staff. The National Guardian's Office closed on 30 June 2026, with some functions moving to NHS England (FACTS S-RC, S-NGO).

n.1: Social media is not a route for raising concerns and risks breaching confidentiality (NMC social media guidance).
n.2: The National Guardian's Office closed on 30 June 2026 and does not review individual cases.
n.3: A referral to the regulator is not the next step when internal routes such as the FTSU Guardian have not been used.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: George Hall, 80, has a NEWS2 score of 1. His nurse, Precious, feels uneasy: he is quieter than usual and has not eaten, though nothing specific is abnormal. She is unsure whether to act on this feeling. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase his observations and discuss her concern with the medical team
Ask the healthcare assistant to repeat the observations at the next round
Record her impression and continue observations at the planned frequency
Wait until his score reaches 5 so that escalation is clearly justified
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NEWS2 supports, and does not replace, clinical judgement (RCP 2017; NICE NG253). For scores of 1-4 the registered nurse decides on monitoring frequency and escalation. Acting on clinical concern under uncertainty, by increasing monitoring and escalating, is safe practice (P6.11 accept and manage uncertainty; Code 13.3 ask for help).

n.1: Repeating routine observations later does not address her clinical concern now.
n.2: Recording a concern without acting on it leaves a possible deterioration unaddressed.
n.3: Waiting for a threshold ignores the nurse's assessment and may delay recognition of deterioration.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: During a late shift on an adult surgical ward, a healthcare assistant tells Ruby, the nurse in charge, that Mr Peter Grant, 70, asked for analgesia 45 minutes ago and has still not received it because both nurses in his bay are busy. What should Ruby do?
o: Complete an incident report at the end of the shift and continue with the current allocation
Record the delay in Mr Grant's notes and discuss the bay workload at the next team meeting
Arrange for Mr Grant's analgesia to be given now and escalate the red flag on staffing
Ask the healthcare assistant to tell Mr Grant that a nurse will come once the bay is quieter
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NICE SG1 Safe staffing for nursing in adult inpatient wards (2014) lists a delay of more than 30 minutes in providing pain relief as a nursing red flag. A red flag should prompt an immediate escalation response by the registered nurse in charge, for example allocating additional staff (rec 1.4.3, Box 2). Mr Grant's pain is dealt with first.

n.0: Reporting is useful but does not relieve his pain or address the staffing problem now.
n.1: Documenting and deferring discussion does not meet the immediate escalation response that SG1 requires.
n.3: This prolongs his pain and treats a recognised red flag as routine.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: On a medical ward the early shift requires 40 hours of registered nurse time. Because of sickness, 30 hours of registered nurse time is available. Two registered nurses are on duty. According to NICE SG1, is this a nursing red flag event?
