o: Yes, because any shortfall in registered nurse time is a red flag
No, because the shortfall is exactly 25% and not more than 25%
Yes, because the 10-hour shortfall is more than 8 hours
No, because two registered nurses are present on the ward
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NICE SG1 Box 2: a red flag is a shortfall of more than 8 hours or 25% of registered nurse time, whichever is reached first, compared with the requirement for the shift. Working: shortfall = 40 - 30 = 10 hours. 10 hours is more than 8 hours, so the red flag is triggered even though 10/40 is exactly 25% (SG1 gives 40 hours with under 32 available as its example).

n.0: SG1 sets thresholds; a shortfall below 8 hours and 25% is not itself a red flag.
n.1: The 8-hour limit is reached first; 'whichever is reached first' means the 25% figure does not need to be exceeded.
n.3: Having at least two registered nurses avoids a different red flag; it does not cancel the shortfall red flag.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: At 21:00 Yusuf arrives to take charge of a 24-bed ward for the night. One registered nurse has phoned in sick and no replacement has been found, leaving Yusuf as the only registered nurse with three healthcare assistants. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the shift and complete an incident report at the end of the night describing it
Start the shift and allocate the medicines round to the most senior healthcare assistant
Escalate immediately to the site manager, as fewer than two registered nurses is a red flag
Ask the day staff to stay until midnight and then manage the remainder of the shift himself
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NICE SG1 Box 2 lists fewer than 2 registered nurses present on a ward during any shift as a nursing red flag, which requires an immediate escalation response. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt action on risks to safety and effective management of staff and resources.

n.0: Reporting after the shift leaves the risk unmanaged throughout the night.
n.1: Healthcare assistants cannot be delegated tasks outside their competence, such as a full registered nurse medicines round (Code 11.1).
n.3: A short extension by tired day staff does not solve the shortfall for most of the night and bypasses escalation.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Wendy, a registered nurse on a general medical ward, is told to care for a patient receiving non-invasive ventilation who has been moved from the respiratory unit. She has had no training in non-invasive ventilation. What should Wendy do?
o: Decline to be on the ward until a nurse with the right training is found
Accept the patient and ask the respiratory team for help if problems arise
Tell the nurse in charge she lacks the competence and escalate the concern now
Accept the patient after reading the trust's policy on non-invasive ventilation
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Code 13: recognise and work within the limits of your competence, and (13.3) ask for help from a suitably qualified professional for anything beyond it. Code 16.2: raise concerns immediately if asked to provide care outside your scope. Skill mix is part of safe staffing (P6.2); the gap must be escalated so a competent nurse or support is provided.

n.0: Leaving the ward abandons her other patients; the right response is to raise and escalate the concern while continuing other care.
n.1: Accepting care she cannot provide safely puts the patient at risk until something goes wrong.
n.3: Reading a policy does not provide the training and competence needed for this care.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A ward manager is reviewing staffing on an acute adult medical ward. Which statement about nurse-to-patient ratios reflects NICE SG1 (2014)?
o: A ratio of one registered nurse to six patients applies on all wards, day and night
A ratio of one registered nurse to eight patients is a legal minimum in England
There is no single ratio, but over 8 patients per nurse by day is linked to harm
Staffing ratios for adult wards are set by the NMC for each type of hospital ward
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NICE SG1 rec 1.5.3: there is no single nursing staff-to-patient ratio for all acute adult wards, but there is evidence of increased risk of harm when a registered nurse cares for more than 8 patients on day shifts, which should prompt close monitoring of red flags and safe nursing indicators.

n.0: SG1 does not set a 1:6 ratio; it uses patients' nursing needs and professional judgement.
n.1: The 1:8 figure is an evidence threshold for monitoring, not a legal minimum in England.
n.3: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not set ward staffing ratios.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A registered nurse on a surgical ward calls in sick. The bed manager suggests replacing her with an extra healthcare assistant because the total number of staff on shift would stay the same. Six patients on the ward have intravenous antibiotics due. What is the best response from the nurse in charge?
o: Accept the healthcare assistant, as total staff numbers meet the ward's planned establishment
Ask the healthcare assistant to give the IV antibiotics under her direct supervision
Accept the healthcare assistant and give all six patients' IV antibiotics herself
Explain that registered nurse tasks cannot be covered and escalate the skill mix gap
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Safety depends on skill mix as well as numbers (P6.2; NICE SG1 Box 1 takes skill mix into account). Registered nurse tasks such as IV medicines and assessment cannot be delegated to a healthcare assistant (Code 11.1), so the gap must be escalated.

n.0: Matching headcount ignores the registered nurse time that patients' needs require.
n.1: IV antibiotic administration is outside a healthcare assistant's role; supervision does not make delegation appropriate.
n.2: Taking on extra IV work on top of her own role risks delayed doses elsewhere and hides the shortfall.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Elif, a ward manager, is preparing a business case for an additional registered nurse on night shifts. Which evidence would most strengthen her case?
o: Comments from staff that the ward has felt busier over recent months
The staffing levels of a similar ward in a neighbouring hospital trust
Red flag reports, acuity data and safe nursing indicators, linked to costs
The number of complaints she has personally received about night care
Patient Safety & Quality.w: A basic business case sets out the problem with objective evidence, the options and their costs and benefits (P7.12 develop a basic business case using finance, resources and safe staffing). NICE SG1 recommends recording red flag events and safe nursing indicators so they can inform establishment reviews.

n.0: Staff impressions are useful context but are subjective and not linked to patient need or cost.
n.1: Another ward's staffing does not show this ward's patients' needs.
n.3: Complaint numbers are a partial measure and do not demonstrate the staffing requirement or its cost.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A charge nurse asks what a basic business case for funding two additional healthcare assistant posts should contain. Which content is most appropriate?
o: Last year's off-duty rotas to show how often extra shifts were filled
A list of the staff who support the request, with their signatures
The problem, the options considered, their costs and the expected benefits
Details of recent incidents including the patients' names and dates of birth
Patient Safety & Quality.w: A business case explains why change is needed, the options (including doing nothing), costs, expected benefits to patients and the organisation, and how success will be measured (P7.12). Evidence should be anonymised to protect confidentiality (Code 5).

n.0: Past rotas may support part of the argument but are not the core content of a business case.
n.1: Support from colleagues does not show need, cost or benefit.
n.3: Identifiable patient information is not needed and would breach confidentiality; anonymised data should be used.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A train derails near a town and the local acute trust is told to expect over 40 casualties, more than the emergency department can manage with normal arrangements. Under NHS emergency preparedness guidance, how is this event best classified?
o: A business continuity incident
A serious incident
A major incident
A critical incident
Patient Safety & Quality.w: NHS England EPRR guidance classes incidents as business continuity, critical or major. A major incident is an event with serious consequences that requires special arrangements by one or more emergency responder agencies; in the NHS this includes casualties in numbers or types that require special arrangements (JESIP/Cabinet Office definition used by NHS England; P6.12).

n.0: A business continuity incident disrupts an organisation's normal service delivery, for example an IT failure; it is not defined by a surge of casualties needing a multi-agency response.
n.1: 'Serious incident' was a patient safety category under the former Serious Incident Framework, not an emergency preparedness classification.
n.3: A critical incident is a localised, principally internal escalation where an organisation loses the ability to deliver critical services; an external mass casualty event needing multi-agency arrangements is a major incident.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool (MITT), Lucy is triaging casualties after an explosion at a shopping centre. A man with cuts to his face and arms is walking around asking for help, with no catastrophic bleeding. Which category should she assign?
o: P2
P3
P1
Dead
Patient Safety & Quality.w: MITT (NHS England 2023) first checks for catastrophic bleeding (P1); if absent, anyone who is walking is categorised P3 (minor) before further physiological assessment (P6.12).

n.0: P2 is reached after the walking, breathing, voice and respiratory rate steps in a casualty who cannot walk.
n.2: P1 is for catastrophic bleeding or abnormal findings later in the algorithm; a walking casualty without catastrophic bleeding is not P1.
n.3: The man is walking and talking; 'dead' applies to a casualty who does not breathe after the airway is opened.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: At a major incident, Daniel reaches a young woman lying on the ground with a lower leg wound that is spurting blood. She is conscious. Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool, what should he do?
o: Categorise her as P2 because she is conscious and breathing
Ask her to walk to the casualty clearing area for assessment
Apply pressure or a tourniquet and categorise her as P1
Assess her breathing rate first and then decide her triage category
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Catastrophic bleeding is the first step in MITT (NHS England 2023): control it with pressure, a tourniquet or haemostatic packing and categorise the casualty as P1 (P6.12).

n.0: Being conscious does not lower the priority of catastrophic bleeding, which makes the casualty P1.
n.1: Walking her would worsen the bleeding and delay life-saving control.
n.3: Catastrophic bleeding is assessed and controlled before breathing in MITT; delaying control risks death from haemorrhage.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Before the ambulance service arrives, off-duty nurse Imran stops at a multi-vehicle collision on a dual carriageway. Traffic is still moving past and one car is leaking fuel. Several people appear injured. What should Imran do first?
o: Start assessing the nearest injured person in the car that is leaking fuel
Check that the scene is safe, then call 999 and describe the incident clearly
Move all the injured people away from the vehicles to the hard shoulder
Leave the scene, as he is off duty and is not covered by trust indemnity
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Code 15.1-15.3: offer help in an emergency within the limits of your knowledge and competence, taking account of your own safety. Scene safety comes first, then early alert to emergency services with clear information (the M/ETHANE structure) so the right response is sent (P6.12).

n.0: Approaching a leaking vehicle beside moving traffic before assessing danger risks creating another casualty.
n.2: Moving injured people without assessment can worsen injuries and exposes Imran to traffic.
n.3: The Code expects registrants to offer help in emergencies outside work, within competence and safety.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Joanne is the first health professional at a road traffic collision and is passing information to the ambulance control room using the M/ETHANE structure. What does the 'H' in M/ETHANE stand for?
o: Hospital
Head injuries
Hazards
Help needed
Patient Safety & Quality.w: M/ETHANE (JESIP joint doctrine): Major incident declared or standby; Exact location; Type of incident; Hazards (present and potential); Access routes; Number of casualties; Emergency services present and required (P6.12).

n.0: The receiving hospital is decided by the ambulance service; it is not an M/ETHANE heading.
n.1: Injury types inform casualty numbers and severity but are not the 'H' heading.
n.3: Resources needed are reported under 'Emergency services', not 'H'.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A major incident is declared at Sophie's hospital after a factory fire. Sophie is the nurse in charge of a medical ward. The ward's major incident action card is in the office. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Follow the action card, for example by identifying patients fit for discharge
Phone off-duty colleagues personally and ask them to come in to work
Carry on with routine ward work until casualties start arriving on the ward
Send two of her nurses straight to the emergency department to help
Patient Safety & Quality.w: In a hospital major incident, staff follow their role-specific action cards and the trust's command structure. Ward nurses in charge typically help create capacity, for example by identifying patients who can safely be discharged or moved, and release staff only when the incident control team requests them (P6.12 roles at different levels of seniority).

n.1: Calling in staff is coordinated centrally through the trust's call-in procedure to avoid exhausting the workforce for later phases.
n.2: Waiting passively loses time to create the capacity the hospital will need.
n.3: Self-deploying staff disrupts the coordinated response and leaves the ward short; staff are released when requested by incident control.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: During a major incident, Amir is triaging with the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool. A man is unable to walk, has no catastrophic bleeding, is breathing and responds to voice. His respiratory rate is 32/min. Which category is correct?
o: P2, because he is breathing and responds to voice
P1, because his respiratory rate is outside 12 to 23
P3, because he has no catastrophic bleeding
Dead, because he cannot walk and is breathing fast
Patient Safety & Quality.w: MITT (NHS England 2023) steps: catastrophic bleeding (no); walking (no); breathing (yes); responds to voice (yes); respiratory rate 12-23? A rate of 32 is outside this range, so the casualty is P1. Two steps: work through the algorithm in order, then apply the respiratory rate criterion (P6.12).

n.0: Breathing and responding to voice move him on to the respiratory rate check; an abnormal rate makes him P1, not P2.
n.2: P3 is for casualties who can walk; this man cannot.
n.3: 'Dead' applies to a casualty who does not breathe after the airway is opened; this man is breathing.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Caroline, an off-duty theatre nurse, hears on the news that a major incident has been declared at her hospital after a building collapse. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make herself available and respond if the trust contacts her
Drive to the scene of the collapse to help the ambulance crews
Go straight to the emergency department to offer her help
Phone the theatre suite to ask whether she should come in
Patient Safety & Quality.w: In a major incident, staff are called in through the trust's coordinated call-in process so that the right skills arrive at the right time and staff remain for later phases. Self-deployment to the scene or hospital can hamper command and control, and phone lines are needed for the response (P6.12).

n.1: Health staff at the scene are deployed by the ambulance service; self-deploying can add to the risk and confusion.
n.2: Self-presenting bypasses the hospital's command structure, and the trust may need her rested for later shifts.
n.3: Calling the department ties up phone lines needed for the incident response.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Priya, a registered nurse on a care of older people ward, is preparing to hoist Alan Hughes, 78, from bed to chair. While checking the sling she notices that one of the seams is frayed and partly torn. Two healthcare assistants are waiting to help. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Transfer Mr Hughes by lifting him with the two healthcare assistants instead of using the hoist
Reinforce the torn seam with strong tape and complete the transfer with the hoist as planned
Use the sling for this transfer with an extra person present, then report the damage afterwards
Withdraw the sling from use, label it as faulty, report it and fetch a suitable replacement
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Faulty lifting equipment must be taken out of use and reported so that nobody else uses it, and the planned safe system of work (hoist with an intact sling) should continue with a replacement. This applies the employee duty under s7 Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 to take reasonable care for others, LOLER 1998 (equipment for lifting people must be safe) and Code 19 (preserve safety).

n.0: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 require hazardous manual handling to be avoided where reasonably practicable; a manual lift of a hoist-dependent person replaces one hazard with another.
n.1: Improvised repairs to lifting equipment are unsafe and conceal the defect; damaged slings must be withdrawn and replaced, not patched.
n.2: An extra person does not make a torn sling safe; using it exposes Mr Hughes to a fall and delays reporting a known hazard.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: A first-year student nurse asks Tom, her practice supervisor, what the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires of her personally as an employee on the ward. Which statement by Tom is correct?
o: You must ensure the health, safety and welfare of all staff on the ward so far as reasonably practicable
You must report every injury you sustain at work directly to the Health and Safety Executive yourself
You must write a formal risk assessment before carrying out each care task that involves any risk to you
You must take reasonable care of yourself and others affected by what you do, and cooperate with your employer
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 places two duties on every employee: to take reasonable care for their own health and safety and that of other people who may be affected by their acts or omissions, and to cooperate with the employer so that the employer can meet its own duties (FACTS S-HSE).

n.0: Ensuring the health, safety and welfare of employees so far as reasonably practicable is the employer's general duty (s2), not the individual employee's duty.
n.1: RIDDOR reports are made by the responsible person (usually the employer); the employee reports the injury through the local incident system.
n.2: Formal risk assessment is an employer duty under the management regulations; employees follow the assessments and safe systems of work their employer provides.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Kerry, a healthcare assistant, injures her back while helping a patient who began to fall. She is unable to do her normal work for ten days. The ward manager is preparing the RIDDOR report as the responsible person. Within what timescale must the report be made?
o: Within 10 days of the incident
Within 15 days of the incident
Within 7 days of the incident
Within 15 days of her return to work
Patient Safety & Quality.w: Under RIDDOR 2013 an injury that incapacitates a worker for more than seven consecutive days (not counting the day of the accident but including weekends and rest days) must be reported within 15 days of the accident (HSE, RIDDOR: when do I report).

n.0: Ten days is the deadline for the written report of a specified injury or death, not for an over-7-day incapacitation.
n.2: Seven days is the length of incapacitation that makes the injury reportable, not the reporting deadline.
n.3: The 15-day period runs from the date of the accident, not from the worker's return to work.

Patient Safety & Quality.q: Sam, a community nurse, has just given a subcutaneous injection of enoxaparin to Mrs Ada Kowalski, 69, in her home using a prefilled syringe with a safety device. What is the safest way to deal with the used syringe?
o: Separate the needle from the syringe and place each part in the correct waste stream
Place the used syringe in a rigid tray and dispose of it in the sharps bin in the car
Activate the safety device and place the needle and syringe as one unit in the sharps bin at once
Recap the needle with a one-handed scoop technique and dispose of it at the next clinic visit
Patient Safety & Quality.w: The Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 and the National IPC Manual require safer sharps to be used as designed, no recapping, and disposal at the point of use by the user, with the needle and syringe discarded as one unit into a sharps container (FACTS S-HSE, S-NIPCM).

n.0: Needles must not be disassembled from syringes; the unit is discarded intact.
n.1: Carrying an exposed used sharp away from the point of use increases the risk of injury; a portable sharps container should be taken to the point of use.
n.3: Recapping is a recognised cause of needlestick injury and is prohibited by the Sharps Regulations; carrying a recapped needle to another visit adds further risk.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Kyle, a staff nurse, notices that Bev, a healthcare assistant, has become quiet and withdrawn since a relative criticised her in front of colleagues. Bev's care remains of a good standard. What is the most appropriate way for Kyle to support and motivate her?
o: Give Bev lighter tasks for the next few shifts so that she can recover
Speak with Bev privately, acknowledge her good care and ask how she is
Report Bev's change in mood to the ward manager for a formal welfare review
Tell Bev that complaints are part of the job and she should not take it personally
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Leaders guide, support and motivate others (P5.6) and the Code asks registrants to work cooperatively and support the staff they are responsible for (Code 8, 25.2). Specific recognition and a private, supportive conversation help restore confidence and show that her work is valued.

n.0: Changing her work without discussion may suggest a lack of confidence in her.
n.2: Escalating to a formal process before talking with her is disproportionate.
n.3: Dismissing her feelings is unsupportive and unlikely to restore motivation.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: The Department of Health and Social Care opens a public consultation on changes to nurse education funding. Mariam, a staff nurse, has concerns about the effect on recruitment to her mental health service. What is the most appropriate way for her to influence the policy?
o: Post her views on social media, naming her employer and the vacancies
Respond to the consultation with evidence, directly or through her union
Ask her manager to raise it with the patients' families at visiting
Write to the NMC and ask it to block the proposed funding changes
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: P5.12 and P7.13 ask nurses to understand mechanisms for influencing public policy and to use political awareness. Responding to consultations with evidence, individually or through professional bodies and unions, is a legitimate and effective route, consistent with Code 20 (professionalism).

n.0: Naming her employer and service on social media risks breaching Code 20.10 and confidentiality, and is not a formal route of influence.
n.2: Involving visiting families is inappropriate and does not feed into the consultation.
n.3: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not control government education funding.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Incident reporting on a surgical ward has fallen sharply since a new manager publicly criticised a nurse who reported an error. Staff say they now worry about being blamed. Which action by the matron would best improve the ward's safety culture?
o: Remind staff in writing that failing to report is a breach of the Code
Model openness, thank staff for reporting and share the learning
Make incident reporting a target in each nurse's annual appraisal
Ask the manager to review each report before it is submitted
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Organisational culture is shaped by leaders' behaviour. A just, open culture where reporting is thanked and learning shared encourages reporting (P5.1 group and organisational dynamics and culture; Code 16.5 and 25.1; PSIRF).

n.0: Threats increase fear and do not rebuild trust.
n.2: Targets can encourage low-value reports without addressing the fear that is suppressing reporting.
n.3: Managerial filtering of reports adds to the fear and may suppress reporting further.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A new community nursing team has been formed by merging two teams. In the first few weeks there are disagreements about who covers which visits and how handovers should run. What should the team leader, Fiona, do first?
o: Allocate the visits herself and ask the team to follow the new system
Meet the whole team to clarify roles and agree ways of working together
Wait for the team to settle, as early disagreement usually fades with time
Ask the two former team leaders to decide the arrangements between them
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: In newly formed groups, uncertainty about roles commonly causes conflict. Leaders help by bringing the team together to clarify roles and agree shared ways of working, which builds cohesion and safe handovers (P5.1 group dynamics; AnnexA.4.2.2 active listening to team concerns).

n.0: Imposing a system without involving the team misses their knowledge and may prolong conflict.
n.2: Leaving role confusion unresolved risks missed visits and unsafe handovers.
n.3: Delegating to the former leaders may entrench the two old teams rather than build one team.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: At the start of an early shift, Nina, a staff nurse, is allocated four patients on a medical ward. Which patient should she see first?
o: Mr Ali, 66, whose insulin is due with breakfast in 45 minutes
Mrs Dunn, 74, whose respiratory rate is 28/min, SpO2 89% and who is newly confused
Ms Reid, 52, who reports post-operative pain of 5/10, last analgesia 3 hours ago
Mr Shaw, 59, who is to be discharged today and needs his discharge letter
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Prioritisation uses an ABCDE approach and early warning scores: Mrs Dunn has a respiratory rate of 28 (scores 3), SpO2 89% (scores 3) and new confusion (scores 3) on NEWS2 (RCP 2017), indicating possible life-threatening deterioration needing immediate assessment and escalation (P5.5 lead and manage care of a group of people with prioritisation).

n.0: Time-critical insulin matters, but there are 45 minutes before it is due and he is not unwell.
n.2: Her pain needs prompt attention, possibly by another team member, but is not life-threatening.
n.3: Discharge paperwork can safely wait while a deteriorating patient is assessed.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Marta, a registered nurse, asks Lewis, a healthcare assistant who is trained and assessed in clinical observations, to record observations on three stable patients in her bay. What must Marta do to delegate this task appropriately?
o: Tell Lewis which patients to observe and leave the escalation decisions to him
Explain what to report and when, check he understands and review the results
Ask Lewis to record the observations and to calculate the NEWS2 for each patient
Ask Lewis to observe the patients if he feels confident and has time this morning
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Code 11.1-11.3: delegate only within the other person's competence, make sure they understand the instructions and are supervised and supported, and confirm the outcome meets the required standard. AnnexA.4.1.2 requires clear instructions and checking understanding when delegating. Marta remains accountable for the decision to delegate and for reviewing findings.

n.0: Escalation decisions require registered nurse assessment; leaving them to Lewis passes on responsibility Marta cannot delegate in this way.
n.2: Recording a score without clear thresholds for reporting and review does not meet Code 11.2-11.3.
n.3: Delegation must be clear and planned; leaving it to his confidence and time does not ensure the care is done.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: On a busy surgical ward, a doctor asks Holly, a staff nurse, to get a healthcare assistant to give a prescribed dose of intravenous antibiotic so that it is not late. The healthcare assistant has not been trained in IV administration. What should Holly do?
o: Delay the dose until the evening medicines round, when more nurses are on duty
Give the IV dose herself or arrange for another competent registrant to give it
Delegate the IV dose and supervise the healthcare assistant closely at the bedside
Ask the doctor to give the dose, as the healthcare assistant is not trained
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Code 11.1: delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence. An untrained healthcare assistant cannot safely give IV medicines, so the dose must be given by a competent registrant without undue delay (Code 18.1; P5.4 roles and scope of practice of team members).

n.0: Delaying a prescribed antibiotic risks harm when a competent nurse can give it now.
n.2: Supervision does not make delegation appropriate when the person lacks the training and competence for the task.
n.3: The doctor could give it, but medicine administration is within Holly's own role; passing it back adds delay without a reason.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Before a short handover, Graham, a staff nurse, needs to ask a healthcare assistant to monitor Mr Okafor, 70, who had a hypotensive episode earlier. Which instruction is clearest?
o: 'Please check Mr Okafor's BP and pulse at 14:00 and tell me at once if systolic is under 100.'
'Please keep an eye on Mr Okafor this afternoon and let me know how he gets on.'
'Please do the usual observations on everyone in bay 2, including Mr Okafor, this afternoon.'
'Please do Mr Okafor's observations when you have time and tell me if anything looks off.'
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: AnnexA.1.11 requires clear verbal, digital or written information and instructions when delegating or handing over. An instruction stating what to do, when, and exactly what to report and when removes ambiguity (Code 11.2; AnnexA.4.1.2).

n.1: 'Keep an eye on' does not specify what to measure, when, or what to report.
n.2: A general bay instruction does not flag Mr Okafor's specific risk or what to report.
n.3: There is no time set or threshold for reporting; 'anything off' depends on the assistant's interpretation.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Priti, a registered nurse, delegates a simple wound dressing to Dean, a registered nursing associate who is competent in this task. Dean applies the wrong dressing type. Who is accountable for what?
o: Priti for the decision to delegate; Dean for how he carried out the dressing
Priti is accountable for the dressing, as Dean was working under her direction
The ward manager is accountable, as the allocation of staff was set by her each shift
Dean is accountable for all aspects, as he is a registered professional in his own right
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The Code (standard 11) makes the registrant accountable for decisions to delegate and for confirming outcomes. Nursing associates are NMC registrants bound by the Code, so Dean is accountable for his own practice in carrying out the task (P5.4; FACTS S-CODE).

n.1: Dean is a registrant accountable for his own actions in carrying out the dressing; Priti's accountability is for the decision to delegate and for confirming the outcome.
n.2: The manager is accountable for her own decisions, but this does not remove Priti's or Dean's accountability.
n.3: Priti remains accountable for her decision to delegate and for confirming the outcome (Code 11.3).

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Femi, the nurse in charge of a 28-bed surgical ward, is allocating patients. Sara, a newly registered nurse, is in her first week of preceptorship. One bay includes Mr Clarke, 58, who has a new tracheostomy. Sara has not yet been trained in tracheostomy care. Which allocation is most appropriate?
o: Give Sara no patients and ask her to shadow Femi while Femi coordinates the ward
Give Sara the bay and ask a healthcare assistant to look after Mr Clarke's tracheostomy
Give Sara the bay with Mr Clarke so that she can learn tracheostomy care quickly
Give Sara a bay of stable patients with a named nurse to support her during the shift
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Assigning care means matching patients' needs to staff competence and providing support (P5.5 prioritisation, delegation and assignment of care; Code 11.1 and standard 13 (work within the limits of competence)). A preceptee should care for patients within her competence with a named support, while a nurse trained in tracheostomy care looks after Mr Clarke.

n.0: A registered preceptee can safely take a supported caseload; withholding all patients wastes capacity and slows her development.
n.1: Tracheostomy care is outside a healthcare assistant's role unless specifically trained, and Sara could not supervise it.
n.2: Learning tracheostomy care needs training and supervision; allocating an untrained nurse puts Mr Clarke at risk.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Ten minutes apart, Tariq, the nurse in charge, is told that Mr Lee, 63, has new central chest pain and that Mrs Burns, 81, was found sitting on the floor and has been helped back to bed by a healthcare assistant. She says she is fine. What should Tariq do?
o: Assess Mrs Burns first, as any fall needs a post-fall assessment before other care
Ask Mrs Burns' family to sit with her and see Mr Lee once she has been checked
Ask the healthcare assistant to record Mr Lee's ECG while he reviews Mrs Burns
Assess Mr Lee now and ask the assistant to record Mrs Burns' observations meanwhile
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: New central chest pain is potentially life-threatening and needs immediate registered nurse assessment and escalation. Mrs Burns still needs a post-fall assessment, but interim observations can be delegated to a competent healthcare assistant until Tariq reviews her (P5.5 prioritisation, delegation and assignment of care; Code 11). Two steps: prioritise, then delegate appropriately.

n.0: Mrs Burns needs assessment, but a potential acute coronary syndrome takes priority over a fall in a patient who reports feeling well.
n.1: Families are not a substitute for clinical observation, and this delays Mr Lee's assessment.
n.2: Recording an ECG may be within a trained assistant's role, but Tariq should assess the patient with chest pain himself first.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: On a medical ward, Mrs Hall's daughter asks who can prescribe a new laxative for her mother this afternoon. The doctors are busy in clinic. Which team member could prescribe it?
o: The ward pharmacy technician during the medicines round
A registered nursing associate with three years' experience
Any registered nurse following the doctor's verbal agreement
A registered nurse with a recorded prescribing qualification
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Only nurses and midwives with a recorded prescribing qualification on the NMC register can prescribe; nursing associates do not prescribe (FACTS S-CODE, Code 18). Knowing the scope of practice of each team member is part of P5.4.

n.0: Pharmacy technicians support medicines management but do not prescribe.
n.1: Nursing associates are not able to prescribe, whatever their experience.
n.2: A registered nurse without a prescribing qualification cannot prescribe, even with a doctor's verbal agreement.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Kezia, a second-year adult nursing student, is ending her placement on a surgical ward. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment (SSSA), who conducts the assessment that confirms her achievement of proficiencies for this placement?
o: Her practice assessor, informed by feedback from her supervisors
Her practice supervisor, who has worked most shifts with her
Her academic assessor, who visits the ward at the end of placement
The ward manager, who signs off all students on the ward
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under the SSSA (NMC 2018), practice supervisors support and supervise and contribute feedback; the practice assessor conducts the assessment and confirms achievement of practice proficiencies, drawing on that feedback; the academic assessor works with the practice assessor on progression decisions (P5.8).

n.1: Practice supervisors contribute to assessment through feedback but do not confirm achievement of proficiencies.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement for progression with the practice assessor, but does not assess practice on the ward.
n.3: SSSA roles are defined by function, not by management position; the ward manager has no automatic assessment role.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Owen, a nursing student on a stroke unit, is spending a day working with Leanne, a registered physiotherapist, to learn about mobilisation. Under the SSSA, can Leanne act as Owen's practice supervisor for that day?
o: Yes, as a registered health or social care professional
Yes, but the ward manager must countersign her feedback
No, unless she has completed a practice assessor course
No, as practice supervisors must be registered nurses
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The SSSA allows students to be supervised by any registered health and social care professional, not only NMC registrants, so long-standing interprofessional learning is supported. The physiotherapist can supervise and give feedback within her expertise (P5.8; FACTS S-SSSA).

n.1: The SSSA sets no requirement for a manager to countersign a supervisor's feedback.
n.2: Practice supervisors need to be prepared for the role, but practice assessor preparation is a different requirement.
n.3: NMC registrants are well placed to supervise, but supervision is not restricted to nurses under the SSSA.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Ruth, a practice supervisor, observed her student speak abruptly to a patient who was slow to answer during an admission assessment. The rest of the student's admission work was thorough. How should Ruth give feedback?
o: Wait until the final interview so the feedback is part of the formal assessment
Discuss it privately and soon, naming the strengths and the behaviour, then agree next steps
Write it in the student's document without discussion so that there is a clear record
Mention it to the student briefly at the bedside so that the patient hears the correction
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Constructive feedback is timely, private, specific about the behaviour and its effect, balanced with genuine strengths, and ends with agreed actions (AnnexA.4.1.3 unambiguous, constructive feedback on strengths, weaknesses and potential; P5.9).

n.0: Delaying feedback to the end of placement denies the student time to improve.
n.2: Records should reflect feedback that has been discussed; writing it without discussion is not constructive.
n.3: Correcting a student in front of a patient is humiliating and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Jamal, a first-year student nurse, is visibly upset after caring for a patient who died unexpectedly on his shift. Later that day his practice supervisor, Helen, has time to talk. What is the most helpful approach?
o: Invite him to talk through the event and reflect on his feelings and learning
Ask him to write a reflective account for his portfolio before his next shift
Reassure him that he will get used to deaths with more experience
Suggest he takes the rest of the week off and speaks to occupational health
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Supervisors encourage colleagues and students to reflect on practice (AnnexA.4.1.4) and support their wellbeing. A supportive conversation that explores feelings and learning helps the student process the event, with further support offered if needed (P5.8 promote reflection).

n.1: Written reflection may help later, but setting a task first misses the need for supportive discussion now.
n.2: This dismisses his distress and does not support reflection.
n.3: Some students need time off or occupational health input, but the first step is to listen and explore with him.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Zara, a first-year student nurse, asks to insert a urinary catheter for a patient. She has not yet been taught or practised the procedure. Her practice supervisor, Ama, is busy. What is the most appropriate response from Ama?
o: Carry out the procedure with Zara observing and explain each step
Ask a healthcare assistant to supervise Zara during the catheterisation
Ask Zara to read the procedure policy and then insert the catheter
Let Zara insert the catheter while Ama finishes her other tasks nearby
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Delegation must be within the person's competence (Code 11.1). A student who has not been taught a procedure should first observe and then practise under direct supervision. Ama can use the opportunity to teach (P5.8 support and supervise students; AnnexA.4.1.1 clear explanations when teaching).

n.1: Supervision must come from someone competent in the procedure and in supporting the student; this does not meet the student's learning needs.
n.2: Reading a policy does not provide the skill and assessed competence needed.
n.3: Indirect supervision is unsafe for an aseptic invasive procedure the student has not learned.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Halfway through placement, Steph, a practice supervisor, is concerned that her third-year student repeatedly forgets to escalate abnormal observations. What should Steph record and do?
o: Write in the document that the student has an attitude problem with escalation
Raise it verbally with the student and leave any record until the final review
Keep private notes until the final interview so the student is not distracted
Record specific dated examples in the document and inform the practice assessor
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Unambiguous records of performance (AnnexA.4.1.5) are factual, specific and dated, so the student knows what must improve and the practice assessor can act early with an action plan (SSSA; P5.8 documenting performance).

n.0: Vague, judgemental labels are not evidence and do not tell the student what to change.
n.1: Concerns raised verbally without a record leave no evidence for the assessor or the student's action plan.
n.2: Private notes hidden from the student remove the chance to improve and are not transparent.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Imogen, a staff nurse, sees a colleague starting to move Mr Price, 84, from bed to chair using an under-arm drag lift. His care plan states that he must be hoisted. What should Imogen do?
o: Ask her colleague to stop, help hoist Mr Price, then discuss it privately
Help her colleague complete the transfer and mention it to the ward manager later
Speak to her colleague about it privately at the end of the shift
Report the colleague on the incident system without speaking to her about it
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Code 16 requires acting without delay if there is a risk to patient safety. Imogen should stop the unsafe practice first, ensure Mr Price is moved safely according to his care plan, and then challenge constructively in private, agreeing any learning needs (P5.9 challenge and give constructive feedback about care delivered by others). Two steps: make safe, then feedback.

n.1: Joining an unsafe technique exposes Mr Price and both staff to injury.
n.2: Waiting until later allows the unsafe transfer to continue now.
n.3: Reporting may be appropriate, but the immediate risk must be stopped first and a direct conversation supports learning.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: On a home visit, community nurse Faye watches Mrs Dobson give her husband his insulin. She injects into the same small area of his abdomen each time and Faye notices lumpy skin there. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the GP to review the insulin dose at the next appointment
Show her how to rotate sites, observe her practice and document it
Take over all of Mr Dobson's insulin injections from now on
Leave an injection technique leaflet for Mrs Dobson to read
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Nurses monitor and evaluate the quality of care delivered by lay carers (P5.7). Teaching site rotation, observing Mrs Dobson's technique and recording the plan supports safe care and independence; lumpy injection sites can alter insulin absorption.

n.0: Dose review may be needed later, but the technique problem must be addressed directly now.
n.2: Taking over removes the couple's independence when the issue can be corrected by teaching.
n.3: A leaflet without demonstration and observation does not confirm the technique has changed.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward manager, Leon, has noticed over three weeks that a staff nurse, Abi, regularly completes her patients' records several hours after care. Patient care has otherwise been good. What is Leon's most appropriate first step?
o: Start a formal capability process with a written warning
Meet Abi privately, give examples, explore reasons and agree a plan
Refer Abi to the NMC for failing to keep records as required
Move Abi to a different ward with a lighter workload
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Performance management starts with an informal, supportive conversation using specific examples, exploring causes (for example workload or skills) and agreeing objectives, support and a review date, escalating to formal processes only if problems continue (P5.3 principles and processes of performance management; Code 10.1 records completed at the time or as soon as possible after).

n.0: Formal processes are disproportionate before an informal discussion and support have been tried.
n.2: This is a local performance issue, not a fitness to practise concern at this stage.
n.3: Moving her does not address the reasons for the delay or support her improvement.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Carol, a healthcare assistant, tells Ifeoma, the nurse in charge, that she is anxious about the new 12-hour shift pattern because of her childcare. The ward is busy. Which response best shows active listening?
o: 'Everyone has had to adjust to the new shifts, so I am sure you will manage.'
'Lots of people find it easier once they settle in, so try it for a month first.'
'It sounds as if the longer shifts are making childcare hard. Can you tell me more?'
'You should talk to the ward manager, as I cannot change the shift pattern.'
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Active listening involves giving attention, reflecting back the person's concern and inviting them to say more, which shows the concern has been heard before solutions are discussed (AnnexA.4.2.2 active listening to team members' concerns and anxieties).

n.0: This dismisses her individual concern and closes the conversation.
n.1: Offering reassurance and advice before understanding the problem is not active listening.
n.3: Signposting may be needed later, but responding first with a referral shows she has not been heard.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Two staff nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses' station about who should admit a new patient. Patients and visitors nearby are watching. Lorna is the nurse in charge. What should Lorna do first?
o: Admit the new patient herself so that the disagreement is no longer relevant
Calmly ask them both to step into the office and talk the issue through there
Tell both nurses firmly that they will each be reported to the ward manager
Leave them to resolve it between themselves, as they are both experienced nurses
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: A calm presence and moving the conflict to a private place protects patients' dignity and the team's professionalism and allows the issue to be resolved (AnnexA.4.2.3 calm presence when dealing with conflict; Code 20.1 and 20.3). The admission can then be allocated clearly.

n.0: Taking the task herself avoids the conflict without addressing it and adds to her workload.
n.2: Threatening sanctions in public escalates the conflict and does not resolve the allocation.
n.3: A public argument is affecting patients now; the nurse in charge needs to intervene.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: For a week, Sean, a staff nurse, has noticed that a colleague often takes long breaks, leaving her bay without registered nurse cover. Two call bells went unanswered yesterday. Which approach is most appropriate for Sean to take?
o: Talk to her privately, describe what he has seen and its effect on patients
Report her to the ward manager without discussing the matter with her first
Mention the long breaks during the safety huddle so the whole team is aware
Cover her bay himself during her breaks to make sure that patients are safe
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Effective confrontation is private, specific and focused on behaviour and its impact on patients, inviting the other person's view and agreeing a solution. Escalation follows if the problem continues (AnnexA.4.2.4 appropriate and effective confrontation strategies; Code 8 and 16).

n.1: Escalation may be needed later, but a direct conversation is the proportionate first step.
n.2: Raising an individual's behaviour in front of the team is humiliating and may provoke defensiveness.
n.3: Covering for her hides the problem and stretches his own care.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: The son of a patient on a medical ward is shouting at the nurses' station because he was not told his father had been moved to another bay. He is red-faced and pacing. What should the nurse, Bryony, do first?
o: Call security straight away so that he can be escorted off the ward
Tell him firmly that shouting is unacceptable and that he must lower his voice
Speak calmly, acknowledge his frustration and offer to talk somewhere quieter
Explain that the move happened because of bed pressures beyond her control
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: De-escalation uses a calm tone and non-threatening body language, acknowledges the person's feelings, and moves the conversation away from an audience, while keeping a safe distance and exit route (AnnexA.4.2.5 de-escalation strategies when dealing with conflict).

n.0: Security may be needed if there is a risk of violence, but there is no threat here and calling them first may escalate the situation.
n.1: Leading with a demand can escalate anger before his concern is acknowledged.
n.3: Explaining reasons before acknowledging his feelings can sound defensive and does not de-escalate.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: At 23:00 the site manager asks Kwame, the nurse in charge, to transfer Mrs Lowry, 88, who has delirium, to another ward to free a bed. Kwame is concerned that a night move will worsen her delirium. Another patient in his ward is medically stable and awake. What is the best approach?
o: Refuse any transfer and tell the site manager to find a bed on another ward
Agree to the move and complete an incident report about it the next day
Explain the risk to Mrs Lowry and propose moving the stable patient instead
Agree to move Mrs Lowry, as the site manager has authority over beds
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Negotiation explores both parties' needs and seeks a solution that meets them: the site manager needs a bed; Kwame needs to protect a vulnerable patient (moving people with delirium, especially at night, can worsen confusion). Offering an alternative is effective negotiation and advocacy (AnnexA.4.2.6.1; AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4).

n.0: Refusing outright without offering a solution ignores the site's legitimate need and is unlikely to resolve the problem.
n.1: Reporting afterwards does not prevent foreseeable harm that negotiation could avoid now.
n.3: Authority over beds does not remove Kwame's duty to advocate for a patient at risk of harm.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Kapoor, 67, has capacity and has told Hayley, his nurse, that he does not want the proposed amputation and would prefer palliative wound care. On the ward round the surgeon starts to describe the operation date without asking his views. What should Hayley do?
o: Say that Mr Kapoor has shared views about the operation and invite him to explain them
Record Mr Kapoor's wishes in his nursing notes once the ward round has finished
Wait until after the ward round and then ask Mr Kapoor whether he has changed his mind
Tell the surgeon that Mr Kapoor has asked her to cancel the operation on his behalf
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Advocacy means making sure the person's own voice is heard in decisions about their care (AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4 act as an advocate for the vulnerable; Code 2.5 respect the right to refuse treatment). Inviting Mr Kapoor to speak supports his autonomy without speaking over him (MCA 2005 s1 principles).

n.1: Recording his wishes is necessary but does not ensure they are heard in the decision being made now.
n.2: Waiting allows a decision to be made without him; he has already expressed his wishes.
n.3: Hayley should not overstate or speak for him when he can speak for himself.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: At a weekly multidisciplinary meeting on a rehabilitation ward, the team plans discharge for Mrs Grey, 80, next week. Ewan, her named nurse, has noticed that she has become confused and agitated each night for the past four nights, which is not recorded in the medical notes. What should Ewan do?
o: Wait until the team asks for nursing views before mentioning the confusion
Record the night-time confusion in the nursing notes after the meeting ends
Share his observations at the meeting and ask for her plan to be reviewed
Tell Mrs Grey's daughter so that she can raise it with the consultant
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Nurses contribute effectively and proactively in the interdisciplinary team (P1.18), sharing information that affects safety (Code 8.2 and 8.5). New nightly confusion may indicate delirium and affects safe discharge, so it must be raised in the decision meeting.

n.0: Waiting to be asked is not proactive and may mean the information is not shared before the decision.
n.1: Records matter, but documentation after the meeting misses the decision point.
n.3: Passing clinical information through a relative is an indirect and unreliable way to inform the team.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: After several months of tension and two formal grievances, a mental health ward manager wants to help the team learn from difficult experiences and improve how they work together. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Hold a single team-building social event outside of working hours
Set up regular facilitated team reflection sessions to discuss practice
Ask each team member to send any concerns to her by email in confidence
Rotate staff with other wards for six months to reduce the tension
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Regular, facilitated group reflection allows staff to share experiences, understand each other's perspectives and agree improvements, which supports team relationships and learning (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; AnnexA.4.1.4 encouraging reflection).

n.0: A one-off social event may help morale but is not a structured way to reflect on practice.
n.2: Individual emails may surface concerns but do not support shared team learning.
n.3: Rotating staff disrupts continuity of care and avoids rather than addresses team issues.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A community nurse in England is asked by a student which organisation in their integrated care system plans NHS services for the local population and manages the local NHS budget. What is the correct answer?
o: The integrated care partnership (ICP)
The upper-tier local authority
The local provider collaborative
The integrated care board (ICB)
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Each of the 36 integrated care systems in England has one integrated care board, an NHS organisation responsible for planning health services for its population and managing the NHS budget (Health and Care Act 2022; ICSs legally established 1 July 2022) (P7.6; FACTS S-ICS).

n.0: The ICP is a joint committee of NHS bodies and upper-tier councils that develops the integrated care strategy; it does not hold the NHS budget.
n.1: Upper-tier local authorities are responsible for social care and public health, not NHS budgets.
n.2: Provider collaboratives bring trusts together to plan and deliver services but do not hold the ICS's NHS budget.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: At a team meeting, a district nursing team leader explains the integrated care partnership (ICP) in her area. Which statement about the ICP is correct?
o: It inspects and rates the quality of local health services
It is the NHS body that commissions hospital and GP services
It is a joint committee that develops the integrated care strategy
It employs the community nurses who work in the local area
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The ICP is a joint committee run by the NHS organisations and upper-tier local authorities in each ICS, with wider partners such as the voluntary sector. It must develop a long-term integrated care strategy to improve health, care and wellbeing (NHS England, What is integrated care?; P7.1).

n.0: Inspection and rating are carried out by the Care Quality Commission in England.
n.1: Planning NHS services and managing the budget is the role of the integrated care board.
n.3: Community nurses are employed by provider organisations, not by the ICP.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Agnes Doyle, 84, lives alone and is recovering from pneumonia on a medical ward in England. She will need help with personal care at home. Which organisation is responsible for assessing her need for care and support at home?
o: Her GP practice
The integrated care board
The local authority
The acute hospital trust
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under the Care Act 2014, local authorities assess adults who appear to need care and support and are responsible for social care (and public health) in their area. The ward nurse refers so assessment can be planned before discharge (P7.1 interagency working; FACTS S-CA, S-ICS).

n.0: The GP provides health care but does not carry out Care Act assessments.
n.1: The ICB plans and funds NHS health services, not adult social care assessments.
n.3: Hospital staff contribute to discharge planning, but the statutory needs assessment is the local authority's duty.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Harold Wright, 76, is on a stroke unit. He coughs and his voice sounds wet when he drinks water. The nurse has stopped oral intake. Which member of the multidisciplinary team should assess his swallow?
o: The specialist stroke dietitian
The stroke unit occupational therapist
The speech and language therapist
The respiratory physiotherapist
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Speech and language therapists assess and manage swallowing difficulties (dysphagia) and advise on safe food and fluid consistencies. Knowing team members' roles supports timely referral (P5.4 roles and scope of practice of interdisciplinary team members; Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.0: Dietitians advise on nutritional needs and supplements but do not carry out swallow assessments.
n.1: Occupational therapists support daily living activities and equipment, not swallow assessment.
n.3: Physiotherapists address mobility and respiratory function; they do not assess swallowing.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Leila Hassan, 71, is recovering from a hip fracture. She lives in a first-floor flat and is worried about managing her bath and kitchen safely at home. Which professional is best placed to assess her for equipment and adaptations?
o: A district nursing sister
An occupational therapist
A hospital social worker
A community physiotherapist
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Occupational therapists assess a person's ability to carry out activities of daily living and recommend equipment and home adaptations, often through a home visit (P5.4; NICE NG249 recommends home hazard assessment ideally by an occupational therapist).

n.0: District nurses provide nursing care at home but are not the lead for daily living equipment assessment.
n.2: Social workers coordinate care and support arrangements but do not assess for equipment.
n.3: Physiotherapists focus on mobility, strength and exercise rather than assessing the home environment for equipment.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Jason, 45, has alcohol dependence and no fixed address. He is medically fit for discharge after treatment for pancreatitis and agrees to support being arranged. What is the most appropriate approach by his nurse, Fatima?
o: Ask his GP to arrange housing and alcohol support after he has left hospital
Keep him in hospital until a permanent tenancy has been secured for him
Give him a list of local hostels and alcohol services on the day of discharge
Involve the housing team and alcohol service before discharge, with his consent
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Interagency working means involving partner agencies early so that a person with complex needs leaves hospital with coordinated support (P7.1 partnership, collaboration and interagency working; P7.5). Under the Homelessness Reduction Act 2017 public bodies including hospitals refer people at risk of homelessness to the local housing authority with consent.

n.0: Passing the task to the GP after discharge leaves Jason without support at the point of greatest risk.
n.1: Keeping a medically fit person in hospital until permanent housing is found is not proportionate and may never resolve.
n.2: Signposting on the day of discharge does not coordinate support and risks readmission.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Becca, a care home nurse, receives Mr Ian Moss, 79, back from hospital. The discharge letter says his furosemide was stopped, but the boxes sent with him and the care home's medicines record still include it. The GP practice is open. What should Becca do?
o: Contact the hospital or GP to reconcile the medicines and report the gap
Stop the furosemide, as the discharge letter is the most recent document
Continue the furosemide until the next routine GP visit
Ask Mr Moss which tablets he has been taking and follow his answer
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Transitions between settings are a common point of medicines error. Discrepancies are resolved by medicines reconciliation with the prescriber and the information gap is reported for learning (P7.6 complexities of care across integrated settings; NICE NG5 Medicines optimisation; Code 18).

n.1: Acting on one document without clarifying a conflict risks error if the letter itself is wrong.
n.2: Continuing a possibly stopped diuretic for days risks harm while the discrepancy is unresolved.
n.3: Mr Moss's account is useful information but does not replace clarification with the prescriber.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: An integrated frailty service involves a hospital, community nursing, social care and a voluntary sector partner. The service lead, Ade, wants to evaluate the quality of people's experience of care across the whole pathway. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Measure the average length of hospital stay for people in the service
Compare each organisation's complaint numbers separately for the past year
Ask people and families for feedback on their whole journey across services
Survey staff in each organisation about how well they work together
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Evaluating the experience of complex care means asking the people who receive it, and their families, about the whole journey, including transitions between services (P7.7 monitor and evaluate the quality of people's experience of complex care; P6.9).

n.0: Length of stay is an efficiency measure, not a measure of people's experience.
n.1: Complaints in separate organisations show only part of the picture and miss the transitions between services.
n.3: Staff views are useful but do not describe the experience of people using the service.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: During a teaching session on health economics, a student nurse asks what a quality-adjusted life year (QALY) measures. Which answer is correct?
o: A patient's own rating of their satisfaction with care, scored from 0 to 1
Length of life adjusted for its quality, where 1 is a year in full health
The cost to the NHS of keeping one person in hospital for a year
The number of years a person lives after receiving a treatment
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: A QALY combines quantity and quality of life: one year in perfect health counts as 1 QALY, and years lived in poorer health are weighted below 1. NICE uses cost per QALY gained to judge cost-effectiveness (P7.3 principles of health economics; FACTS S-NICETH).

n.0: A QALY uses health-related quality of life, not satisfaction with care.
n.2: This is a cost measure; a QALY measures health benefit, not cost.
n.3: Survival alone ignores quality of life, which the QALY adjusts for.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward pharmacist explains to nursing staff how NICE judges whether a new medicine is cost-effective in its technology appraisals. Since April 2026, what is NICE's standard cost-effectiveness threshold?
o: £100,000 to £300,000 per QALY gained
£20,000 to £30,000 per QALY gained
£30,000 to £50,000 per QALY gained
£25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Following a government decision, NICE's standard threshold in technology appraisals rose from £20,000-£30,000 to £25,000-£35,000 per QALY gained from April 2026 (NICE, Changes to NICE's cost-effectiveness thresholds; P7.4 implications of current health policy).

n.0: This higher range applies to highly specialised technologies for ultra-rare diseases, not the standard threshold.
n.1: This was the threshold before April 2026.
n.2: This is not a NICE threshold range.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A new wound treatment costs £30,000 more per patient than standard care and produces 1.5 more QALYs per patient. Using NICE's standard threshold in force since April 2026, what is the incremental cost per QALY and how does it compare?
o: £30,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, below the threshold range
£45,000 per QALY, above the threshold range
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio = extra cost / extra QALYs = £30,000 / 1.5 = £20,000 per QALY. This is below the standard range of £25,000-£35,000 per QALY, so the treatment would usually be considered cost-effective (P7.3). Two steps: calculate, then compare with the current threshold.

n.0: This ignores the QALY gain and uses the extra cost alone.
n.1: The calculation is right, but £20,000 is below the current £25,000-£35,000 range, not within it.
n.3: This multiplies cost by QALYs instead of dividing.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Siân, a nurse who has worked in England, moves to a hospital in Cardiff. She asks which body independently inspects NHS healthcare services in Wales. What is the correct answer?
o: The Nursing and Midwifery Council
Healthcare Improvement Scotland
Healthcare Inspectorate Wales
The Care Quality Commission
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Health is devolved across the UK. Healthcare Inspectorate Wales inspects healthcare in Wales; the Care Quality Commission regulates in England, Healthcare Improvement Scotland in Scotland and the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority in Northern Ireland (P7.2 devolved UK differences).

n.0: The NMC regulates individual nurses, midwives and nursing associates, not services.
n.1: Healthcare Improvement Scotland covers Scotland.
n.3: The CQC regulates health and adult social care services in England only.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Tasha is a registered nursing associate working in Manchester. She is moving to Edinburgh and asks whether she can practise there in her registered nursing associate role. What is the most accurate answer?
o: No, until she completes a Scottish conversion course for the role
No, because nursing associates are regulated for practice in England
Yes, once she transfers to the Scottish part of the NMC register
Yes, because NMC registration applies in all four UK nations
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Nurses and midwives are regulated by the NMC across the UK, but nursing associates are regulated in England only (FACTS S-CODE). This is an example of devolved differences in health workforce policy (P7.2).

n.0: No Scottish conversion course creates a regulated nursing associate role in Scotland.
n.2: There is no Scottish part of the register for nursing associates.
n.3: This is true for nurses and midwives, but the nursing associate role is regulated in England only.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward's budget is overspent. The manager explains that money spent on agency staff this year means the planned purchase of new pressure-relieving mattresses cannot go ahead. Which economic concept does this illustrate?
o: Value for money
Opportunity cost
Cost-effectiveness
Economies of scale
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Opportunity cost is the benefit lost from the next best use of a resource when it is spent on something else. In a fixed budget, spending on one item means another cannot be funded (P7.3 principles of health economics and resource allocation).

n.0: Value for money describes how well spending achieves outcomes, not the forgone alternative.
n.2: Cost-effectiveness compares the costs and outcomes of alternatives; it is not the loss of the forgone option.
n.3: Economies of scale are lower unit costs from producing more; they are not shown here.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Tomasz, a community nurse, is concerned that a planned reduction in local district nursing posts will affect housebound patients. He wants to use his professional knowledge to influence the decision. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Refuse to accept new referrals until the reduction in posts is withdrawn
Share named patients' stories with a local newspaper to raise awareness
Write to his MP with anonymised evidence about the impact on care
Tell his patients during home visits that they should vote against the council
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Political awareness and influence are part of the nurse's role (P7.13; P5.12). Engaging with elected representatives using anonymised evidence is legitimate, while the Code requires confidentiality (Code 5) and that personal political views are not expressed inappropriately to people in his care (Code 20.7).

n.0: Refusing referrals puts patients at risk and is not a professional way to influence policy.
n.1: Sharing identifiable patient information breaches confidentiality (Code 5).
n.3: Expressing personal political views to patients during care breaches Code 20.7.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Charlie, a mental health nurse in England, asks in October 2026 whether the Mental Health Act 2025 has replaced the 1983 Act for detentions on his ward. Which statement is correct?
o: The 2025 Act received Royal Assent, but most provisions are not yet in force
The 2025 Act applies to new detentions; the 1983 Act applies to existing ones
The 2025 Act is still a Bill and has not yet completed its parliamentary stages
The 2025 Act is fully in force and has replaced the 1983 Act in England
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but most provisions (including changes to sections 3 and 4) were not in force at October 2026. The Mental Health Act 1983 as amended remains the current law for detention (BUILD-PLAN unsettled law note; P7.4 implications of current and future health policy).

n.1: There is no rule of this kind; detentions continue under the 1983 Act as amended until provisions are commenced.
n.2: The Act completed its passage and received Royal Assent in December 2025.
n.3: Most provisions of the 2025 Act await commencement, so the 1983 Act as amended still applies.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Daniel Morgan, 32, has a learning disability and is very anxious about needles. He missed his last two blood test appointments at a busy GP practice clinic. Which reasonable adjustment is most appropriate for the practice nurse to offer?
o: Offer the first appointment of the day with extra time and easy read information
Ask his support worker to bring him in and stay outside the room during the test
Arrange for the test to be done when he next attends hospital as an inpatient
Book him into the next routine clinic slot and send a standard reminder letter
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Equality Act 2010 s20 places a duty to make reasonable adjustments so that disabled people are not at a substantial disadvantage. A quiet first appointment, extra time and accessible information reduce anxiety and support his access (P3.7 principles of reasonable adjustments; P7.9; Accessible Information Standard).

n.1: A familiar support worker can help, but asking them to wait outside removes the support he may need.
n.2: Waiting for an unplanned admission denies him timely, equitable access to routine care.
n.3: Repeating the arrangement that has failed twice makes no adjustment for his disability.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Anita Rao, 68, is admitted for elective surgery. She is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. Her 12-year-old grandson has come with her and offers to interpret. What should the admitting nurse do?
o: Record and flag her need for a BSL interpreter and arrange one to attend
Rely on lip reading by facing Mrs Rao and speaking slowly and clearly
Accept the grandson's offer, as Mrs Rao is comfortable with him interpreting
Use written notes for the admission, as she can read English well
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs arising from disability or sensory loss. A qualified BSL interpreter ensures accurate information and valid consent; children should not be used to interpret clinical information (Code 7.2; P7.9).

n.1: Lip reading is unreliable for complex clinical information and is not her preferred communication method.
n.2: A child interpreter may mistranslate clinical information and is placed in an inappropriate role, risking invalid consent.
n.3: Written English may not be fully accessible to a first-language BSL user, and the standard requires her preferred format.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Peter Clarke, 73, is recovering from a stroke on a rehabilitation ward. He can wash his face and upper body himself, although it takes him 20 minutes. A healthcare assistant suggests washing him to save time. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Agree for weekdays and let Mr Clarke wash himself at weekends when it is quieter
Ask the occupational therapist to decide whether Mr Clarke should wash himself
Agree, as it reduces the risk that Mr Clarke becomes tired before therapy
Encourage Mr Clarke to wash what he can, with prompts and help where needed
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Nurses support people to maintain independence and avoid unnecessary interventions (P7.8). Doing for a person what they can do for themselves reduces function and dignity; rehabilitation depends on practice with support where needed (Code 1.2 fundamentals of care; Code 2).

n.0: Inconsistent practice slows recovery and is driven by staff convenience.
n.1: The occupational therapist may advise, but supporting independence in daily care is part of the nurse's role now.
n.2: Fatigue can be managed through planning; removing the activity undermines his rehabilitation.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Ivy Turner, 86, is admitted with a chest infection and has urinary incontinence at night. A colleague suggests inserting a urinary catheter so her bed stays dry. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Insert the catheter and review it after one week
Use continence pads overnight until she is discharged
Insert the catheter overnight and remove it each morning
Carry out a continence assessment and plan alternatives
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Catheters carry risks of infection and loss of continence function and should not be used for staff convenience. A continence assessment identifies causes and less invasive options such as prompted toileting (P7.8 avoid unnecessary interventions; NICE CG139 urinary catheter use only after considering alternatives).

n.0: Catheterising for convenience exposes her to infection risk without a clinical indication.
n.1: Pads without a continence assessment leave the cause unidentified and may reduce continence and dignity.
n.2: Repeated insertion increases infection and trauma risk and is not a continence plan.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Albert King, 81, has heart failure, type 2 diabetes, COPD and osteoarthritis. He takes 14 different medicines and has had two falls this month. The community nurse visits. What is the most appropriate next step to address his complex needs?
o: Remove the medicines he finds hardest to swallow from his list
Advise him to stop his diuretic on days when he feels dizzy
Request a structured medication review with his GP or pharmacist
Refer him to the falls clinic and leave the medicines unchanged
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Polypharmacy with multiple long-term conditions increases the risk of falls and adverse effects. A structured medication review, including psychotropic and cardiovascular drugs, is part of falls assessment (NICE NG249; NICE NG5 Medicines optimisation; P7.5 comorbidities and complex needs).

n.0: Nurses without prescribing responsibility for him must not stop prescribed medicines on swallowing difficulty alone; the issue needs review.
n.1: Advising him to stop a diuretic without prescriber review risks fluid overload.
n.3: A falls referral is reasonable, but leaving medicines unreviewed ignores a likely contributing factor.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Maria, 29, is from a Gypsy, Roma and Traveller community and lives on an unauthorised site. A GP receptionist has told her she cannot register without proof of address. The practice nurse is asked for advice. What is correct?
o: She must register as a temporary resident, having no fixed address
She can register without proof of address or identification
She can attend the emergency department for routine care instead
She must provide a utility bill before she can register
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NHS England guidance states that anyone in England can register with a GP practice and that proof of address, identification or immigration status is not needed to register. Facilitating equitable access for groups who face barriers is part of P7.9 (Core20PLUS5 recognises such inclusion health groups; Equality Act 2010, race is a protected characteristic).
