n.0: Temporary registration is for people staying in an area for a short time; having no fixed address does not restrict her to it, and she is entitled to full registration.
n.2: Directing routine care to the emergency department is inappropriate and deepens inequality of access.
n.3: Lack of proof of address is not a reason to refuse registration.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Jamie, 24, has a learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. He brings a hospital passport describing how he communicates. On the ward round, staff talk to his mother and ignore Jamie. What should his nurse do?
o: Ask his mother to explain the ward round decisions to Jamie later
Allow the conversation to continue, as his mother knows him best
Share the passport details and invite staff to speak directly to Jamie
Ask the learning disability liaison nurse to attend the next ward round
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Nurses advocate for people who are vulnerable or disabled and make reasonable adjustments (P7.9; Code 3.4; Equality Act 2010 s20). Using the hospital passport and speaking directly to Jamie in his preferred way respects his rights, involves him in decisions and supports any capacity assessment (MCA 2005 s1(3)).

n.0: Passing information on later excludes Jamie from the conversation about his own care.
n.1: His mother's knowledge is valuable, but Jamie must be involved directly in decisions about his care.
n.3: Liaison nurses offer valuable support, but the nurse should advocate for Jamie now rather than wait.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Leo, 19, is autistic and attends a busy emergency department with a wrist injury. He is covering his ears, rocking and becoming more distressed in the noisy waiting room. His triage category means he may wait two hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Suggest he returns tomorrow when the department is likely to be quieter
Move him up the triage queue ahead of patients with more urgent needs
Ask him to wait outside the department until a cubicle becomes free
Offer a quieter space to wait and explain clearly what will happen next
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Reasonable adjustments remove disadvantage arising from disability without compromising others' safety: a quieter waiting space and clear, predictable information reduce sensory overload while clinical priority is maintained (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7; P7.9). Two steps: recognise sensory distress, then select a proportionate adjustment.

n.0: Delaying treatment of an injury is not a reasonable adjustment and may worsen the outcome.
n.1: Triage order is based on clinical urgency; changing it could harm patients with more urgent needs.
n.2: Sending him outside removes him from observation and is not an adjustment that maintains his care.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Edna Fox, 83, is medically fit for discharge after a urinary tract infection. Before admission she managed alone at home. She will now go home with a new package of carers visiting twice a day for personal care. Which discharge pathway applies?
o: Pathway 1
Pathway 2
Pathway 3
Pathway 0
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Hospital discharge and community support guidance (DHSC/NHS England, updated January 2024): pathway 1 is discharge home or to the usual place of residence with new or additional health and/or social care needs (P4.18; P7.10).

n.1: Pathway 2 is a community bed-based setting with recovery support, not home.
n.2: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new or additional care needs; Mrs Fox needs a new care package.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Gordon Bailey, 79, is recovering from a hip fracture repair. He is not yet safe at home but the team expects he will be able to return home after a few weeks of rehabilitation in a community hospital bed. Which discharge pathway is this?
o: Pathway 3
Pathway 2
Pathway 1
Pathway 0
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Pathway 2 is discharge to a community bed-based setting with dedicated recovery support, where short-term care helps the person recover before living independently or receiving longer-term care (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.2: Pathway 1 is discharge home with new support; Mr Bailey is not yet ready to go home.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new needs.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Rita Holmes, 87, lived alone before a fall and is now medically fit for discharge but still slow and unsteady. At the board round, a doctor suggests arranging a permanent nursing home place directly from the ward. What does current discharge guidance in England advise?
o: Discharge her home with no support and review her needs if she falls
Arrange the permanent place now, as hospital is the best place to assess needs
Discharge her for a period of recovery, then assess her long-term needs
Keep Mrs Holmes in hospital until she has fully recovered her mobility
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under discharge to assess, long-term needs are assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery, not in hospital. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home placement for the first time without an opportunity to recover first (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P4.18). Two steps: recognise she is medically fit, then apply discharge to assess.

n.0: She has clear new needs; discharge without support is unsafe.
n.1: Assessing long-term needs in hospital, before recovery, tends to overestimate need; the guidance advises against it.
n.3: Staying in hospital once medically fit risks deconditioning and delays recovery.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Claire Bennett, 42, who has multiple sclerosis, is due for discharge after a relapse. During discharge planning, Sunil, her nurse, learns that her 14-year-old son provides much of her care at home. What should Sunil do?
o: Ask Claire to arrange more help from other family members before discharge
Plan the discharge around the son's school hours, as he already provides her care
Leave the son out of discussions, as he is under 18 and cannot be a carer
Involve the son appropriately and notify the local authority so it can assess him
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NHS trusts must involve unpaid carers, including young carers, in discharge planning as soon as feasible (Care Act 2014 s74 as amended by the Health and Care Act 2022). Where a young carer is identified, the local authority should be notified so it can carry out a young carer's needs assessment, including whether caring is appropriate or excessive (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Other support may help, but the young carer still needs to be identified and referred for assessment.
n.1: Relying on a child's care without assessment may place excessive responsibility on him and ignores safeguarding considerations.
n.2: Young carers are recognised in law and must be identified and involved appropriately, not excluded.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Leonard Ross, 74, is going home after a stroke. His wife, Margaret, will help him with washing and dressing. She tells the nurse she is already exhausted and worried about coping. What should the nurse tell her?
o: She should wait to see how she copes for the first few weeks at home
She can apply for a carer's assessment once he has been home a month
She has a right to a carer's assessment from the local authority
She can ask the GP to prescribe something to help her sleep better
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under section 10 of the Care Act 2014, where a carer appears to have needs for support, the local authority must carry out a carer's assessment. For a new caring role this should ideally happen before caring begins, organised so as not to delay discharge (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Waiting risks carer breakdown; carers' needs should be assessed early.
n.1: There is no one-month waiting period; the local authority's duty arises when it appears she may have needs.
n.3: Sleep problems may need attention, but this does not address her support needs as a carer.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Kwabena Asante, 66, is to be discharged on a newly started oral anticoagulant after a pulmonary embolism. Which final check before he leaves best supports a safe discharge?
o: He has been told to read the patient leaflet supplied with his tablets
He understands his medicine, has a supply, and follow-up is arranged
His observations are within normal limits on the morning of discharge
He has a copy of the discharge letter to hand in to his GP practice
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Safe discharge on a high-risk medicine requires the person to understand the medicine and its risks, have an adequate supply, and have follow-up arranged with information shared with primary care (P4.18 coordinate safe discharge; NICE NG5 medicines-related communication at transfer; Code 7 and 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care).

n.0: A leaflet does not confirm understanding of a high-risk new medicine.
n.2: Stable observations are needed but do not address the medicines and follow-up risks of anticoagulation.
n.3: Relying on the patient to carry the letter delays information reaching the GP; discharge information should be sent directly.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Joan Pike, 90, has social care needs and has been in hospital for a week with heart failure. Several professionals are involved and her daughter is confused about who to contact about discharge plans. According to NICE NG27, what should be in place?
o: A weekly letter to the daughter from the consultant in charge
A named discharge coordinator as the central point of contact
A rule that her daughter contacts the ward sister each morning
A referral to the hospital complaints team to manage contact
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NICE NG27 (2015) recommends a hospital-based multidisciplinary team and a named discharge coordinator who is the central point of contact for the person and their family during discharge planning (P7.10; P4.18).

n.0: A weekly letter is too infrequent and does not provide a single coordinating contact.
n.2: This places responsibility on the family rather than giving them a coordinator.
n.3: Her daughter's confusion is a coordination problem, not a complaint to be managed.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward wants to evaluate how well it plans discharges for people with complex care needs who go home with new support. Which approach would best capture the quality of their experience?
o: Count the number of discharges completed before midday each week
Review the ward's length-of-stay figures against other medical wards
Phone people and carers after discharge to ask about their experience
Audit how many discharge letters reached GPs within 24 hours
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The quality of people's experience of complex care is best evaluated by asking them and their carers directly about the discharge and transition, including whether support started as planned (P7.7 monitor and evaluate the quality of people's experience of complex care; P6.9).

n.0: Discharge timing is a process measure that says little about the person's experience.
n.1: Length of stay measures efficiency, not experience.
n.3: Letter timeliness is an important process measure but does not capture the experience of people and carers.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: During a team meeting, Ellie, a nurse three months after registration, says that leadership is something for ward managers and that her job is to look after her own patients. How does the NMC Code describe leadership for registrants?
o: All registrants have opportunities to show leadership whatever their role
Leadership is required where a nurse is formally in charge of a shift
Leadership is expected once a nurse is appointed to a band 6 role or above
Leadership is expected after completing a recognised leadership course
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Code standard 25 (provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences) applies to every registrant; the NMC states that all registrants have opportunities to show leadership regardless of formal position (P5.6 exhibit leadership potential).

n.1: Being in charge adds responsibilities (Code 25.1), but leadership is expected of all registrants at all times.
n.2: The Code links leadership to professional practice, not to pay band or grade.
n.3: Courses can develop leadership skills, but the Code's expectation does not depend on them.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward is moving from paper charts to electronic observations next month. Several experienced nurses tell Raj, the ward manager, that the system will slow them down and they do not want it. Which approach is most likely to support the change?
o: Ask the nurses who object to work on other wards during the changeover
Involve staff early, explain the reasons, act on concerns and pilot it
Delay the change until every member of the team agrees to it
Set a firm start date and tell staff the system is mandatory from that day
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Effective change management involves the people affected: explaining why the change is needed, listening to and addressing concerns, and testing the change on a small scale so staff can shape it (P5.1 principles of leadership and organisational culture; AnnexA.4.2.1 strengths-based approaches to managing change).

n.0: Removing staff who raise concerns loses their expertise and damages trust in the team.
n.2: Waiting for unanimous agreement can block necessary safety improvements indefinitely.
n.3: Imposing change without engagement tends to increase resistance and workarounds.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: At her appraisal, Joy, a healthcare assistant, is praised by families for her skill in calming people living with dementia who are distressed. Her line manager, Paul, wants to use a strengths-based approach to developing the team. What should Paul do?
o: Concentrate the appraisal on the areas where Joy needs to improve
Move Joy to the dementia unit so that her skills are used there
Ask Joy to spend less time with families so she can do other tasks
Agree a plan for Joy to share her approach and support colleagues
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Strengths-based team development recognises what people do well and builds on it, for example by enabling a team member to share skills and act as a resource, which improves care and motivation (AnnexA.4.2.1; P5.2 strength-based approaches in teams).

n.0: Development needs matter, but a strengths-based approach starts from what the person does well.
n.1: Moving her removes the skill from the team rather than building on it within the team.
n.2: Reducing the activity she excels at undermines a strength that benefits patients and families.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: On a leadership study day, students are asked to distinguish leadership from management. Which activity is best described as leadership rather than management?
o: Preparing the ward's off-duty rota for the next four weeks
Setting a shared vision for care and motivating the team
Recording and reviewing staff sickness absence each month
Monitoring the ward's monthly spending against its budget
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Management is concerned with planning, organising and controlling resources (rotas, budgets, absence); leadership is concerned with direction, vision and influencing and motivating people. Nurses need both (P5.1 principles of effective leadership and management).

n.0: Rota planning organises resources, a management task.
n.2: Absence monitoring is a management process.
n.3: Budget monitoring is a management control activity.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Sana, a nurse who trained in Canada, joins a UK learning disability team and refers to 'people with an intellectual disability'. A colleague asks whether this is the same group. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It is the international term for the group UK services describe as having a learning disability
It refers to specific learning difficulties such as dyslexia, dyscalculia and dyspraxia
It describes a milder condition than a learning disability as defined by UK services
It is the statutory term used for this group in section 1 of the Mental Health Act 1983
Understanding Learning Disability.w: 'Intellectual disability' is the term used internationally (and in ICD-11 as disorders of intellectual development) for the same group described as having a learning disability in UK health and social care.

n.1: Dyslexia and dyspraxia are specific learning difficulties; they do not affect general intellectual ability.
n.2: The terms describe the same range of severity, not a milder group.
n.3: The 1983 Act uses 'learning disability' (s1(4)), not 'intellectual disability'.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Kofi, 20, scored 67 on an IQ test taken during a stressful college assessment. He works part-time, travels alone by bus, cooks for himself and manages his own money. His tutor asks the nurse whether Kofi has a learning disability. What is the best response?
o: Refer him for genetic testing to identify the cause of his learning disability
The definition also needs impaired social functioning, which is not evident
Yes, because a score below 70 confirms a mild learning disability
Repeat the IQ test, because a second score below 70 would confirm it
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Two steps: the definition needs impaired intelligence AND impaired social (adaptive) functioning starting before adulthood. Kofi's daily living skills show no significant impairment of social functioning, so a single IQ score cannot establish a learning disability; adaptive functioning matters as much as IQ.

n.0: Genetic testing does not decide whether the definition is met, and on these facts social functioning is not impaired.
n.2: An IQ score alone does not define a learning disability; adaptive functioning must also be impaired.
n.3: Repeating the test still ignores the adaptive functioning limb, which on these facts is not impaired.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Mrs Hughes asks the nurse whether the speech therapy and support her son Leo, 6, receives will cure his moderate learning disability by the time he is an adult. Which reply is most accurate?
o: It will improve markedly once any underlying medication is fully optimised
It is lifelong, but the right support helps him keep learning new skills
It is lifelong, and skills cannot develop much further once childhood ends
It usually resolves by adulthood when intervention starts before school age
Understanding Learning Disability.w: A learning disability is a lifelong condition with a lasting effect on development (Valuing People 2001), but people continue to learn throughout life and good support increases independence and quality of life.

n.0: Medication does not treat a learning disability itself.
n.2: People with a learning disability keep developing skills across the lifespan; adulthood does not end learning.
n.3: Early intervention improves outcomes, but a learning disability does not resolve.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ellis, 30, is autistic, has a university degree and no impairment of general intelligence. He is admitted to a surgical ward and the ward manager asks whether he should be referred to the learning disability liaison team as 'a patient with a learning disability'. Which statement is accurate?
o: Ellis has a mild learning disability because autism affects social functioning
Ellis is autistic but does not have a learning disability
Ellis must be added to the GP learning disability register before any referral
Ellis falls under the learning disability qualifier in section 1 of the Mental Health Act
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Autism and learning disability are distinct conditions that can, but need not, occur together. Ellis has no impairment of intelligence, so he does not meet the definition, although he may still need autism-related reasonable adjustments (many liaison teams support autistic people too).

n.0: Differences in social communication from autism are not the same as the impaired intelligence required for a learning disability.
n.2: The register is for people with a learning disability; Ellis does not meet that definition.
n.3: The s1(2A) qualifier applies to learning disability; autism is treated as a mental disorder without that qualifier under the 1983 Act.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: A student nurse on placement in a day centre reads that several people there have 'profound and multiple learning disabilities' (PMLD). Which description best fits PMLD?
o: A profound learning disability with physical or sensory impairments and complex health needs
A mild learning disability occurring together with autism, an anxiety disorder and sensory sensitivities
A learning disability acquired after a severe brain injury sustained in adult life
A moderate learning disability with behaviour that challenges and repeated placement breakdowns
Understanding Learning Disability.w: PMLD means a profound learning disability together with additional physical and/or sensory impairments and complex health needs, usually with very limited or no verbal communication.

n.1: Autism and anxiety can coexist with any level of learning disability, but this does not describe PMLD.
n.2: An impairment starting in adult life is not a learning disability, whatever its severity.
n.3: Behaviour that challenges is not a defining feature of PMLD, and the learning disability is profound, not moderate.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ruth, 45, has a moderate learning disability and is moving from her family home to supported living. Her new provider asks the community nurse which assessment will best show the support Ruth needs day to day. What is the best answer?
o: A genetic test to establish the cause of her learning disability
A repeat IQ test to confirm her current severity band
An assessment of adaptive skills such as self-care, safety and money
A review of the diagnosis letter written during her childhood
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Support needs depend on adaptive (social) functioning: self-care, communication, managing money, keeping safe. A severity label or IQ score says little about the specific help a person needs in a new setting.

n.0: Knowing the cause may help with health surveillance but does not show her daily support needs.
n.1: An IQ score does not describe the practical help Ruth needs, and her severity is already known.
n.3: A childhood letter will not reflect Ruth's current skills as an adult.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Jordan, 28, has a mild learning disability and is about to sign a consent form for a hernia repair. He speaks fluently and says 'yes, that's fine' to everything the surgeon explains. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
o: Check what he has understood, as fluent speech can mask poor comprehension
Accept his signature, as a mild learning disability rarely affects consent
Ask his mother, who attends with him, to sign the form on his behalf
Request a formal capacity assessment by a psychiatrist before surgery
Understanding Learning Disability.w: People with a mild learning disability may have expressive language that exceeds their understanding and may agree to please. Asking Jordan to explain the procedure in his own words, with accessible information, checks understanding before consent is relied on (MCA s1(3): all practicable steps).

n.1: Capacity is presumed, but agreement alone does not show that Jordan has understood the information.
n.2: Another adult cannot consent for Jordan; a parent has no legal authority to sign for an adult.
n.3: There is no reason yet to doubt capacity formally; the first step is to check and support understanding, which any clinician can do.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Which example best describes adaptive (social) functioning when assessing whether someone meets the definition of a learning disability?
o: Reaching walking and sitting milestones at the usual age
Having hearing and vision within the typical range
Scoring at the expected level on a verbal reasoning test
Using public transport, handling money and keeping safe
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Adaptive or social functioning is the ability to cope independently with everyday life: self-care, communication, travel, money and personal safety. It is one of the three parts of the Valuing People definition.

n.0: Motor milestones describe physical development, not coping with everyday life.
n.1: Sensory function matters for assessment but is not adaptive functioning.
n.2: Verbal reasoning is part of measured intelligence, not adaptive functioning.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: The LeDeR report on deaths in 2023 (republished January 2026) compared deaths by severity of learning disability. Which finding is accurate?
o: People with a profound learning disability died at an average age of around 70
Age at death did not differ between levels of severity of learning disability
People with a severe or profound learning disability died younger, on average at 58
People with a mild learning disability died youngest because they had less support
Understanding Learning Disability.w: LeDeR 2023 (revised January 2026): average age at death was 63 overall, but people with a severe or profound learning disability died at an average of 58 and were more likely to die of something treatable.

n.0: The average for severe or profound learning disability was 58, not around 70.
n.1: There was a clear difference: 58 for severe or profound against 63 overall.
n.3: The report found the opposite: greater severity was linked to earlier death.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Aisha, 22, has profound and multiple learning disabilities, uses a wheelchair, receives gastrostomy feeds and does not use words. Her care plan is being reviewed on admission to hospital. Which addition is the priority?
o: Standard ward routines so that she is cared for in the same way as others
How Aisha shows pain, pleasure and distress, as described by those who know her
A plan to teach verbal requests for food and drink within three months
A 0 to 10 numerical pain rating scale to be completed at each observation round
Understanding Learning Disability.w: People with PMLD communicate through behaviour, sounds, facial expression and body tone. Recording their usual cues from family and carers (for example a DisDAT profile) lets staff recognise pain and illness against a baseline, a key LeDeR and Equality Act reasonable adjustment learning point.

n.0: Treating everyone the same ignores the duty to make reasonable adjustments for her needs.
n.2: Teaching verbal requests is not realistic or a priority on admission for a person with PMLD.
n.3: A self-report numerical scale needs language and number concepts that Aisha does not use.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Leon, 40, has a severe learning disability and lives in a residential home. Over three weeks he has stopped dressing himself, a skill he has had for years, and spends more time in bed. What should the nurse do first?
o: Compare with his recorded baseline and look for a physical or mental health cause
Increase his support plan so that staff dress him fully each morning
Record that his skills are declining because of his severe learning disability
Refer him straight to the memory service for a dementia assessment
Understanding Learning Disability.w: A new loss of skills is a change from baseline, not part of a stable learning disability. The first step is to establish the change against his baseline and look for treatable causes such as pain, infection, constipation, hypothyroidism, sensory loss or depression, avoiding diagnostic overshadowing.

n.1: Doing tasks for Leon may be needed short term but does not find the cause of the change.
n.2: Attributing new decline to the learning disability is diagnostic overshadowing.
n.3: Dementia is a possibility, but physical and mental health causes should be assessed first.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: A referral letter for Sam, 32, who has a moderate learning disability, says he 'has a mental age of five'. The nurse is preparing his support plan. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Plan consent discussions in the way you would for a five-year-old child
Describe Sam's actual abilities and support needs rather than a mental age
Request a new psychometric test so that the mental age can be updated
Use the mental age to choose activities and toys suitable for a five-year-old
Understanding Learning Disability.w: 'Mental age' is inaccurate and devaluing: Sam is an adult with adult experiences, rights and interests. Describing what he can do and the support he needs is person-centred and respects his rights, including the presumption of capacity under the MCA 2005.

n.0: Adults with a learning disability are presumed to have capacity; child consent rules do not apply.
n.2: Updating a mental age still uses an unhelpful label rather than describing his needs.
n.3: Treating an adult as a young child is devaluing and ignores his adult interests.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Kayla, 6, has a moderate learning disability and a diagnosis of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. A student nurse is sorting causes of learning disability by when they act. How should this cause be classified?
o: Chromosomal, because alcohol alters the number of chromosomes
Prenatal, because alcohol affects the developing brain in the womb
Perinatal, because the damage occurs around the time of birth
Postnatal, because the effects become apparent after birth
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder results from alcohol crossing the placenta and damaging the developing fetal brain, so it is a prenatal (environmental) cause of learning disability.

n.0: Alcohol is a teratogen; it does not change chromosome number as in trisomy 21.
n.2: Perinatal causes act around birth, such as hypoxic injury during labour; alcohol exposure acts during pregnancy.
n.3: Classification depends on when the brain injury happens, not when the effects are noticed.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: A community learning disability nurse is teaching carers about causes of learning disability. Which example is a perinatal cause?
o: Rubella infection in the mother during the first trimester
Bacterial meningitis at 18 months of age
Hypoxic brain injury during a prolonged and complicated birth
An extra copy of chromosome 21 present from conception
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Perinatal causes act around the time of birth: hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury in labour, extreme prematurity and its complications, and severe neonatal jaundice are examples.

n.0: Maternal rubella in early pregnancy is a prenatal (congenital infection) cause.
n.1: Meningitis in later infancy is a postnatal cause.
n.3: Trisomy 21 is a genetic (chromosomal) prenatal cause.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Mo, 7, had bacterial meningitis at 9 months of age. He now has significant difficulty learning new skills and needs help with self-care and keeping safe. His father asks whether this counts as a learning disability. What is the best response?
o: Yes, because the impairment started in childhood and affects his development
Yes, once he reaches 18 and the impairment is confirmed as lasting
No, because an illness-related impairment is classed as a brain injury
No, because a learning disability has to be present from birth
Understanding Learning Disability.w: A learning disability can be caused before, around or after birth; what matters is impaired intelligence and social functioning starting before adulthood with a lasting effect on development (Valuing People 2001). Meningitis in infancy is a recognised postnatal cause.

n.1: Diagnosis does not wait until 18; children are identified and supported throughout childhood.
n.2: The cause does not exclude the definition; injury during childhood development is a recognised cause of learning disability.
n.3: Onset must be before adulthood, not necessarily at birth; postnatal causes in childhood count.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Hannah, 29, attends a pre-conception appointment and asks the practice nurse whether a small amount of wine is safe during pregnancy. Which advice reflects UK guidance on preventing fetal alcohol spectrum disorder?
o: Wine is safer than spirits, so up to one glass a day is acceptable
Alcohol is harmful mainly in the third trimester when the brain grows fastest
The safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all during pregnancy
One or two units once or twice a week is low risk after the first trimester
Understanding Learning Disability.w: The UK Chief Medical Officers' low-risk drinking guidelines (2016) advise that if you are pregnant or planning a pregnancy, the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all, to keep risks to the baby to a minimum.

n.0: The type of drink does not change the risk; it is the alcohol itself that harms the fetus.
n.1: Alcohol can harm the fetus at any stage of pregnancy, including the first trimester.
n.3: The earlier 'one or two units' advice was replaced in 2016; no safe level has been identified.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Olu and Grace ask why their son Ethan, 4, who has a learning disability, is being offered genetic testing when 'nothing will change his condition'. What is the most accurate explanation?
o: Testing can identify a treatment that reverses the learning disability
A known cause can guide checks for linked conditions and inform family planning
Testing is needed before Ethan can be referred to specialist support services
Testing decides whether Ethan is eligible for an annual health check at 14
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Identifying a cause (for example fragile X or a chromosome deletion) can guide health surveillance for associated conditions, give the family information on recurrence risk, and connect them with condition-specific support.

n.0: Knowing the genetic cause does not reverse a learning disability.
n.2: Support is based on need, not on knowing the cause; many people never have a cause identified.
n.3: Annual health checks are offered to anyone aged 14 or over on the GP learning disability register, whatever the cause.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Joan, 56, has a moderate learning disability and lives in supported living. At her annual review the community nurse plans her health monitoring. Which approach is in line with NICE NG96 on growing older with learning disabilities?
o: Focus reviews on behaviour change, because physical decline is an expected part of ageing
Start age-related health checks at 65, the same age as for the general population
Monitor for age-related changes such as hearing and sight loss, dysphagia and osteoporosis
Transfer her care from learning disability services to older people's services at 55
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE NG96 (1.5.14) recommends monitoring people with learning disabilities for age-related conditions including hearing loss, sight problems, dysphagia, epilepsy, thyroid problems, osteoporosis, menopausal symptoms and dementia; these can occur earlier than in the general population.

n.0: Assuming decline is expected is diagnostic overshadowing; changes should be assessed.
n.1: Age-related changes may start earlier, so waiting until 65 risks late detection.
n.3: NG96 does not set an age for transfer; it focuses on a single lead practitioner and coordinated support.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Pat, 82, has cared at home for her son Michael, 55, who has a severe learning disability. She says she is 'managing fine for now' but has had two falls this year. What is the most appropriate action by the community nurse?
o: Advise that Michael should move in with his sister as the next of kin
Wait until Pat says she can no longer cope before raising future plans
Begin planning with Pat and Michael now, including emergency arrangements
Arrange an urgent residential placement for Michael to protect Pat
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE NG96 highlights older family carers: services should plan early with the person and their family for future support, including what happens in an emergency, so that moves are not made in crisis. Pat may also be entitled to a carer's assessment.

n.0: Michael's future home should be planned with him and the family, not assigned to a relative.
n.1: Waiting until a crisis leads to unplanned emergency moves, which NG96 aims to avoid.
n.3: There is no immediate need for a move; decisions must involve Michael and follow his best interests if he lacks capacity.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: A health visitor reviews Ava, 3, who is not yet walking unaided, uses no words and does not play with toys like her peers. Her parents ask whether she has a learning disability. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise a hearing test and no further action if the result is normal
Reassure them that development varies and review again at age 5
Tell them Ava has a learning disability and refer to adult social care
Refer for a developmental assessment with the community paediatric team
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Significant delay across several areas of development in a young child is usually described as global developmental delay and needs specialist assessment by a community paediatrician and multidisciplinary team, including hearing and vision checks, to find causes and start support early.

n.0: Hearing should be checked, but delay in walking and play needs wider assessment whatever the hearing result.
n.1: Waiting two years with significant delay in several areas would delay assessment and support.
n.2: A diagnosis cannot be given at a routine review, and adult social care is not the right service for a child.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ruby's parents have just been told that their newborn daughter has Down syndrome. They ask the nurse what causes the condition. Which explanation is accurate?
o: A deletion on the copy of chromosome 15 from the father
A new variant in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome
An expansion of CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene
An extra copy of chromosome 21 in the baby's cells
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Down syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), most often as standard trisomy, with translocation and mosaic forms less common (NHS.uk).

n.0: A paternal chromosome 15 deletion is the commonest cause of Prader-Willi syndrome.
n.1: MECP2 variants cause Rett syndrome.
n.2: CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 causes fragile X syndrome.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ruby, 4 days old, has Down syndrome. She is feeding well, is pink in air and no murmur was heard on the newborn examination. What should the nurse ensure before discharge from the postnatal ward?
o: Heart checks are deferred until she is old enough to manage an exercise test
A heart assessment is arranged if she becomes breathless or sweaty during feeds
A heart assessment is arranged if a murmur develops at the 6 to 8 week check
A heart assessment is arranged, as about half have a heart condition
Understanding Learning Disability.w: About half of babies with Down syndrome are born with a heart condition (NHS.uk), and serious defects can be present without a murmur or symptoms in the first days, so every baby with Down syndrome should have a planned heart assessment (echocardiogram) early in life.

n.0: Congenital heart defects need assessment in infancy, not years later.
n.1: Waiting for symptoms of heart failure delays diagnosis and surgery planning.
n.2: Waiting for a murmur risks missing a significant defect that may be silent in early weeks.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Robert, 38, has Down syndrome. His thyroid blood tests have been normal every year since childhood and he asks the practice nurse why he still needs them. Which reply is accurate?
o: Testing can drop to every five years once adult results stay normal
Testing continues until 40, when a dementia review replaces it
Testing can stop at 18 once the childhood results have all been normal
Thyroid risk rises with age, so yearly testing continues throughout life
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and the risk rises with age, so people with Down syndrome should have their thyroid tested every year throughout their life (DSMIG / Down's Syndrome Association guidance).

n.0: The recommended interval is yearly for life, not every five years.
n.1: Thyroid testing is not replaced by dementia review; untreated hypothyroidism can mimic dementia.
n.2: Thyroid disease often develops in adulthood, so normal childhood results do not end testing.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Lily, 5, has Down syndrome. Her teacher reports that over the past term she has stopped responding when her name is called and seems 'in her own world'. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Refer to the educational psychologist for an attention assessment
Arrange a hearing assessment, as hearing loss and glue ear are common
Refer to CAMHS because she may be showing new autistic features
Record the change as behaviour linked to her learning disability
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Hearing loss, including glue ear, is common in children with Down syndrome (NHS.uk). A child who stops responding to her name needs her hearing checked first, before other explanations are explored.

n.0: Attention assessment may follow, but hearing is the likely and treatable cause to check first.
n.2: Autism can occur with Down syndrome, but a treatable hearing problem should be excluded first.
n.3: Recording it as part of her learning disability is diagnostic overshadowing.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Carl, 41, has Down syndrome. Over six months he has become slower, gained weight, sleeps more and has less interest in his job. Staff at his home say it must be 'early dementia'. What should the nurse do first?
o: Request thyroid function tests and a physical health review
Refer him straight to the memory clinic for a dementia assessment
Increase his day activities to stimulate his memory and mood
Start a dementia care plan with simplified daily routines
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Two steps: recognise that slowing, weight gain and low mood can be hypothyroidism, which is common in Down syndrome and can mimic dementia or depression; then exclude it (and other physical causes such as sensory loss) before a dementia diagnosis is considered.

n.1: A memory assessment may follow, but treatable causes such as hypothyroidism should be excluded first.
n.2: Extra activity does not address a possible physical cause of his symptoms.
n.3: Planning dementia care before diagnosis risks missing a reversible cause.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Grace, 34, has Down syndrome and lives in a group home. She had pneumonia last winter. In September the practice nurse reviews how to reduce her risk of serious respiratory infection. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the GP to prescribe prophylactic antibiotics through the winter
Offer the annual flu vaccine, as she is in a clinical risk group
Wait until she next develops a cough before reviewing her chest
Advise that she stops attending day services from November to March
Understanding Learning Disability.w: People with Down syndrome have a weakened immune system and are more prone to chest infections and pneumonia (NHS.uk); people with a learning disability are in the clinical risk groups for the annual flu vaccine, and being on the GP register is the gateway to this priority.

n.0: Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not standard and add antimicrobial resistance risk.
n.2: Waiting for symptoms misses the chance to prevent serious infection.
n.3: Withdrawing her from day services restricts her life and is not an evidence-based prevention measure.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Emma, 28, has Down syndrome. Her mother has read about dementia and asks the learning disability nurse when they should talk about it. Which approach follows NICE NG96?
o: Raise the topic once Emma reaches 60, when dementia usually starts
Explain the link early to Emma and her family, and plan a baseline assessment
Discuss it with her mother and not with Emma, to avoid upsetting her
Avoid raising dementia until symptoms appear, to prevent needless worry
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE NG96 (1.5.36) advises explaining early to people with learning disabilities, particularly those with Down syndrome, and their families about the link with dementia. A baseline of skills and abilities in adulthood helps later change to be measured.

n.0: Dementia in Down syndrome usually starts much earlier than 60.
n.2: Emma has a right to accessible information about her own health; excluding her is not person-centred.
n.3: Waiting for symptoms means there is no baseline and no early planning.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Femi, 46, has Down syndrome and attends his annual health check with his support worker. Which question does NICE NG54 recommend asking to identify a possible need for dementia assessment?
o: Whether his behaviour, skills or need for prompting have changed recently
Whether his support workers would rate his mood as low on most days
Whether he can score above 24 on the mini mental state examination
Whether he has had any falls or trips at home in the past twelve months
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE NG54 1.5.4: at annual health checks for adults with Down syndrome, ask about any change in behaviour, loss of skills (including self-care) or a need for more prompting in recent months, which may indicate the need for dementia assessment.

n.1: Low mood should be explored but is not the NG54 dementia prompt.
n.2: The MMSE is not validated for people with a learning disability and is not what NG54 recommends here.
n.3: Falls matter, but NG54 links dementia screening to change in behaviour, skills and prompting.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Isla, 2, developed as expected until about 12 months. Since then she has lost the few words she had, stopped using her hands to pick up toys, and now repeatedly wrings her hands. Her parents report episodes of breath-holding. Which condition is most likely?
o: Prader-Willi syndrome
Rett syndrome
Fragile X syndrome
Angelman syndrome
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Rett syndrome (MECP2, almost exclusively girls) typically shows 6 to 18 months of apparently normal development followed by regression: loss of purposeful hand use with repetitive hand wringing, loss of speech and breathing irregularities (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.0: Prader-Willi presents with infant hypotonia and later hyperphagia, not regression.
n.2: Fragile X causes developmental delay and anxiety but not regression with loss of hand use.
n.3: Angelman syndrome causes severe speech impairment, ataxia and frequent laughter, but not a period of normal development followed by loss of hand use.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Noah, 5, has developmental delay, anxiety and hand-flapping. His paediatrician requests a genetic test. Which result would confirm fragile X syndrome?
o: More than 200 CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene
An extra copy of chromosome 21 in the cells
A pathogenic variant in the MECP2 gene
Loss of the maternal UBE3A gene on chromosome 15
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a full mutation in FMR1 on the X chromosome: more than 200 CGG repeats (typical range about 5 to 40), which silences the gene (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.1: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.
n.2: MECP2 variants cause Rett syndrome.
n.3: Loss of maternal UBE3A causes Angelman syndrome.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ms Ali has two children with fragile X syndrome. Her son has a moderate learning disability; her daughter has mild learning difficulties at school. She asks why her son is more affected. Which explanation is accurate?
o: Boys inherit two copies of the full mutation, one from each parent
Boys have one X chromosome, so they have no second working copy of FMR1
Girls are protected by higher oestrogen levels throughout childhood
The gene is carried on the Y chromosome, which passes from father to son
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Fragile X is X-linked: males have one X chromosome, so a full mutation affects all their cells' FMR1 expression, while females have a second X that usually carries a working copy. Males are therefore usually more severely affected; about a third of females have a learning disability (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.0: Males have one X chromosome, so they cannot inherit a copy from each parent.
n.2: Hormones do not explain the difference; it is due to the number of X chromosomes.
n.3: FMR1 is on the X chromosome, not the Y.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Jake, 16, has fragile X syndrome. At hospital outpatient appointments he becomes very anxious, avoids eye contact and flaps his hands in the busy waiting room. Which reasonable adjustment is most appropriate?
o: Request a dose of PRN lorazepam before every outpatient appointment
Offer the first appointment of the day and a quiet place to wait
Encourage him to hold eye contact so that he engages with the clinician
Ask his mother to wait outside so that he can practise independence
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Anxiety, social avoidance and gaze aversion are common in fragile X. Reducing waiting and sensory load (first or last appointment, a quiet space) is a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010 and avoids unnecessary medication (STOMP).

n.0: Routine sedation for anxiety is not first line; environmental adjustments come first (STOMP).
n.2: Gaze aversion is part of the condition; forcing eye contact increases anxiety.
n.3: Removing a trusted parent increases anxiety and reduces support for communication.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Claire, 30, is the sister of a man with fragile X syndrome. She has no learning disability and asks the practice nurse whether she could pass fragile X to her own children. What is the most accurate response?
o: No, because female carriers of fragile X would have a learning disability themselves
Yes, as women can carry a premutation without symptoms; offer genetic counselling
No, because fragile X arises as a new mutation in each affected child
Yes, and her risk can be judged from the result of her own IQ test
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Premutation carriers (about 55 to 200 CGG repeats) usually do not have a learning disability but can pass on a repeat that expands to a full mutation in their children. Claire should be offered genetic counselling and testing.

n.0: Premutation carriers usually have no learning disability, so her own abilities do not rule out carrier status.
n.2: Fragile X is usually inherited through families with premutations, not a new mutation each time.
n.3: Carrier status is shown by DNA testing of FMR1, not by an IQ test.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Sophie, 14, has Rett syndrome and is reviewed by the community learning disability nurse. Which complication is most important to monitor for as part of her condition?
o: Large ears and joint hypermobility
Curvature of the spine (scoliosis)
Hyperphagia with rapid weight gain
Early-onset Alzheimer's disease
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Scoliosis is a recognised feature of Rett syndrome, alongside seizures, breathing irregularities, slow growth and loss of hand use (MedlinePlus Genetics), and needs regular monitoring and postural care.

n.0: Large ears and flexible joints are features of fragile X syndrome.
n.2: Hyperphagia is characteristic of Prader-Willi syndrome; slow growth is more typical in Rett.
n.3: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease is linked with Down syndrome.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Mia, 20 months, has become withdrawn and has stopped babbling. Her parents are worried about autism. Which finding would most point towards Rett syndrome rather than autism alone?
o: Delay in developing first single words
Reduced eye contact with close family members
Loss of purposeful hand use with hand-wringing
Strong preference for the same daily routines
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Loss of previously acquired purposeful hand use replaced by repetitive hand-wringing, washing or clapping movements is the hallmark of Rett syndrome and is not a feature of autism.

n.0: Speech delay occurs in autism and many other conditions, so it does not distinguish Rett.
n.1: Reduced eye contact is common in autism and does not point to Rett.
n.3: Preference for routines is typical of autism, not specific to Rett.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Isla's parents are told that she has Rett syndrome caused by a MECP2 variant. Neither parent has symptoms. They ask about the chance of a future child being affected. What is the most accurate response?
o: Each future daughter has a 50% risk because the condition is X-linked dominant
Future sons have a higher risk than future daughters of being affected
The risk is 25%, as both parents must carry the variant
Most cases are new variants, so the risk is low; genetic counselling is advised
Understanding Learning Disability.w: More than 99% of Rett syndrome cases arise from a new (de novo) MECP2 variant not present in either parent (MedlinePlus Genetics), so recurrence risk is low, but families should be offered genetic counselling to discuss their individual situation.

n.0: A 50% risk would apply if a parent carried the variant; in nearly all families the variant is new.
n.1: Rett syndrome affects almost exclusively girls.
n.2: Rett is not autosomal recessive, so the 25% figure does not apply.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Leah, 6, has Prader-Willi syndrome. A student nurse on the children's ward asks what causes the condition. Which explanation is accurate?
o: Loss of function of the UBE3A gene on the copy of chromosome 15 from the mother
An extra copy of chromosome 21 present in most of the body's cells
Loss of function of genes on the copy of chromosome 15 from the father
A new variant in the MECP2 gene on one of the two X chromosomes
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of function of genes in the 15q11-q13 region of the paternally inherited chromosome 15: about 70% by paternal deletion and about 25% by maternal uniparental disomy (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.0: Loss of the maternal UBE3A gene causes Angelman syndrome.
n.1: An extra chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome.
n.3: MECP2 variants cause Rett syndrome.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Toby, 7, has a severe learning disability, uses no words, walks with a jerky, unsteady gait and has epilepsy. Staff describe him as laughing often and flapping his hands when excited. Which syndrome is most consistent with this picture?
o: Angelman syndrome
Fragile X syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome
Down syndrome
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Angelman syndrome (loss of maternal UBE3A) causes severe learning disability, minimal or no speech, ataxia, epilepsy, a happy excitable demeanour with frequent laughter and hand-flapping, and sleep problems (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.1: Fragile X usually causes a mild to moderate learning disability with speech, anxiety and social avoidance.
n.2: Prader-Willi typically causes a mild to moderate learning disability with hyperphagia, not ataxia and absent speech.
n.3: Down syndrome does not typically cause absent speech with ataxia and frequent laughter.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: The parents of Ollie, 2 months, who has just been diagnosed with Prader-Willi syndrome, ask what to expect with feeding. Which statement is accurate?
o: Feeding is often difficult in infancy; extreme hunger develops later in childhood
Rapid weight gain in infancy is expected because babies tend to be overfed
Extreme hunger is present from birth, so feeds should be restricted early
Poor feeding in infancy means that appetite will stay low throughout adult life
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Infants with Prader-Willi syndrome have hypotonia, a weak suck and feeding difficulties with poor growth; hyperphagia (extreme hunger) leading to overeating and obesity develops later in childhood (MedlinePlus Genetics).

n.1: Infants tend to have poor weight gain because of hypotonia and weak sucking.
n.2: Hyperphagia is not present at birth; infants usually feed poorly.
n.3: Appetite changes later in childhood to extreme hunger, so it does not stay low.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Dan, 24, has Prader-Willi syndrome and lives in supported living. He has taken food from housemates' cupboards and gained 6 kg in two months. Staff want to lock the kitchen. What must happen first?
o: Assess his capacity on food access and, if lacking, decide in his best interests
Lock the kitchen straight away, because hyperphagia justifies any food restriction
Lock the kitchen once his parents have agreed to it on his behalf
Leave the kitchen open and record his food choices as unwise decisions
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Two steps: locking the kitchen restricts Dan and his housemates, so it needs a lawful basis. Assess his capacity for this decision (MCA s2-3); if he lacks it, make a best interests decision (s4) choosing the least restrictive option (s1(6)), and review it regularly.

n.1: Restrictions need a lawful basis and proportionality; a diagnosis does not authorise any restriction.
n.2: Parents cannot consent on behalf of an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.
n.3: Calling his choices unwise assumes he has capacity, which has not been assessed, given the compulsive nature of hyperphagia.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Kerry, 19, has Prader-Willi syndrome and is attending her annual health check. Which health problem is most important to screen for because of her syndrome?
o: Breathing irregularities while awake, by an overnight study
Congenital heart disease, by arranging an echocardiogram
Type 2 diabetes, linked to weight gain from hyperphagia
Early-onset Alzheimer's disease, by a memory assessment
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Hyperphagia in Prader-Willi syndrome leads to overeating and obesity, with a raised risk of type 2 diabetes (MedlinePlus Genetics). Weight, diet support and diabetes screening are priorities at health checks.

n.0: Breathing irregularities while awake are a feature of Rett syndrome.
n.1: Congenital heart disease is strongly associated with Down syndrome, not Prader-Willi.
n.3: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease is associated with Down syndrome.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Toby, 8, has Angelman syndrome and epilepsy. He is admitted after a fall and keeps laughing while staff examine his swollen wrist. A nurse says he cannot be in much pain because he is laughing. What is the best response?
o: Explain that the laughter is a seizure and give his rescue medication
Explain that frequent laughter is part of his syndrome and does not exclude pain
Agree, as laughter shows he understands and is not frightened by the examination
Agree, as frequent laughter shows he is content and comfortable
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Frequent laughter and a happy demeanour are features of Angelman syndrome, so they cannot be taken as a sign of comfort. Pain should be assessed using his known pain cues and an observational tool, avoiding diagnostic overshadowing.

n.0: Laughter in Angelman syndrome is not usually a seizure; giving rescue medication without seizure activity is unsafe.
n.2: Laughter does not show understanding of the examination or absence of distress.
n.3: Assuming comfort from laughter risks missing pain from a likely injury.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Toby, 8, has Angelman syndrome and uses no spoken words. His new teaching assistant asks how best to communicate with him. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Offer signs, symbols or a communication aid alongside speech
Avoid signs and pictures, so that he is encouraged to develop speech
Speak more loudly, as hearing loss explains the lack of speech
Rely on written instructions, as reading is usually a relative strength
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Severe speech impairment is a core feature of Angelman syndrome. A total communication approach using signs, symbols, objects or a communication aid alongside speech gives him ways to understand and express himself.

n.1: Alternative communication supports rather than blocks speech, and withholding it removes his means of communicating.
n.2: The lack of speech is part of the syndrome, not caused by hearing loss.
n.3: Most people with Angelman syndrome have a severe learning disability and do not read.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: A genetics nurse explains to a student that two children each have the same deletion at 15q11-q13, yet one has Prader-Willi syndrome and the other Angelman syndrome. What determines which syndrome develops?
o: Whether the child also has an extra chromosome 21 present
Which parent the deleted chromosome 15 came from
How many CGG repeats the child carries in FMR1
Whether the child is male or female at birth
Understanding Learning Disability.w: This is genomic imprinting: genes in 15q11-q13 are expressed from one parent's copy only. A deletion on the paternal chromosome 15 causes Prader-Willi syndrome; on the maternal chromosome 15 it causes Angelman syndrome (loss of maternal UBE3A).

n.0: An extra chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome and does not determine these syndromes.
n.2: CGG repeats in FMR1 relate to fragile X syndrome, not chromosome 15.
n.3: Both syndromes affect males and females; sex does not decide which occurs.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: A support worker new to a residential home asks the learning disability nurse what cerebral palsy is. Which description is most accurate?
o: Permanent movement and posture disorders from non-progressive injury to the developing brain
A form of learning disability that is defined by difficulty with movement
An inherited muscle disease that causes gradually increasing weakness from early childhood
A progressive degeneration of the motor neurones in the spinal cord that begins in early childhood
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain. It is often accompanied by epilepsy, dysphagia, reflux, constipation and orthopaedic problems.

n.1: Cerebral palsy is a movement disorder; a learning disability may or may not occur with it.
n.2: Muscular dystrophies are inherited muscle diseases; cerebral palsy arises from the developing brain.
n.3: Motor neurone degeneration is progressive; the brain disturbance in cerebral palsy is not.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Jay, 30, has cerebral palsy and a moderate learning disability. Over a year he has walked less and needs more help to stand. His parents ask whether his cerebral palsy is getting worse. Which reply is most accurate?
o: The change shows the original brain injury is spreading, so an urgent brain scan is needed
Declining mobility in adults with cerebral palsy is usually caused by low motivation and should be managed with encouragement
Cerebral palsy worsens with age, so declining mobility is expected and needs no specific review
The brain injury is not progressive, but hip, spine and pain problems can worsen and need assessment
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Cerebral palsy results from a non-progressive brain disturbance, but musculoskeletal problems (hip displacement, scoliosis, contractures), pain and fatigue can increase over time. A change in function needs assessment rather than being accepted as part of the condition.

n.0: The original injury does not spread; secondary complications are the likely cause.
n.1: Attributing decline to motivation ignores likely physical causes such as pain.
n.2: Accepting decline as expected is diagnostic overshadowing and misses treatable causes.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ellie, 17, has profound and multiple learning disabilities and cerebral palsy and receives gastrostomy feeds. Staff report that she grimaces and coughs when laid flat after feeds, and she has had three chest infections this year. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Hip displacement causing pain on repositioning
Absence seizures triggered by the feeding routine
Gastro-oesophageal reflux with risk of aspiration
Constipation causing abdominal pain after feeds
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Reflux is common in cerebral palsy and PMLD. Distress and coughing when lying flat after feeds, with recurrent chest infections, suggest reflux with aspiration, which needs escalation, upright positioning and review of feeding (LeDeR pneumonia risk factors include reflux and postural problems).

n.0: Hip pain would link to movement, not specifically to lying flat after feeds with coughing.
n.1: Seizures do not explain the link with lying flat, coughing and chest infections.
n.3: Constipation is common but does not explain coughing when flat and recurrent chest infections.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Paul, 48, who had cerebral palsy and a severe learning disability, has died in hospital after aspiration pneumonia. The nurse sees a draft death certificate giving 'cerebral palsy' as the sole cause of death. What should the nurse do?
o: Raise it with the doctor, as the illness that caused death should be recorded
Accept it, as cerebral palsy is a recognised cause of death in adults
Advise leaving the cause of death blank until the LeDeR review is complete
Suggest recording 'learning disability' instead as the underlying condition
Understanding Learning Disability.w: LeDeR learning: people do not die 'of' cerebral palsy or learning disability but of illnesses such as pneumonia. Recording the disability as the sole cause hides avoidable deaths; NHS England guidance is that learning disability should never be given as a cause of death.

n.1: Cerebral palsy alone hides the actual cause, here aspiration pneumonia.
n.2: Death certification is not delayed for LeDeR; the review happens separately after notification.
n.3: Learning disability should not be recorded as a cause of death.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ali, 25, has profound and multiple learning disabilities. He is seen by a speech and language therapist, physiotherapist, dietitian, epilepsy nurse and wheelchair service. His mother says she is overwhelmed by appointments and conflicting advice. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Agree a named lead professional to coordinate care with the family
Transfer coordination of all his care to the GP practice
Reduce input to one service at a time to simplify his care
Ask his mother to coordinate appointments, as she knows Ali best
Understanding Learning Disability.w: People with PMLD have complex needs across many services. A named lead professional (care coordinator) working with the family integrates plans, reduces duplication and supports the carer, in line with NICE NG96 and NMC platform 7 on coordinating care for people with complex needs.

n.1: The GP is important but does not usually coordinate multiple specialist community services.
n.2: Withdrawing services risks harm; each service meets an essential need.
n.3: Placing coordination on a carer who is already overwhelmed increases her burden.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Steve, 36, has cerebral palsy and a severe learning disability and does not use words. He cries out and grips the hoist sling when moved and when staff dress his legs. A support worker suggests adding this to his behaviour plan. What should the nurse do?
o: Assess for hip or other musculoskeletal pain and review his analgesia
Hoist him less often to reduce the number of distressing transfers
Record it as behaviour that challenges to be managed in his support plan
Ask staff to dress him more quickly to shorten the distress
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Hip displacement, contractures and scoliosis are common in cerebral palsy and cause pain on movement. Crying out during transfers and leg dressing is likely pain communication, so it needs assessment and analgesia review rather than a behavioural label (avoid diagnostic overshadowing).

n.1: Reducing transfers affects his care and position changes without treating the cause.
n.2: Labelling pain as behaviour is diagnostic overshadowing and leaves pain untreated.
n.3: Faster dressing does not address the likely source of pain.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Sam, 22, has cerebral palsy with severe dysarthria and uses a communication aid. He does not have a learning disability. On admission, a nurse begins asking his mother questions about his symptoms. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Use simplified language and pictures, as for a person with a learning disability
Speak to Sam directly and allow time for him to use his aid
Continue with his mother, as she understands his speech more quickly
Ask closed yes or no questions throughout to save him effort
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Cerebral palsy does not imply a learning disability. Sam should be addressed directly as the patient, with time to use his communication aid (Accessible Information Standard; NMC Code 7.1-7.3). His mother may help only if he wishes.

n.0: He does not have a learning disability, so simplifying language assumes a need he does not have.
n.2: Directing questions to his mother bypasses Sam and his right to speak for himself.
n.3: Closed questions may help at times, but limiting him to them throughout restricts what he can tell staff.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Rosie, 30, has cerebral palsy and profound and multiple learning disabilities and takes two anti-seizure medicines. Today she is restless and grimacing, her abdomen is distended and her bowel chart shows no bowel movement for five days. What should the nurse do?
o: Recognise likely constipation and escalate for review today
Continue monitoring and recheck the bowel chart in two days
Give her PRN sedation as prescribed for agitation
Increase her water flushes and review again next week
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Two steps: interpret the signs (distension, distress, five days without bowels open, constipating medicines, reduced mobility) as likely constipation, which can be life-threatening and is still contributing to deaths in LeDeR; then escalate for same-day medical review and treatment.

n.1: Waiting two days risks obstruction or perforation.
n.2: Sedation masks distress without treating the cause and may worsen constipation.
n.3: Extra fluid may help prevention but does not treat established constipation with distension, and a week's delay is unsafe.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Liam, 26, has no learning disability. He tells his GP practice nurse that he struggles with social situations and has rigid routines, and asks whether he could be autistic. Which approach is in line with NICE CG142?
o: Use the AQ-10 and record a diagnosis of autism if he scores 6 or above
Request genetic testing before deciding whether to assess for autism
Consider the AQ-10 and offer full assessment if he scores 6 or above
Arrange an MRI brain scan to look for structural signs of autism
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE CG142 1.2.3: for adults with possible autism who do not have a moderate or severe learning disability, consider the AQ-10; a score of 6 or above, or clinical suspicion, should lead to an offer of comprehensive assessment.

n.0: The AQ-10 is a screening tool; it identifies who needs a comprehensive assessment and does not make a diagnosis.
n.1: Genetic tests are not used routinely to diagnose autism.
n.3: CG142 advises against routine neuroimaging for diagnosing autism.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: The father of Chloe, 22, who is being assessed for autism, asks the nurse to arrange a brain scan and blood tests 'to prove it one way or the other'. Which response follows NICE CG142?
o: Arrange an MRI scan if the clinical assessment is inconclusive
Arrange an EEG, because it is the investigation that confirms autism
Arrange blood tests, as a genetic marker confirms most cases of autism
Explain that scans and blood tests are not routine for diagnosing autism
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE CG142 1.2.11: do not routinely use biological tests, genetic tests or neuroimaging for the purposes of diagnosing autism in adults. Diagnosis is made by comprehensive clinical assessment.

n.0: An inconclusive assessment is resolved by further clinical assessment, not routine neuroimaging.
n.1: There is no EEG test that confirms autism; EEG is used if seizures are suspected.
n.2: No single genetic marker confirms autism in most people.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Mr Patel tells the learning disability nurse that he has read online that a gluten-free, casein-free diet will reduce his autistic son's social difficulties, and he wants to start it. His son has no gut symptoms. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer to a dietitian so that the diet can be started safely
Agree, as exclusion diets are low risk and may help some autistic people
Support a three-month trial of the diet and review social skills afterwards
Explain that NICE advises against exclusion diets for the core features of autism
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE advises against exclusion diets such as gluten-free or casein-free diets for the core features of autism (CG170 1.3.2 for children and young people; CG142 1.4.15 for adults, which also covers vitamins, minerals and dietary supplements). The nurse should explain this respectfully and discuss evidence-based support.

n.0: Starting the diet safely still means offering an intervention NICE advises against.
n.1: Restrictive diets can affect nutrition and are not recommended for core features.
n.2: NICE does not recommend trialling exclusion diets for core features of autism.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ben, 9, is autistic and has a moderate learning disability. His mother asks whether a medicine could reduce his repetitive behaviours and help him make friends. What does NICE CG170 advise?
o: Medication is not recommended to treat the core features of autism
An antidepressant can be started to reduce repetitive behaviours
An anticonvulsant can reduce core features if an EEG is normal
A low-dose antipsychotic can be trialled for social difficulties
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE CG170 1.3.2: do not use antipsychotics, antidepressants, anticonvulsants or exclusion diets for the management of the core features of autism in children and young people. Psychosocial interventions are used instead.

n.1: Antidepressants are not recommended for core features of autism in children.
n.2: Anticonvulsants are not recommended for core features whatever the EEG shows.
n.3: Antipsychotics are not recommended for core features; they have a limited role in severe behaviour that challenges.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Kwame, 30, is autistic and has a mild learning disability. His aggression at home has had a limited response to a psychosocial intervention, and his psychiatrist is considering an antipsychotic. Which plan is consistent with NICE CG142?
o: Replace the psychosocial intervention with the antipsychotic to avoid duplication
Prescribe two antipsychotics at low doses to reduce the risk of side effects
Continue the antipsychotic for six months before reviewing whether it has helped
Give it alongside the psychosocial intervention and review benefit at 3 to 4 weeks
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE CG142 1.5.7: consider antipsychotic medication in conjunction with a psychosocial intervention for behaviour that challenges when there has been no or limited response to psychosocial or other interventions. It should be prescribed by a specialist, with quality of life outcomes monitored; review the effects after 3 to 4 weeks and stop it if there is no clinically important response at 6 weeks. This also reflects STOMP.

n.0: Medication should be combined with, not replace, psychosocial intervention.
n.1: Two antipsychotics increase side-effect risk; a single drug at the lowest effective dose is used.
n.2: Review is due at 3 to 4 weeks, not after six months.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Ryan, 12, is autistic and finds noise, bright light and waiting very distressing. He is due for a dental check at a busy community clinic. Which adjustment reflects NICE CG170?
o: Send a written reminder to his parents the day before the visit
Book a mid-morning appointment when the clinic is fully staffed
Ask a staff member to sit with him in the main waiting area throughout
Offer the first or last appointment of the day and a quiet place
Understanding Learning Disability.w: NICE CG170 1.1.9-1.1.10 advises adjusting the environment for autistic children and young people, including attention to lighting, noise and personal space, and offering appointments at the beginning or end of the day to minimise waiting.

n.0: A reminder is helpful but does not reduce the sensory load or wait.
n.1: A mid-morning slot is likely to involve more waiting and a busier environment.
n.2: Company does not remove the noise, light and waiting that cause his distress.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Femi, 34, is autistic. During admission he tells the nurse that he prefers to be called 'an autistic person' rather than 'a person with autism'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Use the term he prefers and record his preference in his notes
Use the term 'suffers from autism', as it is the clinical wording
Explain that person-first language is the required NHS style
Remove any reference to autism from his care plan to respect him
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Person-centred practice (NMC Code 1 and 2) means respecting how someone describes their own identity; many autistic people prefer identity-first language, and NICE's 2021 surveillance updated its own wording to 'autistic people'. Recording the preference helps all staff use it.

n.1: 'Suffers from' is a deficit-based phrase and is not what he asked for.
n.2: There is no NHS rule overriding a person's preferred description of their identity.
n.3: Autism is relevant to his care and reasonable adjustments, so it should stay in his plan.

Understanding Learning Disability.q: Joe, 35, has a severe learning disability. His carers notice that he becomes very distressed when routines change, avoids eye contact and lines up objects. His GP asks how to begin assessing for possible autism. What does NICE CG142 recommend?
o: Use the AQ-10 and refer for full assessment if he scores 6 or above
Arrange neuroimaging to separate autism from his learning disability
Do not assess, as autism cannot be diagnosed alongside a severe learning disability
Consider a brief assessment of autism-related difficulties instead of the AQ-10
Understanding Learning Disability.w: Two steps: recognise that the AQ-10 is for adults without a moderate or severe learning disability; for adults with a moderate or severe learning disability, CG142 1.2.4 advises a brief assessment (asking about social interaction, communication and stereotyped behaviour), leading to comprehensive assessment if indicated.
