n.0: Detailed questioning can contaminate evidence; investigation is for the police and safeguarding team.
n.1: Waiting leaves her at risk and ignores a clear communication.
n.3: Approaching the alleged abuser may put Lucy at risk and compromise evidence.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: At a residential service for people with learning disabilities, a nurse notices that everyone is woken at 6am, clothing is shared from a communal store, and visitors may come only on Sundays. Which category of abuse is most likely?
o: Organisational abuse
Discriminatory abuse
Domestic abuse
Self-neglect
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: Organisational (institutional) abuse includes neglect and poor practice within a service, such as rigid routines, lack of personal possessions and restricted visiting that suit the service rather than individuals (Care and Support Statutory Guidance ch.14).

n.1: Discriminatory abuse targets a protected characteristic; here the pattern comes from the service's regime.
n.2: Domestic abuse occurs within family or intimate relationships.
n.3: Self-neglect concerns a person's own care of themselves.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Kelly, 39, has a moderate learning disability and lacks capacity to manage her finances. A neighbour has started collecting her benefits and keeps most of the money, giving Kelly a small allowance. Kelly says she likes the neighbour and is happy. What should the community nurse do?
o: Raise a safeguarding concern, as Kelly meets the section 42 criteria
Respect Kelly's wishes, as she is happy with the arrangement
Ask the neighbour to keep receipts for everything that is spent
Apply to become Kelly's benefits appointee to control the money
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: Two steps: Kelly has care and support needs, is at risk of financial abuse and, lacking capacity about money, cannot protect herself (Care Act s42); so raise a safeguarding concern. Her wishes are important but do not remove the duty to protect.

n.1: Her wishes matter but she lacks capacity about finances and is at risk.
n.2: Receipts do not stop the neighbour keeping her money and do not address the abuse.
n.3: A nurse becoming her appointee creates a conflict of interest and bypasses safeguarding.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Paul, 31, has a mild learning disability and lives in supported living. He tells his keyworker he has a girlfriend he met at college. A support worker says people like Paul 'shouldn't really be in relationships'. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Support it, as Paul has the same right to relationships as anyone else
Ask the GP to decide whether the relationship is in Paul's best interests
Discourage the relationship until his family have given their agreement
Allow the relationship with staff supervising all of their meetings
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: People with a learning disability have the same right to private and family life, including relationships, as everyone else (Article 8 HRA; UNCRPD Article 23). Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)), and staff should support Paul, including with accessible information about relationships and safety.

n.1: Best interests decisions apply only to people lacking capacity, and decisions about sexual relations cannot be made for a person under the MCA (s27).
n.2: An adult's relationships do not need family approval.
n.3: Blanket supervision is a disproportionate restriction without any identified risk.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: A nurse is preparing to assess whether Lily, 25, who has a learning disability, has capacity to decide to engage in sexual relations. Following A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52, which information must Lily be able to understand as part of the decision?
o: That her family must be told about any sexual relationship she has
That a written agreement is needed before any sexual activity
That marriage is required before sexual activity becomes lawful
That the other person must be able to consent and consent throughout
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: In JB the Supreme Court upheld the Court of Appeal: the information relevant to the decision includes that the other person must have the capacity to consent to the sexual activity and must in fact consent before and throughout it, as well as the mechanics of sex, health risks and the risk of pregnancy.

n.0: An adult does not need to tell her family about a relationship.
n.1: There is no legal requirement for a written agreement.
n.2: Sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful without marriage.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Mia, 19, has a mild learning disability and asks her community nurse about contraception because she has a new boyfriend. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give accessible information and offer support to attend a sexual health clinic
Discuss contraception with her mother so that she can explain it to Mia
Advise Mia to wait until staff have formally assessed her capacity
Arrange a contraceptive implant for Mia in her best interests
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: Mia is presumed to have capacity (MCA s1(2)) and has the right to sexual health information and services. Accessible (easy read, pictorial) information and support to attend a clinic is a reasonable adjustment and respects her confidentiality.

n.1: Speaking to her mother breaches her confidentiality and bypasses Mia.
n.2: Capacity is presumed; there is no reason given to doubt it.
n.3: There is no basis for a best interests decision when she is presumed to have capacity and is asking for information.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: A nurse learns that Dan, a support worker, has begun a sexual relationship with Jess, 28, a woman with a learning disability whom he supports at her home. Jess says she consents and is happy. What is the correct position?
o: It is lawful if Jess is assessed as having capacity to consent to sex
It is lawful, because both are adults and Jess has said she consents
It is a likely criminal offence by a care worker and must be raised as safeguarding
It is a disciplinary matter for his employer rather than a safeguarding issue
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: The Sexual Offences Act 2003 (ss38-41) makes sexual activity by a care worker with a person with a mental disorder, including a learning disability, an offence whether or not the person appears to consent, because of the imbalance of power in the care relationship. A safeguarding concern and police referral are required.

n.0: The care worker offences apply even if the person has capacity.
n.1: Apparent consent is not a defence to the care worker offences.
n.3: Employer discipline does not replace safeguarding and police involvement.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Sasha, 24, has a mild learning disability and is 20 weeks pregnant. A professional suggests a referral to children's social care 'because of her learning disability'. There are no other concerns. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Assess her support needs as a parent and offer adapted support
Wait until the baby is born before considering any support
Plan for the baby to be placed with her grandparents at birth
Make a child protection referral because of her learning disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: A learning disability alone is not evidence that a child is at risk. Parents with a learning disability should have their needs assessed early and receive adapted, ongoing support; referral to children's social care follows if there are actual concerns about the child (balanced safeguarding; Equality Act 2010).

n.1: Delaying support until after birth misses the chance to prepare and support her.
n.2: Planning removal without evidence of risk breaches Article 8 and is discriminatory.
n.3: A diagnosis alone is not a child protection concern and assuming risk is discriminatory.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Sasha, 24, has a mild learning disability and has just had her first baby. She is learning to make up formula feeds safely before discharge home. Which teaching approach is most likely to help?
o: Show the steps practically with pictures and repeat them over time
Explain the full process once in detail on the day of discharge
Ask her partner to make all the feeds until she feels confident
Give her the standard written leaflet on formula feeds to take home and keep
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: People with a learning disability learn best through practical demonstration, accessible pictorial step-by-step guides, repetition and positive reinforcement (NMC Annexe A 2.6). Ongoing support at home should continue after discharge.

n.1: A single detailed explanation is hard to retain and does not allow practice.
n.2: This removes her opportunity to learn and parent her baby.
n.3: A standard leaflet may not be accessible to Sasha.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Tom, 30, has a severe learning disability and lives in a group home. Staff report that he has started masturbating in the shared lounge. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask the GP to prescribe medication to reduce his sex drive
Lock his bedroom during the day so he spends time in shared areas
Support him to learn that his bedroom is a private place for this
Raise a safeguarding concern that Tom is sexually abusing others
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: Sexual expression is a normal part of life. The aim is to teach and support privacy, using consistent, accessible prompts and guiding him to his room, as part of a person-centred plan. Medication to suppress sexuality is not a first-line response (STOMP).

n.0: Using medication to suppress libido is a restrictive response that does not teach privacy.
n.1: Locking his room removes the private place he needs and is a blanket restriction.
n.3: Masturbation in a shared space needs support and teaching; it is not in itself sexual abuse of others.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Leah, 23, has a moderate learning disability and lives with her parents. She wants to move in with her boyfriend. Her parents strongly object and ask the nurse to stop her. What should the nurse do?
o: Advise Leah to wait until she is 25, when the decision becomes hers
Follow her parents' wishes, as they are her main carers
Assess her capacity with accessible information; if present, support her choice
Arrange a best interests meeting with her parents to decide where Leah lives
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: Two steps: capacity is presumed and decision-specific, so if in doubt it is assessed for where to live, using accessible information and all practicable steps (MCA s1-3); if Leah has capacity, the decision is hers, and her parents' views do not override it.

n.0: Adults make their own decisions from 18 (and the MCA applies from 16); there is no age 25 rule.
n.1: Parents of an adult cannot decide where she lives unless they hold legal authority.
n.3: A best interests meeting is premature; it applies only if she lacks capacity.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Josh, 25, has a moderate learning disability and is refusing a blood test on the medical ward. The doctor says, 'He has a learning disability, so he can't consent; just do it in his best interests.' What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Ask his mother to give consent for the test as his next of kin
Explain that capacity is assessed for this decision, not assumed from diagnosis
Agree, as a moderate learning disability means he cannot weigh up information
Agree, as a blood test is a minor procedure that needs no consent
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it; s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a condition. Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed for this blood test.

n.0: A next of kin cannot consent for an adult without a relevant LPA or deputyship.
n.2: A diagnosis of learning disability never by itself establishes lack of capacity.
n.3: Every intervention, including a blood test, needs valid consent or another lawful basis.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Mel, 38, has a moderate learning disability and needs a tooth extraction under local anaesthetic. Before anyone concludes that she lacks capacity to decide, which step is most important?
o: Ask her a series of yes or no questions to check her understanding
Give her the standard information leaflet used for all patients
Explain the procedure verbally twice and then ask for her decision
Use pictures and her communication passport, with someone who knows her
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: MCA s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. For Mel this means accessible information, her usual communication methods, a supporter who knows her, and the right time and place.

n.0: Yes or no questions risk acquiescence and do not show real understanding.
n.1: A standard leaflet is not accessible for many people with a moderate learning disability.
n.2: Repeating spoken information does not adapt it to her communication needs.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Adam, 30, has a mild learning disability and lives in his own flat with some support. He has been assessed as having capacity about his diet. He chooses to eat takeaway food most nights despite advice about his weight. What should the community nurse do?
o: Ask his support workers to stop him from ordering takeaway food
Ask the GP to make a best interests decision about his diet
Record that he lacks capacity because the choice harms his health
Respect his decision and keep offering accessible health information
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: MCA s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Adam has capacity, so his choice stands; the nurse continues health promotion in an accessible way.

n.0: Restricting a capacitous adult's choices has no legal basis.
n.1: Best interests decisions are made for people who lack capacity, which Adam does not.
n.2: An unwise choice does not establish a lack of capacity.

Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.t: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.q: Ravi, 29, has a learning disability. During a capacity assessment about a hernia operation he understands and weighs the information and gives a clear decision, but the next day he cannot remember the discussion. Does his short retention prevent him having capacity for the decision?
o: Yes, because he must be able to write down what he has been told
Yes, because retention for at least a week is needed for surgery
No, because retaining it long enough to make the decision is enough
Yes, because he must be able to recall the information the following day
Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning.w: MCA s3(3): the fact that a person can retain information relevant to a decision for a short period only does not prevent them from being regarded as able to make the decision. Aids such as an easy read summary can help him later.

n.0: Writing is not required; the test concerns understanding, retaining, using or weighing, and communicating.
n.1: There is no minimum retention period such as a week.
n.3: The Act does not require recall the next day.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Lee, 45, who has a moderate learning disability, dies on a surgical ward after a bowel obstruction was recognised late. The ward sister tells Chloe, his named nurse, that the trust's own incident review will cover everything so no other notification is needed. What is the most appropriate action for Chloe?
o: Notify LeDeR and report the delayed diagnosis through the incident system
Ask Lee's GP to notify LeDeR, because notifications must come from primary care
Wait for the trust review to finish and then decide whether LeDeR is needed
Notify the coroner and leave the review of Lee's care to the inquest
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Anyone can notify LeDeR, including hospital staff (leder.nhs.uk), and a delay in recognising illness should also be reported as a patient safety incident so the organisation can learn (PSIRF; Code 19). The two processes run alongside each other.

n.1: LeDeR accepts notifications from anyone, including ward nurses and families; there is no primary care rule.
n.2: Waiting delays the national review and risks the death never being notified; both processes can start now.
n.3: An inquest decides how the person died; it does not replace LeDeR's review of the person's care or the trust's incident learning.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: An integrated care board's LeDeR reviews found that several people waited weeks for blood tests and scans because hospital staff had not planned adjustments such as longer slots or sedation. Hana, a learning disability liaison nurse, is asked to propose one change. Which proposal best addresses this learning?
o: Admit adults with a learning disability to a side room on every admission
Check the reasonable adjustment flag before tests and plan adjustments in advance
Refer every adult with a learning disability to the liaison team after admission
Ask families to attend each appointment so they can explain needs to staff
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: LeDeR repeatedly identifies missing reasonable adjustments and delays to tests and treatment. The Equality Act 2010 duty is anticipatory, and the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag exists so that recorded adjustments are seen and acted on before care is delivered (LeDeR 2023; DAPB4019).

n.0: A blanket side room is not person-centred and does not address the planning failure behind the delayed tests.
n.2: Referral after admission comes too late for outpatient tests and scans; adjustments need planning before the appointment.
n.3: Families are valuable partners, but the duty to adjust rests with the service; relying on relatives shifts the burden and fails people without family.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ruth, 58, has a mild learning disability and lives with support. Her bowel cancer screening kit has been returned unused twice, and her support worker says Ruth found the instructions confusing. LeDeR has highlighted later diagnosis of bowel cancer in people with a learning disability. What should the community nurse do first?
o: Use an easy read guide and support Ruth to decide about completing the kit
Record that Ruth has declined screening and remove her from the recall list
Ask the GP to refer Ruth straight for colonoscopy because she is high risk
Wait until her next annual health check to raise screening with the GP
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: LeDeR reports bowel cancer diagnosed later and more often fatal in people with a learning disability, with low screening uptake. The barrier here is accessible information, so the first step is easy read material and support to make an informed choice (MCA s1(3) all practicable steps; Accessible Information Standard).

n.1: Returning a kit unused because the instructions were confusing is not an informed refusal; recording a decline would perpetuate the inequality.
n.2: Ruth has no symptoms; screening starts with the home test kit, and jumping to an invasive test without her informed consent is inappropriate.
n.3: Waiting adds months of delay when the barrier can be addressed now.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Priya, a community learning disability nurse, is preparing a briefing for her ICB on the January 2026 republished LeDeR report for 2023. She wants one accurate headline about how many adult deaths were rated avoidable. Which statement should she use?
o: About 2 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable, matching the general population
About 1 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
About 4 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
About 7 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The revised 2023 report rated 40.2% of adult deaths as avoidable (about 4 in 10), slightly higher than first published before the report was withdrawn for data errors and republished on 27 January 2026 (LeDeR 2023 revised).

n.0: About 22% is the comparable general population figure cited for 2022; people with a learning disability were roughly twice as likely to die avoidably.
n.1: 1 in 10 greatly understates the reported figure of about 40%.
n.3: 7 in 10 overstates the reported figure of about 40%.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Tunde, a student learning disability nurse, is writing an essay on how healthcare for people with a learning disability came under scrutiny. He needs the 2007 Mencap report that described the deaths of six people in NHS care and argued that the NHS institutionally discriminated against them. Which report is this?
o: Death by Indifference
Healthcare for All
The Confidential Inquiry (CIPOLD)
Building the Right Support
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Mencap's Death by Indifference (2007) set out six avoidable deaths of people with a learning disability in NHS care and alleged institutional discrimination. On publication the Health Secretary ordered an independent inquiry led by Sir Jonathan Michael (Mencap).

n.1: Healthcare for All (2008) was the independent inquiry set up in response to Death by Indifference, not the Mencap report itself.
n.2: CIPOLD (2013) reviewed a large population of deaths in south west England; it did not focus on six cases.
n.3: Building the Right Support (2015) is the national plan to reduce inpatient care after Winterbourne View.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ffion, a practice educator, is teaching newly qualified nurses about the Confidential Inquiry into Premature Deaths of People with Learning Disabilities (CIPOLD, 2013). Which finding about life expectancy should she present?
o: Men died about 20 years and women about 13 years earlier than the general population
Men and women each died about 10 years earlier than the general population
Men died about 13 years and women about 20 years earlier than the general population
Men died about 5 years and women about 8 years earlier than the general population
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: CIPOLD (Heslop et al., 2013) found men with a learning disability died on average 13 years earlier, and women 20 years earlier, than men and women in the general population.

n.0: The figures are reversed; the gap was larger for women (20 years) than for men (13 years).
n.1: CIPOLD found different gaps for men and women (13 and 20 years), both longer than 10 years.
n.3: These figures greatly understate the gaps CIPOLD reported.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: During a governance meeting, Marcus, a learning disability nurse consultant, explains that one CIPOLD recommendation led to a permanent national programme in England. Which change followed from that recommendation?
o: A national programme reviewing the deaths of people with a learning disability
A legal duty to offer annual health checks to people on GP registers
A statutory right to an independent mental capacity advocate
Statutory learning disability and autism training for CQC-registered providers
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: CIPOLD recommended a national learning disability mortality review body; this became the LeDeR programme, which now reviews the deaths of people with a learning disability and autistic people (CIPOLD 2013; LeDeR).

n.1: Annual health checks are an NHS contractual scheme that predates CIPOLD; they are not a legal duty created by it.
n.2: IMCAs were created by the Mental Capacity Act 2005, before CIPOLD reported.
n.3: Statutory training came from section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 after Oliver McGowan's death, not from CIPOLD.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Jodie, a nurse new to a community learning disability team, is told that a 2011 BBC Panorama programme exposed the abuse of patients at Winterbourne View, a private inpatient hospital. Which national programme was the government's direct response?
o: The Transforming Care programme
The LeDeR mortality review programme
The Valuing People white paper
The STOMP medicines programme
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: After Winterbourne View the Department of Health published Transforming Care (2012), which aimed to move people out of inpatient units into community support; this led to Building the Right Support (2015) and the 2022 action plan (Commons Library SN07058).

n.1: LeDeR reviews deaths and grew from CIPOLD's recommendations, not the Winterbourne View response.
n.2: Valuing People was the 2001 learning disability white paper, ten years before Winterbourne View.
n.3: STOMP (2016) tackles overuse of psychotropic medicines; it was not the direct policy response to Winterbourne View.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Nadia, a learning disability nurse, is preparing a briefing on inpatient care. She needs to state the Building the Right Support target for people with a learning disability and autistic people in mental health inpatient settings in England, and whether it was met. Which statement is accurate?
o: Close every specialist inpatient unit by March 2020; the target was missed
Halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 compared with 2015; the target was missed
Reduce inpatient numbers by a quarter by March 2030; progress is on track
Halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 compared with 2015; the target was met
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The Building the Right Support action plan (July 2022) aimed to halve the number of inpatients by March 2024 against March 2015. In February 2025 there were 2,055 inpatients, down about 29% from 2,905, so the target was missed (Commons Library SN07058).

n.0: The policy aimed to reduce reliance on inpatient care, not to close all specialist units by 2020.
n.2: The target was a halving by March 2024, not a quarter by 2030.
n.3: The target was not met; the fall was about 29%, short of 50%.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Kemi, a newly qualified nurse on an assessment and treatment unit, notices staff mocking a patient, restraint episodes left unrecorded and families discouraged from visiting the ward. Mindful of the lessons of Winterbourne View and Whorlton Hall, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Speak privately to the staff involved and monitor whether it continues
Record her observations in her reflective account for revalidation
Raise the concern at the next team meeting so standards can be agreed together
Escalate promptly to senior managers and the safeguarding lead
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: These are warning signs of a closed culture and possible abuse. The Code requires nurses to act without delay where there is a risk to patient safety, raising and escalating concerns (standard 16 and 16.1), and to raise concerns immediately where a person is vulnerable or at risk (standard 17 and 17.1), using whistleblowing routes if needed; safeguarding procedures must be followed (Care Act 2014 s42).

n.0: Informal monitoring allows abuse to continue and leaves no formal record; escalation is required.
n.1: Reflection is no substitute for acting; patients remain at risk while nothing is reported.
n.2: Waiting for a team meeting delays protection and may expose the concern to the people involved.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Owen, a learning disability liaison nurse, is presenting CIPOLD data to hospital consultants. He wants to compare the proportion of deaths from causes amenable to good-quality healthcare in people with and without a learning disability. Which comparison is correct?
o: 20% in people with a learning disability compared with 13% in the general population
50% in people with a learning disability compared with 25% in the general population
37% in people with a learning disability compared with 13% in the general population
13% in people with a learning disability compared with 37% in the general population
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: CIPOLD (2013) found 37% of deaths of people with a learning disability were from causes amenable to good-quality healthcare, compared with 13% in the general population.

n.0: 20% understates the CIPOLD figure of 37% for people with a learning disability.
n.1: These are not the CIPOLD figures; 37% and 13% were reported.
n.3: The figures are reversed; people with a learning disability had the higher proportion.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Bethan, a ward manager, asks her learning disability liaison nurse which theme runs through Death by Indifference, CIPOLD and the LeDeR reports, so that staff training can target it. Which theme should the liaison nurse identify?
o: A shortage of specialist learning disability inpatient beds nationally
Too many early referrals to specialist palliative care services
Over-reliance on community nurses in place of GP review
Delayed diagnosis and treatment, with family concerns not acted on
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: All three identify delays in recognising and treating illness, failures to make reasonable adjustments, diagnostic overshadowing and not listening to families and carers who know the person (Death by Indifference 2007; CIPOLD 2013; LeDeR 2023).

n.0: National policy aims to reduce reliance on inpatient beds; the reports did not identify bed shortages as the cause of avoidable deaths.
n.1: The reports raised concerns about end-of-life decisions, but early palliative referral was not a recurring cause of avoidable death.
n.2: The reports did not attribute deaths to community nurses replacing GP review.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Mia, 14, has a moderate learning disability and is on her GP practice's learning disability register. Her mother asks the school nurse whether Mia can now have a learning disability annual health check. What is the correct answer?
o: Yes, but checks are offered every three years until she is 18
No, the checks start at 18 once she moves to adult services
Yes, a free check is offered each year from age 14
No, the checks start at 16 when she can consent for herself
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Anyone aged 14 or over on the GP learning disability register can have a free annual health check once a year (NHS.uk, Annual health checks, reviewed September 2025). Starting at 14 also supports transition planning.

n.0: The check is annual from 14, not three-yearly.
n.1: Checks begin at 14 so they overlap with transition planning; they do not wait for adult services.
n.3: The scheme starts at 14, not 16; at 14 consent is handled through Gillick competence or by a person with parental responsibility, not by delaying the check.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Jordan, 29, has a learning disability and has just had his annual health check. The practice nurse found raised blood pressure and that he has not seen a dentist for three years. Where should the agreed actions be recorded so Jordan and his supporters can follow them?
o: In his hospital passport held by the ward
In a behaviour support plan written by the team
In a health action plan agreed with Jordan
In a care and support plan from the local authority
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Actions from the annual health check are written into a health action plan, which sets out what will be done, by whom and when, in a format the person can use (NHS.uk, Annual health checks).

n.0: A hospital passport tells hospital staff about the person on admission; it is not where annual health check actions are tracked.
n.1: A behaviour support plan addresses behaviour that challenges, not general health actions such as blood pressure and dental care.
n.3: A Care Act care and support plan covers social care needs; health actions belong in the health action plan.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Lucy, 33, has a mild learning disability and lives alone with a few hours of support. She has never been invited for a learning disability annual health check, and the community nurse finds she is not on her GP practice's learning disability register. What should the nurse do first?
o: Arrange for the community team to carry out the annual check at home
With Lucy's agreement, ask the practice to add her to the register
Advise Lucy to request a health check at the local walk-in centre
Ask the GP to book her an NHS Health Check, which covers the same review
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Being on the GP learning disability register is the gateway to annual health checks, health action plans and many reasonable adjustments; only about a quarter of people with a learning disability are on registers (NHS.uk; Mencap).

n.0: Annual health checks are provided by GP practices; the gap here is the missing register entry.
n.2: Walk-in centres do not provide learning disability annual health checks or hold the register.
n.3: The NHS Health Check is a different programme for adults aged 40 to 74 and does not replace the learning disability annual check.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ahmed, 41, has a severe learning disability and limited speech. His GP practice is booking his annual health check. Following NICE NG11, who should ideally attend with him?
o: A social worker from the local authority
An independent mental capacity advocate
A family member or carer who knows him well
A positive behaviour support practitioner
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: NICE NG11 (1.2.1) recommends that the annual physical health check is carried out with a family member, carer or other person who knows the person well, so changes from their usual presentation can be recognised.

n.0: A social worker is not routinely needed and may not know Ahmed's usual health and behaviour.
n.1: An IMCA is instructed for specific serious decisions when there is no one appropriate to consult; it is not the person NICE names for health checks.
n.3: A PBS practitioner may contribute where behaviour is a concern, but NICE recommends someone who knows the person well.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Simone, 37, has Down syndrome and attends her annual health check with her support worker. She has no new symptoms. Alongside the standard check, which additional test should be offered every year?
o: An X-ray of the cervical spine
A resting electrocardiogram
A cervical screening test
A thyroid function blood test
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and the risk rises with age, so thyroid function should be tested every year throughout life (DSMIG thyroid guideline; Down's Syndrome Association).

n.0: Routine X-ray screening of the neck is not recommended in adults without symptoms.
n.1: Heart problems are common from birth, but an annual ECG is not part of routine surveillance in an adult without symptoms.
n.2: Cervical screening follows the national recall schedule of several years between tests, not an annual test.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Kieran, 26, has a learning disability and takes risperidone prescribed for behaviour that challenges. His learning disability nurse is helping the GP practice prepare his annual health check. According to NICE NG11, which area should the check specifically review?
o: A full functional assessment of his behaviour by a clinical psychologist
His medicines and side effects, and links between behaviour and physical health
A capacity assessment covering each of his major life decisions
A repeat IQ test to confirm the severity of his learning disability
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: NICE NG11 (1.2.1) says the annual health check should include reviewing behaviour that challenges and any links with physical health, and reviewing medication including side effects.

n.0: Functional assessment is a specialist process when behaviour is a concern, not a routine element of the GP check.
n.2: Capacity is decision-specific and assessed when a decision arises, not as a blanket review at the health check.
n.3: Re-testing IQ is not part of the annual health check and does not change his care.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Jamal, 31, is autistic with a learning disability. He has not attended his annual health check for two years; letters were sent each time. The practice manager suggests removing him from the recall list. What should the community learning disability nurse do?
o: Send a second standard reminder letter with a fixed appointment time
Find out the barriers with Jamal and his supporters and plan adjustments
Agree to removal, as two missed appointments show an informed refusal
Ask the GP to complete the check from his records without seeing him
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Non-attendance often reflects barriers such as inaccessible letters, waiting rooms or anxiety. The Equality Act 2010 s20 duty requires adjustments, so the nurse should explore barriers and arrange adjustments such as easy read invitations, a quiet first appointment or a home visit (NICE NG11; Accessible Information Standard).

n.0: Repeating the same inaccessible approach is unlikely to work; the barriers need identifying first.
n.2: Missed appointments after standard letters do not show an informed decision; removing him would widen the inequality.
n.3: A records review misses the physical examination and conversation that make the check useful.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Paula, 46, has Down syndrome. At her annual health check her sister says that over recent months Paula needs more prompting to dress and has lost interest in her day centre. Paula has no physical complaints. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse?
o: Refer Paula to the memory clinic and ask that a cholinesterase inhibitor is started
Increase Paula's support hours and review the change at next year's check
Reassure her sister that this slowing is expected with age in Down syndrome
Record the change and arrange thyroid tests and an assessment for dementia
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: NICE NG54 (1.5.4) advises asking adults with Down syndrome at the annual check about changes in behaviour, loss of skills or needing more prompting, which may indicate the need for dementia assessment. Reversible causes such as hypothyroidism must be excluded (DSMIG).

n.0: Referral may be appropriate after assessment, but treatment cannot be decided before a diagnosis and reversible causes are excluded.
n.1: Waiting a year delays diagnosis of treatable causes and of dementia.
n.2: Loss of skills is a possible sign of dementia or a treatable condition, so it should not be dismissed as normal ageing.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Sophie, a student nurse on an acute medical ward, hears that Callum, 27, who has a learning disability, has brought his hospital passport. She asks her mentor what a hospital passport is. Which description is correct?
o: A legal record of his best interests decisions, signed by his consultant
A trust form completed by the admitting nurse that replaces the nursing assessment
A person-held document telling staff what they must know about him and how to support him
A GP summary of diagnoses and medicines sent with the referral letter
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: A hospital (health) passport is held by the person and travels with them. It records things staff must know (allergies, medicines, communication, how the person shows pain, capacity and consent information), things that are important to them, and likes and dislikes.

n.0: Best interests decisions are recorded in the clinical record under the Mental Capacity Act; the passport is not a legal decision record.
n.1: The passport is the person's own document and supports, not replaces, the nursing assessment.
n.3: A GP summary is a clinical referral document; the passport is person-held and describes how to support the person.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ellie, 35, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to an orthopaedic ward with a fractured wrist. Her support worker hands the nurse Ellie's hospital passport. What should the admitting nurse do with it?
o: Complete the trust admission assessment first and read the passport later
Photocopy it and give the original back for the support worker to take home
File it in the medical notes so it is available if questions arise
Read it, use it to plan care and keep it with Ellie for all staff to use
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The passport is only useful if staff read and act on it. It should inform the care plan from admission and stay with the person, at the bedside, so every member of staff can see how to communicate with and support Ellie.

n.0: Leaving it until later means the admission assessment misses key information about communication, pain and allergies.
n.1: Sending the original home removes it from the person; a photocopy filed away is unlikely to be read by all staff.
n.2: Filed in the notes, the passport is easily missed by staff who need it at the bedside.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Gareth, a learning disability liaison nurse, is training outpatient staff on the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag. A nurse asks what the flag is. Which answer is correct?
o: A GP code showing that a person is on the learning disability register
A paper sticker placed on the front of the person's hospital notes
A national record of a person's reasonable adjustments, visible to services
A local alert that each trust designs for its own patient system
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag (Information Standard DAPB4019) is a national record on the National Care Records Service of the adjustments a disabled person needs, so that health and adult social care services in England can see and meet them (NHS England).

n.0: The GP learning disability register is separate; the flag records specific adjustments for any disabled person.
n.1: A paper sticker is a local, non-shareable marker; the flag is digital and national.
n.3: The flag is a national standard, not a locally designed alert, so it can be seen across organisations.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Rhys, 22, has a learning disability and is writing his hospital passport with his mother and community nurse. They want the first page to cover things staff must know. Which item belongs in that section?
o: The name of the college he attends
His favourite television programmes and music
How he shows that he is in pain
His preferred times to have a shower
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The 'things you must know' section covers safety-critical information: allergies, medicines, communication, how the person shows pain or distress, and capacity and consent information. Preferences sit in later sections.

n.0: His college is background information, not something staff must know to keep him safe.
n.1: Favourite programmes are helpful 'likes' but not safety-critical information.
n.3: Shower times are a personal preference for the 'things that are important to me' or likes section.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Nia, 40, has a learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. Her hospital passport lists her medicines, but the nurse notices it names an antiepileptic that her GP record shows was stopped a year ago. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her family to update the passport after discharge and continue as listed
Stop using the passport and rely on the trust's own records for her stay
Give the medicines listed on the passport, as it is written by those who know her
Reconcile her medicines with current records and update the passport with Nia
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Medicines reconciliation on admission must use current, verified sources. Passports go out of date, so the nurse should confirm the current medicines and support Nia and those close to her to update the passport so it stays accurate (Code 10.2, 18).

n.0: Continuing an inaccurate list risks a medication error now; the update should not wait until discharge.
n.1: The passport still contains valuable information on communication, pain and preferences; it needs correcting, not discarding.
n.2: Giving a discontinued antiepileptic could cause harm; passport medicine lists must be checked against current records.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Femi, 30, is autistic with a learning disability. The hospital learning disability team knows he needs the first appointment of the day, a quiet waiting area and his mother present, but these adjustments are recorded only in local notes. He is about to be referred to another trust. What should the liaison nurse do?
o: Record his adjustments on the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag
Add the adjustments to the trust's own electronic alert system
Telephone the other trust's clinic to explain the adjustments
Give Femi's mother a letter listing the adjustments to bring along
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag (DAPB4019) records adjustments nationally so that every organisation providing NHS or publicly funded care can see them; providers in England had to implement it fully by 30 September 2026 (NHS England).

n.1: A local alert is not visible to the receiving trust, which is the gap here.
n.2: A phone call may help this once but leaves no lasting record for other services and future referrals.
n.3: A letter places the burden on his mother and may be lost; the duty to share sits with services.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Oliver, 52, has a learning disability and needs information in easy read with pictures. This is recorded and flagged on his hospital record. He is now being discharged with a referral to the community heart failure team. Under the Accessible Information Standard, what should the discharging nurse do?
o: Ask Oliver to tell the heart failure team about his needs at their first visit
Include his information and communication needs in the referral
Send the referral as normal, since the heart failure team will assess him
Give Oliver an easy read discharge leaflet and leave the referral as written
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet (and review) information and communication needs. 'Share' means including these needs in referrals, discharge and handover so the next service is ready.

n.0: The standard places the duty to share on services, not on the person.
n.2: Leaving the needs out means the next service will send inaccessible information before any assessment.
n.3: An accessible leaflet meets his need today but does not share it with the next service.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Zara, 24, is being discharged from hospital after an appendicectomy. A ward nurse plans to keep Zara's hospital passport in the medical notes 'in case she is readmitted'. Zara's support worker objects. What should the nurse in charge do?
o: Keep the passport on the ward so it is ready for any readmission
Return it to Zara, updated with anything learned during her stay
Scan the passport into the record and destroy the paper copy
Send the passport to her GP to hold with her medical record
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The hospital passport belongs to the person and travels with them to every appointment and admission. Updating it with Zara before she leaves keeps it accurate for next time.

n.0: Keeping it on the ward means it will not be with Zara at other hospitals or appointments.
n.2: Destroying her own document without consent is inappropriate; it is hers to keep.
n.3: The GP does not hold the passport; it is person-held so it can travel with Zara.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: During induction to a learning disability liaison team, Lauren, a newly qualified nurse, is asked to define diagnostic overshadowing as it is used in LeDeR reviews. Which definition is correct?
o: Relying on a family's account in place of the clinical observations
Prescribing medicines to manage behaviour in place of practical support
Attributing signs of illness to the person's learning disability or autism
Delaying treatment until a formal best interests decision has been made
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Diagnostic overshadowing is attributing signs or symptoms of physical or mental ill health to the person's learning disability or autism (for example, 'that is just his behaviour'), so the underlying illness is missed. It recurs in LeDeR, CIPOLD and the Oliver McGowan case.

n.0: Listening to families usually protects against overshadowing; this does not define it.
n.1: This describes overmedication, which STOMP addresses; it is not overshadowing.
n.3: Delays around best interests decisions are a separate problem, not the definition of overshadowing.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ben, 31, has a severe learning disability and no speech. Over two days he has stopped eating and has been pushing staff away. A support worker writes in the notes, 'Ben is being difficult again, it is his learning disability.' Which concept best describes this note?
o: Diagnostic overshadowing
Learned helplessness
Behavioural extinction
Positive risk-taking
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Explaining a new change in eating and behaviour as part of Ben's learning disability, without considering pain or illness, is diagnostic overshadowing. Behaviour change is a common way people without speech communicate pain or illness.

n.1: Learned helplessness describes passivity after repeated loss of control; it does not fit a note blaming the disability.
n.2: Extinction is a behavioural term for a behaviour fading when it is no longer reinforced; it does not describe this note.
n.3: Positive risk-taking is a planned approach to supporting choice and independence, not a missed illness.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Josh, 19, has a learning disability and autism. His family say he has been hitting the side of his head much more than usual for three days and is sleeping poorly. Staff at his college want to restart his behaviour support plan. What should the learning disability nurse do first?
o: Reduce demands at college until the behaviour returns to his usual level
Ask the GP to review the dose of his regular medication for behaviour
Restart the behaviour support plan and record each incident on an ABC chart
Arrange a physical assessment for causes of pain such as ear or dental problems
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: A new or increased behaviour may communicate pain or illness. Hitting the side of the head with poor sleep can indicate ear infection or dental pain, so a physical assessment comes before behavioural interventions (NICE NG11 assessment; LeDeR learning on overshadowing).

n.0: Reducing demands may ease distress but leaves a possible painful condition untreated.
n.1: Changing psychotropic medication without assessing for pain repeats the overshadowing error.
n.2: Behavioural recording may be useful later, but treating this as behaviour first risks missing a physical cause.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Diane is the mother of Peter, 44, who has a learning disability and is on a medical ward. At visiting she tells the nurse, 'He is not himself; he usually chats to everyone and today he will not look at me.' His NEWS2 score is 1. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reassure her that his observations are stable and the team will monitor him
Ask how this differs from his usual self and repeat a full assessment now
Suggest he may be tired from the ward routine and review after he has slept
Explain that a score of 1 means his care continues with routine observations
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Family and carers know the person's baseline and often notice 'soft signs' of deterioration before observations change. Their concern is clinical information: explore the change and reassess, escalating if needed (LeDeR learning; NICE NG11 and NG54 on involving people who know the person).

n.0: Stable observations do not exclude deterioration in someone whose baseline differs; this dismisses key information.
n.2: Attributing the change to tiredness without assessment is a form of overshadowing.
n.3: Relying on NEWS2 alone ignores a reported change from his usual presentation.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Leah, 28, has a moderate learning disability. Over six weeks she has stopped going to her art group, is tearful and is waking at 4 am. Day centre staff say this is 'part of her learning disability'. Following NICE NG54, what should the community learning disability nurse do?
o: Agree a new activity timetable to re-engage Leah with her art group
Advise staff to give less attention to tearfulness so it is not reinforced
Refer Leah for an annual health check at the next routine date
Assess for depression, allowing for how it may present differently
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: NICE NG54 (1.1.2) says practitioners should take into account that mental health problems may present differently in people with a learning disability. Withdrawal, tearfulness and early waking suggest possible depression, which should be assessed rather than attributed to the learning disability.

n.0: Re-engagement may help later but does not assess a possible depressive illness.
n.1: Withdrawing attention from distress treats a possible illness as behaviour and repeats the overshadowing.
n.2: Waiting for the next routine check delays assessment of a six-week change.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ryan, 37, has a learning disability. Over a month he has started pushing his plate away and shouting at mealtimes, and he has lost 3 kg. His support team ask for a behaviour support plan for 'mealtime aggression'. What is the most appropriate action for the learning disability nurse?
o: Write a support plan with clear limits on behaviour at mealtimes
Refer to speech and language therapy for a swallowing assessment
Change his diet to softer foods until the behaviour settles
Arrange assessment for physical causes such as dental pain or reflux
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Behaviour linked to eating, with weight loss, points to a possible physical cause such as dental pain, reflux or constipation. A physical health assessment comes first; treating it as behaviour would be diagnostic overshadowing (NICE NG11 1.2 and 1.5 assessment).

n.0: A behavioural plan without ruling out pain risks missing the cause of his distress and weight loss.
n.1: A swallowing assessment may be needed later, but there are no signs of dysphagia such as coughing; pain causes need assessing first.
n.2: Changing food texture without assessment is not evidence-based and may hide the cause.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Marcus, 18, is autistic and has epilepsy and a mild learning disability. Two days after starting an antipsychotic on a ward, he is found with his eyes fixed upwards, his neck twisted and he is distressed. A healthcare assistant says he is 'doing his behaviours'. What should the nurse do?
o: Give his prescribed PRN medicine for agitation and reassess in an hour
Recognise a possible acute dystonic reaction and seek urgent medical review
Use distraction and his calming strategies from his support plan
Record the episode on an ABC chart and observe him for patterns
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Upward fixed gaze and neck twisting after starting an antipsychotic suggest an oculogyric crisis, an acute dystonic reaction needing urgent medical treatment. In Oliver McGowan's case, such a reaction was mistaken for behaviour (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.0: Further sedation or antipsychotic PRN could worsen the reaction; medical review is needed now.
n.2: Calming strategies do not treat a drug-induced dystonia.
n.3: Recording the episode as behaviour delays treatment of a medical emergency.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Sana, a staff nurse, believes that Ivy, 50, who has a learning disability, has abdominal pain: Ivy keeps rocking and holding her stomach, which her carers say is new. The registrar says, 'She does that; it is her learning disability,' and declines to review her. What should Sana do?
o: Accept the decision and document the registrar's view in the notes
Give simple analgesia and monitor the rocking over the next shift
Restate the change from baseline using SBAR and escalate further
Ask Ivy's carers to raise the concern with the registrar themselves
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Carers report a new change from baseline. The Code requires nurses to act as an advocate for the vulnerable, challenging poor practice (3.4), and to raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns (16.1). Using structured communication (SBAR) with the evidence, and escalating to a senior doctor if still declined, challenges diagnostic overshadowing.

n.0: Accepting the decision leaves possible abdominal pathology unassessed despite clear evidence of change.
n.1: Analgesia without diagnosis may mask a surgical cause and does not address the refusal to review.
n.3: The nurse holds the professional duty to escalate; passing it to carers is inappropriate.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ethan, 23, is autistic with a mild learning disability. He becomes very distressed in busy waiting rooms and left his last outpatient appointment before being seen. The clinic nurse is rebooking his diabetes review. Which adjustment is most likely to help?
o: Book the first or last appointment of the day with a quiet place to wait
Book a mid-morning appointment and ask him to arrive 30 minutes early
Offer a telephone review so he does not need to attend in person
Ask his GP to take over his diabetes review from the clinic
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Appointments at the start or end of the day minimise waiting (an adjustment NICE gives in CG170 1.1.10), and a quiet waiting space reduces sensory overload (NICE CG142 1.1.8 on adjusting the environment for autistic adults; Equality Act 2010 s20). This keeps the face-to-face review he needs.

n.1: Arriving early lengthens the wait in the environment that caused distress.
n.2: A telephone call cannot replace the examination and tests a diabetes review needs, so it removes care rather than adjusting it.
n.3: Moving his care elsewhere avoids the duty to adjust and may not suit his needs.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Molly, 45, has a learning disability and needs a double-length dental appointment so she can become familiar with the room and equipment. The practice manager says Molly will have to pay an extra fee for the longer slot. What is the correct position under the Equality Act 2010?
o: Molly can be charged if the adjustment costs more than a set amount
Molly can be charged a reduced fee for the additional time
Molly's family can be charged in place of Molly herself
Molly must not be charged for the cost of a reasonable adjustment
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Section 20(7) of the Equality Act 2010 states that a disabled person must not be required to pay for the costs of complying with the duty to make reasonable adjustments.

n.0: There is no cost threshold above which the disabled person can be charged; cost is considered when deciding what is reasonable.
n.1: A reduced fee is still a charge for the adjustment, which s20(7) prohibits.
n.2: Passing the cost to family is still charging for the adjustment and is not permitted.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Kai, 30, has a learning disability and is booked for a planned hip operation in four weeks. His community nurse wants the hospital to be ready with the adjustments he needs. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Ask the surgeon to add his needs to the operation consent form
Give Kai's mother a list of his needs to hand to the ward on admission
Wait for the pre-assessment letter and then raise his needs with the clinic
Contact the hospital learning disability liaison nurse to plan the admission
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Hospital learning disability liaison nurses help plan reasonable adjustments before admission, such as a pre-admission visit, a side room, carers staying, timing on the list and communication support. Planning ahead meets the anticipatory duty (Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: The consent form records consent to a procedure; it is not a tool for planning adjustments.
n.1: Relying on family to brief staff on the day leaves no time to plan adjustments such as theatre timing or a side room.
n.2: Waiting delays planning; four weeks is the time to arrange adjustments.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Alys, 38, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to a medical ward. Her long-standing support worker asks to stay overnight because Alys becomes frightened in unfamiliar places. Ward visiting ends at 8 pm. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse in charge?
o: Agree a trial stay and review whether to extend it in the morning
Ask the support worker to return at 8 am to help with personal care
Explain that ward visiting times apply to all visitors equally
Agree she can stay and plan how she will support Alys's care
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Allowing a familiar carer to stay is a recognised reasonable adjustment (Equality Act 2010 s20). Agreeing roles in advance helps staff work with the carer while remaining responsible for Alys's nursing care.

n.0: Making the stay a trial overnight adds uncertainty for Alys without reason; her need for a familiar person is already known.
n.1: Returning in the morning leaves Alys frightened overnight, which is when she most needs support.
n.2: Applying the same rule to everyone can put a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage; the duty is to adjust.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: An outpatient manager tells Dev, a learning disability liaison nurse, 'We make adjustments when a patient asks for them.' Dev explains the duty that applies to service providers such as NHS trusts under the Equality Act 2010. Which statement is correct?
o: The duty is anticipatory, so services must plan adjustments in advance
The duty applies to physical features such as ramps and toilets
The duty starts when a disabled person or carer asks for an adjustment
The duty applies once a learning disability diagnosis is confirmed
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: For service providers the reasonable adjustment duty is anticipatory: services must think ahead about what disabled people generally may need and plan adjustments before anyone asks (Equality Act 2010 s20 and Sch 2).

n.1: Physical features are one of three requirements; the duty also covers practices and auxiliary aids.
n.2: Waiting for a request puts the burden on disabled people; the provider duty is anticipatory.
n.3: The duty protects disabled people generally and does not depend on a confirmed diagnosis before planning starts.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Tariq, 26, has a mild learning disability and capacity to decide about blood tests. He has a strong fear of needles and pulled away at his last two attempts. He needs regular blood tests to monitor his lithium. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Record that he has refused blood tests and inform the prescriber
Arrange a graded desensitisation programme with numbing cream
Ask the GP to prescribe a sedative before the next attempt
Ask two staff to hold his arm still for a quick test
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Tariq has capacity, so holding him would be unlawful restraint. A reasonable adjustment such as gradual desensitisation over several visits, with a familiar person and topical anaesthetic, supports him to have the test he needs (MCA 2005 s1; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: His fear is a barrier that adjustments can address; recording refusal without trying them risks unsafe lithium monitoring.
n.2: Sedation is a restrictive option to consider only after less restrictive adjustments have been tried, and needs his consent.
n.3: Holding a person with capacity against his will is assault and not a reasonable adjustment.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Jasmine, 34, has a profound learning disability and lacks capacity to consent to dental treatment. She needs a tooth extraction under general anaesthetic. Her blood tests and ear examination are also overdue because she cannot tolerate them while awake. What is the best adjustment to propose?
o: Plan, in her best interests, to do the other checks under the same anaesthetic
Ask her GP to try the blood tests again with extra staff support
Book separate appointments for the blood tests and ear examination later
Carry out the extraction and delay the other checks to her annual check
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Coordinating procedures under one general anaesthetic is a recognised reasonable adjustment that avoids repeated distress and anaesthetic risk. Because Jasmine lacks capacity, the plan must be agreed as being in her best interests with those close to her (MCA 2005 s4; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.1: Repeating the tests while she is awake, with more staff to support or hold her, is more restrictive and she has not tolerated them awake.
n.2: Separate appointments she cannot tolerate while awake are likely to fail again.
n.3: Delaying the checks misses a safe opportunity and leaves health needs unmet.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Bea, 29, is autistic and has a learning disability. She attends the emergency department with a wrist injury and is rocking and covering her ears in the busy waiting area. The triage nurse estimates a three-hour wait. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Move her ahead of other patients so she is seen straight away
Give her ear defenders and ask her to stay in the waiting area
Ask her carer to take her home and return when the department is quieter
Move her to a quieter area while she keeps her place in the queue
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: A quiet space is a reasonable adjustment that removes the sensory disadvantage while clinical priority is still decided by triage (Equality Act 2010 s20; NICE CG142 1.1.8 on adjusting noise and the environment for autistic adults).

n.0: Priority should follow clinical need; the adjustment is to the environment, not to the triage order.
n.1: Ear defenders may help a little, but keeping her in the busy area leaves the main barrier in place.
n.2: Sending her home delays treatment of an injury.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ivan, a newly appointed nurse at an acute trust, is booked onto the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training on Learning Disability and Autism. A colleague asks why the training carries Oliver's name. Which explanation is accurate?
o: He was a man with a learning disability whose death at Winterbourne View prompted the national inquiry
He was a learning disability nurse who designed the first national training curriculum
He was an autistic man with a learning disability who campaigned for training in his twenties
He was an autistic teenager who died after being given an antipsychotic his family had opposed
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Oliver McGowan was an autistic teenager with a mild learning disability, epilepsy and cerebral palsy who died in 2016 after a severe reaction to antipsychotic medication that he and his family had asked doctors not to give. His parents campaigned for mandatory training (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.0: Winterbourne View was an abuse scandal exposed in 2011; Oliver did not die there.
n.1: Oliver was a patient, not a nurse or curriculum designer.
n.2: Oliver died as a teenager in 2016; the campaign was led by his parents after his death.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Comfort manages a CQC-registered home care agency. She asks the local learning disability nurse which staff the legal requirement for learning disability and autism training covers. Which answer is correct?
o: All staff of CQC-registered providers, trained to suit their role
Staff in NHS trusts, with independent home care agencies exempt
Registered nurses and doctors, with care staff covered by local policy
Staff whose job descriptions name learning disability or autism work
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 requires every CQC-registered provider of health and adult social care in England to ensure its staff receive learning disability and autism training appropriate to their role, from 1 July 2022 (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice).

n.1: Independent CQC-registered providers, including home care agencies, are covered.
n.2: Care staff are covered by the legal requirement, not left to local policy.
n.3: The requirement covers staff across services, not just roles labelled as learning disability or autism work.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ruby works as a receptionist in a GP surgery and needs general awareness of learning disability and autism. Her practice manager books her onto the Tier 1 package of the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training. What does this package consist of?
o: A three-hour classroom session led by a learning disability nurse
A 90-minute e-learning module and a one-hour live online interactive session
A one-day face-to-face session followed by a 90-minute e-learning module
A 90-minute e-learning module with an assessed workbook and no live session
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The Tier 1 package is for staff who need general awareness: a 90-minute e-learning module plus a one-hour live online interactive session with at least one person with a learning disability and one autistic person (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.0: The package is not a nurse-led classroom session; it must be co-delivered by people with lived experience.
n.2: A one-day face-to-face session is the Tier 2 package for staff who provide care and support.
n.3: The live interactive session is a required part of Tier 1; e-learning alone does not meet it.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Ahmed is a registered nurse on an acute medical ward who regularly cares for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Which Oliver McGowan training package is appropriate for his role?
o: Tier 3, the specialist module for consultant-level practitioners
Tier 2, the e-learning and a one-day face-to-face session
Tier 1, repeated each year in place of further training
Tier 1, the e-learning and one-hour online interactive session
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Tier 2 capabilities are for health and social care staff who provide care and support to people with a learning disability or autistic people; the Tier 2 package is the 90-minute e-learning plus a one-day face-to-face session (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice).

n.0: Tier 3 capabilities are for highly autonomous professionals leading complex care; it is not a separate Oliver McGowan package for ward nurses.
n.2: Repeating Tier 1 does not provide the Tier 2 capabilities his role needs.
n.3: Tier 1 is for staff who need general awareness, such as reception staff, not those providing direct care.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: A trust's education lead proposes delivering the Tier 2 face-to-face day using two experienced learning disability nurses as trainers to save costs. Clinical nurse educator Hamza reviews the plan against the Oliver McGowan Code of Practice. What should he advise?
o: The day must include a family carer of a person with a learning disability
The plan is acceptable if a person with lived experience reviews the slides first
It must be co-delivered by a person with a learning disability and an autistic person
The plan is acceptable if both nurses hold a learning disability qualification
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The Tier 2 one-day session must be co-delivered by at least one person with a learning disability and one autistic person, who are trained as trainers (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.0: Family carers are valued, but the Code specifies a person with a learning disability and an autistic person as co-trainers.
n.1: Reviewing slides is not co-delivery; they must deliver the session.
n.3: Professional qualifications do not replace co-delivery by people with lived experience.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Eve, a practice development nurse, is writing a policy on learning disability and autism training. She needs to cite the legal source and start date of the requirement for CQC-registered providers. Which citation is correct?
o: Care Act 2014 section 42, in force from 1 April 2015
Equality Act 2010 section 20, in force from 1 October 2010
Mental Capacity Act 2005 section 1, in force from 1 October 2007
Health and Care Act 2022 section 181, in force from 1 July 2022
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 introduced the requirement, through the Health and Social Care Act 2008 and regulation 18 of the 2014 Regulations, that from 1 July 2022 CQC-registered providers ensure staff receive learning disability and autism training appropriate to their role (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.0: Section 42 of the Care Act 2014 is the safeguarding enquiry duty.
n.1: Section 20 of the Equality Act 2010 is the reasonable adjustment duty.
n.2: Section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 sets out its five principles.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Noah, 17, is autistic with a mild learning disability and epilepsy. His hospital passport and his parents state he reacted badly to antipsychotics in the past. On admission an antipsychotic is prescribed for agitation. What should the nurse do before giving it?
o: Raise the history with the prescriber and ask for a review first
Withhold all of his medicines until his parents arrive on the ward
Ask his parents to sign a form agreeing to the medicine being given
Give the dose as prescribed and monitor him closely for side effects
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The lesson of Oliver McGowan's death is to listen to the person and family and act on documented adverse reactions. The Code requires nurses to listen and respond to people's concerns (standard 2), raise concerns (16.1) and reduce the likelihood of harm (19.1); the prescriber must review before administration.

n.1: Withholding all medicines, including antiepileptics, could cause harm; the concern is this one prescription.
n.2: A parental signature does not address the clinical risk and the decision belongs with the prescriber and Noah.
n.3: Giving a medicine with a recorded serious reaction without review repeats the failure in Oliver's care.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: A care home manager tells Leo, a visiting learning disability nurse, that the Oliver McGowan Code of Practice is 'only guidance, so we can ignore it'. Which response from Leo is accurate?
o: It is a statutory code that CQC takes into account, and departures need good reasons
It is voluntary best practice that providers can choose whether to adopt
It is binding on NHS trusts, with independent care homes encouraged to follow it
It replaces the legal training requirement, so following it is the whole duty
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The Secretary of State must issue the code under the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (s21A, inserted by the 2022 Act). CQC takes the code into account, and a provider that departs from it must give good reasons and show it meets the requirement another way (Oliver McGowan Code of Practice, 2025).

n.1: The code has a statutory basis and CQC considers it when assessing compliance; it is not optional best practice.
n.2: It applies to all CQC-registered providers, including independent care homes.
n.3: The legal requirement is in the 2022 Act and 2014 Regulations; the code explains how to meet it.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Amara is a newly registered learning disability nurse in a supported living service. Harry, 52, whom she supported for two years, has died in hospital, and her manager says his death will be notified to LeDeR. Amara asks what LeDeR is for. Which description is correct?
o: A coroner's process that decides the legal cause of death and any fault
A police investigation into whether neglect contributed to his death
A service improvement programme that reviews deaths to learn and improve care
A Care Quality Commission inspection that rates the service where he lived
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: LeDeR (Learning from lives and deaths: people with a learning disability and autistic people) is an NHS England service improvement programme. Reviews look at the person's life and care to identify learning that improves services and reduces avoidable deaths; it does not apportion blame (LeDeR, KCL national reports).

n.0: Determining the legal cause of death is the coroner's role at an inquest; LeDeR is not a court process and does not find fault.
n.1: Suspected criminal neglect is a police and safeguarding matter; LeDeR is a learning programme, not a criminal investigation.
n.3: CQC inspects and rates registered services; a LeDeR review is about learning from the person's life and death, not rating a provider.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Samuel, a staff nurse on a medical ward, is caring for the family of Daniel, 34, an autistic man without a learning disability who has died after a short illness. Samuel is unsure whether a LeDeR notification is appropriate. What is the correct position?
o: Yes, LeDeR reviews the deaths of autistic people as well as people with a learning disability
No, his death is reviewed by the trust's structured judgement review in place of LeDeR
Yes, but the notification is made by the coroner once the inquest has concluded
