No, LeDeR reviews an autistic person's death when a learning disability is also diagnosed
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: Since 2021 the programme has been 'Learning from lives and deaths: people with a learning disability and autistic people', so the deaths of autistic adults are reviewed whether or not they also have a learning disability. Anyone, including ward staff and family, can notify a death (leder.nhs.uk).

n.1: A trust mortality review can take place as well, but it does not replace the national LeDeR review.
n.2: Notification does not wait for, or come from, the coroner; anyone can notify LeDeR, including hospital staff and family.
n.3: Autistic people are included in their own right; a co-existing learning disability is not required.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: During a team teaching session, Kofi, a community learning disability nurse, presents the republished (January 2026) LeDeR report on deaths in 2023. A student asks which causes of death were most common among the people reviewed. Which answer should Kofi give?
o: Dementia, chronic kidney disease and stroke
Cancer, pneumonia and lung infections, and heart conditions
Accidents, suicide and drug or alcohol overdoses
Epilepsy, choking incidents and complications of constipation
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The revised 2023 LeDeR report found the most common causes of death were cancer, pneumonia and other lung infections, and heart problems (LeDeR 2023 report, republished 27 January 2026).

n.0: These causes occur but were not the leading groups in the 2023 report.
n.2: External causes such as accidents and suicide were not among the leading causes for people with a learning disability.
n.3: Epilepsy, choking and constipation still contribute to deaths and are key learning themes, but they were not the most common causes.

Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.q: Grace, a student nurse, reads in the revised 2023 LeDeR report that the average age at death of people with a learning disability was 63. She asks her practice assessor how this compared for people with a severe or profound learning disability. Which figure is correct?
o: About 68 years, older than the overall average
About 58 years, younger than the overall average
About 63 years, the same as the overall average
About 48 years, fifteen years below the overall average
Health Inequalities and Reasonable Adjus.w: The revised 2023 LeDeR report gives an average age at death of 63 for people with a learning disability, and 58 for people with a severe or profound learning disability, who were also more likely to die of something treatable (LeDeR 2023, republished January 2026).

n.0: People with more severe learning disabilities died younger, not older, than the overall average.
n.2: The report found a clear gap by severity; the average was not the same.
n.3: 48 is too low; the reported average for severe or profound learning disability was 58.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Neil, 49, has Down syndrome. Over three months his support staff say he has stopped following spoken instructions and seems 'stubborn'. He still responds well to signs and pictures. What should the learning disability nurse arrange first?
o: A review of his behaviour support plan with the support team
A referral to speech and language therapy for a new communication plan
A hearing assessment, including a check for ear wax
A dementia assessment with the memory service
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Hearing loss is common in people with Down syndrome (NHS.uk). A recent failure to follow speech while still responding to visual signs suggests reduced hearing, so ear wax and hearing must be checked first before other explanations (diagnostic overshadowing).

n.0: Calling him stubborn risks overshadowing a sensory problem; hearing comes first.
n.1: SLT input may help later, but the change points to a hearing problem that needs assessing first.
n.3: Dementia must be considered in Down syndrome, but a treatable sensory cause should be excluded first.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Tom, 23, has a severe learning disability. He uses vocal sounds and some gestures, and staff are not sure what many of them mean. Incidents of distress are increasing, possibly because he cannot make himself understood. What is the most appropriate referral?
o: To a clinical psychologist for a functional assessment of behaviour
To audiology for a hearing aid fitting
To speech and language therapy for a communication assessment
To his GP for a review of medication for anxiety
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Speech and language therapists assess communication and recommend approaches such as signs, objects of reference or a communication passport. Improving how Tom can express himself may reduce distress.

n.0: Behaviour assessment may also help, but the identified problem is communication, which SLT assesses.
n.1: There is no evidence of hearing loss; a hearing aid fitting needs a hearing assessment first.
n.3: Medication does not address his difficulty being understood and risks overmedication (STOMP).

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Sam, 35, has a moderate learning disability. He understands some speech and uses a few signs and a photo book. He needs a blood test tomorrow. Which approach should the nurse use to prepare him?
o: Use simple speech with his signs, photos of the clinic and a demonstration
Explain the test in speech, and give his support worker a leaflet to read to him
Show him the photo book in place of speech, as pictures are clearer
Explain the test on the day so he does not worry overnight
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Combining speech with the signs and photos Sam already uses, plus a demonstration, is total communication: using every channel that works for him so he understands and can be involved in the decision (Annexe A 2.5).

n.1: A standard leaflet read aloud is a single channel and may be inaccessible for Sam.
n.2: Removing speech takes away a channel he partly understands; total communication combines methods.
n.3: Leaving explanation until the day removes time to process and prepare, which can increase distress.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Ayesha, 30, has a learning disability and uses her own signs, which her support worker understands. During a consultation the doctor directs all questions to the support worker. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the support worker to leave so Ayesha can answer for herself
Arrange a separate meeting with the support worker to gather the history
Ask the doctor to speak to Ayesha, with the support worker helping interpret
Let the support worker answer, as she knows Ayesha best
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Communication should be directed to the person, with others helping only to support understanding. This respects Ayesha's dignity and right to be involved (Code 2.1, 7; Annexe A 2.5; MCA s1(3)).

n.0: Removing the person who understands her signs would make communication harder.
n.1: A separate meeting still bypasses Ayesha and misses the chance to hear from her.
n.3: Talking about Ayesha rather than to her excludes her from her own care.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Kerry, a nurse joining a learning disability respite service, sees staff signing while they talk to Lily, 12. Her colleague explains that they use Makaton. Which description of Makaton is correct?
o: Signs and symbols used alongside speech to support understanding and expression
A sign language with its own grammar, used in place of spoken English
A set of everyday objects that stand for activities, people or places
A picture exchange system in which the person hands over cards to request items
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Makaton is a language programme that uses signs and symbols together with speech, signing key words in spoken word order, to support both understanding and expression.

n.1: This describes British Sign Language, which has its own grammar; Makaton is used with speech.
n.2: This describes objects of reference.
n.3: This describes PECS (Picture Exchange Communication System).

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Adam, 30, has a learning disability and uses Makaton. A healthcare assistant who has learned some signs explains Adam's meal choices by signing silently so as not to 'confuse him with words'. What advice should the nurse give?
o: Use speech and save signing for when Adam seems confused
Write the choices down for Adam and point to each one
Sign every word of each sentence while staying silent
Sign key words while speaking, in normal word order
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Makaton signs are used with speech, signing the key words in spoken word order. Speech plus sign gives two channels and supports understanding.

n.0: Waiting until confusion appears loses the benefit of signs supporting understanding from the start.
n.1: Written words may not be accessible to Adam; he uses Makaton.
n.2: Makaton signs key words, not every word, and is not used silently.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Bryony, 38, has a profound learning disability and does not use pictures or signs. Staff want to help her anticipate that she is going swimming. Using objects of reference, what should they do?
o: Show her a photograph of the swimming pool
Sign 'swimming' in Makaton as they tell her
Give her a piece of her swimming towel to hold
Hand her a symbol card for swimming
Communication in Learning Disability.w: An object of reference is a real object that stands for an activity, person or place, such as a towel for swimming, used with people who do not yet understand pictures or signs. It must be used consistently.

n.0: Photographs are more abstract than objects; Bryony does not use pictures.
n.1: Bryony does not use signs, so a sign alone will not convey the activity.
n.3: Symbols are more abstract than pictures and are not meaningful for her.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Kian, 5, is autistic and does not speak. His team starts the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS). In the first phase, what is Kian taught to do?
o: Hand a picture to a partner to receive the item he wants
Choose between two pictures to get the item he prefers
Answer the question 'What do you want?' with a picture
Build an 'I want' sentence strip with a picture of the item
Communication in Learning Disability.w: PECS Phase 1 is the physically assisted exchange: the person learns to pick up a single picture and hand it to a communication partner in exchange for a desired item (Bondy and Frost, PECS).

n.1: Choosing between pictures is Phase 3, picture discrimination.
n.2: Responding to 'What do you want?' is Phase 5.
n.3: Sentence strips are Phase 4, sentence structure.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Ruby, 7, is autistic and uses PECS. She now walks across the room to her communication book and hands a single picture to adults to request items. Her teacher asks what the next PECS phase will teach. Which answer is correct?
o: Answering 'What do you want?' using a sentence strip
Commenting on things she sees, such as 'I see a dog'
Building a sentence strip with 'I want' and an item picture
Choosing the correct picture from two or more pictures
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Ruby has achieved Phase 2 (distance and persistence). Phase 3 is picture discrimination: choosing the right picture from several. Phase 4 then adds sentence structure (PECS).

n.0: Responding to 'What do you want?' is Phase 5.
n.1: Commenting is Phase 6, the final phase.
n.2: Sentence structure is Phase 4, after discrimination in Phase 3.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Leo, 9, is autistic and uses PECS. He reliably picks the right picture from a page of choices. His speech and language therapist introduces a strip with an 'I want' card, to which he adds an item picture before handing it over. Which PECS phase has Leo reached?
o: Phase 3, picture discrimination
Phase 4, sentence structure
Phase 2, distance and persistence
Phase 6, commenting
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Phase 4 teaches sentence structure: the person builds a sentence strip with 'I want' plus the item picture and exchanges the whole strip (PECS).

n.0: Leo has already mastered Phase 3 discrimination; building a sentence is the next phase.
n.2: Phase 2 teaches travelling to the book and partner, not sentence building.
n.3: Phase 6 teaches commenting, such as 'I see' or 'I hear', not requesting.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Daisy, 19, is autistic and uses a picture communication book. She is admitted to a children's ward after a fall. The nurse notices the book has been packed away in her bag in the locker. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep the book within Daisy's reach and use it when talking with her
Ask her parents to take the book home until she is discharged
Make a set of the ward's own picture cards to use during her stay
Leave the book in the locker so it does not get lost on the ward
Communication in Learning Disability.w: A personal communication aid is Daisy's voice. It must be kept with her and used by staff so she can understand and express needs, including pain (Annexe A 2.4; Accessible Information Standard 'meet').

n.1: Sending it home removes her means of communication during admission.
n.2: Unfamiliar ward cards are less useful than her own book, which she already knows how to use.
n.3: Locked away, the book cannot be used, leaving Daisy unable to communicate.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Mo, 44, has a profound learning disability and uses objects of reference. At home a spoon means lunch, but at his day centre a plate is used for lunch and a spoon for cooking sessions. He has become distressed at both places. What should the learning disability nurse recommend?
o: Let each setting keep its own objects as Mo will learn both
Replace the objects with photographs so the meanings are clearer
Stop using objects until Mo shows he understands their meaning
Agree one set of objects with the same meanings in both settings
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Objects of reference work only if each object consistently means the same thing for the person across settings. Agreeing one shared set, often recorded in a communication passport, reduces confusion and distress.

n.0: Different meanings for the same object are the cause of Mo's confusion.
n.1: Photographs are more abstract and Mo uses objects; the problem is inconsistency, not the type of cue.
n.2: Removing his communication system would increase distress and take away his means of anticipating events.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Harriet, a learning disability nurse, is helping a GP practice turn its flu vaccination letter into easy read for patients on its learning disability register. Which approach matches easy read?
o: Long paragraphs in plain words with a glossary of medical terms at the end
Capital letters throughout so that every word is easier to read
Short sentences in everyday words, each idea with a picture beside it
Bullet points with medical terms in bold so they stand out for readers
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Easy read uses short sentences, everyday words, one idea per sentence and a supporting picture beside the text it illustrates, so people with a learning disability can understand written information (Accessible Information Standard context).

n.0: Long paragraphs and a glossary still overload the reader; easy read uses short sentences with pictures.
n.1: Text in capitals is harder to read because word shapes are lost.
n.3: Medical terms remain a barrier even when highlighted.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Ewan, 36, has a mild learning disability and is having a colonoscopy. The standard letter says: 'Please refrain from consuming food after midnight prior to your procedure.' Which easy read version is best?
o: Refrain from eating after midnight before your procedure.
Do not eat or drink anything after midnight, please.
Do not eat any food after 12 o'clock at night.
No food after 00:00 before your colonoscopy procedure.
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Easy read uses everyday words, one idea per sentence and familiar time words (such as 12 o'clock at night). The best version keeps the original meaning (no food) without adding or changing instructions.

n.0: 'Refrain' and 'procedure' remain hard words.
n.1: This changes the instruction by adding drinks, which the original letter did not restrict.
n.3: The 24-hour time and medical term make it harder to understand.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: A community learning disability team has produced an easy read leaflet about bowel screening. Before printing it, the team leader asks Cara, a nurse, how to check that it works for the people it is meant for. What should Cara suggest?
o: Ask family carers whether they think it looks clear enough
Test it with people with a learning disability and revise it
Check that it uses fewer than a set number of words per page
Ask the health promotion team to proofread it for spelling
Communication in Learning Disability.w: The best test of accessible information is whether the intended readers understand it, so easy read should be co-produced or checked with people with a learning disability (Accessible Information Standard; person-centred health promotion, P2.10).

n.0: Carers' views help, but the people who will use the leaflet should test it.
n.2: Word counts do not prove understanding; testing with readers does.
n.3: Spelling checks do not show whether readers with a learning disability understand it.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Ollie, 21, has a moderate learning disability and is learning to brush his teeth independently. His nurse breaks the task into steps. Which approach to reinforcement is most likely to help him learn?
o: Correct each mistake as it happens and praise the finished task
Praise him straight after each step he completes
Praise him at the end of the week if he has brushed every day
Offer a reward once he can complete all steps without help
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Immediate positive reinforcement of each step, with repetition, helps people with a learning disability learn new skills (Annexe A, repetition and positive reinforcement).

n.0: Focusing on correction with praise only at the end gives little reinforcement for each step learned.
n.2: Delayed praise is weakly linked to the behaviour and is less effective.
n.3: Waiting until full independence means no reinforcement during learning.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Clinic staff plan to send Delyth, 50, an easy read appointment letter. Delyth has a profound learning disability, does not read and relies on objects and her sister to understand plans. Her record notes these needs. What should the clinic do?
o: Send the easy read letter as it is the accessible format for this group
Send the letter to Delyth's sister and agree how she will prepare Delyth
Send a standard letter, since easy read will not help Delyth read it
Phone Delyth directly on the day to remind her of the appointment
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Accessible information must meet the individual's recorded needs, not a group label. Delyth does not read, so contact through her sister, agreed with Delyth's support and using her objects, meets her need (Accessible Information Standard 'meet').

n.0: Easy read requires some reading; it does not meet Delyth's recorded needs.
n.2: A standard letter meets nobody's need; the solution is the route recorded for her.
n.3: A phone call on the day gives no time to prepare and Delyth does not use the phone.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: A practice nurse is updating records under the Accessible Information Standard for Kevin, 33, who has a learning disability. Which entry best meets the standard?
o: 'Requires easy read letters; support worker Jo reads them with him.'
'Learning disability: needs extra help with any letters we send.'
'Vulnerable adult: discuss all information with his carers first.'
'Unable to read: send all his letters to his mother instead.'
Communication in Learning Disability.w: The Accessible Information Standard requires a person's specific information and communication needs (format and support) to be recorded, flagged and met, not just a diagnosis or vague label (DAPB1605).

n.1: A diagnosis plus vague help does not tell staff what format or support to provide.
n.2: 'Vulnerable adult' is not a communication need and does not tell staff what to do.
n.3: Routing all letters to his mother is not his recorded preference and may breach confidentiality.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Sinead, a learning disability nurse, is running healthy eating support for Josh, 29, who has a mild learning disability and type 2 diabetes. Which plan is most likely to help Josh learn and keep the key messages?
o: Short repeated sessions using pictures, practice and praise
A leaflet from the diabetes clinic for Josh to read at home
A weekly text message with a different healthy eating tip
One detailed hour-long session covering all dietary advice
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Repetition, practical learning with pictures and positive reinforcement help people with a learning disability understand and retain health information (Annexe A; P2.10 health promotion using accessible methods).

n.1: A standard leaflet may be inaccessible and gives no repetition or practice.
n.2: A new tip each week lacks repetition of the key messages and practice.
n.3: A single long session overloads processing and memory.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Yusuf, 27, has a mild learning disability and is due to have a dental extraction. The dentist gives him an easy read leaflet and asks him to sign the consent form at his next visit. What should the nurse supporting Yusuf do?
o: Ask his father to sign the form, as the leaflet explains it to the family
Go through the leaflet with him, check his understanding and give time to decide
Ask Yusuf to sign the consent form now, as he has the easy read leaflet
Arrange a best interests meeting, since he needed an easy read leaflet
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Easy read supports, but does not replace, the consent discussion. Taking all practicable steps (MCA s1(3)) means explaining, checking understanding in his own words and giving time. Needing accessible information does not mean he lacks capacity.

n.0: An adult with capacity gives his own consent; a family member cannot consent for him.
n.2: Having a leaflet does not show understanding; consent needs discussion first.
n.3: Needing accessible information does not indicate a lack of capacity, so best interests does not apply.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Priti, a newly qualified nurse in a residential service, is asked to use intensive interaction with Rowan, 26, who has a profound learning disability. She asks her manager what the approach involves. Which description is correct?
o: Signing key words to Rowan as staff speak to him during care
Teaching Rowan to request objects by exchanging picture cards
Following Rowan's lead and responding to his sounds and movements
Giving Rowan a structured daily timetable of tasks with rewards
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Intensive interaction teaches the fundamentals of communication by following the person's lead, imitating and responding to their sounds, movements and expressions, so the person experiences being listened to and enjoying another person's company (Hewett and Nind).

n.0: Signing key words with speech is Makaton.
n.1: Exchanging pictures to request items is PECS.
n.3: A task timetable with rewards is a structured teaching approach, not intensive interaction.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: A community learning disability team is deciding who would benefit most from intensive interaction. For which person is the approach most suitable?
o: Maya, 34, with a mild learning disability who reads easy read well
Callum, 28, with a profound learning disability and very limited communication
Sean, 45, who has dementia after many years of fluent speech
Lena, 19, with a moderate learning disability who uses Makaton fluently
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Intensive interaction is used with people at early stages of communication development, such as people with profound and multiple learning disabilities and some autistic people with limited communication.

n.0: Maya already communicates through reading and speech; she does not need early communication fundamentals.
n.2: Sean's needs relate to dementia; he already has established communication.
n.3: Lena is a fluent Makaton user and already has a working communication system.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Isla, 30, has a profound learning disability. She often rocks and makes humming sounds. During an intensive interaction session, what should the nurse do?
o: Ask Isla simple questions and wait for a response each time
Gently redirect the rocking towards a more purposeful activity
Join in with Isla's humming and rhythm, then wait for her response
Offer a picture choice of activities every few minutes
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Intensive interaction uses imitation and responsive joining-in with the person's own sounds and movements, then pausing for them to respond, creating turn-taking from the person's own behaviour.

n.0: Questions are staff-led and assume language skills Isla may not have.
n.1: Redirecting her behaviour takes control away from Isla and stops her leading the interaction.
n.3: Picture choices are a different approach and interrupt the shared interaction.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: A support worker asks Ola, a learning disability nurse, what the 'fundamentals of communication' are that intensive interaction aims to develop. Which group of skills should Ola describe?
o: Eye contact, turn-taking and enjoying being with another person
Following instructions, sitting still and finishing set tasks
Reading, writing and using symbols to make everyday choices
Using signs, gestures and photographs to request items
Communication in Learning Disability.w: The fundamentals of communication include giving attention, eye contact, facial expression, turn-taking, and enjoying being with another person; these come before language (intensive interaction literature, Hewett and Nind).

n.1: Compliance skills are not the fundamentals of communication.
n.2: Literacy and symbols are later skills built on the fundamentals.
n.3: These are specific communication systems, not the underlying fundamentals.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: During an intensive interaction session, Sasha, a support worker, holds up a ball and repeatedly asks Ryan, 32, who has a profound learning disability, 'What colour is this?' Ryan looks away. What feedback should the nurse give Sasha?
o: Ask more slowly and wait longer before repeating the question
Let Ryan lead, and respond to what he chooses to do
Offer Ryan a choice of two coloured balls to make it easier
Give Ryan praise each time he looks at the ball
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Intensive interaction is led by the person, not by staff questions or tasks. Staff wait, observe and respond to what the person initiates, so the person experiences control and success.

n.0: Slowing the same question keeps the session staff-led and task-focused.
n.2: A choice of balls is still a staff-set task rather than following Ryan.
n.3: Rewarding attention to the ball keeps the agenda with staff.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Ten minutes into an intensive interaction session, Kofi, 40, who has a profound learning disability, turns his body away, closes his eyes and stops vocalising. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Move round to face him so he can see her again
Increase the volume and energy of her sounds to regain interest
Gently touch his arm to bring his attention back to her
Give him space and stay available in case he re-engages
Communication in Learning Disability.w: The person controls the interaction. Turning away and closing his eyes signal a need to pause, so the nurse respects this, gives space and stays available, which builds trust (intensive interaction principles; Annexe A 1.3 non-verbal cues).

n.0: Moving into his view overrides his signal that he wants a break.
n.1: Escalating stimulation ignores his cue and may cause distress.
n.2: Touch to regain attention overrides his clear non-verbal signal.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Ana, a nurse, is about to start intensive interaction with Leon, 23, who has a profound learning disability and uses a wheelchair. Which non-verbal approach should she use?
o: Sit at his eye level with a relaxed, responsive face and body
Stand in front of him and keep constant eye contact
Sit behind him and talk so he can hear her voice clearly
Stand beside his wheelchair so she does not crowd him
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Being at the person's level with a relaxed, open and responsive manner invites interaction. Non-verbal communication (position, facial expression, body language) is central to Annexe A 1.3 and intensive interaction.

n.1: Standing over him with constant eye contact can feel intimidating.
n.2: Sitting behind him prevents shared attention and facial communication.
n.3: Standing over a seated person is less inviting and makes eye contact hard.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Staff have used intensive interaction with Nell, 37, who has a profound learning disability, for three months. The team wants to know whether she is making progress. What is the best way to evaluate this?
o: Repeat her IQ assessment to measure cognitive change
Record observations of her eye contact and turn-taking over time
Ask Nell's family whether she seems happier than she was before
Count how many tasks she completes each day
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Progress in intensive interaction is shown by changes in the fundamentals of communication (attention, eye contact, turn-taking, length of shared interaction), so regular recorded observations, sometimes with video, are used.

n.0: IQ testing does not measure the fundamentals of communication.
n.2: Family views help but are not a structured record of communication progress.
n.3: Task completion measures compliance, not communication.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Cerys, a community learning disability nurse, introduces the Disability Distress Assessment Tool (DisDAT) for Ellis, 42, who has a profound learning disability and no speech. His support team asks what DisDAT does. Which answer is correct?
o: It gives a numerical pain score that guides the dose of analgesia
It diagnoses the physical cause of distress from a checklist of signs
It measures how severe Ellis's learning disability is
It records Ellis's usual content and distress cues as a baseline
Communication in Learning Disability.w: DisDAT documents how a person looks and behaves when content and when distressed (face, eyes, skin, vocal sounds, habits and mannerisms, posture). This creates a baseline so changes can be recognised. It is not a scoring tool (DisDAT, Northumberland Tyne and Wear NHS Trust and St Oswald's Hospice).

n.0: DisDAT is descriptive and individual; it does not produce a score or set doses.
n.1: DisDAT helps identify distress, not its cause; clinical assessment finds the cause.
n.2: DisDAT is about distress cues, not severity of learning disability.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Using his DisDAT, staff recognise that Abdul, 39, who has a severe learning disability, is showing his distress cues: grimacing, rubbing his hands and refusing food. What should the nurse do next?
o: Give his PRN medicine for agitation as written in his care plan
Start his behaviour support plan's de-escalation strategies
Assess for possible causes such as pain, infection or constipation
Record the cues and review them again tomorrow
Communication in Learning Disability.w: DisDAT identifies that the person is distressed, not why. The next step is a clinical assessment for causes such as pain, infection, constipation, dental problems or emotional causes, then treating the cause and reassessing.

n.0: Sedative PRN treats the behaviour without finding the cause and may mask pain.
n.1: De-escalation addresses behaviour but leaves a possible physical cause untreated.
n.3: Waiting a day delays treatment of a possibly painful condition.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: A supported living team plans to complete a DisDAT for Freya, 31, who has a profound learning disability. When and with whom should it ideally be completed?
o: When Freya is unwell, by the nurse who is assessing her pain
At her annual health check, by the GP using her medical record
When Freya is well, with family and staff who know her best
During an admission, by ward staff observing her for the first time
Communication in Learning Disability.w: DisDAT is completed by people who know the person well, ideally when they are well, so their usual content cues are captured as a baseline. Distress cues are then recognisable when they appear.

n.0: Completing it only when unwell gives no content baseline to compare against.
n.1: The GP and records lack the day-to-day detail that close carers hold.
n.3: Ward staff who have just met Freya cannot describe her usual cues.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Joe, 25, has a severe learning disability and no speech. Over a day he has repeatedly pulled at his right ear and pushed his food away. Staff note this is new for him. What is the most likely meaning of this behaviour?
o: He is seeking attention because staff have been busy
He is bored with his meals and wants different food
He is communicating pain, possibly from his ear or mouth
He is showing a new habit that can be safely ignored
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Behaviour is communication. A new behaviour focused on one part of the body, with reduced eating, suggests pain such as ear infection or dental pain, which needs physical assessment (diagnostic overshadowing; LeDeR learning).

n.0: Explaining a new, body-focused behaviour as attention-seeking is diagnostic overshadowing.
n.1: Boredom does not explain ear pulling; pain is more likely and must be excluded.
n.3: A new behaviour may signal pain and should be assessed, not dismissed.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Chloe, 22, has a profound learning disability. Her DisDAT records that she makes loud moaning sounds when she is happy and goes silent and still when distressed. On admission a new nurse hears her moaning and plans to give PRN analgesia. What should the nurse do first?
o: Check her DisDAT and look for her other cues before deciding
Ask the doctor to prescribe regular analgesia in case of pain
Calculate a pain score using a numerical rating scale
Give the analgesia, since moaning is a common sign of pain
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Cues are individual. Chloe's DisDAT shows moaning is a content cue, so the nurse should compare her presentation with the baseline and other cues before deciding she is in pain (DisDAT; Annexe B 3.1).

n.1: Prescribing regular analgesia without evidence of pain is not person-centred.
n.2: A numerical scale requires self-report, which Chloe cannot give.
n.3: General assumptions about pain signs can be wrong for an individual; her own cues must guide the decision.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Dominic, 47, has a severe learning disability. He is usually very active, walking around the house and humming. For two days he has stayed in his chair, quiet and still. Staff say he is 'having a calm few days'. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Encourage him to join activities to lift his mood
Note the change and review him again at the end of the week
Treat this as a possible sign of pain or illness and assess him
Agree that this is positive and continue to monitor him
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Distress and pain may show as withdrawal and reduced activity, not only as agitation. A marked change from Dominic's baseline needs assessment for pain or illness (DisDAT; deteriorating patient learning from LeDeR).

n.0: Encouraging activity ignores a possible physical cause.
n.1: Waiting a week risks delayed diagnosis.
n.3: Interpreting withdrawal as calm may miss pain or illness.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Rania, 33, has a severe learning disability. Staff think her rocking and grimacing may be due to period pain, and she is given prescribed paracetamol. How should the nurse evaluate whether this has worked?
o: Reassess her using the same distress cues after a suitable interval
Assume it has worked if she does not ask for more
Ask Rania whether she feels better using a yes or no question
Check her temperature to see whether it has fallen
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Evaluation uses the same individual cues as the assessment: if her distress cues settle after a suitable interval for paracetamol, pain was a likely cause; if not, other causes must be explored (Annexe B 3.1; DisDAT).

n.1: Not asking for more is not evidence of relief in someone who cannot easily ask.
n.2: Yes or no questions are unreliable for Rania because of acquiescence and limited understanding.
n.3: Temperature is not a measure of pain relief.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Owen, 51, has a severe learning disability and limited understanding of language. He is admitted after a fall and may have a fractured hip. Which approach to pain assessment is most appropriate?
o: A 0 to 10 numerical rating scale explained with simple words
Asking 'Are you in pain?' each hour during observations
An observational tool based on his individual cues, with his carers
A faces scale, asking him to point to the face that matches his pain
Communication in Learning Disability.w: People who cannot self-report need observational assessment based on their own cues, ideally using a baseline such as DisDAT and input from carers who know them (Annexe B 3.1).

n.0: Numerical scales require understanding of numbers and abstract rating.
n.1: A yes or no question is unreliable because of limited understanding and acquiescence.
n.3: Faces scales still need him to match an abstract picture to his feeling, which he may not be able to do.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Archie, 11, is autistic and has a mild learning disability. He is due to have his tonsils removed next month and becomes very anxious about new situations. His community nurse suggests writing a Social Story. What is the purpose of a Social Story?
o: To record Archie's medical history for the anaesthetist to read
To describe what will happen and why, so the situation is predictable
To reward Archie with stickers each time he stays calm at hospital
To teach Archie the medical words used by hospital staff
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Social Stories, created by Carol Gray (1991), describe a situation, event or activity in a clear, reassuring way, so an autistic person knows what to expect. They are widely used to prepare people for hospital visits and procedures.

n.0: Medical history belongs in the clinical record or hospital passport.
n.2: Rewards are a behavioural strategy; a Social Story gives information to make events predictable.
n.3: Social Stories use everyday language to explain events, not to teach medical vocabulary.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Poppy, 24, has a moderate learning disability and autism. She is having a blood test, a weight check and then a chat with the doctor at clinic. She copes better when she knows what is coming next. Which tool will best help during the appointment?
o: A verbal explanation of the whole appointment at the start
A visual schedule showing each step in order with pictures
A leaflet describing the conditions the clinic treats
A written list of the clinic's opening times and staff names
Communication in Learning Disability.w: A visual schedule (for example a 'now and next' board) shows steps in order with pictures, making the sequence predictable and reducing anxiety for autistic people and people with a learning disability (NICE CG142 1.1.8 visual supports for autistic adults).

n.0: A single spoken explanation is hard to retain and gives no ongoing reference.
n.2: Information on conditions does not prepare her for the steps of her visit.
n.3: Opening times and staff names do not show her what will happen next.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Max, 33, has a moderate learning disability and is anxious about his planned knee operation. His learning disability liaison nurse is planning reasonable adjustments. Which adjustment is most likely to reduce his anxiety on the day?
o: Arranging a pre-admission visit to see the ward and meet staff
Admitting him the night before so he can settle in overnight
Keeping details from him until the day so he does not worry
Giving him a sedative premedication on arrival at the ward
Communication in Learning Disability.w: A pre-admission visit lets the person see the environment and meet staff in advance, making the day familiar and predictable. This is a common reasonable adjustment (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7).

n.1: An extra night in an unfamiliar ward may increase anxiety rather than reduce it.
n.2: Withholding information makes the day less predictable and may increase distress.
n.3: Sedation is a more restrictive option and does not replace preparation.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Lewis, 29, is autistic with a learning disability and needs an MRI scan. He is very sensitive to noise and has refused scans before. The scan is in six weeks. What should the learning disability nurse plan?
o: Book the scan under general anaesthetic without trying preparation
Tell Lewis about the scan on the morning so he has less time to worry
Ask the radiographer to complete the scan as quickly as possible
Graded preparation with photos, scanner sounds and a practice visit
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Graded desensitisation builds familiarity with each part of the experience over time and is a reasonable adjustment that may avoid sedation or anaesthetic (Equality Act 2010 s20; least restrictive option, MCA s1(6)).

n.0: General anaesthetic carries risks; less restrictive preparation should be tried first where time allows.
n.1: Late notice removes preparation time and may increase distress.
n.2: Speed does not address his sensory sensitivity or prior refusals.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Jas, a learning disability nurse, is writing a Social Story for Riley, 15, who is autistic and is having a blood test. Which sentence fits the Social Story approach best?
o: The nurse will put a band on my arm. It will feel tight for a short time.
If I do not keep still, the nurse will have to try again.
Most young people are brave and do not cry when they have blood taken.
The needle is tiny, so it will not hurt me when it goes in.
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Social Stories use descriptive, accurate and reassuring sentences, often in the first person, that explain what will happen and how it may feel. They avoid threats, comparisons and false promises (Carol Gray).

n.1: This frames the story as a warning, which can increase anxiety.
n.2: Comparisons and pressure to be 'brave' are not descriptive and can cause shame.
n.3: Promising it will not hurt is inaccurate and can damage trust.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Graham, 46, has a moderate learning disability. His mother, who lived with him, died suddenly last night. His support team asks the community nurse how to tell him. Which approach is best?
o: Wait until after the funeral so he is not upset during it
Ask his GP to tell him at his next appointment
Tell him plainly that she has died, with someone he trusts present
Tell him his mother has 'gone to sleep' to soften the news for him
Communication in Learning Disability.w: People with a learning disability need honest, concrete words (such as 'died') delivered by someone they trust in a familiar place, with time to repeat information and include them in mourning rituals. Euphemisms confuse and delays exclude (Annexe A 2.9).

n.0: Delaying the news excludes him from the funeral and grieving with family.
n.1: Waiting for a routine appointment delays the news and removes the support of familiar people.
n.3: Euphemisms like 'gone to sleep' are confusing and can cause fear of sleep.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Wendy, 52, has a mild learning disability and has just been diagnosed with breast cancer. Her brother asks the team not to tell her because 'she will not cope'. Wendy has asked staff why she had the scan. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Hear his concerns, then plan staged, accessible disclosure to Wendy
Agree to the brother's request, as he knows Wendy best
Ask the brother to decide when Wendy should be told
Tell Wendy the full diagnosis and treatment plan in one meeting
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Wendy has a right to information about her health and is asking for it. The team should listen to her brother's concerns but plan honest, accessible disclosure in small chunks with pictures and checking understanding (Code 2, 4, 7; Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations).

n.1: Withholding a diagnosis from someone who is asking breaches her rights and prevents her making decisions.
n.2: The decision belongs with the team and Wendy, not her brother.
n.3: Giving all the information at once overloads understanding; staged disclosure is more effective.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Hamid, 20, is autistic and uses a picture schedule prepared for his day-case procedure. On arrival he learns that theatre is running two hours late. He starts pacing and flapping his hands. What should the nurse do first?
o: Update his schedule with him, adding a waiting activity
Ask his carer to take him for a long walk until theatre calls
Give him the prescribed PRN medicine to help him wait calmly
Reassure him verbally that everything is fine and he will go soon
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Unexpected change is distressing for many autistic people. Promptly updating the visual schedule and adding a planned waiting activity restores predictability (NICE CG142 1.1.8 visual supports for autistic adults; Annexe A 2.8).

n.1: Leaving without a clear plan adds uncertainty and may cause him to miss his slot.
n.2: PRN sedation is a more restrictive response when an adjustment can address the cause.
n.3: Vague reassurance does not restore predictability and 'soon' may be inaccurate.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Holly, a student nurse in a community learning disability team, hears her assessor say the team uses a 'total communication' approach. Holly asks what this means in practice. Which description is correct?
o: Using one agreed system, such as Makaton, across all services the person attends
Combining speech, signs, symbols, objects and gestures to suit the person
Replacing speech with pictures for every person who has a learning disability
Asking a speech and language therapist to lead every conversation with the person
Communication in Learning Disability.w: Total communication means using every available channel (speech, signs, symbols, photographs, objects, gestures, body language and technology), tailored to the individual, so the person can understand and be understood.

n.0: Using one system for everyone is the opposite of total communication, which combines methods to suit the person.
n.2: Pictures help some people but not all; total communication adds channels rather than removing speech.
n.3: SLTs assess and advise, but everyone supporting the person uses total communication day to day.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Ffion, 32, has a severe learning disability and is starting at a new day service. Her family bring a communication passport to her first visit. Staff ask what it is for. Which explanation is correct?
o: It records the legal decisions made in Ffion's best interests
It describes how Ffion communicates and how to communicate with her
It sets out the goals agreed in Ffion's person-centred plan
It records Ffion's medical history and current medicines for staff
Communication in Learning Disability.w: A communication passport is a person-centred document describing how the person communicates (what their sounds, signs and behaviours mean) and how others can best communicate with them, so new staff can understand her quickly.

n.0: Best interests decisions are recorded in the care record under the Mental Capacity Act.
n.2: Goals belong in the person-centred plan; the passport is about communication.
n.3: Medical history and medicines are in the clinical record or hospital passport, not the communication passport.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Gary, 40, has a mild learning disability. The nurse explains a change to his insulin and asks, 'Do you understand?' Gary smiles and says 'yes', as he does to most questions. What is the best way to check his understanding?
o: Ask him again more slowly whether he understands the change
Give him a printed copy of the instructions and ask him to sign it
Ask his support worker whether Gary has understood the change
Ask Gary to show or tell her in his own words what he will do
Communication in Learning Disability.w: People with a learning disability may agree with questions to please or to avoid looking unsure (acquiescence). Asking the person to explain or demonstrate in their own words checks real understanding (teach-back; Annexe A 1.6 check understanding; Code 7.4).

n.0: Repeating a closed yes or no question is likely to get the same answer.
n.1: A signature on a printed sheet does not show understanding and may be inaccessible.
n.2: His support worker cannot confirm what Gary himself understands.

Communication in Learning Disability.q: Rosa, 27, has a moderate learning disability and is being told about her new antibiotic. Which way of speaking is most likely to help her understand?
o: Medical terms explained afterwards in a written leaflet she can keep
A full explanation in one go so that she hears every detail together
A raised voice and slower speech to make sure every word is heard
Short sentences with one idea each, key words stressed and time to respond
Communication in Learning Disability.w: People with a learning disability often need more time to process information. Short sentences, one idea at a time, key words, pauses and checking understanding support communication (Annexe A 1.6; NMC Code 7.1 and 7.4).

n.0: Jargon is a barrier; a leaflet afterwards does not fix an inaccessible explanation.
n.1: Too much information at once overloads processing and reduces understanding.
n.2: Raising the voice does not help understanding unless she has hearing loss and can seem aggressive.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Tom, 30, has a severe learning disability. His PBS plan includes a reactive strategy of two-person holding when he hits other residents. In the last month the hold has been used nine times, compared with once a month previously. What should the learning disability nurse do next?
o: Ask staff to start the hold earlier so that it ends each episode more quickly
Request a GP review to start PRN medication for use before the hold is needed
Review the functional assessment and the proactive strategies in the plan
Add a third member of staff to each hold to reduce the risk of injury
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: A rise in restrictive interventions signals that the proactive parts of the plan are not meeting Tom's needs. NICE NG11 says reactive strategies are used alongside proactive ones and that restrictive interventions should be reviewed and reduced (1.9.4-1.9.6); the next step is to revisit the functional assessment and the primary and secondary strategies.

n.0: Using the hold earlier increases restriction and does nothing about why the behaviour has increased.
n.1: PRN medication is a restrictive intervention in its own right; NG11 puts it after psychosocial review, not as the next step here.
n.3: Changing the hold manages the incident but leaves the cause unaddressed; reduction of restriction is the goal.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A support worker asks Hannah, a learning disability nurse, why a PBS plan for Lily, 22, includes teaching her to hand over a 'break' card. Lily throws objects to escape tasks she finds hard. What is the best explanation?
o: The card replaces throwing with a safer way of getting the same outcome
The card lets staff record how often Lily wants a break during the day
The card gives Lily a reward that makes her less likely to throw objects again
The card is a reactive strategy that staff can use once Lily starts throwing
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Teaching a functionally equivalent replacement behaviour is a core proactive PBS strategy (functional communication training): if throwing serves escape, the card gives Lily an acceptable, reliable way to request a break, so the behaviour is no longer needed (PBS model; NICE NG11 1.6.1 strategies to develop an alternative behaviour that achieves the same function).

n.1: Data collection may follow, but the purpose of the card is to give Lily a replacement behaviour.
n.2: The card is not a reward contingent on not throwing; it is a communication tool that meets the same need.
n.3: Teaching a new skill is primary prevention, used before any throwing, not a reactive strategy.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ravi, 45, has a moderate learning disability and lives in a residential home. His PBS plan was written 18 months ago. Since then he has moved bedroom, his mother has died and he has started new medication for epilepsy. He is now shouting at staff most evenings. What is the priority action?
o: Arrange bereavement counselling for Ravi before any changes to his support
Remind staff to follow the existing PBS plan more consistently in the evenings
Ask the GP to increase Ravi's epilepsy medication to improve his seizure control
Review the plan, starting with a physical health check and a new functional assessment
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Two-step reasoning: major changes in his life, health and medication mean the old plan may no longer match his needs, and new behaviour may reflect pain, side effects or grief. NICE NG11 asks for assessments to be reviewed after any significant change (1.5.2) and for physical and mental health, medication side effects and recent life events to be taken into account (1.5.5); a physical check avoids diagnostic overshadowing.

n.0: Grief may be relevant, but it should be one part of a full review that also excludes physical causes and side effects.
n.1: Insisting on an out-of-date plan ignores the changes that may now be driving the behaviour.
n.2: There is no evidence of poor seizure control; a medication change could add side effects without addressing the cause.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Sofia, 28, has a severe learning disability. Her PBS plan includes a planned restrictive intervention: briefly holding her wrists if she scratches her face hard enough to bleed. A new nurse asks what must also be in place for this to be lawful and ethical. Which answer is best?
o: A Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards authorisation covering the use of physical holds
A signed instruction from the consultant psychiatrist authorising the hold for Sofia
A record that Sofia's family agreed to the hold when the plan was written
A best interests decision that it is necessary and proportionate, with review
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG11 1.9.5-1.9.6: planned restrictive interventions must be lawful (MCA, HRA), in the person's best interests where they lack capacity, a reasonable, necessary and proportionate response to the risk, the least restrictive option, documented, debriefed and reviewed within a reduction programme.

n.0: DoLS authorises a deprivation of liberty in a care home or hospital; it is not the authority for a brief planned hold, which rests on MCA ss5-6.
n.1: A doctor's instruction does not replace the MCA best interests process and proportionality test.
n.2: Families must be consulted, but family agreement does not on its own make an intervention lawful for an adult who lacks capacity.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Callum, 24, has a severe learning disability. Staff record that he screams and pushes his plate away at most mealtimes. The learning disability nurse starts an ABC chart. What should staff write in the 'A' column?
o: Staff members' views on why Callum behaves this way at meals
How staff responded and what happened straight afterwards
What happened just before Callum screamed and pushed his plate
Exactly what Callum did and how long the screaming lasted
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: ABC recording captures the Antecedent (what happened immediately before, the trigger), the Behaviour (a clear description of what the person did) and the Consequence (what happened afterwards). Antecedents point to triggers and setting events (NICE NG11 1.5.9-1.5.10).

n.0: Opinions about cause are not part of ABC data; the record should be objective observation.
n.1: Staff responses and what followed are recorded in the 'C' (consequence) column.
n.3: A description of what he did and its duration belongs in the 'B' (behaviour) column.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Grace, 32, has a moderate learning disability. ABC records show that she tips over her chair each time staff ask her to start a cleaning task, and staff then let her sit in the lounge instead. Which function is the behaviour most likely to serve?
o: Sensory stimulation
Access to a preferred item
Gaining attention from staff
Escape from a demand
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: The four functions of behaviour are escape or avoidance, social attention, access to tangibles and sensory (automatic) reinforcement. The behaviour follows a demand and results in the task being removed, which points to escape (NICE NG11 1.5 functional assessment).

n.0: Sensory behaviour occurs across settings regardless of demands; this pattern is tied to a task request.
n.1: She is not given a specific item or activity she was asking for; the demand is removed.
n.2: Nothing in the records shows that staff attention follows the behaviour; the consequence is that the task stops.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Daniel, 40, has a profound learning disability and rocks and flicks his fingers in front of his eyes for long periods, including when he is alone in his room and nothing is being asked of him. Which function is most likely?
o: Social attention
Escape from a demand
Access to a tangible item or activity
Sensory or automatic reinforcement
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Behaviour that continues when the person is alone, with no demands and no social consequence, is most likely maintained by the sensory feedback it produces (automatic reinforcement), one of the four functions identified in functional assessment.

n.0: The behaviour persists when nobody is with him, so attention does not maintain it.
n.1: There are no demands present for him to escape, so escape is unlikely.
n.2: He does not gain an object or activity as a result of the behaviour.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A student nurse on a learning disability placement asks why the team spends weeks on a functional assessment before writing a behaviour support plan for Ayesha, 27. What is the best explanation?
o: It shows why the behaviour happens so support can target that need
It gives evidence that the behaviour is severe enough for admission
It identifies which staff members are causing the behaviour to happen
It is needed so that a referral for medication can be accepted
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG11 1.5.6 recommends a written formulation of what led to the behaviour and the function it serves; this understanding is the basis for a support plan that meets the need, rather than simply suppressing the behaviour.

n.1: NG11 aims to support people in the least restrictive setting close to home, not to build a case for admission.
n.2: Staff interactions are one possible influence, but the assessment is not designed to find fault with individuals.
n.3: Medication is not the purpose of functional assessment; NG11 puts psychological and environmental approaches first.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ben, 35, has a moderate learning disability. ABC charts show he hits out on some days when asked to get dressed but not on others. Night staff notes show the incidents follow nights when he slept less than four hours. How should the nurse describe the poor sleep in the formulation?
o: A consequence that keeps the behaviour going
A trigger that immediately precedes the behaviour
A setting event that makes the behaviour more likely
The function the behaviour serves for Ben
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Setting events are background conditions (poor sleep, pain, hunger, illness) that change how likely a trigger is to provoke the behaviour. NICE NG11 1.5.9 asks for setting events to be identified alongside triggers and maintaining consequences.

n.0: Consequences follow the behaviour; poor sleep comes before it.
n.1: The immediate trigger is the request to get dressed; poor sleep is a background condition, not the antecedent.
n.3: The function is what the behaviour achieves (for example escape); sleep loss influences likelihood but is not a function.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Fatima, 29, has a severe learning disability and has started slapping her cheek in the last fortnight. Her support staff believe she does it for attention and want to start a functional assessment straight away. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask staff to give Fatima less attention when she slaps her cheek
Begin ABC charts so the function can be identified within a week
Ask the GP to prescribe PRN medication while the assessment is done
Arrange a physical health review, including her teeth and ears
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Two-step reasoning: a new behaviour directed at one part of the face may signal pain (for example dental abscess or ear infection). NICE NG11 asks for physical health problems to be taken into account in assessment (1.5.5) and, for recent-onset behaviour, whether physical health changes are associated with it (1.5.11); assessing this first avoids diagnostic overshadowing.

n.0: Withdrawing attention assumes the function without assessment and could leave pain untreated.
n.1: ABC data are useful, but recent onset and the location of the slapping make a physical cause the first thing to exclude.
n.2: Medication before assessment risks masking a treatable cause and is contrary to NG11 and STOMP.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A functional assessment for Leo, 23, who has a learning disability, has been completed and a support plan started. Six weeks later, the nurse is evaluating the plan. Which measure best shows whether the plan is working?
o: The number of staff who have read and signed the plan
The number of PRN doses given during the six weeks
Staff ratings of whether Leo seems calmer than he was before the plan
Behaviour and quality-of-life data compared with the baseline
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG11 1.5.10 asks for a baseline of the behaviour (frequency, severity, duration) and of quality of life, so that the effect of interventions can be measured against it; evaluation compares current data with that baseline (P3.15).

n.0: Staff sign-off shows the plan was shared, not whether it changed outcomes for Leo.
n.1: PRN use is one indicator, but on its own it does not measure behaviour or quality of life against the baseline.
n.2: Impressions are less reliable than measured data compared with the baseline.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Noah, 31, has a moderate learning disability. ABC records show he grabs other people's drinks in the café. Each time, staff buy him his own drink to calm the situation. The episodes have increased from twice to eight times a week. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The café is too noisy and is causing sensory overload
Staff are giving him attention, which maintains the behaviour
He is thirsty because his fluid intake at home is too low
Buying a drink acts as a consequence that reinforces the grabbing
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: The behaviour reliably produces access to a tangible (his own drink), and its frequency has risen since this response began, showing the consequence is reinforcing it. Functional assessment looks at consequences that maintain behaviour (NICE NG11 1.5.9).

n.0: Nothing in the records points to noise as a trigger; the pattern fits access to a drink.
n.1: The consistent consequence is the drink itself; attention is not what changes after the behaviour.
n.2: Thirst could be checked, but it would not explain the rise linked to staff buying a drink each time.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: In a supported living service, staff keep the kitchen cupboards locked because Alfie, 33, who has Prader-Willi syndrome, eats food compulsively. A new support worker asks the learning disability nurse what kind of practice this is. Which answer is correct?
o: A mechanical restrictive practice
A seclusion-based restrictive practice
An environmental restrictive practice
A chemical restrictive practice
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Locking doors or cupboards to limit a person's access to their environment or belongings is an environmental restriction. Like all restrictive practices it needs a lawful basis (for example an MCA best interests decision), must be the least restrictive option and should be reviewed (NICE NG11 1.9; MCA 2005 s1(6)).

n.0: Mechanical restraint uses a device (for example arm splints or a belt) to restrict movement; locked cupboards restrict access, not movement.
n.1: Seclusion is confining a person alone in a room they cannot leave, which is not what is happening.
n.3: Chemical restraint is the use of medication to control behaviour, which is not described here.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Sara, 25, has a severe learning disability. Staff on an assessment unit often give her PRN lorazepam when she shouts in the corridor, although she is not harming anyone. Which concern should the learning disability nurse raise?
o: The PRN should be changed to a regular dose so that she is calmer all day
Shouting in a corridor should be managed with seclusion rather than drugs
The PRN use may be chemical restraint without a clear, proportionate need
The lorazepam dose may be too low to be effective at reducing her shouting
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Medication used to control behaviour is a restrictive intervention (chemical restraint). NICE NG11 1.8.4 and 1.9 say PRN should be used for as short a time as possible, recorded and reviewed, and restrictive interventions must be necessary and proportionate to a real risk; shouting without risk of harm does not meet that test (STOMP).

n.0: Regular sedation would increase restriction and contradicts STOMP and NG11.
n.1: Seclusion is more restrictive and is not justified by shouting that poses no risk of harm.
n.3: Raising the dose increases restriction without addressing whether medication is justified at all.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: After staff use a two-person hold to stop Kieran, 20, from hitting another resident, the learning disability nurse leads the response. Kieran has a moderate learning disability. Which action should follow once everyone is safe?
o: Ask the GP for regular sedation to prevent further incidents
Add the hold to Kieran's plan as the first response for the future
Move Kieran to another service so that the other resident is protected
Record the hold and hold a debrief with Kieran and with staff
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG11 1.9.6: every restrictive intervention is recorded and followed by a debrief with the person (in an accessible way) and with staff, to support recovery and learn how to prevent recurrence; data feed into the reduction programme.

n.0: Regular sedation is chemical restraint and is not supported by NG11 or STOMP after one incident.
n.1: Restrictive interventions are a last resort; making the hold the first response increases restriction.
n.2: A placement move is a major decision that is not justified by a single incident and does not address the cause.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A learning disability nurse is teaching staff about restraint under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 for adults who lack capacity. Which statement correctly describes when restraint is lawful under s6?
o: When it is needed to make the person follow the daily routine
When it is in the person's best interests and the family have agreed
When it prevents harm to the person and is proportionate to that harm
When it is written in the care plan and signed by the manager
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: MCA 2005 s6: restraint is permitted only if the person taking action reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to the person who lacks capacity, and the act is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. It must also be in the person's best interests (s5).

n.0: Securing compliance with a routine is not prevention of harm and does not meet s6.
n.1: Family agreement is not the legal test; s6 requires necessity to prevent harm and proportionality.
n.3: Documentation is good practice, but a signed plan does not make a disproportionate restraint lawful.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: An inpatient unit for autistic people and people with a learning disability is reviewing its use of force. The ward manager asks which law, often called Seni's Law, sets duties such as a use-of-force policy, training and recording. Which Act is this?
o: Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018
Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014
Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019
Mental Capacity Act 2005
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: The Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018 (Seni's Law) applies to mental health units, including inpatient units for people with a learning disability or autistic people. It requires a responsible person, a use-of-force policy, information for patients, staff training and records of any use of force.

n.1: These regulations set CQC fundamental standards for registered providers; they are not Seni's Law and do not set the unit use-of-force duties.
n.2: The 2019 Act created the Liberty Protection Safeguards, which are not in force; it is not Seni's Law.
n.3: The MCA governs restraint of people who lack capacity generally, but it is not Seni's Law and does not set unit use-of-force duties.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Evie, 37, has a profound learning disability and pulls out her gastrostomy tube. Staff suggest arm splints at all times. The nurse wants the least restrictive option. Which plan is best?
o: Use arm splints at night and remove them for meals during the day
Ask the GP to prescribe sedation so that she does not pull the tube
Fit splints day and night and review them at the next annual review
Use a tube cover and abdominal binder, agreed in a best interests review
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: MCA 2005 s1(6) requires the less restrictive option to be considered. A tube cover or binder protects the gastrostomy with far less restriction of movement than splints, and any restriction must be agreed through a best interests decision and reviewed (NICE NG11 1.9.5).

n.0: Night-time splints still restrict her movement for long periods when a less restrictive device could protect the tube.
n.1: Sedation is chemical restraint and is more restrictive than protecting the tube directly.
n.2: Continuous splints are highly restrictive, and waiting a year to review breaches the duty to minimise restriction.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Monthly data on a learning disability inpatient unit show 40 physical restraints, mostly on three patients and mostly between 4pm and 6pm when staff change shifts. The nurse in charge is asked to lead a reduction plan. Which first step is best?
o: Train all staff in additional holding techniques for late afternoon
Analyse the incidents with patients and staff to find and change the triggers
Increase PRN medication at 3pm for the three patients involved
Ask the three patients' families to visit outside the 4pm to 6pm period
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Two-step reasoning: the data show a pattern (time, people), so the next step is to understand why. NICE NG11 1.9.4 requires a restrictive intervention reduction programme that uses incident data and involves people and staff to change practice, such as how handovers are staffed and how the patients are supported at that time.

n.0: More holding training prepares staff to restrain, rather than reducing the need for restraint.
n.2: Scheduled PRN is chemical restraint and swaps one restriction for another.
n.3: Nothing suggests visits cause the incidents; the pattern points to the shift change.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: During an incident, Harvey, 22, who has a learning disability, falls to the floor face down while staff are holding him. One staff member suggests keeping him there until he calms. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep him face down and count his breathing rate every five minutes
Help him into a seated or side position and monitor his breathing
Keep him face down with weight across his shoulders until he is calm
Leave him face down and ask all staff to step back and observe
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Prone (face down) restraint carries a serious risk of positional asphyxia; Department of Health 'Positive and Proactive Care' (2014) says people must not be deliberately held face down. Staff should release or move to a safer position as soon as possible and monitor airway, breathing and wellbeing throughout (NICE NG10/NG11 principles).

n.0: Monitoring every five minutes does not remove the danger of continuing to hold him face down.
n.2: Pressure on the back or shoulders in the prone position greatly increases the risk of asphyxia.
n.3: Stepping back without helping him change position leaves him in an unsafe position and unmonitored at close range.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Joel, 19, is autistic and has a learning disability. His placement at home is breaking down after several crises, and his family fear he may be admitted to a mental health hospital. The community learning disability nurse wants the integrated care board to know he is at risk. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask for Joel to be added to the dynamic support register
Add Joel to the GP learning disability register
Refer Joel for an inpatient bed so one is ready if needed
Request a Mental Health Act assessment as a precaution
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: The dynamic support register (DSR) records people with a learning disability and autistic people at risk of admission to a mental health inpatient setting, so that extra support and a community C(E)TR can be arranged to avoid admission (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy, 2023).

n.1: The GP register is the gateway to annual health checks, not the tool for flagging risk of admission.
n.2: Planning a bed in advance works against the aim of keeping Joel at home with more support.
n.3: An MHA assessment is not a precaution and would not trigger the community support the DSR gives.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A student nurse asks what a Care and Treatment Review (CTR) is for an adult with a learning disability at risk of admission. Which answer is best?
o: A formal complaint process for families who are unhappy with care
An independent review of whether care is safe and community options are used
A Care Act needs assessment completed by a local authority social worker
A review of whether the person meets the criteria for detention
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: C(E)TRs bring an independent panel to look at whether the person's care, (education) and treatment are safe and effective, whether community alternatives to admission have been used and what is needed to avoid admission or speed discharge (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy).

n.0: Complaints have their own process; a CTR reviews care and treatment, not complaints.
n.2: A Care Act assessment determines eligible care and support needs; a CTR is a different, NHS-led review.
n.3: Detention criteria are decided under the Mental Health Act by AMHPs and doctors, not by a CTR.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A community learning disability nurse is arranging a C(E)TR for Zara, 15. Which panel members must be present in addition to the chair?
o: Zara's GP and her head teacher
A clinical expert and an expert by experience
A police officer and a safeguarding lead
A consultant psychiatrist and an approved mental health professional
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Under the NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy (2023) every review panel includes a chair (usually the commissioner), an independent clinical expert and an independent expert by experience (a person with lived experience or a family carer).

n.0: The GP and school provide information; the independent panel members are a clinical expert and an expert by experience.
n.2: Police and safeguarding leads are not core C(E)TR panel members.
n.3: These professionals may contribute evidence but are not the required independent panel members.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ethan, 28, has a learning disability and was admitted urgently to an assessment and treatment unit without a pre-admission review. Under the NHS England C(E)TR policy, by when should a post-admission CTR take place?
o: Within 3 months of admission
Within 72 hours of admission
Within 14 days of admission
Within 28 days of admission
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: The NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy (2023) sets post-admission reviews within 28 days for adults and within 14 days for children and young people, where no review took place before admission.

n.0: Three months is far longer than the policy allows and would delay planning for discharge.
n.1: 72 hours is the length of some Mental Health Act holding powers (for example section 5(2) or section 4), not the CTR timescale.
n.2: 14 days is the timescale for children and young people; Ethan is an adult.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ruby, 24, has a learning disability and has been on an inpatient unit for 14 months. Her clinical team say she no longer needs hospital care, but no community provider has been found. Her mother asks what can help. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Request a C(E)TR to identify discharge barriers and who will act on them
Suggest a transfer to a nearer hospital until a provider is found
Ask the consultant to apply for Ruby to be detained under section 3
Advise that Ruby must stay until her discharge plan is fully funded
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Two-step reasoning: Ruby is clinically ready for discharge but delayed by a lack of community support.
