C(E)TRs review barriers to discharge and set actions with named owners; Building the Right Support aims to reduce long inpatient stays and develop community services (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy; BRS).

n.1: A move to another hospital keeps her in inpatient care she no longer needs.
n.2: Detention is not justified when she no longer needs hospital treatment and would not help discharge.
n.3: Waiting passively accepts an inappropriate delay rather than challenging the barriers.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A ward manager asks a learning disability nurse what the national Building the Right Support programme set out to achieve for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Which answer is correct?
o: To increase specialist inpatient beds so that people are treated near home
To reduce reliance on inpatient care by developing community support
To make Care and Treatment Reviews a requirement under the Care Act 2014
To transfer all learning disability services to local authority control
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Building the Right Support (2015) and its 2022 action plan aim to reduce the number of people with a learning disability and autistic people in mental health inpatient settings by developing community services; the action plan target was to halve inpatient numbers from 2015 levels by March 2024, which was missed (BRS; Commons Library SN07058).

n.0: The aim was to reduce, not increase, reliance on inpatient beds.
n.2: C(E)TRs are NHS England policy; the Care Act 2014 did not make them statutory.
n.3: The programme involves NHS and local government jointly; it did not transfer services to councils.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Lucas, 30, has a learning disability and is on the dynamic support register, rated at high risk of admission. His behaviour has escalated over a week, and his support provider says it can no longer cope. What should the community nurse do first?
o: Tell the provider to give notice so that the council must act quickly
Arrange for Lucas to go to the emergency department for assessment
Request an urgent community C(E)TR and extra support to keep him at home
Ask the GP to start an antipsychotic to settle him over the weekend
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: For people at high risk on the DSR, the policy is a community C(E)TR and intensive support to avoid admission where possible, with the least restrictive setting close to home (NHS England DSR and C(E)TR policy; NICE NG11 1.1 and NG93).

n.0: Encouraging the placement to end raises the risk of admission rather than reducing it.
n.1: A busy emergency department is an unfamiliar, noisy setting for a behavioural crisis and is likely to increase distress and the risk of admission.
n.3: NG11 does not support starting an antipsychotic before psychosocial review; this may also breach STOMP.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A nurse hears that the Mental Health Act 2025 changes how people with a learning disability can be detained. A colleague says that from now on a person cannot be detained under section 3 because of a learning disability. What is the correct position in October 2026?
o: Correct, the change came into force with the new Code of Practice in 2026
Incorrect, the change has been enacted but is not yet in force
Incorrect, the 2025 Act did not change the rules for learning disability
Correct, the 2025 Act removed learning disability from section 3 on Royal Assent
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 (Royal Assent 18 Dec 2025) will stop learning disability or autism alone justifying s3 detention, but ss3-4 and Sch 1 are prospective and not in force; the 1983 Act as amended applies, including the 'abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct' qualifier for s3 (MHA83 s1(2A)-(2B)).

n.0: No commencement has brought the s3 change into force, and a code of practice cannot do so.
n.2: The 2025 Act does contain this change; it is simply not yet in force.
n.3: Royal Assent did not bring this change into force; legislation.gov.uk shows the provisions as prospective.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Megan, 36, has a severe learning disability and little speech. Over two months she has stopped joining activities she loved, sleeps badly, eats less and has lost the ability to dress herself. Her support staff think she is 'just being lazy'. What should the learning disability nurse consider first?
o: That Megan may be depressed and needs a mental and physical health assessment
That Megan is choosing not to take part and her choice should be respected
That Megan's loss of skills is part of her learning disability
That a reward chart will help Megan regain her dressing skills
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG54 1.1.2 says presentation of mental health problems differs in people with a learning disability: withdrawal, loss of skills and changes in sleep and appetite may signal depression. A full assessment (and exclusion of physical causes) avoids diagnostic overshadowing.

n.1: Choice matters, but a broad change in mood, sleep, appetite and skills points to illness rather than preference.
n.2: A learning disability is lifelong and stable; a new loss of skills needs investigation, not attribution to the disability.
n.3: A reward chart assumes motivation is the problem and could delay assessment of an illness.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A learning disability nurse is assessing the mental health of Kofi, 29, who has a moderate learning disability and limited verbal communication. According to NICE NG54, who should usually be involved in the assessment?
o: Kofi, with his family or carers who know him well
His GP, using his records from the annual health check
Kofi, seen privately so that his confidentiality is protected
His consultant psychiatrist, without carers present
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG54 1.7.5 says assess recent changes in behaviour using information from family members, carers and staff as well as records, taking into account their relationship with the person; they can describe change from Kofi's usual presentation and help with communication.

n.1: Records help, but an assessment needs Kofi himself and those who know him, not records alone.
n.2: Confidentiality matters, but excluding everyone who knows Kofi would lose crucial information about change from his baseline.
n.3: Specialist input may be needed, but excluding carers loses the knowledge of his usual behaviour.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ellie, 23, has a mild learning disability and has been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. She would like a talking therapy. Which approach is most consistent with NICE NG54?
o: Offer a psychological intervention adapted to her communication and needs
Offer an antidepressant first and review the need for therapy in six months
Advise that talking therapies are unsuitable for people with a learning disability
Refer her to a general group therapy course with no adjustments
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG54 1.8.2-1.8.3 says tailor psychological interventions to the person's understanding, communication and sensory needs and agree goals with them (and carers if appropriate); for anxiety, 1.8.6-1.8.7 suggest relaxation therapy or graded exposure, adapted for people with learning disabilities.

n.1: Medication is not the first offer when she wants therapy, and delaying therapy is not supported.
n.2: Psychological therapies are recommended when adapted; excluding Ellie would be discriminatory.
n.3: Without adjustments a standard group is unlikely to meet her needs and fails the reasonable adjustment duty.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Sam, 41, has a moderate learning disability and lives in a group home. Since the death of a housemate he has been tearful and has told staff 'I want to be with Pete in heaven'. Staff think he does not understand what he is saying. What should the nurse do?
o: Wait until the next annual health check to raise it with the GP
Ask Sam directly and gently about thoughts of ending his life
Reassure staff that Sam is grieving and needs no further action
Distract Sam from talking about Pete to avoid upsetting him
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: People with a learning disability can experience suicidal thoughts and must not be assumed not to mean what they say. Asking directly and gently about suicidal thoughts is the first step to assessing and managing any risk, and research indicates that asking does not increase suicidal thinking. Mental health problems are common in people with a learning disability and may present differently (NICE NG54 1.2.8).

n.0: Delaying months leaves a possible risk unassessed now.
n.2: Grief is likely, but the statement needs exploring before deciding no action is needed.
n.3: Avoiding the subject denies Sam support and leaves any risk unassessed.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Asif, 32, has a moderate learning disability. His sister reports he has been talking to someone who is not there, and he is frightened in his room at night. Staff say he has always talked to himself. What is the best next step for the learning disability nurse?
o: Move him to a different bedroom and see whether his fear settles over a week
Compare with his known baseline and arrange a mental health assessment
Ask the GP to start an antipsychotic to help him sleep at night
Record that this is his usual self-talk and close the concern
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Two-step reasoning: self-talk can be normal for some people with a learning disability, so the nurse first compares with the person's baseline; a change in content (frightened, responding to voices) suggests possible psychosis and needs a specialist mental health assessment (NICE NG54 1.1.2 differences in presentation; 1.6.5 refer suspected serious mental illness to a psychiatrist with expertise in learning disabilities).

n.0: Changing rooms may help comfort but does not assess a possible mental illness.
n.2: Medication before assessment is not appropriate and conflicts with STOMP.
n.3: Dismissing the change as usual self-talk is diagnostic overshadowing; the sister describes something new.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A community nurse uses a PAS-ADD checklist with support staff caring for Olivia, 45, who has a learning disability. What is the purpose of this tool?
o: To measure Olivia's IQ and adaptive functioning
To diagnose a specific mental illness without a clinical assessment
To screen for possible mental health problems needing full assessment
To assess Olivia's capacity to consent to treatment
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: The PAS-ADD family of tools (Psychiatric Assessment Schedules for Adults with Developmental Disabilities) includes checklists completed by carers to screen for possible mental health problems, prompting referral for full assessment. They support, but do not replace, clinical diagnosis.

n.0: IQ and adaptive functioning are measured with different psychometric tools.
n.1: A screening checklist identifies possible problems; diagnosis requires clinical assessment.
n.3: Capacity is assessed under the MCA for a specific decision, not with a PAS-ADD checklist.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Hollie, 27, has a moderate learning disability and depression and finds it hard to describe how she feels. Her psychiatrist starts an antidepressant. Which approach to dosing best reflects NICE NG54?
o: Stop the tablets if her mood has not improved after one week
Start at the maximum licensed dose so that her mood improves quickly
Aim for the lowest effective dose, watching for side effects she may not report
Keep the dose low and below the therapeutic range to avoid any side effects
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG54 1.9.5: when deciding the initial dose and increases, aim for the lowest effective dose, taking account of side effects and the person's difficulty in reporting them, and avoid sub-therapeutic doses. 1.9.4: monitor benefits and harms using agreed outcome measures that reflect communication needs.

n.0: Antidepressants usually take weeks to work; one week is too soon to judge and stopping abruptly is not advised.
n.1: Starting at the maximum dose ignores her higher risk of side effects she may be unable to report.
n.3: NG54 1.9.5 warns against sub-therapeutic doses that may not treat the depression effectively.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ibrahim, 38, has a severe learning disability. For three weeks he has been more agitated, slapping his face and refusing food. Staff ask for a referral to the mental health team for 'challenging behaviour'. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase his PRN medication until the referral is seen
Ask staff to reduce his activities to lower his stress
Make the referral now and start an ABC chart while waiting to be seen
Arrange a physical check to exclude pain, constipation or infection
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG54 and NG11 advise excluding physical health problems, including pain, that may cause or worsen changes in behaviour or mental state. Face slapping and food refusal could indicate dental or ear pain, constipation or infection; physical assessment first prevents overshadowing.

n.0: Increasing PRN masks distress and is a restrictive response contrary to STOMP.
n.1: Reducing activities lowers quality of life and does not find the cause.
n.2: Referral may be needed later, but a physical cause should be excluded first.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Tyler, 20, is autistic and has a learning disability. He is admitted to a busy medical ward with a chest infection. He covers his ears, rocks and shouts when the bay is noisy. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Explain firmly that shouting disturbs other patients in the bay
Ask the doctor to prescribe PRN lorazepam to help him settle
Move Tyler to a quieter side room and reduce noise and lighting
Ask his family to go home so that he has fewer people around him
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Tyler is showing signs of sensory overload. NICE CG142 1.1.8 advises adjusting the environment for autistic adults (noise, lighting, personal space) as a reasonable adjustment; a quieter room addresses the cause and is the least restrictive response.

n.0: Firm verbal correction does not reduce sensory overload and may increase distress.
n.1: Medication would be chemical restraint for a distress response the environment can address, contrary to STOMP.
n.3: Familiar people usually reduce anxiety; sending them away removes his main support.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Maya, 17, is autistic. Her outpatient appointment has been moved to a different clinic room at short notice and she has become very anxious in the waiting area. Which reasonable adjustment would best prevent this next time?
o: Ask Maya's mother to attend instead of Maya to save her stress
Give advance notice of any change with a photo of the new room
Offer Maya a sedative to take an hour before each appointment
Book the longest available slot in the middle of the clinic day
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Unexpected change commonly drives anxiety in autistic people. Advance warning and visual information make change predictable; CG170 1.1.10 also suggests appointments at the start or end of the day to minimise waiting.

n.0: Excluding Maya removes her right to take part in her own care.
n.2: Routine sedation is not a reasonable adjustment and is contrary to STOMP and STAMP.
n.3: Long waits in the middle of a busy clinic day are likely to increase anxiety; start or end of day is preferred.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Jacob, 26, is autistic with a moderate learning disability. During a fire alarm test at his day service he stops responding, sits very still and does not answer questions for 20 minutes. Which response by staff is best?
o: Record it as non-compliance in his daily notes
Guide him to a quiet space, stay calm and give him time
Keep asking him questions to keep him engaged
Call an ambulance because he is not responding to speech
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Withdrawal and reduced responsiveness after overwhelming sensory input can be a shutdown response. Reducing demands and stimulation, staying nearby calmly and allowing recovery time is the supportive approach (NICE CG142 1.1.8 adjusting noise and the environment for autistic adults).

n.0: This is a response to overload, not a choice to refuse, so recording it as non-compliance is inaccurate.
n.2: Repeated questions add demands and sensory input and may prolong the shutdown.
n.3: He is breathing, sitting and recovering after a known trigger; there is no sign of a medical emergency.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A ward is preparing for the planned admission of Aiden, 34, an autistic man with a learning disability, for dental treatment under general anaesthetic. Which preparation is most likely to reduce his anxiety on the day?
o: Admission the evening before so that he can settle on the ward
A bed in the middle of a large bay so that staff can see him easily
A visual schedule of the day, agreed with Aiden and his carers
A detailed verbal explanation from the anaesthetist on arrival
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Predictability reduces anxiety. Visual supports (NICE CG142 1.1.8) prepared with the person and carers in advance let Aiden know what will happen and when; this is a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: An extra night in an unfamiliar ward is likely to increase anxiety unless he has asked for it.
n.1: A busy open bay increases sensory input; a quiet space is preferable.
n.3: A detailed verbal explanation on arrival is too late and may overload him; visual information beforehand is better.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Isla, 15, is autistic. Her parents report she has become increasingly anxious since moving to secondary school, with stomach aches every morning and refusal to leave the house. What should the nurse recognise?
o: Her anxiety may be a co-occurring condition that needs assessment
Stomach aches are not linked to anxiety in autistic young people
Anxiety is part of autism and does not need separate support
School refusal is a behaviour that a reward chart will resolve
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Anxiety disorders commonly co-occur with autism and can present physically (stomach aches) and through avoidance. NICE NG54 1.7.4 asks assessors to look for problems linked to behavioural phenotypes, for example anxiety in autistic people, so they can be treated; CG170 covers interventions for coexisting problems.

n.1: Anxiety commonly causes physical symptoms such as stomach aches, especially in young people.
n.2: Assuming anxiety is simply part of autism is diagnostic overshadowing; co-occurring anxiety can be treated.
n.3: A reward chart ignores the anxiety driving the avoidance and is not an assessment.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ravi, 30, is autistic with a learning disability and is in hospital after a fall. He becomes distressed every morning when a different nurse arrives. Staff are short and have to rotate allocation. Which is the best adjustment?
o: Ask the ward to allocate him whichever nurse is least busy
Let him stay in bed until he has calmed down each morning
Explain to Ravi that staff changes are unavoidable on a busy ward
Use a photo board each morning showing who is caring for him that day
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Two-step reasoning: the trigger is unpredictability, and constant staff cannot be guaranteed, so the next best adjustment is to make the change predictable with visual information (NICE CG142 1.1.8 visual supports for autistic adults). Where possible, consistent staffing should also be considered.

n.0: Allocation by workload increases unpredictability rather than reducing it.
n.1: Staying in bed delays recovery after a fall and does not address the trigger.
n.2: An explanation alone does not reduce the unpredictability causing his distress.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Chloe, 22, is autistic and has a moderate learning disability. She is due a blood test and has had distressing experiences with needles. Her care team is planning the test. Which approach is best?
o: Postpone the test until Chloe asks to have it done
Use gradual desensitisation and a quiet planned visit
Hold Chloe still so the test is over quickly
Take the blood while Chloe is asleep at night
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Gradual desensitisation (step-by-step exposure, visual stories, practice visits) and a planned quiet appointment are reasonable adjustments that reduce anxiety and the need for restraint. Any restriction requires capacity assessment and best interests decisions (MCA 2005).

n.0: Waiting for her to ask may delay necessary care; the duty is to adjust so that the test can happen.
n.2: Holding is a restrictive intervention and a last resort; it is not the first plan for an anxious person.
n.3: A procedure on a sleeping person without consent or a best interests decision is unlawful and harmful to trust.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A support worker asks why Bella, 28, an autistic woman, flaps her hands and hums when she is excited or anxious and whether staff should stop it. What is the best response from the nurse?
o: Allow it, as it may help her regulate and is not harmful
Stop it gently, as it draws attention in public places
Replace it with a reward each time she keeps her hands still
Report it to the GP as a possible new seizure type
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Repetitive movements (stimming) often help autistic people regulate emotion and sensory input. Stopping harmless self-regulation can increase distress; it should be respected unless it causes harm (person-centred, neurodiversity-affirming practice).

n.1: Concern about how it looks is not a reason to stop a harmless way of regulating herself.
n.2: Rewarding suppression aims to change her rather than meet her needs, which can increase anxiety.
n.3: This is longstanding and linked to emotion; nothing suggests a new seizure.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Nadia, 49, has Down syndrome and lives in supported living. Over six months she has started needing prompts to wash and dress, and has become forgetful and withdrawn. Staff wonder if she has dementia. Which should the nurse ask the GP to check first?
o: Her IQ score compared with childhood
Her serum cholesterol and lipid profile
An urgent CT head scan
Thyroid function, hearing and vision
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and can mimic dementia or depression; hearing and vision loss also cause apparent cognitive decline. These treatable causes should be excluded before a dementia diagnosis (DSMIG/DSA thyroid guidance; NICE NG54 1.7.4 review physical health).

n.0: IQ tests do not measure change reliably and do not exclude treatable causes; adaptive behaviour compared with a baseline is used instead.
n.1: Lipids are part of general health checks but do not explain new loss of skills.
n.2: Neuroimaging is not the first step; reversible causes such as thyroid and sensory problems are checked first.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A learning disability nurse is supporting Ben, 25, who has Down syndrome, at his annual health check. NICE NG54 recommends a particular assessment for all adults with Down syndrome to help detect later decline. Which is it?
o: Genetic testing for the APP gene
A yearly brain MRI from the age of 25
A baseline memory clinic referral at age 25
A baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG54 1.7.13: complete a baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour with all adults with Down's syndrome, so that later changes in skills can be measured against it.

n.0: Genetic testing does not establish a functional baseline and is not recommended for this purpose.
n.1: Routine imaging is not recommended for screening.
n.2: Memory clinic referral is for suspected dementia, not a routine baseline.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ella, 38, has Down syndrome. Her brother asks why her annual health check includes questions about changes in behaviour and skills. Which explanation is correct?
o: Her learning disability is expected to worsen steadily from age 30
People with Down syndrome develop Alzheimer's dementia earlier than others
Behaviour change is a common side effect of her thyroid medication
Questions about skills are part of every adult's annual health check
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: An extra copy of the APP gene on chromosome 21 means people with Down syndrome have a much higher risk of Alzheimer's disease at a younger age. NICE NG54 1.5.4 asks at annual health checks about changes in behaviour, loss of skills or needing more prompting, which may suggest the need for dementia assessment.

n.0: A learning disability does not progressively worsen; new decline suggests another cause such as dementia.
n.2: Correctly dosed levothyroxine does not commonly cause behaviour change; the questions screen for dementia.
n.3: These specific questions are recommended for adults with Down syndrome because of their dementia risk.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A carer asks a learning disability nurse why Alzheimer's disease is more common in people with Down syndrome. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Repeated ear infections in childhood damage areas of the brain
An extra copy of the APP gene on chromosome 21 raises amyloid levels
Long-term thyroid medication causes amyloid plaques to form
Congenital heart disease reduces blood supply to the brain over time
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Chromosome 21 carries the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene; three copies lead to increased amyloid and Alzheimer's pathology, present in virtually all adults with Down syndrome by about age 40 (Nature Reviews Neurology 2019).

n.0: Ear infections cause hearing loss, not Alzheimer's pathology.
n.2: Thyroid replacement does not cause amyloid plaques.
n.3: Heart disease affects cardiovascular health but is not the mechanism for Alzheimer's in Down syndrome.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Peter, 52, has Down syndrome and diagnosed Alzheimer's dementia. He lives in a shared house and is becoming disorientated at night. Staff propose locking his bedroom door so he does not wander. What should the nurse advise?
o: Assess capacity and look at less restrictive options first
Lock the door at night, as this is the safest plan for Peter
Ask the GP for a sedative so that he sleeps through the night
Arrange an urgent move to a nursing home with locked doors
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Locking Peter in is a significant restriction. Under the MCA 2005 his capacity must be assessed, any decision made in his best interests and less restrictive options considered first (night lights, signage, sensor alerts, waking staff) (MCA s1(6), s4).

n.1: Locking him in without a best interests process is unlawful restraint and could be a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: Sedation increases falls and aspiration risk and is chemical restraint.
n.3: A move is a major decision; less restrictive support in his home should be explored first.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Amira, 46, has Down syndrome. Her support staff report she has lost interest in activities, is tearful and sleeps poorly. She can still dress and cook with her usual prompts. Which possibility should be assessed alongside dementia?
o: Lack of motivation
Normal ageing
Learned helplessness
Depression
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Depression can mimic early dementia (withdrawal, poor sleep, apparent decline) and is treatable. NICE NG54 asks for full assessment of mental and physical health; her preserved skills make depression a strong alternative to exclude.

n.0: Labelling the change as lack of motivation is diagnostic overshadowing.
n.1: Tearfulness and loss of interest are not part of normal ageing.
n.2: This is a behavioural concept, not a diagnosis to exclude; it would not explain tearfulness and poor sleep.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A community nurse is monitoring Joseph, 55, who has Down syndrome and suspected dementia. Which tool would NICE NG54 suggest to supplement the assessment?
o: The standard Mini-Mental State Examination, unadapted
Dementia Questionnaire for People with Learning Disabilities
The Abbey Pain Scale designed for people living with dementia
The Waterlow score
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG54 1.7.12: consider supplementing a dementia assessment with measures designed for people with learning disabilities, such as the DLD, the Down Syndrome Dementia Scale or the DSQIID, plus cognitive and adaptive measures over time.

n.0: Standard cognitive tests are not designed for people with learning disabilities and are hard to interpret (NG54 1.7.9).
n.2: The Abbey scale assesses pain in people with dementia, not dementia itself.
n.3: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Lucy, 21, has Down syndrome. Her parents ask the nurse when they should start talking with her about the link between Down syndrome and dementia. Which advice reflects NICE NG96?
o: Wait until Lucy shows the first signs of memory loss
Leave the conversation to her GP when she reaches 40
Explain early and accessibly to Lucy and her family
Talk to her parents and avoid upsetting Lucy
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG96 1.5.36 advises explaining early to people with learning disabilities, particularly Down syndrome, and their families about the link with dementia, using accessible information so they can plan.

n.0: Waiting until symptoms appear prevents planning while Lucy can take part fully.
n.1: NG96 advises early discussion; delaying to 40 is not supported.
n.3: Excluding Lucy denies her information about her own health.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A family carer asks a learning disability nurse what STOMP is. Her son Liam, 30, has a learning disability and takes risperidone for behaviour that challenges. Which description is correct?
o: A medicines review that pharmacists complete when a person turns 18
A scheme that pays GPs to prescribe fewer antidepressants
A rule that people with a learning disability must not take antipsychotics
A national programme to stop the overuse of psychotropic medicines
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: STOMP (stopping over medication of people with a learning disability, autistic people or both) is an NHS England programme launched in 2016. It aims to stop inappropriate use of psychotropic medicines and to ensure the right medicine for the right reason, with regular review and non-drug alternatives; it is not anti-medication (NHS England STOMP).

n.0: STOMP is not tied to an age-18 review; STAMP covers children and young people.
n.1: STOMP is a health and care improvement programme, not a GP payment scheme for antidepressants.
n.2: STOMP supports appropriate use; antipsychotics remain right for some people, for example those with psychosis.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Grace, 9, is autistic and has a learning disability. She has taken a sedative for sleep and behaviour for two years, and her parents ask whether she still needs it. Her paediatrician is reviewing it. Which national programme specifically supports appropriate psychotropic prescribing for children and young people?
o: ReSPECT
STOMP
STAMP
LeDeR
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: STAMP (Supporting Treatment and Appropriate Medication in Paediatrics) was launched in December 2018 by NHS England with the RCPCH, BACD and Council for Disabled Children, extending STOMP principles to children and young people.

n.0: ReSPECT is an emergency care and treatment planning process.
n.1: STOMP is the overarching programme mainly focused on adults; STAMP is the paediatric pledge.
n.3: LeDeR reviews deaths of people with a learning disability and autistic people.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Callum, 35, has a learning disability and started olanzapine six months ago for behaviour that challenges. Staff notice he has gained 9 kg, coughs during meals and has hard stools. Which explanation should the nurse consider?
o: These are expected and need no change to his care plan
These are signs his dose is too low and should be increased
These are unrelated problems linked to his lack of exercise
These may be antipsychotic side effects needing urgent review
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Antipsychotics can cause weight gain and metabolic effects, swallowing difficulty and constipation (anticholinergic effects), which raise the risks of aspiration pneumonia and bowel obstruction; pneumonia and constipation both recur in LeDeR reviews of avoidable deaths. NICE NG11 1.8.4 requires side effects to be monitored and the medicine reviewed.

n.0: Choking risk and constipation are serious and must prompt review, not acceptance.
n.1: Side effects do not indicate under-dosing; raising the dose would worsen them.
n.2: The timing after starting olanzapine makes side effects the most likely common cause.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A GP asks for the learning disability nurse's view on starting an antipsychotic for Ryan, 24, who has behaviour that challenges. Psychological interventions have not yet been tried. What should the nurse advise, in line with NICE NG11?
o: Try psychological and environmental interventions first
Start a low dose now and review in six months
Start a PRN antipsychotic for use during incidents
Start two drugs at low doses to reduce side effects
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG11 1.8.2: consider antipsychotics only if psychological or other interventions alone have not produced change within an agreed time, treatment of coexisting physical or mental health problems has not helped, or the risk is very severe; and only in combination with psychological interventions.

n.1: Medication before psychological approaches is contrary to NG11, and six months is far beyond the 3-4 week review.
n.2: PRN use is still antipsychotic treatment and should be as short as possible after other approaches.
n.3: NG11 advises a single drug at the lowest effective dose, not combinations.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Zoe, 28, has a learning disability and started risperidone for severe self-injury four weeks ago, alongside a psychological intervention. Under NICE NG11, if there is no meaningful response, by when should the antipsychotic be stopped?
o: After 6 weeks
After 12 weeks
After 6 months
After 2 weeks
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG11 1.8.4: review effectiveness and side effects after 3-4 weeks and stop the antipsychotic if there is no indication of a response at 6 weeks.

n.1: Twelve weeks exceeds the 6-week limit set by NG11.
n.2: Six months would expose Zoe to side effects without benefit for far too long.
n.3: Two weeks is too early; NG11 sets the first review at 3-4 weeks.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Ahmed, 50, has a learning disability and has taken haloperidol for 15 years. He has never had psychotic symptoms. His behaviour has been settled for several years. What should the nurse recommend at his medication review?
o: Switch him to a newer antipsychotic that has fewer side effects
Continue the dose because his behaviour is now stable
Consider a gradual, monitored reduction with specialist support
Stop the haloperidol today because it is not indicated
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Two-step reasoning: there is no psychosis, so the indication is behaviour; stable behaviour makes a reduction worth considering. NICE NG54 1.9.7: for people taking antipsychotics without psychotic symptoms, consider reducing or discontinuing long-term prescriptions, review after reduction, consider specialist referral and document reasons annually if continued. Withdrawal should be gradual.

n.0: Switching continues antipsychotic use without addressing whether any is needed.
n.1: Stability is a reason to review, not to continue indefinitely; NG54 asks for reduction to be considered.
n.3: Abrupt withdrawal after 15 years risks withdrawal effects and relapse; reduction should be gradual.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Molly, 33, has a learning disability and a PRN antipsychotic for agitation. Her records show it was given 14 times last month, often in the early evening. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse?
o: Remove the PRN from her chart without discussion with the prescriber
Review the PRN use, look for triggers and request a medicines review
Ask the GP to make the PRN a regular evening dose
Continue as now, because each dose was within the prescribed limit
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG11 1.8.4 says PRN antipsychotics should be used for as short a time as possible and their use recorded and reviewed. Frequent use at a regular time suggests an unmet need or trigger that should be explored, with a prescriber review (STOMP).

n.0: Nurses cannot unilaterally stop a prescribed medicine; changes need the prescriber.
n.2: Converting to a regular dose increases medication exposure without understanding the cause.
n.3: Staying within limits does not answer whether the medicine is needed so often.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Daniel, 27, has a learning disability and epilepsy. His psychiatrist plans to start an antipsychotic for psychosis. Which consideration does NICE NG54 specifically highlight before starting?
o: His anti-seizure medicine should be stopped while the antipsychotic is started
Antipsychotics may lower the seizure threshold, so consult the epilepsy team
Antipsychotics are contraindicated in people who have epilepsy
He should be admitted to hospital for the first week of treatment
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: NICE NG54 1.9.3: before starting medication, take account of interactions and effects on other conditions, consulting specialists when necessary, for example neurologists providing epilepsy care when prescribing antipsychotics that may lower the seizure threshold.

n.0: Stopping anti-seizure medication would risk seizures and status epilepticus.
n.2: Epilepsy is a reason for caution and consultation, not an absolute bar to antipsychotics for psychosis.
n.3: Admission is not routinely required to start an antipsychotic.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Jamal, 26, has a moderate learning disability and lives in supported living. Staff report that he has started hitting his head with his hand several times a day. The service manager asks the learning disability nurse what a positive behaviour support (PBS) approach will aim to achieve first. Which answer is best?
o: Refer Jamal to his GP for medication to reduce his agitation and the head hitting
Reduce the behaviour quickly by agreeing consequences that staff apply every time it happens
Keep Jamal safe by planning a restrictive intervention that staff use when he hits his head
Improve Jamal's quality of life by understanding and meeting the needs behind the behaviour
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: PBS is a values-led, person-centred framework. It combines a functional understanding of the behaviour with multi-component support whose primary aim is a better quality of life; reduction in behaviour that challenges follows from meeting the person's needs (PBS definition, Gore et al. 2013; NICE NG11 focus on improving support rather than changing the person).

n.0: NICE NG11 places psychological and environmental interventions first; medication is not the first aim of a PBS approach.
n.1: Imposing consequences is a punishment-based approach; PBS changes the environment and support to meet the need the behaviour serves.
n.2: Reactive and restrictive strategies are a last resort within a PBS plan (NICE NG11 1.9.1), not the outcome it sets out to achieve.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: A learning disability nurse is writing a positive behaviour support plan for Elena, 34, who has a severe learning disability and bites her hand when the day centre becomes noisy. Which strategy is an example of primary prevention?
o: Offering Elena her ear defenders once she starts biting her hand
Moving Elena's activities to a quieter room before the centre gets busy
Recording each biting episode on an ABC chart after it has finished
Guiding Elena's hand away from her mouth when she begins to bite
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Primary prevention strategies are proactive: they change the environment, meet the person's needs and teach skills so that the behaviour is less likely to happen at all. Altering the setting before the known trigger (noise) arises is primary prevention (PBS model; NICE NG11 1.6.1 proactive strategies such as reducing noise).

n.0: Offering a support once early signs or the behaviour have begun is a secondary (de-escalation) strategy, not primary prevention.
n.2: ABC recording is part of functional assessment and monitoring, not a prevention strategy in the plan.
n.3: Physically guiding her hand away during the behaviour is a reactive strategy used to keep her safe.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Owen, 19, is autistic and has a learning disability. His PBS plan says that when he begins pacing and repeating 'bus, bus', staff should calmly offer him his picture schedule and a walk outside. Which part of the plan does this describe?
o: Reactive strategies
Primary prevention strategies
Post-incident support strategies
Secondary prevention strategies
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: Secondary prevention strategies respond to early warning signs (here pacing and repetitive speech) with de-escalation, such as redirection, reassurance or offering a preferred activity, to stop the situation escalating to a crisis (PBS model).

n.0: Reactive strategies are used once the behaviour is happening to keep everyone safe, not at the early warning stage.
n.1: Primary strategies are proactive and in place all the time, before any early warning signs appear.
n.2: Post-incident support follows an episode (recovery, debrief and review), not the early signs before it.

Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.q: Priya, a newly registered nurse in a community learning disability team, is asked who should be involved in developing a positive behaviour support plan for Mark, 41, who has a moderate learning disability. Which approach is best?
o: Develop it with Mark, his family and the staff who support him day to day
Develop it with the team psychologist, then hand it to staff to put into practice
Develop it with the service manager, who will sign it off for the staff team
Develop it with Mark's GP, who knows his physical health history best
Behaviour, Mental Health and Medication.w: PBS is person-centred and collaborative: the plan is co-produced with the person, family carers and the staff who support them, because they know the person's needs, triggers and communication and must be able to use the plan consistently (NICE NG11 1.1.1 working in partnership, 1.3.1 involving family in developing the plan, 1.5.2 full involvement in assessment; PBS values).

n.1: Specialist input is valuable, but a plan written by one professional and handed down is not co-produced and is less likely to be used consistently.
n.2: Management sign-off may be part of governance, but involving the manager in place of Mark and his supporters misses the people who know him best.
n.3: The GP's input on physical health is useful, but the GP is not the core partner in designing day-to-day behaviour support.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Sean, 34, has a severe learning disability and epilepsy. Over a month his seizures have increased. Staff find tablets in his bedding and he spits out his evening dose. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the GP to increase his anti-seizure medicine dose
Give his tablets covertly in his food from tonight
Find out why he refuses and review the formulation with the prescriber
Record each refusal and keep offering the tablets at the usual times
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Two-step reasoning: the seizure increase is likely due to missed doses, so the cause of refusal must be found (taste, tablet size, swallowing difficulty, side effects, timing) and a solution such as a liquid formulation agreed with the prescriber and pharmacist. Non-adherence is a modifiable SUDEP risk factor (NG217 10.1.2).

n.0: A higher dose will not help if he is not taking the tablets and may cause toxicity when he does.
n.1: Covert administration needs a capacity assessment, best interests decision and pharmacist advice first.
n.3: Simply recording leaves seizures and SUDEP risk unaddressed.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Freya, 29, has a learning disability and epilepsy. She wants to start swimming at her local leisure centre. Her support worker thinks she should not be allowed. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Suggest she swims after her seizures have stopped for five years
Support a risk assessment and plan so that she can swim safely
Agree she should not swim because drowning is a risk
Advise her to swim in the shallow end without any supervision
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: People with epilepsy should be supported to live full lives; risks are managed through individual risk assessment and planning (for example a trained companion who knows her seizures, lifeguard awareness), rather than blanket restriction (NG217 principles; positive risk-taking; MCA unwise decisions).

n.0: There is no five-year seizure-free rule for swimming; individual risk assessment applies.
n.2: A blanket ban is overly restrictive; the risk can be reduced with planning.
n.3: Swimming unsupervised is unsafe for a person with active seizures, even in shallow water.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A learning disability nurse is reviewing the epilepsy care plan for Abdul, 45, who has a profound learning disability. Which should be included in his individualised plan?
o: His seizure types, triggers, first aid and rescue medication
A blanket instruction to call 999 for any seizure he has
Information on his seizures that is kept by his neurologist
Advice to restrain his limbs during a seizure to prevent injury
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG217 recommends an individualised care plan, agreed with the person and carers, describing seizure types and triggers, what to do during and after seizures, any emergency medication and when to call for help (7.1.12 for emergency plans).

n.1: Calling 999 for every seizure is not needed; the plan should specify when emergency help is required.
n.2: The plan must be shared with those who support Abdul daily, not held by the neurologist.
n.3: Restraining limbs during a seizure can cause injury and is not recommended.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Michael, 52, has Down syndrome. He has had no seizures in his life until now, when he has two tonic-clonic seizures in a month. His family say he has also become more forgetful. Which condition should the nurse be aware this could indicate?
o: A side effect of his thyroid medication
Normal ageing in people with Down syndrome
Late-onset epilepsy linked to Alzheimer's disease
Childhood absence epilepsy recurring in adulthood
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: In Down syndrome epilepsy has a second, late-onset peak closely linked to the emergence of Alzheimer's disease (late-onset myoclonic epilepsy in Down syndrome, often with tonic-clonic seizures; PubMed 25661268). New seizures with memory decline need specialist assessment for both epilepsy and dementia (NICE NG54 1.5.4 and 1.7.12).

n.0: Thyroid replacement at correct doses does not commonly cause seizures.
n.1: New seizures and memory loss are not part of normal ageing and must be investigated.
n.3: Absence seizures are brief lapses, not tonic-clonic seizures, and Michael had no seizures in childhood.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ruby, 31, has a learning disability and epilepsy. At her day centre she has a tonic-clonic seizure. Her individual emergency plan says to give buccal midazolam if a seizure lasts 5 minutes. The seizure has now lasted 5 minutes. What should the trained nurse do?
o: Call 999 and wait for paramedics to give any medication
Place a soft object between her teeth and then give the midazolam
Wait until the seizure has lasted 10 minutes, then give the midazolam
Give buccal midazolam as set out in Ruby's emergency plan
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus. NICE NG217 7.1.1-7.1.2: provide emergency treatment and, if the person has an individualised emergency management plan immediately available, give medication as detailed in it.

n.0: The plan authorises trained staff to give rescue medication now; waiting for paramedics delays treatment.
n.1: Nothing should be placed between the teeth during a seizure; it can cause injury and airway obstruction.
n.2: Waiting longer than the plan states delays treatment of status epilepticus and raises the risk of harm.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A learning disability nurse is teaching support staff about seizure emergencies. A support worker asks how long a convulsive seizure must last before it is treated as status epilepticus. What is the correct answer?
o: 5 minutes or more
10 minutes or more
2 minutes or more
30 minutes or more
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG217 7.1.1 defines convulsive status epilepticus for treatment purposes as seizures lasting 5 minutes or more, which need immediate emergency treatment.

n.1: Ten minutes is the upper end of the window for a second benzodiazepine dose, not the definition.
n.2: Two minutes is within the usual duration of a self-limiting tonic-clonic seizure.
n.3: Thirty minutes is an older definition; waiting this long delays treatment.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Liam, 24, has a learning disability and epilepsy. He is having a convulsive seizure at home that has lasted 6 minutes. He has no emergency plan with him and his carer has buccal midazolam prescribed for him. What does NICE NG217 recommend as first-line treatment in the community?
o: Buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam immediately
Intravenous lorazepam once paramedics arrive
An extra dose of his usual anti-seizure tablets
Oral diazepam tablets crushed into water
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG217 7.1.3: if no individualised plan is immediately available, give a benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam) immediately as first-line treatment in the community; IV lorazepam is used where IV access and resuscitation facilities are immediately available.

n.1: IV lorazepam is appropriate when IV access and resuscitation facilities are available, but buccal or rectal treatment should not be delayed waiting for it.
n.2: Usual oral tablets are not emergency treatment and cannot be swallowed safely during a seizure.
n.3: Nothing should be given by mouth during a convulsive seizure because of the choking risk.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ahmed, 36, has a learning disability and is in supported living. His carer gave buccal midazolam 3 minutes ago for a seizure that had lasted 5 minutes, but he is still convulsing. His plan does not say otherwise. What should happen now?
o: Wait 20 minutes for the midazolam to take full effect
Put him in a cool bath to bring the seizure to an end
Give a second dose of midazolam straight away
Call 999 for emergency help
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG217 7.1.7: if convulsive status epilepticus does not respond to the first dose of benzodiazepine, call emergency services in the community. A second dose is considered if the seizure has not stopped 5 to 10 minutes after the first (7.1.8).

n.0: Waiting 20 minutes without calling for help delays emergency treatment.
n.1: A bath is dangerous during a seizure because of drowning risk.
n.2: A second dose is considered only after 5 to 10 minutes; giving it at 3 minutes is too early.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Fatima, 40, has a profound learning disability. She received buccal midazolam 7 minutes ago and is still having a tonic-clonic seizure. An ambulance has been called. Her plan allows a second dose. What is the next step?
o: Give the second dose of benzodiazepine as her plan allows
Give rectal diazepam in addition to a second buccal dose
Give a dose of her regular oral levetiracetam
Wait for paramedics before giving any further medicine
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG217 7.1.8: follow the individualised plan or give a second dose of benzodiazepine if the seizure does not stop within 5 to 10 minutes of the first. Second-line IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate is given by clinicians if two doses fail (7.1.9).

n.1: Giving two benzodiazepines together risks respiratory depression; only one second dose is given.
n.2: Oral medicine cannot be given safely during a seizure; second-line levetiracetam is given intravenously by clinicians.
n.3: Her plan and NG217 support a second dose now; waiting delays treatment.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A support worker who has completed buccal midazolam training is preparing to give it to Owen, 29, during a prolonged seizure. Where should the midazolam be given?
o: Onto the back of the throat
Into the nostril
Between the gum and the cheek
Under the tongue (sublingual)
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Buccal midazolam is given into the buccal cavity, between the gum and the cheek, where it is absorbed through the lining of the mouth. Half may be given on each side if the person's plan states so.

n.0: Giving liquid onto the back of the throat risks aspiration.
n.1: Intranasal midazolam exists but is a different preparation and route from buccal midazolam.
n.3: Sublingual administration is not the buccal route, and the tongue may obstruct during a seizure.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Grace, 27, has a learning disability and epilepsy and was treated in hospital for convulsive status epilepticus. She has no emergency management plan. What does NICE NG217 recommend before she goes home?
o: Advise her family to call 999 for every seizure
Start her on night-time sedation to prevent recurrence
Arrange for her to live in a care home with nursing
Agree an individualised emergency management plan with her
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG217 7.1.12: after an episode of convulsive status epilepticus, agree an emergency management plan with the person if they do not already have one and there is concern that it may recur.

n.0: A plan specifies when to give rescue medicine and call 999; calling for every seizure is not needed.
n.1: Sedation is not recommended to prevent status epilepticus and adds risk.
n.2: A move to nursing care is a major decision not justified by one episode.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ben, 45, has a learning disability and diabetes treated with insulin. He has a prolonged seizure, which stops after buccal midazolam. He is drowsy and breathing normally. What should the nurse check promptly as a possible cause?
o: Capillary blood glucose
Urinalysis for protein
Peak expiratory flow
Serum cholesterol
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Two-step reasoning: once the seizure has stopped and airway and breathing are secure, consider underlying causes. NICE NG217 7.1.4 lists hypoglycaemia among possible causes of status epilepticus; Ben uses insulin, so a capillary glucose check is a priority.

n.1: Proteinuria is not an acute cause of seizure in this context.
n.2: Peak flow assesses asthma and is not useful in a drowsy post-ictal person.
n.3: Cholesterol does not cause an acute seizure.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Daisy, 44, has a severe learning disability and cerebral palsy. Her carers report she coughs during drinks, her voice sounds 'gurgly' after meals and she has had two chest infections this year. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer Daisy to speech and language therapy for assessment
Switch Daisy to a soft diet and review it after a month
Thicken all of her drinks to IDDSI level 4 from today
Ask her GP to prescribe antibiotics to keep at home
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Coughing on drinks, a wet voice after eating and recurrent chest infections are signs of dysphagia and possible aspiration. The person should be referred to speech and language therapy for assessment and an individual eating and drinking plan (LeDeR pneumonia report; NHS England RightCare aspiration pneumonia scenario).

n.1: Changing texture without assessment may not address the risk and may be inappropriate.
n.2: Thickening levels must be set by SLT assessment; guessing a level can cause dehydration or still be unsafe.
n.3: Rescue antibiotics do not address the cause, which is unassessed dysphagia.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Following an SLT assessment last month, Tom, 37, who has a learning disability and dysphagia, has a new drinks chart. A support worker in his supported living service asks the nurse what IDDSI level 2 on the chart means. Which description is correct?
o: Slightly thick
Extremely thick
Mildly thick
Moderately thick
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: IDDSI drinks levels: 0 thin, 1 slightly thick, 2 mildly thick, 3 moderately thick, 4 extremely thick (IDDSI framework).

n.0: Slightly thick is level 1.
n.1: Extremely thick is level 4.
n.3: Moderately thick is level 3.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Asif, 52, has a learning disability and his speech and language therapist has recommended an IDDSI level 5 diet. A new carer asks what this is. Which description is correct?
o: Soft and bite-sized pieces that can be mashed with a fork
Regular everyday food of any texture
Minced and moist food with small soft lumps
Pureed food with no lumps that holds its shape on a spoon
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: IDDSI food levels: 3 liquidised, 4 pureed, 5 minced and moist (small lumps about 4 mm for adults), 6 soft and bite-sized (about 15 mm pieces for adults), 7 regular (IDDSI framework).

n.0: Soft and bite-sized food is level 6.
n.1: Regular food is level 7.
n.3: Smooth pureed food with no lumps is level 4.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Mia, 30, has a profound learning disability and an SLT eating and drinking plan. She is about to be given her lunch. Which position is safest during the meal?
o: Semi-reclined in her chair with her feet raised
Lying on her side in bed facing the carer
Reclined at 45 degrees with her head tilted back
Sitting upright with her chin slightly tucked
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Sitting as upright as possible, with the head in midline and the chin slightly tucked, protects the airway during swallowing; her SLT plan and 24-hour postural care plan give the specific position (SLT dysphagia guidance).

n.0: A semi-reclined position increases the risk of food entering the airway.
n.1: Side-lying is not a safe eating position unless a specialist plan states it.
n.2: Reclining with the head tilted back opens the airway to food and fluid, increasing aspiration risk.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Jamie, 41, has a learning disability and his SLT plan says IDDSI level 1 slightly thick drinks. A carer has made up his tea with a new brand of thickener. The nurse wants to check that the drink matches level 1 before it is given. Which test should she use?
o: The fork drip test
The IDDSI flow test
The fork pressure test
The spoon tilt test
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: The IDDSI flow test classifies drinks levels 0-3 by how much remains in a standard 10 mL slip-tip syringe after 10 seconds: under 1 mL thin, 1-4 mL slightly thick (level 1), 4-8 mL mildly thick (level 2), more than 8 mL moderately thick (IDDSI testing methods).

n.0: The fork drip test checks thicker textures (IDDSI levels 3 to 5), not whether a drink is level 1.
n.2: The fork pressure test checks how soft foods are (IDDSI levels 4 to 7), not the thickness of a drink.
n.3: The spoon tilt test checks the cohesiveness and stickiness of thick textures such as pureed food, not the flow of a slightly thick drink.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ethan, 35, has a learning disability and an SLT plan for level 2 mildly thick drinks. At a family party his brother gives him a glass of fizzy lemonade, saying 'just this once'. Ethan has capacity to make this decision and understands the risks. What should the nurse do?
o: Add thickener to the lemonade before handing it to him
Respect his choice and support him to drink as safely as possible
Take the glass away because it breaches his eating and drinking plan
Ask the brother to leave because he has put Ethan at risk
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Two-step reasoning: Ethan has capacity for this decision, so under the MCA 2005 s1(4) he may make an unwise choice. The nurse supports him to reduce risk (upright, small sips, supervision) and records it; many services use a risk feeding (eating and drinking with acknowledged risks) plan agreed with SLT.

n.0: Thickening his drink overrides the choice he has made with capacity about what to drink.
n.2: Overriding a capacitous decision is unlawful; the plan supports him, it does not bind him.
n.3: Excluding his brother is disproportionate and harms Ethan's relationships.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Isla, 26, has a learning disability and dysphagia. Her weight has dropped by 4 kg in two months, and staff say meals now take over an hour and she often refuses food. What is the priority?
o: Offer larger portions at each meal to restore her weight
Record her weight monthly and review in three months
Give her meals faster so that she does not tire
Refer back to SLT and a dietitian for urgent review
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Prolonged meals, food refusal and weight loss suggest her swallowing has worsened or the plan no longer meets her needs; she needs prompt SLT re-assessment and dietetic review (NICE CG32 nutrition support principles; LeDeR learning on dysphagia).

n.0: Larger portions may increase fatigue and aspiration risk without addressing the cause.
n.1: Waiting three months allows further weight loss and aspiration risk.
n.2: Faster feeding increases aspiration risk; pacing should match her swallow.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Chris, 39, has a learning disability and an SLT plan for level 6 soft and bite-sized food. On a hospital ward, he is served a meal of steak and chips. What should the nurse do?
o: Mash the meal with a fork so that it is easier to swallow
Cut the steak into small pieces and give him the meal
Return it and order a level 6 meal that matches his plan
Give him the chips and record that he refused the steak
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Food must match the IDDSI level in the SLT plan. Steak is tough and cannot be made soft and bite-sized by cutting; level 6 pieces must be soft enough to mash with a fork and about 15 mm for adults (IDDSI framework). Errors in texture are a recognised cause of choking deaths.

n.0: Mashing does not produce a consistent tested texture; the right meal should be provided.
n.1: Cutting tough meat into pieces does not make it soft enough for level 6.
n.3: Chips may also not meet level 6, and this leaves him without a proper meal.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Aaron, a learning disability nurse, is teaching a new supported living team about the health risks faced by the people they support. A support worker asks which serious illness LeDeR reports as one of the most common causes of death, often linked to aspiration. Which illness is it?
o: Asthma
Kidney failure
Pneumonia
Meningitis
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: LeDeR reports consistently list pneumonia and other lung infections among the most common causes of death, alongside cancer and heart conditions; in 2021 pneumonia accounted for 35% of respiratory deaths reported to LeDeR, many linked to aspiration (LeDeR 2023 report; LeDeR pneumonia report 2024).

n.0: Asthma is not among the leading causes of death in LeDeR reports.
n.1: Kidney failure is not among the leading causes highlighted.
n.3: Meningitis is not a leading cause of death in LeDeR reports.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Jacob, 48, has a profound learning disability, dysphagia and reflux. He spends most of the day in a reclined wheelchair and is often semi-reclined for meals because staff find it easier. Which change would most reduce his risk of aspiration pneumonia?
o: Sit him upright for meals and afterwards, as his postural plan sets out
Move his main meal to late evening so that he can rest afterwards
Ask the GP to increase his antipsychotic to calm him at mealtimes
Offer thin drinks so that swallowing takes less effort for him
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Reclined positions during and after eating increase aspiration risk, especially with dysphagia and reflux. Upright positioning in line with his 24-hour postural care plan protects his airway (LeDeR pneumonia report; NHS England RightCare aspiration pneumonia scenario).

n.1: Lying down soon after a large evening meal increases reflux and aspiration risk.
n.2: Sedating medicine impairs swallowing and airway protection and raises aspiration risk.
n.3: Thin drinks move faster and are harder to control, increasing aspiration risk if his plan specifies thickened fluids.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Sophie, 36, has a severe learning disability and dysphagia. Her SLT reports that her videofluoroscopy showed food entering her airway without any cough. Staff say she never coughs at mealtimes so cannot be aspirating. What should the nurse explain?
o: Aspiration without coughing is harmless
Coughing is required for aspiration to occur
Videofluoroscopy often gives false results
Silent aspiration can occur without coughing
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Silent aspiration is entry of material into the airway without a protective cough. It is common in people with neurological impairment and can only be detected by instrumental assessment or by recognising indirect signs such as recurrent chest infections; absence of coughing does not mean the swallow is safe.

n.0: Silent aspiration can cause pneumonia and is a serious risk.
n.1: Aspiration can happen with or without coughing.
n.2: Videofluoroscopy is a standard instrumental test for detecting aspiration.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ellie, 39, has a profound learning disability and dysphagia. Which daily measure is most important for reducing her risk of aspiration pneumonia, alongside her eating and drinking plan?
o: Daily chest X-rays
Keeping her lying flat after meals
Thorough oral care at least twice a day
Restricting all fluids after 6pm each day
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Good oral hygiene reduces the bacterial load that can be aspirated into the lungs, and is part of prevention with SLT-led eating and drinking plans and 24-hour postural care (NHS England RightCare aspiration pneumonia scenario).

n.0: Routine daily X-rays are not a preventive measure and expose her to radiation.
n.1: Lying flat after meals increases the risk of reflux and aspiration; she should stay upright.
n.3: Restricting fluids risks dehydration and constipation without reducing aspiration.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Harry, 55, has a severe learning disability and dysphagia. His carers notice he is more sleepy than usual, eating less, and breathing slightly faster. His temperature is 37.4°C. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the observations and recheck them tomorrow
Complete full observations and seek same-day medical review
Encourage more fluids and review in 48 hours
Tell the carers this is likely tiredness after a busy weekend
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Two-step reasoning: subtle changes (drowsiness, eating less, faster breathing) in a person with dysphagia may be early signs of chest infection, which may present without a high fever. The nurse should complete full observations (for example NEWS2) and escalate for same-day review, acting on carer concern (LeDeR learning on delayed recognition).

n.0: Waiting until tomorrow risks delayed treatment of a possible pneumonia.
n.2: Fluids are sensible but a 48-hour delay is unsafe given his risk factors.
n.3: Attributing the changes to tiredness is diagnostic overshadowing.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Katie, 42, has a learning disability and has had three chest infections in six months, each treated with antibiotics by her GP. No one has reviewed why they keep happening. What should the learning disability nurse recommend?
o: Request a review of swallowing, posture and oral care to find the cause
Request a flu vaccine as the main preventive step
Ask for a rescue pack of antibiotics to keep at home
Advise that recurrent infections are expected in learning disability
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Recurrent chest infections can be a sign of aspiration. LeDeR learning shows treating each infection without investigating cause misses dysphagia, postural problems and poor oral care; a multidisciplinary review (SLT, physiotherapy, postural care) targets prevention.

n.1: Vaccination is important but does not address likely aspiration.
n.2: Rescue antibiotics treat episodes but do not address the cause.
n.3: Accepting recurrent infection as expected is diagnostic overshadowing.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ali, 33, has a profound learning disability and is fed by gastrostomy. His mother asks whether he can still get aspiration pneumonia, as he no longer eats by mouth. What should the nurse explain?
o: No, aspiration happens during eating by mouth
Yes, saliva and refluxed feed can still be aspirated
Yes, when the feeding tube becomes blocked
No, a gastrostomy removes the risk of aspiration
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: People who are tube fed can still aspirate oral secretions and refluxed stomach contents. Positioning (head raised during and after feeds), oral care and reflux management remain important (NHS England RightCare aspiration pneumonia scenario).

n.0: Aspiration can occur from secretions and reflux as well as eating.
n.2: Tube blockage is not what causes aspiration; reflux and secretions are.
n.3: A gastrostomy reduces oral intake risks but not aspiration of saliva or refluxed feed.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A LeDeR review of the death of Paul, 51, who had a learning disability, found his death certificate gave 'cerebral palsy' as the cause of death; he died of aspiration pneumonia. Why does LeDeR treat this as an issue?
o: Cerebral palsy should be listed after the learning disability
The actual illness that caused his death was hidden
LeDeR reviews do not look at the recorded cause of death
Pneumonia deaths are certified by the coroner, not a doctor
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: LeDeR highlights that people do not die 'of' cerebral palsy or a learning disability but of illnesses such as pneumonia; recording the disability as the cause hides potentially preventable causes and prevents learning (LeDeR 2023 report).

n.0: The order of the conditions is not the problem; the disability should not be given as the cause of death.
n.2: LeDeR reviews do consider cause of death information, including certificates.
n.3: Doctors routinely certify deaths from pneumonia; it does not need certifying by the coroner.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Jordan, 37, has a severe learning disability and cerebral palsy and lives in a residential home. His bowel chart shows Bristol type 1 stools every four or five days. He takes an anticholinergic medicine for drooling. A new support worker asks why this matters. What should the nurse explain?
o: Infrequent stools need action once he reports abdominal pain
Constipation can lead to obstruction and has contributed to deaths
Bristol type 1 stools show that his diet has enough fibre
Hard stools are expected in people with cerebral palsy
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Bristol type 1 (separate hard lumps) indicates constipation. In people with a learning disability constipation is common, is worsened by immobility and anticholinergic medicines, and can cause bowel obstruction, perforation and aspiration from vomiting; LeDeR reports constipation still contributing to deaths (LeDeR 2023).

n.0: Jordan may not be able to report pain; waiting for a complaint is unsafe.
n.2: Type 1 stools suggest constipation, not adequate fibre.
n.3: Treating constipation as expected is diagnostic overshadowing; it needs active management.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ava, 29, has a profound learning disability and no speech. Over two days she has become restless, is pushing food away and is pressing on her abdomen. Her bowel chart shows no stool for six days. What is the most likely explanation to assess first?
o: Boredom because her day centre is closed
Constipation causing abdominal pain
Dental pain from a new tooth
Behaviour that challenges needing a PBS review
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Behaviour change (restlessness, food refusal, pressing the abdomen) may be how Ava communicates pain. With no stool for six days, constipation is the most likely cause and should be assessed promptly, avoiding diagnostic overshadowing (LeDeR; NHS England constipation resources).

n.0: Boredom does not explain six days without a bowel movement and abdominal pressing.
n.2: Pressing on the abdomen and absent stools point to the bowel rather than the teeth.
n.3: Labelling the change as behaviour misses a likely physical cause.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A learning disability nurse is reviewing the medicines of Nathan, 42, who has a learning disability, schizophrenia and hypothyroidism. He has had three episodes of severe constipation this year. Which of his medicines is most likely to be contributing?
o: Clozapine 300 mg daily
Paracetamol 1 g when needed
Folic acid 5 mg weekly
Levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Clozapine strongly slows gut motility (MHRA warning on potentially fatal clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility). Other constipating medicines common in LD include antipsychotics, anticholinergics, some anti-seizure medicines and opioids.

n.1: Paracetamol does not usually cause constipation.
n.2: Folic acid is not a recognised cause of constipation.
n.3: Correctly dosed levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism, which itself causes constipation.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Staff supporting Ryan, 24, who has a learning disability, have recorded 'bowels opened' each day for a week. The nurse wants a more useful record. What should the bowel chart include?
o: The name of the staff member on shift
Date and time, Bristol stool type and amount
The number of toilet visits he makes each day
Ryan's mood on each day of the week
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: A bowel chart should record date and time, stool type using the Bristol Stool Chart, amount and any concerns (pain, straining, blood), so that constipation or overflow can be spotted early.

n.0: Staff names do not describe bowel function.
n.2: Toilet visits do not show whether stool was passed or its type.
n.3: Mood may be relevant to behaviour, but it does not describe bowel function.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Bethany, 46, has a learning disability and has had no proper bowel movement for eight days. Staff now report frequent small amounts of liquid stool leaking into her pad. They plan to give loperamide for diarrhoea. What should the nurse advise?
o: Start a stool chart and review in a week
Withhold it and seek review for impaction with overflow
Give the loperamide as planned and monitor her fluid intake
Give extra fluids and restart her normal diet
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Two-step reasoning: liquid leakage after days without a proper stool suggests overflow around impacted faeces. Antidiarrhoeal treatment would worsen the impaction; she needs urgent medical assessment and treatment of constipation.
