n.0: Waiting a week risks obstruction and perforation.
n.2: Loperamide slows the bowel and would worsen faecal impaction.
n.3: Fluids help but do not address the impaction needing medical treatment.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Oliver, 51, has a profound learning disability and takes clozapine. He has had no stool for four days, has vomited twice and his abdomen is distended and tender. What is the priority?
o: Give a laxative and recheck tomorrow
Increase his fibre intake for the next week
Record the vomiting and encourage fluids
Arrange urgent medical assessment today
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Vomiting, distension and tenderness with constipation in a person taking clozapine may indicate bowel obstruction from clozapine-induced hypomotility, which can be fatal; this is an emergency needing same-day medical assessment (MHRA clozapine warning; LeDeR).

n.0: A laxative and delay are inappropriate when there are signs of obstruction.
n.1: Fibre can worsen obstruction and does not address the emergency.
n.2: Recording and fluids alone delay emergency treatment.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A nurse is planning bowel care for Amelia, 34, who has a learning disability, uses a wheelchair and takes several constipating medicines. Which proactive plan is best?
o: Agree a bowel plan covering fluids, fibre, activity and review
Give an enema each week to keep her bowel clear
Give a laxative when there has been no stool for seven days
Wait for Amelia to ask for help before acting
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: A proactive bowel care plan addresses known risks (immobility, medicines) with fluids, diet, movement, routine toileting, prescribed laxatives where needed, Bristol chart monitoring and clear actions and timescales for escalation (NHS England constipation resources).

n.1: Routine weekly enemas are invasive and not first-line prevention.
n.2: Seven days without stool is too long a threshold for someone at high risk.
n.3: Amelia may not be able to report symptoms; waiting is unsafe.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Noah, 27, has a learning disability and constipation. A support worker says he refuses prune juice and fibre-rich foods. What is the best approach for the nurse?
o: Tell Noah he must drink the juice so he avoids going to hospital
Hide fibre supplements in his food
Agree acceptable food and drink with him and review laxatives
Stop offering choices and give the same meal each day
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Person-centred care involves Noah in finding foods and drinks he accepts, using accessible information, and reviewing medical treatment if diet alone is not enough. Covert administration would need a capacity assessment and best interests process.

n.0: Threats are coercive and do not respect his choices.
n.1: Hiding supplements is covert administration without lawful process.
n.3: Removing choice is restrictive and unlikely to help.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Carla, a learning disability nurse, is explaining 24-hour postural care to the family of Toby, 15, who has cerebral palsy and a profound learning disability. Which statement best describes its purpose?
o: To help Toby learn to walk independently by adulthood
To prevent pressure ulcers on Toby's heels
To improve Toby's posture during the school day
To protect body shape when lying, sitting and standing
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: 24-hour postural care uses supported positioning across the whole day and night (lying, sitting, standing) to protect body shape, reducing hip dislocation, scoliosis and chest problems that follow when a person stays in asymmetric positions (LeDeR pneumonia report; NHS England postural care resources).

n.0: Postural care protects body shape; it does not aim to achieve independent walking.
n.1: Pressure relief is a benefit of good positioning but not the main purpose.
n.2: Daytime posture is part of it, but night-time lying is where many hours are spent and body shape changes.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Lewis, 30, has a profound learning disability and very limited movement. He sleeps every night on his side with both knees dropped to the same side. Over time, which body shape change is most likely?
o: Windswept hips with risk of hip dislocation
Improved lung expansion on the upper side
Flat feet from lack of weight bearing
Stronger trunk muscles from side lying
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Lying in the same asymmetric position for long periods causes the knees to fall to one side, producing a 'windswept' hip pattern, pelvic rotation, hip dislocation and scoliosis. Supported symmetrical lying protects body shape.

n.1: Lying fixed on one side does not improve lung expansion; the asymmetry it causes can lead to scoliosis that restricts the chest over time.
n.2: Foot posture may change, but the classic risk from this position is windswept hips.
n.3: Side lying in one position does not strengthen the trunk; it promotes asymmetry.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A support worker asks why postural care matters for preventing chest infections in Marie, 47, who has a profound learning disability. Which explanation is best?
o: Body shape mainly affects mobility rather than breathing
Chest infections are caused by sleeping in a cold room
Postural care increases the effectiveness of antibiotics
Body shape changes restrict the chest and impair swallowing
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Scoliosis and chest wall distortion reduce lung capacity and airway clearance, and poor head and trunk position impairs swallowing; these raise the risk of aspiration pneumonia, a leading cause of death in LeDeR (LeDeR pneumonia report).

n.0: Body shape distortion is a recognised risk factor for respiratory problems.
n.1: Room temperature is not the mechanism linking posture to chest infections.
n.2: Positioning does not change how antibiotics work.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ben, 22, has a profound learning disability. His physiotherapist recommends a night-time positioning system. His mother worries it will stop him moving. Ben lacks capacity to decide. What should the nurse do?
o: Use it on alternate nights as a compromise
Leave it until Ben is able to choose for himself
Hold a best interests meeting with his mother and physio
Fit the system because the physiotherapist has recommended it
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Night-time positioning can restrict movement, so for a person who lacks capacity it requires a best interests decision under MCA 2005 s4, consulting family and professionals, weighing benefits for body shape against any restriction and considering the least restrictive way to use it.

n.0: An arbitrary compromise is not a reasoned best interests decision.
n.1: Ben is unlikely to gain capacity for this decision, and delay allows body shape to change.
n.3: A professional recommendation does not replace the best interests process.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ruby, 38, has a profound learning disability and has been sitting in her wheelchair for six hours at a day centre. Her postural care plan says she should change position every two hours. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask her family to reposition her when she gets home
Leave Ruby in her chair as she seems content
Tilt the wheelchair back for the rest of the day
Reposition Ruby out of her chair as her plan sets out
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Prolonged sitting in one position increases pressure damage and body shape distortion. The plan's schedule should be followed, using supported lying or standing as set out (24-hour postural care principles).

n.0: Delaying repositioning until she goes home breaches the plan and risks harm.
n.1: Appearing content does not mean her body is protected from prolonged sitting.
n.2: Tilting changes pressure but she has already exceeded the planned time in her chair.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A nurse is reviewing the 24-hour postural care plan of Hassan, 19, who has cerebral palsy. Which measure best shows whether his body shape is being protected over time?
o: Regular body shape measurements recorded and compared
His carers' views on how comfortable he looks each day
The number of hours he spends in his wheelchair
His weight recorded each month
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Body symmetry measurements (for example chest and pelvic measures) taken regularly and compared over time show whether body shape is being protected or deteriorating, and guide changes to the plan.

n.1: Comfort matters, but it does not measure body shape change.
n.2: Time in the chair is a process measure, not an outcome measure of body shape.
n.3: Weight is important but does not measure body shape.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Grace, 26, has a profound learning disability and scoliosis. She is admitted to hospital with a chest infection. Her mother brings her positioning equipment and plan from home. What should the ward nurse do?
o: Ask her mother to take the equipment home to avoid loss
Use the hospital's standard positioning chart and store the equipment
Follow her home postural plan with her mother and physiotherapy
Nurse her flat on her back to make observations easier
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Continuing the person's established postural care plan in hospital is a reasonable adjustment that protects body shape and breathing; families know the plan well, and ward physiotherapy can adapt it to her acute illness (Equality Act 2010 s20; postural care principles).

n.0: Sending the equipment home removes support she needs in hospital.
n.1: A generic chart ignores her individual needs and the plan already in use.
n.3: Lying flat increases aspiration risk and may worsen breathing in scoliosis.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A support worker positions Sam, 35, who has a profound learning disability, for sleep. Which position best supports his body shape at night?
o: Lying on his side with his knees drawn up to his chest
Lying flat on his back with no supports
Lying on his front with his head turned
Supported symmetrical lying with knees and hips aligned
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Supported symmetrical lying, with the pelvis level and knees and hips aligned using positioning supports, protects body shape overnight and reduces windswept hips and scoliosis (24-hour postural care principles).

n.0: A curled side position held for long periods promotes asymmetry and contractures.
n.1: Unsupported supine lying lets the knees fall to one side and can raise aspiration risk.
n.2: Prone lying may compromise breathing and is not a standard night position for him.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Peter, 45, has a severe learning disability and is on a medical ward. His sister says, 'He's not himself, he's gone quiet and isn't humming like he usually does.' His NEWS2 score is 1. What should the nurse do?
o: Recheck his observations at the next routine time
Reassure her that a NEWS2 of 1 is low risk
Act on her concern, reassess fully and escalate
Ask her to write her concerns down for the doctor
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Family carers know the person's baseline and often notice 'soft signs' of deterioration before observations change. LeDeR and CIPOLD learning show that ignoring carer concern contributes to avoidable deaths; the nurse should reassess (full observations, ABCDE) and escalate, using Martha's Rule routes if needed.

n.0: Waiting for routine observations may miss early deterioration.
n.1: A low score does not override a credible concern from someone who knows his baseline.
n.3: Written concerns delay action; the nurse should act now.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: In a supported living service, staff are asked what 'soft signs' of deterioration might look like in Lena, 33, who has a profound learning disability and no speech. Which example best fits?
o: A new oxygen saturation of 88% on air
A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
A systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg
Eating less and sleeping more than usual
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Soft signs are subtle changes from the person's baseline (eating, drinking, sleeping, mobility, mood, behaviour) that may precede changes in vital signs. Recognising them depends on knowing the person's usual presentation.

n.0: Saturation of 88% on air is a measured abnormality, not a soft sign.
n.1: A respiratory rate of 30 is a hard, measured sign that scores highly on NEWS2.
n.2: Systolic BP of 85 is a measured red-flag sign, not a soft sign.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Callum, 39, has a profound learning disability and cerebral palsy. His usual temperature, recorded in his health passport, is 35.8°C. Today it is 37.6°C, and he is drowsier than usual. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: A normal temperature needing no action
A low reading that needs a second thermometer
A sign that his room is too warm
A rise from baseline that may mean infection
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Some people with a profound learning disability have a lower baseline temperature, so 37.6°C is a rise of nearly 2°C for Callum. Interpreting observations against the person's baseline, with the drowsiness, suggests possible infection needing escalation.

n.0: Although within the general normal range, it is a significant rise from his baseline.
n.1: 37.6°C is not a low reading.
n.2: Room temperature does not explain the rise with drowsiness.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ellie, 28, has a learning disability and autism. On admission, her hospital passport says she shows pain by rocking and biting her sleeve. Which use of the passport is most helpful for spotting deterioration?
o: Filing it in her notes for the discharge team
Returning it to her carers at the end of the visit
Recording her usual behaviours as a baseline for comparison
Keeping it in her bedside drawer for her family to read
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: The passport records how the person communicates pain and illness and what is usual for them; using it as a baseline for observation helps staff recognise changes and avoid diagnostic overshadowing.

n.0: Using it only at discharge misses its value during the stay.
n.1: Returning it removes key information while she is in hospital.
n.3: The passport is for staff to use, not to be stored for the family.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Lucas, 41, has a severe learning disability and is admitted with vomiting. Staff note he is shouting more and hitting his head. A healthcare assistant says it is 'just his behaviour'. His abdomen is distended. What should the nurse do first?
o: Complete an ABCDE assessment and escalate
Ask for a PRN sedative to settle him
Request a learning disability liaison review
Ask his carers to sit with him until he settles
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Two-step reasoning: vomiting and a distended abdomen with new distress may signal a serious problem such as bowel obstruction; the behaviour is likely communication of pain. An ABCDE assessment and prompt escalation are needed (avoiding diagnostic overshadowing).

n.1: Sedation could mask deterioration and does not treat the cause.
n.2: Liaison support is useful but should not delay urgent medical assessment.
n.3: Carers help, but this does not address the possible emergency.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Amira, 50, has a profound learning disability. Her NEWS2 score has risen from 2 to 5 over four hours, and her mother reports she is 'very different'. What is the correct escalation?
o: Change her observations to every 12 hours overnight
Repeat her observations again in four hours
Urgent review by a clinician skilled in acute illness
Inform the nurse in charge at the next handover
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: A NEWS2 aggregate of 5 or more triggers an urgent response: urgent review by a clinician with competence in assessing acute illness and at least hourly observations (RCP NEWS2). Her mother's concern adds weight to escalation.

n.0: Twelve-hourly observations are for scores of 0.
n.1: Four-hourly observations are too infrequent for a score of 5.
n.3: Waiting for handover delays an urgent response.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Jack, 34, has a learning disability and lives in a small care home. Staff have noticed over three days that he walks more slowly, refuses his favourite drink and sleeps in the afternoon. His observations are within normal ranges. What is the best action?
o: Note the changes and keep watching for a week
Treat it as low mood and plan more outings
Record soft signs and seek a GP review today
Encourage more activity to wake him up
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: A cluster of soft signs over several days is an early warning even when vital signs are normal. Recording them against his baseline and seeking a same-day review supports early recognition (LeDeR learning on delayed recognition).

n.0: Waiting a week risks missing early illness.
n.1: Assuming low mood without assessment is diagnostic overshadowing.
n.3: Pushing activity does not identify the cause.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A ward is admitting Mohammed, 44, who has a learning disability. The nurse wants to recognise deterioration early. Which information is most useful to gather on admission?
o: His usual baselines from family and his passport
His preferred newspaper and television programmes
His school records and qualifications
His blood group and previous transfusions
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Knowing the person's usual observations, behaviours, eating, sleeping, mobility and how they show pain allows staff to recognise change; family carers and passports are key sources (LeDeR; Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag).

n.1: Preferences support comfort but do not establish clinical baselines.
n.2: Education history does not help recognise physical deterioration.
n.3: Blood group matters only if a transfusion is planned.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Jasmine is 13 and in year 8. She has a severe learning disability and epilepsy and an education, health and care (EHC) plan. Her mother asks when planning for adult services should start. According to NICE NG43 and the Children and Families Act 2014, what is the answer?
o: From age 17, a year before she turns 18
From year 9, at age 13 or 14
From age 16, when the MCA applies
From age 18, when adult services take over
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG43 1.2.1: start planning for adulthood from year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest, or immediately if the young person enters services close to transfer. For young people with EHC plans, the SEND Regulations 2014 (made under the Children and Families Act 2014) reg 20(6) require every review from year 9 to consider what provision is needed to prepare for adulthood and independent living.

n.0: Starting at 17 leaves too little time for a gradual, planned transition.
n.2: The MCA applying from 16 is relevant to decisions, but planning should start earlier, from year 9.
n.3: Starting at 18 means no planning before transfer, which NG43 aims to prevent.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Kai, 16, has a learning disability and complex health needs. Several professionals are involved in his transition. His father says no one knows who is coordinating things. What does NICE NG43 recommend?
o: Wait until adult services allocate a social worker
Identify a named worker to coordinate his transition
Ask the GP to take over all of his care at 18
Ask Kai's father to coordinate all of the services
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG43 1.2.5-1.2.7: help the young person identify a single practitioner as 'named worker' to coordinate transition care and support, link with practitioners and the GP, and support the family; ideally someone with whom the young person has a meaningful relationship.

n.0: Waiting for adult services leaves a gap in coordination before transfer.
n.2: The GP is important but is not expected to take over all specialist care.
n.3: Families should be supported, not left to coordinate complex services alone.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A learning disability nurse is the named worker for Ollie, 17, who is moving to adult services. For how long does NICE NG43 say the named worker should support him around transfer?
o: Until the day of his 18th birthday
For 2 weeks after the transfer has happened
For 1 month before the transfer takes place
6 months or more before and after transfer
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG43 1.2.9: the named worker should support the young person for the time defined in relevant legislation, or a minimum of 6 months before and after transfer, negotiated with the young person, then hand over to someone in adults' services if based in children's services.

n.0: Stopping at 18 ignores the support needed after transfer.
n.1: Two weeks after transfer is much shorter than the 6-month minimum.
n.2: One month before transfer is far shorter than the recommended minimum.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Priya, 18, has a learning disability and has just moved from children's to adult services. Her mother is used to making all health decisions for her. At her first adult appointment, how should the nurse approach decision-making?
o: Wait until Priya's mother arrives before any decision
Assume Priya lacks capacity because of her disability
Ask her mother to sign consent as she did before
Presume Priya has capacity and support her to decide
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Adults (and young people aged 16+ under the MCA) are presumed to have capacity (MCA 2005 s1(2)) and must be given all practicable support to decide (s1(3)). Parental responsibility ends at 18, so a parent cannot consent on behalf of an adult; if Priya lacks capacity for a decision, a best interests process applies.

n.0: Her mother's views matter, but Priya should be supported to decide for herself.
n.1: A learning disability does not by itself mean lack of capacity.
n.2: A parent has no legal power to consent for an adult unless appointed as a deputy or attorney.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Tara, 17, has a profound learning disability. Her family are worried that her care package will stop at 18. Which duty under the Care Act 2014 helps plan for this?
o: A transition assessment before she turns 18
A continuing healthcare checklist at age 21
A carer's assessment once she turns 18
A safeguarding enquiry under section 42
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: The Care Act 2014 requires local authorities to carry out transition assessments for children likely to have needs for care and support after turning 18 where it would be of significant benefit (ss58-66), so that support continues without a gap.

n.1: Continuing healthcare is a different NHS process and is not triggered at 21.
n.2: A carer's assessment is for her family's needs and does not replace planning for Tara's own care.
n.3: Section 42 enquiries concern abuse or neglect, not transition planning.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Marcus, 19, has a learning disability and an EHC plan, and is at a further education college. His mother has been told his EHC plan ends at 19. Under the Children and Families Act 2014, what is correct?
o: EHC plans are replaced at 19 by a health action plan
EHC plans end when a young person leaves school
EHC plans can continue up to age 25 if needed
EHC plans end when a young person turns 18
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Under the Children and Families Act 2014, EHC plans can continue up to age 25 for young people who need more time to complete education or training and achieve their outcomes.

n.0: Health action plans follow annual health checks; they do not replace EHC plans.
n.1: Plans can continue in further education after school.
n.3: EHC plans do not end at 18; they can continue to 25.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ella, 17, has a learning disability and is due to move to adult services next month, the same month her family moves house and she starts a new college. What does NICE NG43 advise about the timing of transfer?
o: Transfer at a time of relative stability, not on a rigid age
Transfer on her 18th birthday whatever else is happening
Transfer as planned, as delay will cause confusion
Transfer after she has settled in adult services
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Two-step reasoning: several big changes coincide, so the timing of transfer should be reconsidered. NICE NG43 1.2.3: the point of transfer should not be based on a rigid age threshold and should take place at a time of relative stability for the young person.

n.1: NG43 says transfer should not be tied to a rigid age.
n.2: Proceeding during multiple changes ignores NG43's advice on stability.
n.3: She cannot settle in adult services before she has been transferred.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Sam, 16, has a learning disability. A nurse is planning his transition meeting. Which approach to his involvement best reflects NICE NG43?
o: Let professionals agree the plan and then share it
Hold the meeting with his parents and inform Sam later
Postpone involving Sam until he is 18
Involve Sam in planning and agree goals with him
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG43 1.1.4 and 1.2.4: transition planning should fully involve the young person, agree goals with them and build their confidence to direct their own care, with the family involved as appropriate; it should be reviewed at least annually.

n.0: A plan agreed without him is not person-centred.
n.1: Excluding Sam from his own planning breaches NG43's person-centred approach.
n.2: Waiting until 18 misses years of planning and skill-building.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Gwen, 58, has a severe learning disability and advanced cancer and cannot describe pain. Her support staff know her well. Which tool would best help them recognise when she is distressed?
o: A 0-10 numerical rating scale
DisDAT
The Glasgow Coma Scale
The Abbey Pain Scale for people with dementia
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: The Disability Distress Assessment Tool (DisDAT) records a person's usual 'content' cues and their 'distress' cues (face, eyes, skin, sounds, habits, posture) to create a baseline, so carers can recognise distress when the person cannot report it. It is not a scoring tool.

n.0: A numerical scale needs the person to self-report, which Gwen cannot do.
n.2: The GCS measures level of consciousness, not distress or pain.
n.3: The Abbey scale was developed for people with dementia and does not build an individual baseline in the same way.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Robert, 62, has a moderate learning disability and has been told he has terminal heart failure. His brother asks staff not to tell Robert he is dying 'because it will upset him'. What should the nurse do?
o: Support Robert to understand his illness in an accessible way
Agree with the brother and avoid any discussion of dying
Tell Robert everything at once so that he knows the facts
Ask the GP to decide whether Robert should be told
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: People with a learning disability have the same right as others to information about their health and to be involved in decisions about their care. Information should be given in an accessible, paced way (easy read, pictures, repetition), checking understanding, while supporting the family (NMC Code 2, 4; MCA principles).

n.1: Withholding information denies Robert the chance to make choices and say goodbye.
n.2: Giving everything at once without adapting it may overwhelm him and limit understanding.
n.3: The decision is not the GP's alone; Robert's right to information comes first.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ahmed, 45, has a learning disability. His mother died last month. Staff report he has become withdrawn, is eating less and sometimes shouts at night. What is the most likely explanation?
o: A side effect of his usual medication
Grief expressed through changes in behaviour
Boredom because his routine has changed
Behaviour that challenges needing a PBS plan
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: People with a learning disability grieve, and grief may show through behaviour change (withdrawal, appetite change, sleep disturbance, anger) rather than words. Recognising grief and offering accessible bereavement support avoids labelling it as challenging behaviour; physical causes should still be considered.

n.0: Nothing suggests a medicine change; the timing fits his bereavement.
n.2: Boredom does not explain the timing after his mother's death.
n.3: Labelling grief as behaviour that challenges is diagnostic overshadowing.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Sarah, 40, has a learning disability. Her father is dying in a hospice. Staff in her supported living home think she should not visit or go to the funeral because she 'won't understand'. What should the nurse advise?
o: Decide for her once her father has died
Support Sarah to choose whether to visit and attend
Agree that she should stay at home to avoid distress
Let her attend the funeral but not visit the hospice
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Including people with a learning disability in saying goodbye and in rituals such as funerals supports healthy grieving. Assumptions that a person 'won't understand' are discriminatory; Sarah should be prepared accessibly and supported to make her own choice.

n.0: Delaying the decision removes her chance to see her father.
n.2: Excluding her denies her the chance to say goodbye and can complicate grief.
n.3: Restricting her to the funeral is a choice made for her, not by her.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Lionel, 66, has a profound learning disability and is in the last days of life. He is grimacing and moaning, which his DisDAT shows are his distress cues. He has a syringe pump. What should the nurse do first?
o: Assess the cause and seek a review of his symptom control
Increase the pump rate to give more medicine
Record the cues and review at the next drug round
Ask his family to sit with him and offer him comfort for now
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Two-step reasoning: his known distress cues suggest uncontrolled symptoms. The nurse should assess possible causes (pain, position, full bladder, constipation, breathlessness) and seek prompt review of anticipatory or as-needed medicines; pump rates should not be changed without a prescription.

n.1: Changing a pump rate without a prescription is unsafe and outside the nurse's authority.
n.2: Waiting until the next round leaves him in distress.
n.3: Comfort helps, but it does not address possible uncontrolled pain.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Dora, 54, has a learning disability and terminal cancer. She has said in pictures that she wants to die in her own bed in her supported living home. Staff worry they cannot manage. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange a hospice place because staff feel unsure
Ask her family to decide where she should die
Admit her to hospital when she becomes more unwell at home
Plan with the palliative care team to support her at home
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Preferred place of death should be respected where possible; reasonable adjustments include training staff, district nursing and specialist palliative care in-reach, anticipatory medicines and equipment (NICE NG142; Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: A hospice may be right for some, but staff uncertainty is not a reason to override her wishes without trying support.
n.1: Dora has expressed her own wish; her family should be involved but not replace her choice.
n.2: Planned hospital admission ignores her stated preference.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Phil, 49, has Down syndrome and dementia. He is now sleeping most of the day, barely drinking and his breathing has changed. Care staff say this is 'just his dementia getting worse'. What should the nurse consider?
o: That he is depressed and needs an antidepressant
That Phil may be dying and needs assessment
That his dementia is progressing and his plan stays the same
That he is tired after a busy week
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Increased sleep, reduced intake and changes in breathing may indicate the last days of life, or a reversible cause such as infection. Recognising possible dying allows assessment, review of reversible causes and planning for comfort (NICE NG31 principles; LeDeR learning on overshadowing).

n.0: Depression does not explain these physical changes.
n.2: Attributing all change to dementia risks missing dying or a treatable illness.
n.3: Tiredness does not explain reduced drinking and changed breathing.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Shona, 35, has a moderate learning disability and her friend at the day centre has died. Staff want to help her understand. Which approach is best?
o: Say her friend has 'gone to sleep' to soften it
Use clear words such as 'died' with pictures
Avoid mentioning the friend so she does not get upset
Tell her the friend has moved to another day centre
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Clear, concrete language ('died', 'dead') with pictures or easy read is easier to understand than euphemisms. 'Gone to sleep' can cause confusion and fear about sleeping; honesty supports grieving.

n.0: Euphemisms are confusing and may cause fear of sleep.
n.2: Avoiding the subject leaves her confused and unsupported.
n.3: Lying undermines trust and prevents her from grieving.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Martin, 46, has a severe learning disability and is admitted with a chest infection. A junior doctor writes on a DNACPR form, 'Reason: learning disability, poor quality of life.' What should the nurse do?
o: Ask Martin's family to sign the form to confirm it
Accept the form, as DNACPR is a medical decision
File the form and review it on discharge
Raise it with the consultant as an invalid reason
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: A learning disability, Down syndrome or autism must never be the reason for a DNACPR decision; decisions must be individual, based on clinical factors and made with the person or, if they lack capacity, in consultation with family under the MCA (NHS England C1146 letter on DNACPR and people with a learning disability and autistic people; Equality Act 2010).

n.0: Family signatures do not validate an unlawful reason; families are consulted, not asked to sign.
n.1: Although clinicians make CPR decisions, a decision based on disability is discriminatory and must be challenged.
n.2: Leaving a discriminatory decision in place risks Martin's life during this admission.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Ruth, 70, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to make decisions about CPR. The consultant decides CPR would not work because of her advanced heart failure. Ruth's niece visits regularly. What must happen before the DNACPR decision is recorded?
o: Apply to the Court of Protection
Obtain her niece's written agreement first
Wait for an IMCA to approve the decision
Consult her niece unless this is impracticable
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: For a person who lacks capacity, the MCA 2005 s4(7) requires consultation with those engaged in caring for them or interested in their welfare; Winspear v City Hospitals Sunderland [2015] confirmed a DNACPR notice should not be made without consulting family unless it is not practicable. The niece is consulted, not asked to consent.

n.0: Court involvement is not routinely needed for DNACPR decisions.
n.1: Relatives without an LPA or deputyship do not give or withhold consent; they are consulted.
n.2: An IMCA is instructed when there is no one appropriate to consult; Ruth has her niece.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: George, 55, has a learning disability, lacks capacity for the decision and needs chemotherapy for bowel cancer. He has no family or friends; only paid support staff are involved. What must happen?
o: Treatment is delayed until a deputy is appointed
The oncologist decides without consulting anyone
His support manager can consent on his behalf
An IMCA must be instructed before the decision
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Under MCA 2005 ss37-38, an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate must be instructed for serious medical treatment by the NHS when the person lacks capacity and there is no one, other than paid carers, appropriate to consult. Chemotherapy is serious medical treatment.

n.0: Deputyship is not needed; the IMCA route allows a timely best interests decision.
n.1: Best interests decisions require consultation; with no family an IMCA is required.
n.2: Paid staff cannot consent for an adult and do not count as 'appropriate to consult' for IMCA purposes.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Claire, 39, has a mild learning disability and a progressive illness. She has capacity and wants to plan her future care. Which approach to advance care planning is best?
o: Ask her parents to write the plan for her
Complete the whole plan quickly in a single meeting
Delay planning until she lacks capacity
Record her wishes accessibly over several conversations
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Advance care planning is a voluntary process of discussion over time. For people with a learning disability it should use accessible information (easy read, pictures), take time and involve those Claire chooses, recording her wishes, values and preferences.

n.0: Claire has capacity; the plan should reflect her wishes, not her parents'.
n.1: A single rushed meeting may not give her time to understand and decide.
n.2: Planning while she has capacity lets her own wishes guide future decisions.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: A care home holds a list of residents with a learning disability marked 'not for CPR', made during an outbreak without individual assessment. What should the learning disability nurse do?
o: Keep the list but review it after the outbreak
Escalate it as an unlawful blanket decision
Ask each resident to sign the list
Accept it, as decisions during outbreaks differ
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Blanket DNACPR decisions applied to groups are unlawful and discriminatory; each decision must be individual and made with the person or in consultation with those close to them (NHS England C1146 letter; CQC review of DNACPR decisions; Human Rights Act Article 2 and 14). This should be escalated as a safeguarding and governance concern.

n.0: Keeping an unlawful list puts residents at risk now.
n.2: Signatures do not make a blanket policy lawful or individual.
n.3: Outbreaks do not make blanket decisions lawful.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Tony, 60, has a learning disability and lacks capacity. His sister holds a registered health and welfare Lasting Power of Attorney that expressly covers life-sustaining treatment. Doctors are considering stopping antibiotics. Who makes the decision?
o: His sister, as attorney, in his best interests
The consultant, after informing his sister
An IMCA appointed by the hospital
The Court of Protection, on application
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Under MCA 2005 s9-11, a health and welfare attorney can make decisions about life-sustaining treatment if the LPA expressly authorises it, acting in the person's best interests. Doctors advise on clinical options but the attorney makes the decision.

n.1: Where a valid LPA covers the decision, the attorney decides, not the clinician alone.
n.2: An IMCA is not needed when there is an attorney to make the decision.
n.3: Court involvement is needed for disputes, not for every decision when an attorney exists.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Kevin, 52, has a learning disability and has died of pneumonia. The doctor is completing the medical certificate of cause of death. Kevin's support worker sees 'learning disability' written as the cause. What should happen?
o: The support worker should amend the certificate
The disability should not be recorded as the cause
It is acceptable when pneumonia is also listed
It is correct because his disability made him vulnerable
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Learning disability should not be recorded as a cause of death; the illness that caused death (here pneumonia) should be recorded so that deaths can be understood and learned from (NHS England C1146 letter; LeDeR).

n.0: A support worker has no authority to alter a medical certificate; concerns are raised with the certifying doctor or the medical examiner.
n.2: Accurate recording matters for learning and for LeDeR.
n.3: Vulnerability is not a cause of death; recording it hides the illness.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Nina, 44, has a moderate learning disability and capacity to decide about CPR. Her consultant believes CPR would be unlikely to succeed. Nina says she wants CPR. What should happen?
o: Ask her mother to decide instead of Nina
Record that Nina lacks capacity because she disagrees
Record DNACPR now and discuss it with her at a later review
Explain sensitively why CPR may not work and involve Nina
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Patients with capacity must be involved in discussions about DNACPR; the clinician explains the reasons in an accessible way. A patient cannot demand treatment that will not work, but should be informed unless it would cause physical or psychological harm (Tracey v Cambridge University Hospitals [2014]; Resuscitation Council UK/BMA/RCN guidance).

n.0: Nina has capacity, so her mother cannot decide for her.
n.1: Disagreement with clinicians is not evidence of lack of capacity (MCA s1(4)).
n.2: Under Tracey, a patient with capacity should be involved when the decision is made unless discussion would cause harm; delaying the discussion is not lawful.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Kieran, 32, has a severe learning disability and epilepsy and lives in supported living. His seizures are hard to describe and staff record them as 'had a funny turn'. What should the learning disability nurse put in place first to improve his epilepsy care?
o: A seizure diary recording each event, its length and recovery
A request for the GP to increase his anti-seizure medicine dose
A daily log of how many hours Kieran sleeps each night
A plan to call 999 for every event that staff witness
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Accurate seizure records (description, time, duration, triggers, recovery, any video with consent) let the specialist judge seizure type and control and adjust treatment. NICE NG217 supports individualised care plans built on accurate information from the person and carers.

n.1: Changing doses without accurate information risks side effects without improving control.
n.2: Sleep can be a trigger worth noting, but it does not describe the seizures themselves.
n.3: An ambulance for every event is not appropriate; his emergency plan should define when to call 999.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Jade, 26, has a learning disability and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, some at night. Her mother asks what sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) is and whether anything reduces the risk. Which response is best?
o: Uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures raise SUDEP risk, and this can be reduced
SUDEP is linked to daytime focal seizures and not to night-time ones
SUDEP risk falls once a person has a learning disability diagnosis
SUDEP is rare, so families do not need to be told about it until later
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG217 10.1.2 and 10.1.4: discuss SUDEP from diagnosis with the person, family and carers; modifiable risk factors include generalised or focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, uncontrolled seizures, non-adherence, alcohol or drug misuse, living alone and sleeping alone without supervision.

n.1: Tonic-clonic seizures, especially unwitnessed nocturnal ones, are the main risk factors.
n.2: A learning disability does not reduce the risk; people with LD and epilepsy are a higher-risk group.
n.3: NG217 recommends discussing SUDEP risk with people and their families and carers.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Oscar, 40, has a learning disability and epilepsy with frequent nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures. He sleeps alone in his flat with no overnight support. Which NICE NG217 recommendation is most relevant?
o: Discuss night-time supervision, such as a night monitor
Wake him every two hours to check whether he is breathing
Ask him to sleep on his back so that seizures are easier to see
Move him to a care home so that staff are on duty every night
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: NICE NG217 10.2.1: discuss the possibility of introducing or increasing night-time supervision (for example a night monitor) for people who have seizures during sleep and have been assessed to be at higher risk of epilepsy-related death; living alone and sleeping alone without supervision are modifiable SUDEP risk factors (10.1.2). The discussion respects Oscar's choice and privacy.

n.1: Two-hourly waking disturbs sleep, which can itself trigger seizures, and is not the recommended approach.
n.2: Lying on the back increases the risk of airway obstruction during and after a seizure.
n.3: A move is a major restriction; monitoring can usually be arranged in his own home.

Physical Health, Transitions and End of.t: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.q: Lily, 23, has a mild learning disability and focal seizures that are not well controlled. She has just started a new relationship and is not using contraception. Her neurologist is reviewing her anti-seizure medicine. Which medicine needs the strictest safety measures because of the risks in pregnancy?
o: Clobazam
Levetiracetam
Lamotrigine
Valproate
Physical Health, Transitions and End of.w: Valproate carries a high risk of birth defects and neurodevelopmental disorders. MHRA measures reflected in NICE NG217 (updated 2025) mean valproate must not be started in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, and a pregnancy prevention programme applies to women and girls who could become pregnant.

n.0: Clobazam is not the medicine with the pregnancy prevention programme.
n.1: Levetiracetam is not subject to the valproate pregnancy prevention programme.
n.2: Lamotrigine is among the options considered for women who could become pregnant; it does not carry valproate's restrictions.
